en: The King of Samādhis Sūtra, Manifested as the Equality of the Essential Nature of All Phenomena. Chapter One: The Introduction.
Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagṛha on Vulture Peak Mountain together with a great saṅgha of bhikṣus— fully numbering one hundred thousand million bhikṣuṇīs— and together with eighty million bodhisattvas,

all of whom were bound to only one more birth, renowned for their supernormal powers, and had gathered from the world-systems of the ten directions having attained mastery over the dhāraṇīs and sūtras.

They had gone forth to satisfy all sentient beings with the gift of the Dharma; they were skilled in proclaiming the knowledge of the great superknowledges; they had attained the supreme perfection of all the perfections;

they were skilled in the knowledge of the establishment of all bodhisattva samādhis and meditative attainments; they were praised, lauded, and extolled by all the Buddhas; they were skilled in traversing all buddha-fields; they were skilled in the knowledge that terrifies all Māras; and they were skilled in the knowledge of all phenomena as they truly are.
They were skilled in knowing the superior and inferior faculties of all sentient beings; skilled in the wisdom that undertakes the worship of all the Buddha’s activities;
unstained by any worldly dharmas; adorned in body, speech, and mind; clad in the armor of great loving-kindness and great compassion;
with minds undiminished through great vigor for incalculable eons; uttering the great lion’s roar; and having overcome all rival disputants.
They were sealed with the seal of irreversibility and had received the consecration of all the Buddha-dharmas,
namely: the bodhisattva mahāsattva named Meru,
and Sumeru.
And with Mahāmeru,
Meruśikharidhara,
and Merupradīparāja;
And with Merukūṭa,
and Merudhvaja,
and Merugaja.
And by Saṃghaṭṭanarāja on the peak of Mount Meru,
and by Merusvara,
and by Megharāja.
And by Dundubhisvara,
and by Ratnapāṇi,
and by Ratnākara.
And by Ratnaketu,
and by Ratnaśikhara,
and by Ratnasaṃbhava, and by Ratnaprabhāsa.
And with Ratnayaṣṭi,
and with Ratnamudrāhasta,
and with Ratnavyūha.
And with Ratnajālin,
and Ratnaprabha,
and Ratnadvīpa.
And by Ratiṃkara,
and by Dharmavyūha,
and by Vyūharāja.
And with that which is adorned by the primary marks,
and with the array of tones, and with the radiance of the purity of tones.
And with Ratnakūṭa,
and Ratnacūḍa,
and Daśaśataraśmikṛtārcis, and Jyotirasena;
And by Candrabhānu;
and by Sahacittotpādadharmacakrapravartin;
and by Śubhakanakaviśuddhiprabha.
And by the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva named Satatam-abhayam-dadāna (Ever-Giving Fearlessness),
together with all the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas of the Bhadrakalpa headed by Ajita-bodhisattva,
and with the sixty Anupama-cittas (Incomparable-Minded Ones) headed by Mañjuśrī.
And with the sixteen virtuous men, headed by Bhadrapāla;
and with the sons of the gods belonging to the retinue of the Four Great Kings, headed by the Four Great Kings; and so forth.
The Blessed One was honored, revered, esteemed, worshipped, adored, and respected by the sons of the gods of the Brahma-realm, headed by Brahmā himself, as well as by other gods,

nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans— both those of great renown and those of immense majesty. He was worthy of being saluted, worshipped, and prostrated to by all four assemblies and by the world including its gods.

There, the Blessed One, surrounded and honored by an assembly of many hundreds of thousands, was teaching the Dharma— good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end— and he fully proclaimed the holy life that is meaningful, well-phrased, unique, complete, pure, and pristine.

Now at that time, in that very assembly, there was a youth named Candraprabha who was present and seated; he had performed services for previous Victors, planted roots of merit, remembered his past lives,
possessed inspired eloquence, had set out in the Mahāyāna, and was devoted to great compassion.

Then the youth Candraprabha rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ground, and bowing with palms joined toward the Blessed One, addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"I would like to ask the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened Buddha, about a certain matter."
"If the Blessed One would grant me the opportunity to have my questions answered," [Candraprabha said].

When this was said, the Blessed One addressed the youth Candraprabha: "Ask, O youth, whatever you desire of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One; with the explanation of each question asked, I shall satisfy your mind."

"I am omniscient, O youth, a perfectly awakened one; I am all-seeing, having attained the preeminence of power and fearlessness regarding all phenomena, and I am endowed with the knowledge of unobstructed liberation.
There is nothing, O youth, among all phenomena that is unknown, unseen, unheard, unperceived, unrealized, or not fully awakened to by the Tathāgata throughout infinite and boundless world-systems.
Therefore, O youth, let there be for you the opportunity to question and inquire of the Tathāgata."
I shall satisfy your mind by providing the answer to each and every question that you ask.
Then, indeed, the youth Candraprabha—satisfied, elated, joyful, delighted, and filled with gladness and cheer—at that moment addressed the Blessed One in verses:
"O Perfectly Awakened One, Lord of the World, Illuminator! How do those who practice attain inconceivable wisdom? O Benefactor, please explain this to us."

O Lord of Men, speaker of truth, bull among men, worthy of worship by gods and kings: how does one practice so as to obtain the incomparable, supreme, and foremost path? O Protector, please explain this excellent question that has been asked.
I ask with a resolute intention; no deceit exists in me.
There is no other witness for me besides the Supreme Person.
"I have vast vows and a longing; O Lion of the Śākyas, you know my conduct. I shall not be one who merely speaks words; speak to me quickly, O Lord of Men, regarding practice."
Which dharmas that provide sustenance are of great benefit in the Buddha-vehicle?
Explain them, O Great Hero, you who have reached the further shore of all dharmas. (SRS 1.5)
O Protector, tell me the Dharma that is beneficial, so that a person may practice it and become one of sharp wisdom;
one who is free from fear and terror, undaunted, and does not abandon the aggregate of ethical discipline;
and who, having eliminated pride, attachment, aversion, and delusion, wanders on the path of conduct with all faults stilled.
How does one not abandon ethical discipline? How does one not neglect meditative concentration? How does one resort to the forest? And how does wisdom proceed?
How does one who guards their ethical discipline find delight in the sublime teaching of the One Possessing Ten Powers?
How does the aggregate of ethical discipline become flawless, and how does one weigh the intrinsic nature of the conditioned?
How does the wise one become pure in body and speech?
With an unafflicted mind, he cultivates the wisdom of the Buddha.
How does one become pure in bodily action, and how are the faults of speech avoided?
How does one become undefiled in mind? O Best of Men, answer my question.

Then the Blessed One said this to the youth Candraprabha: "Young man, a bodhisattva mahāsattva endowed with one single quality acquires these virtues and swiftly awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
What is that one quality?"
In this regard, young man, a bodhisattva mahāsattva possesses a mind that is equal toward all beings, a mind intent on their welfare, an unobstructed mind, and an impartial mind.
Endowed with this single quality, young man, a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains these virtues and swiftly awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One addressed the youth Candraprabha in verses:
"If a bodhisattva proceeds by undertaking a single quality, he obtains these virtues and swiftly awakens to enlightenment. (SRS 1.11)
And no one can obstruct the mind of that bodhisattva who possesses an unobstructed mind;
he conceives neither stubbornness nor malice regarding the distinguished qualities as they have been proclaimed.
Having cultivated an even mind, an even ripening is manifested:
their soles of the feet become even, and their conduct and sphere of activity are even.
Having cultivated a mind that is even and free from unevenness, rid of faults and barrenness, and abandoned all doubt,
their feet become excellent in soles, perfectly level, supremely radiant, pure, and beautiful to behold.
The Bodhisattva shines throughout the ten directions, pervading the Buddha-fields with the radiance of his glory;
when he attains the stage of peace, he establishes many beings in the wisdom of a Buddha.

In this regard, young man, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who possesses a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings, a mind of benefit, an unobstructed mind, and a non-discriminatory mind, attains this samādhi called "The Manifestation of the Equality of the Essential Nature of All Phenomena. And what, young man, is that samādhi called "The Manifestation of the Equality of the Essential Nature of All Phenomena" which he attains?
And what, young man, is this samādhi called "The Manifestation of the Equality of the Essential Nature of All Phenomena"? It is, namely, restraint of the body and restraint of speech.
Restraint of the mind,
purity of action,
and transcendence of the object of focus.
Thorough knowledge of the aggregates,
equanimity regarding the elements,
and the removal of the sense bases.
The abandonment of craving;
the entry into the realization of non-arising;
and the illumination of causes.
The non-perishing of the fruit of karma,
the vision of the Dharma,
and the cultivation of the path.
Encountering the Tathāgatas,
possessing sharp wisdom,
and penetrating the truths.
Knowledge of the Dharma; knowledge of the entry into the analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid);
knowledge of the distinctions between syllables and phrases.
The transcending of entities,
the full comprehension of sounds,
and the attainment of joy.
The experience of joy in the Dharma;
uprightness;
and gentleness.
Rectitude,
straightforwardness, freedom from frowning, and gentleness.
Virtuous conduct; amiability; sweetness of speech.
A smiling face;
being the first to speak;
and saying, "Come, welcome."
Freedom from laziness;
reverence for the teacher;
and service to the teacher.
Contentment with one's rebirth;
insatiability regarding wholesome qualities;
and purity of livelihood.
Not abandoning residence in the forest;
knowledge of the arrangement of the stages;
and the non-forgetting of mindfulness.
Skillfulness regarding the aggregates, skillfulness regarding the elements, and skillfulness regarding the sense bases.
The entry into the realization of the superknowledges;
the removal of the afflictions;
and the total eradication of the connection with habitual tendencies.
The progression toward specific knowledge;
the natural outflow of cultivation;
and skillfulness in emerging from transgressions.
The suppression of active outbursts,
the abandonment of latent tendencies,
and the transcendence of existence.
Recollection of past lives;
freedom from doubt;
and a mind focused on the Dharma regarding the ripening of karma.
Sharpness of knowledge in the pursuit of learning,
thirst for knowledge,
and the realization of knowledge.
The stage of a well-bred horse;
a mind like a mountain;
immovability.
Immobility; the knowledge of abiding on the stage of non-retrogression;
and the natural outflow of wholesome qualities.
Aloofness from unwholesome qualities,
the non-manifestation of afflictions,
and the non-abandonment of the training.
The establishment of meditative concentration;
knowledge of intentions;
and knowledge of the specific modes of rebirth among sentient beings.
The knowledge of equality;
the knowledge of the connection between utterances;
and the renunciation of the household life.
Disenchantment with the three realms,
a mind free from despondency,
and non-attachment to phenomena.
The upholding of the true Dharma, the protection of the Dharma,
and conviction in the ripening of karma.
Skill in the Vinaya,
the settling of legal disputes, and the absence of contention.
Absence of dispute;
the stage of patience; the undertaking of patience.
Equanimity toward the realms of existence;
skill in the discernment of phenomena;
and the mind of renunciation.
Skill in the definitive determination of phenomena;
knowledge of the distinctions between the words of the Dharma; and skill in the production of the words of the Dharma.
The knowledge of skill in articulating the distinctions between what is meaningful and what is meaningless;
the knowledge of the past limit; and the knowledge of the future limit.
Knowledge of the present;
knowledge of the equality of the three times;
and knowledge of the purity of the three spheres.
Knowledge of the states of the body; knowledge of the states of the mind;
and the preservation of the modes of conduct.
The disturbance of the postures,
the modification of the postures,
and the gracefulness of the postures.
Knowledge of skill regarding what is beneficial and what is harmful;
speaking appropriately;
and knowledge of the world.
The state of relinquishing what has been acquired, having hands ever extended in generosity,
and a mind free from grasping.
A sense of shame and dread of blame; a feeling of revulsion toward unwholesome states of mind;
and not abandoning the ascetic virtues (dhūtaguṇa).
The undertaking of virtuous conduct;
pleasant behavior;
and rising from one's seat and offering a seat to one's teachers.
The subduing of pride,
the firm control of the mind,
and the knowledge of the arising of the thought [of awakening].
The knowledge of the penetration of meaning,
the knowledge of the penetration of knowledge,
and the awakening to knowledge.
The departure from ignorance;
the knowledge of entering the mind;
and the knowledge of awakening to the intrinsic nature of the mind.
Knowledge of skill regarding the taking up and casting off of food;
knowledge of all sounds;
knowledge of the establishment of etymological definitions.
Knowledge that discerns the meaning,
avoidance of what is meaningless,
and association with virtuous persons.
Associating with virtuous persons,
avoiding base persons,
and the accomplishment of the meditative absorptions.
And therein: non-tasting [of meditative states],
the miraculous transformations of supernormal knowledge,
and the knowledge that penetrates the intrinsic nature of names, conventions, and designations.
The eradication of designations,
disenchantment with conditioned phenomena,
and lack of desire for honors.
Equanimity toward lack of respect;
lack of desire for gain;
and absence of dejection in the face of loss.
There is no longing for fame,
no resentment toward ill repute,
and no attachment to praise.
Absence of despondency in the face of blame; absence of attachment in the face of pleasure;
and absence of aversion in the face of suffering.
Non-appropriation of conditioned phenomena;
non-attachment to true praise;
and patient acceptance of false praise.
Avoiding intimacy with householders and renunciants; shunning improper spheres of activity;
and frequenting the proper sphere of activity.
Perfection of conduct,
avoidance of improper conduct,
and not bringing reproach upon families.
The protection of the teaching;
speaking little;
speaking with moderation.
Skill in responding,
subduing adversaries,
and proceeding at the appropriate time.
Avoiding improper times;
not placing trust in ordinary worldlings;
and not treating those who are suffering with contempt.
And the giving of wealth to them;
the non-humiliation of the poor;
and compassion toward those of immoral conduct.
Being a source of benefit,
possessing a compassionate mind,
and favoring others through the Dharma.
The relinquishing of material things;
the state of not being established in accumulation; and the praising of ethical discipline.
The reviling of immorality;
the cultivation of honesty toward those who possess ethical discipline;
and the relinquishment of all one's possessions.
Inviting through superior intention,
acting according to what has been said,
and constant application.
Reverential experience of joy;
knowledge through analogies;
and skill in former connections.
Being preceded by the roots of virtue;
skill in means;
and the abandonment of signs.
The turning away from conceptualization,
the thorough knowledge of all things,
and the accomplishment of the sūtras.
Skill in the Vinaya,
the definitive determination of the truths,
and the entry into the realization of liberation.
The quality of speaking with categorical certainty;
the non-abandonment of knowledge and vision as they truly are;
and the quality of speaking without hesitation.
The cultivation of emptiness,
the practice of the signless,
and the discernment of the nature of the wishless.
The attainment of fearlessness;
illumination through wisdom;
and firmness in ethical discipline.
Entry into meditative attainments,
the acquisition of wisdom,
and delighting in solitude.
Self-knowledge, limited knowledge, and contentment.
The clarity of the mind;
the avoidance of dogmatic views;
and the attainment of dhāraṇīs.
The descent into knowledge;
the knowledge of the correct and incorrect, of the stages, and of practice;
and the gateway to the method of logical reasoning.
The cause;
the path; the practice.
The message, the instruction, and the admonition.
The practice;
the conformable patience; the stage of patience.
The departure from impatience;
the ground of knowledge;
the abandonment of ignorance.
The foundation of knowledge;
the stage of the practice of yoga; the domain of the bodhisattva.
Associating with virtuous persons; avoiding non-virtuous persons;
and the knowledge that penetrates and realizes the intrinsic nature of all phenomena.
The stage of a Buddha has been proclaimed by the Tathāgata;
it is rejoiced in by the wise and rejected by the foolish.
It is difficult to be understood by the śrāvakas;
it is fully realized by the pratyekabuddhas;
it is not the domain of the non-Buddhist outsiders.
It is embraced by the bodhisattvas and followed by those endowed with the ten powers.
Worthy of worship by the gods;
worthy of salutation by Brahmā; worthy of approach by the Śakras.
She is to be saluted by the nāgas, rejoiced in by the yakṣas, and praised by the kinnaras.
It is to be praised by the mahoragas,
cultivated by the bodhisattvas,
and mastered by the wise.
It is the unsurpassed wealth;
it is a gift free from worldly taint;
it is the medicine for the sick.
It is the joy of those with peaceful minds;
it is the treasury of gnosis;
it is the inexhaustible source of eloquence.
It is the method of the sūtras,
the departure from the treasury,
and the domain of the heroes.
Thorough knowledge of the triple world is a raft for those crossing to the further shore, and a boat for those caught in the midst of the flood.
Fame belongs to those who desire renown;
praise belongs to the Buddhas; and eulogy belongs to the Tathāgatas.
It is a hymn of praise to those possessing the ten powers;
it is the virtue of the bodhisattvas;
it is the equanimity of the compassionate ones.
Loving-kindness is for those who wish to pacify harm;
sympathetic joy is for those who practice tranquility;
and consolation is for those of the Mahāyāna.
It is the practice of those who roar the lion’s roar;
it is the path to the wisdom of a Buddha;
it is the liberation of all sentient beings.
It is the seal of all phenomena,
the bringer of all-knowledge,
and the pleasure grove of all bodhisattvas.
It is the terrorizing of Māra’s army; it is the vidyā for those seeking security;
it is the goal for those who have accomplished their purpose.
It is the protection for those caught in the midst of enemies;
it is the subduing of adversaries in accordance with the Dharma;
and it is the source of truth for the grounds of self-confidence.
The search for beings is the precursor for the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
it is the adornment of the Dharma-body.
It is the natural outflow of conduct,
an ornament for the sons of the Buddha,
and the delight of those who desire liberation.
It is the joy of the eldest sons [of the Buddha];
it is the fulfillment of the wisdom of a Buddha;
it is not the domain of any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
It is the purification of the mind,
the complete purity of the body,
and the perfection of the gateways to liberation.
It is the absence of defilement in the wisdom of a Buddha;
it is the non-arrival of passion and the departure of hatred.
It is not the ground of delusion;
it is the arrival of knowledge;
it is the arising of true insight.
The abandonment of ignorance;
the satisfaction of those for whom liberation is the essence; the contentment of those for whom meditative concentration is the essence.
The eye for those who desire to see; supernormal knowledge for those who desire to perform transformations;
and supernatural power for those who desire to bring about accomplishments.
It is the dhāraṇī for those seeking what they have heard;
it is the non-forgetting of mindfulness;
it is the empowerment of the Buddhas.
The skillful means of the Leaders are subtle and difficult to understand for those who have not applied themselves;
they are unknowable by those who are not liberated.
The turning of syllables is difficult to discern through mere sound;
it is understood by the wise and known by those who are gentle.
It has been penetrated by those with few desires, mastered by those who have initiated vigor,
and maintained by those possessed of mindfulness.
The exhaustion of suffering;
the non-arising of all phenomena; the teaching of the single principle regarding all states of existence, destinies, births, and bases.
Young man, this is called the samādhi named "The Manifestation of the Equality of the Essential Nature of All Phenomena."

Furthermore, while this discourse on all phenomena, this teaching on meditative concentration, was being spoken by the Blessed One, eighty *nayutas* of beings among the human and divine populations who had performed prior preparations attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
And ninety-six *nayutas* attained the conformable patient acceptance (*ānulomikī-kṣānti*).
Thirty-nine nayutas attained the patient acceptance that accords with the sound [of the Dharma].

The minds of one hundred thousand fully ordained monks were liberated from the outflows through non-clinging. And for six million beings among the host of gods and humans, the dust-free and stainless Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena was purified.
The minds of eighty thousand monks were liberated from the outflows through non-clinging;
five hundred laymen attained the fruit of non-returning;
and six hundred laywomen attained the fruit of once-returning.
And this trichiliocosm, the great trichiliocosm world-system, shook, trembled, and quaked; it moved, swayed, and trembled violently;
it quivered, quivered intensely, and quivered all over.
It was shaken, violently shaken, and utterly shaken;
it resounded, resonated, and thoroughly resounded;
it thundered, roared, and completely roared.
The eastern direction sinks and the western direction rises;
the western direction sinks and the eastern direction rises; the northern direction sinks and the southern direction rises.
The southern direction sinks down while the northern direction rises;
the periphery sinks down while the center rises;
the periphery rises while the center sinks down.

An immeasurable radiance appeared in the world, and the entire world-system— including its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, as well as its generation of recluses and brahmins— was illuminated and pervaded by that light. Even these two, the moon and the sun, though possessing such great supernormal power, such great majesty, and such great renown, did not shine, did not glow, and did not radiate.
Even those intermediate spaces between worlds, which are shrouded in blinding darkness,
were suffused by that radiance; and even those beings who had been born therein, [were illuminated].
They, too, recognized one another and said: "Indeed, friends, another being has also been reborn here,
as far down as the great Avīci hell."
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Introduction," in the *Śrī-Samādhirāja*.

Chapter Two: The Previous Deeds of Śālendrarāja. Then, at that time, the Blessed One further elucidated this very chapter on previous deeds for the youth Candraprabha in detail by means of verses: [The Buddha said: “O son of noble family, listen well and attend closely. I shall now proclaim in full the former conduct of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Śālendrarāja. In the past, many hundreds of thousands of eons ago, there was a world-system named *Vicitrasaṃsthāna*. In that world-system, there was a kalpa named *Ratnaprabhāsa*, and therein appeared a Tathāgata named *Ratnasaṃbhava*. That Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, was endowed with knowledge and conduct, the Sugata, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of men to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One. At that time, there was a king named *Śālendrarāja*; he ruled over the four continents, possessed of great power and majesty. His capital city was named *Vaijayantī*, adorned with seven kinds of jewels and most magnificent. Within that city, there was a park named *Nandana*; it was filled with various flowers and fruits, and surrounded by a wall of seven precious substances. Therein stood a jeweled tower, high and vast, reaching up to the Brahma-world. At that time, the Tathāgata Ratnasaṃbhava was dwelling in that park, surrounded by a great assembly. The King Śālendrarāja, having heard of this, went forth from his city with a retinue of eighty-four thousand ministers. He went to the presence of the Buddha Ratnasaṃbhava, prostrated at his feet, and circumambulated him three times. Then he sat down to one side, and with palms joined, addressed the Buddha: ‘World-Honored One, I have long desired to ask; now, out of compassion, please grant me the opportunity. What is the name of this park? And what is the name of this tower? The Buddha then told the King: ‘This park is named Nandana, and this tower is named Vaijayanta. The King then asked the Buddha: ‘World-Honored One, how long has it been since this park and tower were established? The Buddha told the King: ‘It has been immeasurable, incalculable, and beyond all calculation— since the time when the Tathāgata Ratnasaṃbhava first attained enlightenment. The King then asked the Buddha: ‘World-Honored One, how long will the lifespan of that Tathāgata last? The Buddha told the King: ‘The lifespan of that Tathāgata will last for immeasurable, incalculable eons, and after his parinirvāṇa, his True Dharma will remain for twice as long. The King then asked the Buddha: ‘World-Honored One, what is the name of that Tathāgata’s father? The Buddha told the King: ‘His father’s name is *Mahātejas*, and his mother’s name is *Mahāprabhā*. The King then asked the Buddha: ‘World-Honored One, what is the name of that Tathāgata’s son? The Buddha told the King: ‘His son is named *Ratnajālin*, who has already set his mind upon supreme enlightenment. The King then asked the Buddha: ‘World-Honored One, what is the name of that Tathāgata’s principal attendant? The Buddha told the King: ‘His principal attendant is named *Dharmarāja*, who is wise, eloquent, and possesses great power. The King then asked the Buddha: ‘World-Honored One, what is the name of that Tathāgata’s chief female disciple? The Buddha told the King: ‘His chief female disciple is named *Prabhāvatī*, who is pure in conduct and possesses great wisdom. The King then asked the Buddha: ‘World-Honored One, what is the name of that Tathāgata’s *bodhi-tree*? The Buddha told the King: ‘The name of that Tathāgata’s *bodhi-tree* is called *Mahāvyūha*; its height is one hundred yojanas, and its circumference is fifty yojanas. Its leaves, flowers, and fruits are all made of the seven jewels, emitting a light that illuminates the ten directions. The King then asked the Buddha: ‘World-Honored One, what is the name of that Tathāgata’s *parinirvāṇa-stūpa*? The Buddha told the King: ‘The stūpa of that Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa is named *Mahāratnavyūha*; its height is one hundred thousand yojanas, and its circumference is fifty thousand yojanas. It is adorned with the seven precious substances, and covered with a net of gold. Within it are enshrined the relics of that Tathāgata, which emit a light that illuminates the ten directions. The King then asked the Buddha: ‘World-Honored One, how many disciples does that Tathāgata have? The Buddha told the King: ‘The disciples of that Tathāgata number two hundred thousand koṭis; all are Arhats, free from outflows, with minds like great elephants, having done what was to be done. The King then asked the Buddha: ‘World-Honored One, how many Bodhisattvas does that Tathāgata have? The Buddha told the King: ‘The Bodhisattvas of that Tathāgata number eight hundred thousand koṭis; all are irreversible, possessing the five supernormal powers, and they have already perfected the six perfections. The King then asked the Buddha: ‘World-Honored One, what is the name of that Tathāgata’s *dharmaparyāya*? The Buddha told the King: ‘The name of that Tathāgata’s *dharmaparyāya* is called *Mahāvyūha*; it is profound and subtle, difficult to understand, and can transform and guide all sentient beings. The King then asked the Buddha: ‘World-Honored One, how long will the True Dharma of that Tathāgata remain? The Buddha told the King: ‘The True Dharma of that Tathāgata will remain for immeasurable, incalculable eons; after the True Dharma has vanished, the Semblance Dharma will remain for twice as long. The King then asked the Buddha: ‘World-Honored One, what is the name of that Tathāgata’s land? The Buddha told the King: ‘The name of that Tathāgata’s land is called *Padmavyūha*; it is level, smooth, and pleasant, adorned with the seven precious substances. There are no hells, animals, or hungry ghosts; there is no suffering, only joy and bliss. Gods and humans dwell together in peace, all practicing the path to supreme enlightenment. The King then asked the Buddha: ‘World-Honored One, how did you first plant the roots of merit? The Buddha told the King: ‘In the past, during the time of the Tathāgata Ratnasaṃbhava, I was a king named *Śālendrarāja*. Having heard the Buddha preach the *Mahāvyūha Sūtra*, I immediately set my mind upon supreme enlightenment. I offered to the Buddha a jeweled tower, and vowed to become a Buddha in the future. Because of that root of merit, I have now attained this supreme enlightenment. The King then asked the Buddha: ‘World-Honored One, how did you first conceive the thought of enlightenment? The Buddha told the King: ‘In the past, I saw a Pratyekabuddha whose body was emitting a brilliant light. Seeing this, I immediately conceived the thought of enlightenment, vowing to become a Buddha in the future. The King then asked the Buddha: ‘World-Honored One, how did you first offer alms to a Buddha? The Buddha told the King: ‘In the past, I saw a Pratyekabuddha who had come to beg for food at my door. I immediately prepared the finest food and offered it to him with a sincere heart. The King then asked the Buddha: ‘World-Honored One, how did you first build a monastery? The Buddha told the King: ‘In the past, I saw a Pratyek
He remembers sixty billion of those who possessed the ten powers; in a former life they dwelt upon Vulture Peak.
While I was formerly practicing the conduct for awakening, they taught me this supreme, peaceful samādhi.
The last among them was the Lord of the World, Prabhankara;
he who was named Śālendrarāja was questioned by me.
I was a kṣatriya, the most excellent of kings and lord of the earth;
and of my sons, there were no fewer than five hundred.
Ten million monasteries were built for that Buddha;
some were made of exquisite sandalwood, and others were made of jewels.
There was a king named Bhīṣmottara, beloved and pleasing to many people;
he performed distinguished worship of the Buddha for eighteen thousand koṭis of years.
The lifespan of that Jina, the supreme among bipeds, the Guide Śālendrarāja,
who was beyond reproach, was then seventy-six thousand koṭis of years.

At that time, the Saṅgha of that Supreme among Men consisted of eighty thousand times ten thousand disciples— those who possessed the three knowledges and the six superknowledges, who had conquered their senses, whose outflows were exhausted, and who bore their final bodies.
In many ways, he performed worship unto me, the Jina, the supreme among bipeds; for the sake of the world including the gods, he always aspired for this samādhi. (SRS 2.8)
Having gone forth together with my son and wife into the presence of the Jina Śālendrarāja,
I inquired about this samādhi for fourteen thousand billion years.
Eighty thousand million verses, and another hundred billion *bimbara* units—
this chapter on the samādhi was received by him from the presence of that Sugata.
Hands, head, wife, as well as sons, abundant jewels, and likewise food and drink—
there is no object whatsoever that I have not previously sacrificed, desiring this supreme samādhi.
I remember thousands of millions of Buddhas, and even more than that, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
they stood here on Vulture Peak and taught this supreme, peaceful samādhi.
And all those named Śākyarṣabha, and all their sons named Rāhula, and those named Ānanda who were attendants— all of them, having gone forth from the city called Kapila, became renunciants.
Kolita and Śāriputra, in a former age, were both named Agra; they were all protectors, and their world-system was likewise named Sama, and all of them appeared during a time of degeneration.
All those lords of men were honored by me while practicing this conduct of awakening; whatever offerings there are for the Victors, all of them were made by me while seeking this samādhi.
This samādhi is obtained through practice; many kinds of practice have been taught.
For one who is established in all virtues, this samādhi is not difficult to attain.
For one who is not greedy for tastes, who is free from longing, unattached to families, and without envy;
who dwells in motherly compassion and is without malice—for such a person, this samādhi is not difficult to attain.
For one who is indifferent to honor and gain, whose livelihood is pure, who possesses nothing,
whose ethical conduct is purified, and who is confident, this samādhi is not difficult to attain.
For one who has initiated vigor, who is untiring, who is intent upon the forest, who abides in the ascetic practices (dhuta),
and who is established in the patience of selflessness— for such a person, this samādhi is not difficult to attain.
For one whose mind is well-tamed and not agitated, who is established in proper deportment and conduct,
who is devoted to renunciation and free from stinginess— for such a person, this samādhi is not difficult to attain.

The secondary marks and primary characteristics, these eighteen qualities of a Buddha proclaimed by the Leader— these powers and fearlessnesses are not difficult to obtain for one who upholds this peaceful samādhi.
If all those beings seen by the Buddha with his eye were to become Buddhas at one and the same time,
and if the lifespan of each one of them were to be inconceivable billions of kalpas; // SRS_2.22 //
If each one of them were to have as many heads as there are grains of sand in all the oceans,
and if upon every one of those heads there were just as many tongues;

All those benefits have been proclaimed for one who would merely retain this verse from this samādhi; how much more so for one who, having trained, should uphold it! Not even a small portion has been fully described.
Having undertaken the ascetic qualities (*dhūta-guṇa*), he dwells [in them], and gods, asuras, yakṣas, and guhyakas long for him;
kings become his followers—he who maintains this peaceful samādhi so difficult to attain.
He is embraced by the Victors, and gods and nāgas always follow him as attendants;
his adversaries cannot withstand his splendor—he who maintains this peaceful samādhi so difficult to attain.
His eloquence becomes infinite; he speaks thousands of infinite sūtras.
There is never any obstruction for him who maintains this peaceful samādhi.
Those who, in the future time of great terror, having heard this samādhi, shall uphold it, will behold the Buddha Amitābha, the Leader, as well as the world-system Sukhāvatī.
Having revealed these benefits, the Teacher himself, the Self-Existent One, makes this request:
"In the future time after I have passed into parinirvāṇa, you must maintain this pure samādhi. (SRS 2.29)
Whatever Buddhas there are in the ten directions, whether of the past or even the present—
all those Victors have trained in this samādhi and awaken to the stainless, unconditioned enlightenment.
Thus ends the second chapter of the *Śrī-samādhirāja*, titled "The Previous Life of Śālendrarāja."
(Vaidya 13) Chapter 3:
The Exposition of the Praise of the Qualities of the Real.
Thereupon, the Blessed One again addressed the youth Candraprabha: "Therefore, then..."

O Kumāra, whichever bodhisattva mahāsattva desires to proclaim the true praise of the qualities of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, so that there may be no exhaustion either in meaning or in phrasing, and so that all his speech may issue forth sustained by the Buddha—
Therefore, young man, for the sake of all sentient beings, this samādhi must be taken up, mastered, maintained, recited, promulgated, taught, and studied by the bodhisattva mahāsattva;
it must be cultivated through the meditation on non-conflict, practiced extensively, and explained in detail to others.
And what, young man, are those true qualities of a Buddha belonging to the Tathāgata?

In this regard, young man, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having gone to the forest, or to the foot of a tree, or to an open space, or into the midst of an empty dwelling, trains himself thus: "In such a way is that Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat..."
The Perfectly Awakened One, endowed with knowledge and conduct, the Sugata, the knower of the world, the unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed,
the teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One— he, the Tathāgata, is the natural outflow of merits.
It is the non-perishing of the roots of virtue;
it is adorned with patience;
it is the source of stores of merit.
He is adorned with the secondary marks,
blossomed with the primary marks,
and is well-proportioned in his range of activity.
It is not disagreeable to behold;
it is a source of delight for those resolved through faith;
and it is unsurpassed by means of wisdom.
He is invincible by all powers;
he is the teacher of all sentient beings;
he is the father of the bodhisattvas.
He is a king for the noble persons (āryapudgala);
he is a caravan leader for beginners;
he is immeasurable in his wisdom.
He is infinite in his eloquence,
pure in his voice,
and delightful in his resonance.
Incomparable in form,
peerless in body,
and unstained by sensual desires.
Unstained by forms,
unmixed with the formless,
liberated from sufferings.
He is completely liberated from the aggregates,
dissociated from the elements,
and restrained within the sense bases.
Concealed by knots,
yet liberated from fevers;
completely freed from craving.
He has crossed over the flood;
he is perfected in knowledge;
he is established in the knowledge of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, of the past, future, and present.
He is not established in nirvāṇa; he is established in the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi);
he is established on the ground that is to be beheld by all sentient beings.
Young man, these are the true qualities of a Buddha belonging to the Tathāgata.

Endowed with these praises of the Buddha-qualities, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having attained this samādhi, elucidates the true praise of the Buddha-qualities of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, with an uninterrupted eloquence; thus, he does not reach exhaustion either in meaning or in phrasing.
And every word of his issues forth sustained by the Buddha.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
"It is not easy to speak all the praises of the Jina, even by speaking for many thousands of eons."
In the same way, the Victors have accumulated these qualities while seeking this supreme, peaceful samādhi.
In the past, with an undaunted mind, while seeking this supreme, peaceful samādhi, I gave away maidens who were exceedingly beautiful to behold, with adorned limbs and full of charm.
In that same way, with an undaunted mind, I gave away wealth, grain, female and male slaves, as well as jewels, pearls, gold, and silver, while seeking this supreme, peaceful samādhi.
In the past, while seeking this supreme, peaceful samādhi, I gave to the Leaders necklaces of pearls variegated with jewel-gems, beautiful garments, conch shells, and golden threads.
For immeasurable and infinite millions of eons, having generated a supreme and unsurpassed mind, I have offered the most fragrant *vārṣika* flowers at the shrines of the Jinas.
In that very same way, when I was in the midst of the assembly, having generated a sense of reverence, I gave a gift of Dharma;
yet never did the thought arise in me: "May I become the knower of this gift of Dharma."
In order to fully acquire these qualities, I have constantly resorted to the excellent forest where there is little noise;
may I always be abundant in compassion, and may my mind forever attain the wisdom of a Buddha.

I have never had any attachment anywhere, even toward my own most beloved things, for the sake of enjoying them. I give away abundant gifts of merit so that my mind may always attain the wisdom of a Buddha.
He is disposed to share all sweetness, possesses a smiling face, retains what he has heard, and has a melodious voice;
his speech is exceedingly sweet, he is beloved by many, and I am never satiated by the sight of him.

I have not been envious for even a moment, nor has there ever been jealousy throughout millions of existences. I was always fully satisfied with alms-food, having rejected all invitations without exception.
Those who are of great learning and retainers of what they have heard, who would even memorize a single four-line verse from this [teaching],
have always been honored by me, having generated a supreme and unsurpassed love for them.
I have given manifold and infinite gifts, and likewise have guarded my ethical discipline for a long time;
I have performed many acts of worship toward the Leaders, seeking this supreme, peaceful samādhi.
If one were to give a gift by filling vast, diverse, and infinite world-systems with precious jewels,
the merit of one who maintains even a single verse from this samādhi would be far more sublime.
Whatever flowers there may be, as many as they are, and likewise fragrances that are delightful and sublime—
with these, those desiring merit might worship the Jina for many, infinite, and immeasurable eons.
Even if there were as many musical instruments as exist on earth, and abundant food, drink, and clothing,
one who desires merit might honor the Jina with these for many, infinite, and immeasurable eons.

And if a person, having generated the thought of awakening, should think, "I shall become a Victor, a self-arisen King of Dharma," the merit of one who maintains even a single verse of this [sūtra] with a concentrated mind is far more sublime than that. (SRS 3.16)

Even if one were to speak of its benefits for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the broad Ganges, it could not be fully exhausted while being proclaimed; for such is the vastness of the merit from maintaining this samādhi.
Therefore, young man, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should take up, preserve, recite, and master this [teaching].
Having taken it up, preserved it, recited it, and mastered it, he should apply himself to the practice of the cultivation of non-affliction (*araṇā-bhāvanā-yoga*).

This will be for the benefit of many people, for the happiness of many people, out of compassion for the world, and for the welfare, benefit, and happiness of a great multitude of beings, both gods and humans.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
"Therefore, having heard these most auspicious benefits of the Buddhas, quickly take up this samādhi praised by the Buddhas."
In former births, seventy-three koṭis of Buddhas were honored;
by all those Buddhas, this sūtra was proclaimed.
This sūtra is declared to be the conqueror of great compassion;
having trained in this great learning, the qualities of a Buddha are not difficult to attain.
In the future time, after the Leader of the World has passed into nirvāṇa,
there will be many unrestrained monks who have no interest in great learning.

They will speak in praise of ethical discipline while being indifferent to ethical discipline; they will speak in praise of meditative concentration while being indifferent to meditative concentration.
They will speak in praise of wisdom while being themselves devoid of wisdom;
they will speak much about liberation while being themselves devoid of liberation.
Just as someone might speak of the qualities of sandalwood, saying:
"Such is this kind of sandalwood, a species of fragrance that is delightful."
Then, suppose another person were to ask that man:
"Have you taken any sandalwood of which you speak?"
He would reply to that man: "I speak of fragrance and color;
by means of it I maintain my livelihood, yet I do not know that fragrance myself."
Thus, in the future time, even for those who are not engaged in yoga, there will be a livelihood through the praise of ethical conduct,
yet they themselves will possess no ethical conduct.
Thus, even regarding yoga, those who are uncommitted will make their living by means of the praise of meditative concentration;
in the final age, this meditative concentration will not truly exist for them.
Thus, in the future time, for those who are not engaged in yoga, the praise of wisdom will become their livelihood, yet they will possess no true wisdom.
In this way, even though they are unapplied to yoga, their livelihood will be by means of the praise of liberation;
yet in the final age, liberation itself will not be theirs.

Just as some man who is poor might be held in contempt by the great multitude, yet later he finds a hidden treasure and, having become a lord of wealth, would be honored by people; so it is with this.
In this way, as long as this samādhi has not been attained, the bodhisattva here is not highly esteemed by gods,
humans, kumbhāṇḍas, or rākṣasas, just as a man who is poor and destitute of wealth is among other men.
But when this incomparable treasure of the Dharma has been obtained by the wise one on this stage, gods and humans feel longing for it; he bestows that unsurpassed wealth upon all beings.
Therefore, having heard these supreme and most excellent benefits proclaimed by the Jina, abandon all kinship, gain, and pleasure; aim for this tranquil, sublime samādhi.
Whatever Buddhas there are in the ten directions who have attained perfect nirvāṇa, as well as those yet to come and those present now—
all of them, having trained here in this samādhi, awakened to incomparable and inconceivable enlightenment.
The youth Candraprabha, with a joyful heart, stood before the Jina and spoke these words:
"When the Best of Men has entered parinirvāṇa, I shall uphold this sūtra during this time of great hardship."
Having abandoned body and life, as well as whatever happiness exists in the world,
even in that time of great danger, I shall maintain this supreme, peaceful samādhi.
Having generated great compassion for the mass of sentient beings upon seeing those who have fallen into extreme suffering and are without a protector,
I shall bestow loving-kindness upon them and teach this supreme, peaceful samādhi.
At that time, no fewer than five hundred arose there as upholders of this samādhi;
O Youth, you were the leader among them in the sublime undertaking of this excellent sūtra.
Thus ends the third chapter of the *Śrī-samādhirāja*, titled "The Exposition of the Description of the Qualities of Reality."
Chapter Four: Recollection of the Buddha.
Then, the youth Candraprabha said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, it is said: 'Samādhi, samādhi.'"
"For which phenomenon is this a designation: 'samādhi'?
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the youth Candraprabha: "Young man, what is called 'samādhi, samādhi' is the settling of the mind; it is non-arising."
Without rebirth;
knowledge of rebirth;
having laid down the burden.
The wisdom of the Tathāgata; the bull-like sovereignty of a Buddha; the healing of passion.
The subsiding of the defilements,
the abandonment of delusion,
and the practice of proper application.
The avoidance of what is improper,
the desire for unwholesome qualities,
and the longing for liberation from saṃsāra.
The practice of resolute intention;
the cultivation of wakefulness;
and the non-abandonment of abandonment.
The protection of pure dharmas;
lack of confidence in rebirths;
and the absence of volitional construction.
It is the non-attention toward internal bases of cognition resulting from karmic actions, the non-engagement with external bases of cognition,
and the absence of self-exaltation.
Not disparaging others; lack of attachment to wholesome things;
and lack of trust in ordinary worldlings.
The natural outflow of ethical discipline is being difficult to assail and possessing great majesty.
Knowledge of the self;
lack of fickleness;
and abiding in the perfection of the modes of deportment.
Absence of ill-will,
absence of harshness,
and non-oppression of others.
Protecting one's friends;
guarding secret mantras;
and non-violence.
Non-oppression of those who possess ethical discipline;
gentleness of speech;
and non-reliance on anything within the entire triple world.
Emptiness in all phenomena is the patient acceptance that accords with reality; the intense aspiration for the knowledge of omniscience is called "concentration," O Youth. It is called concentration.
Young man, that very practice— or non-practice— with respect to such dharmas as these is called "samādhi."
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:

"The door to the Deathless has been opened by me; I have declared the true nature of phenomena as it is. I have demonstrated the manner of rebirth as it is, and I have revealed Nirvana along with its benefits."
One should always avoid evil friends and cultivate virtuous friends;
having abandoned the crowds, one should dwell in the forests and constantly develop a mind of loving-kindness.
Pure ethical conduct must always be guarded, and nourishment in the dhuta practices must always be sought;
renunciation and wisdom must be cultivated.
Then this samādhi will not be difficult to attain.
Then, having attained this ground of peace, upon which the vast ground of the śrāvakas is no longer present,
you shall directly perceive the Dharma of the Sugata and obtain the inconceivable qualities of a Buddha.
Seeing those people who possess the intelligence of worthy vessels, you should inspire them toward the thought of awakening;
by establishing them in unsurpassed knowledge, this King of Samādhis will not be difficult to attain.
For one who seeks this [teaching], if envy should arise again while they are reflecting upon the flow of nutriment here,
and whether in its pursuit or its enjoyment, this samādhi will not be difficult to attain.
If this King of Samādhis is indeed emptiness, then those of pure conduct stand at its summit;
those who are always concentrated on the nature of phenomena, yet are foolish and unpracticed in yoga, do not know it.
For those who desire this peaceful samādhi, the notion of fear never arises;
having cultivated this ground of perfect tranquility, they always behold the Supreme among Men.
Whoever recollects the Tathāgatas by way of their physical forms becomes one whose faculties are tranquil and whose mind is peaceful;
with an undeluded mind, always in meditative equipoise, he is like the ocean in both learning and wisdom.
For when a bodhisattva, established in this samādhi, walks back and forth upon the walking-path,
he beholds thousands of millions of buddhas, and even more than that, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
The mind of a person who would grasp at a measure for the qualities of a Buddha would go mad;
for that which is immeasurable has no measure, and the Guides are inconceivable in all their virtues.
There is no being in the ten directions who is equal to the Lord of the World, much less superior;
for you all, endowed with the qualities of omniscience, shall desire and attain the wisdom of a Buddha.
With a body of golden hue, the Lord of the World is serene in every way;
he whose mind is focused here upon this object of perception is called a "concentrated" bodhisattva.
Having understood the unconditioned and the conditioned, the wise one, through the dissolution of the perception of signs,
becomes established in the signless, knowing all phenomena to be empty.
He who is established in the dharma-body understands all things to be non-existent;
because the perception of non-existence has been fully cultivated, he does not perceive the Lord of Jinas by means of the form-body.
I announce and declare to you: in whatever way a person engages in much discursive thought, in that very way his mind becomes characterized by those thoughts, being dependent upon them.
For a person who thus recollects the Lord of Munis— by way of his physical form, his wisdom, and his immeasurability—
and who constantly cultivates mindfulness of him, their mind becomes inclined toward him and flows toward him.

Standing upon his walking path and not relying on sitting down, he yearned for the knowledge of the Best of Men; yearning thus, he made a solemn vow for enlightenment: "May I become the unsurpassed Victor in the world."
He perceives the Buddha and sees the Buddha, and he contemplates the true nature (*dharmatā*) of the Buddhas;
established here in this samādhi, he pays homage to the Buddhas of great majesty. (SRS 4.19)
With body and speech, and with a serene mind, he constantly speaks the praises of the Buddhas;
for his mental continuum is thus cultivated,
that he beholds the Protectors of the World day and night.
Even when he becomes ill and afflicted, and the sensation leading to death arises,
his mindfulness directed toward the Buddha is not lost, nor is he overwhelmed by those sensations.

For in this way, having investigated and understood that the emptiness of phenomena applies to both the future and the present, he is established in such a method of Dharma; thus, his mind does not grow weary as he practices the conduct of the bodhisattva path.
Therefore, having heard these benefits, generate the aspiration for incomparable awakening;
do not suffer in the future, for the sight of the most excellent Sugatas is very difficult to obtain.
Suppose I were to speak the sublime Dharma, yet having heard it, you did not practice it;
like a sick person who takes medicine and clothing but is unable to remove their own disease.
Therefore, one who knows the rules, is discerning, and always desires this samādhi, should cultivate ethical discipline, learning, and renunciation; then this samādhi will not be difficult to attain.
Thus ends the fourth chapter of the *Śrīsamādhirāja*, titled "Recollection of the Buddha."
(Vaidya 23) Chapter Five: The Chapter on Ghoṣadatta.
Thereupon, the Blessed One addressed the youth Candraprabha: "In the past, O youth, in times long gone..."

In an incalculable, more than incalculable, vast, immeasurable, inconceivable, and limitless *kalpa* ago— at that time and at that moment— the Blessed One named Ghoṣadatta appeared in the world as a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, perfect in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a Teacher.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, was among both gods and humans.
At that time, on that occasion, there was a first assembly of eighty koṭis of disciples for that Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha Ghoṣadatta;
the second assembly of disciples consisted of seventy koṭis of Arhats.
The third assembly consisted of sixty koṭis of arhat śrāvakas.
Furthermore, at that time, the lifespan of that Blessed One, Ghoṣadatta, the Arhat and Perfectly Enlightened One, was forty thousand years.
And this Jambudvīpa was prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, delightful, and crowded with many people.
Furthermore, at that time, there were two kings in this Jambudvīpa,
named Dṛḍhabala and Mahābala.
Of them, one king enjoyed half of Jambudvīpa.
The second one also enjoys half [of the kingdom], which is prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, delightful, and crowded with many people.

At that time, on that occasion, in the realm of King Mahābala, the Blessed One Ghoṣadatta, the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha, appeared. Thus, Prince, King Mahābala invited that Tathāgata Ghoṣadatta, together with the assembly of Bodhisattvas and the assembly of monks, for a full thousand years, providing them with appropriate and blameless requisites for their use.
With robes, alms-food, bedding and seats, and medicinal requisites for the sick;

and at that time, O youth, on that occasion, there was abundant gain, honor, and renown for that Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Ghoṣadatta, as well as for his community of Bodhisattvas and his community of Śrāvakas.
The faithful brahmins and householders provided abundant offerings and honors for the Blessed One Ghoṣadatta, the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha, as well as for the community of bodhisattvas.

Those faithful brahmins and householders were dedicated to providing offerings and honors for the Blessed One Ghoṣadatta, the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha, and to performing worldly material worship; that is to say, they acted in imitation of King Mahābala himself. Thus it was.

O Kumāra, this thought occurred to that Blessed One Ghoṣadatta: "Alas, these beings are falling away from the undertaking of the ethical precepts and the poṣadha, from approaching the Tathāgatas, from attending upon the Tathāgatas, from living the holy life, and from the state of being a monk who has gone forth and received full ordination.
These beings, immediately thereafter, have come to value pleasure above all else."
For what reason?
Because immediately following that, this pleasure arises, namely, the worship consisting of worldly material offerings.
These beings value the present life and value future lives, but they do not reach the ultimate goal for the sake of the roots of virtue.
In this regard, young man, what is this "valuing corrupt dharmas"?
It is, namely, the intent toward the five strands of sensual pleasure.
In this regard, young man, what is this "valuing the future life"?
Namely, taking the heavenly realm as one's objective support. And what is the prioritization of the roots of goodness that lead to ultimate finality?
It is namely, ultimate purity.
Ultimate liberation;
ultimate security;
ultimate dwelling in the holy life.
The ultimate end;
the ultimate consummation of the roots of virtue;
the ultimate parinirvāṇa.
"May I teach the Dharma to these beings in such a way that these beings might worship the Tathāgata through the unsurpassed worship of the Dharma and the practice of the Dharma.
Then, O youth, at that time, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Ghoṣadatta, with the intention of inspiring awe in King Mahābala and those brahmins and householders,
spoke these verses:
When those who serve one another through the giving of gifts lack mutual respect for each other,
the Buddhas— the wise ones whose latent tendencies have been abandoned— do not praise such service.
Those men who teach the Dharma for the benefit of living beings become such that they are well-served;
their mutual love is so indestructible that even ten million Māras would be unable to break it.
For all those people who serve with worldly gain, the benefit is merely visible in this life;
but for those who cultivate the Dharma free from worldly gain, there is indeed a great benefit for human beings.
Having established a mind free from worldly attachment and having proclaimed the Dharma free from worldly attachment,
those whose love is likewise free from worldly attachment quickly become Buddhas.
One who never indulges in sensual desires, having abandoned craving for children and wives,
and does not dwell in a loathsome household, shall attain unsurpassed, supreme enlightenment.
Those who avoid sensual desires as one avoids a pit of fire, having abandoned craving for children and wives, and who,
out of fear of the household life, go forth into homelessness— for them, this supreme enlightenment is not difficult to attain.
There has never been a Buddha in the past, nor will there be one in the future, nor does one exist now;
yet by those who have remained thus in the midst of the household life, this supreme, foremost awakening has been attained.
Having abandoned kingship like a lump of spittle, one who desires solitude should dwell in the forests;
having abandoned the afflictions and struck down Māra, they awaken to the stainless, unconditioned enlightenment.

If one were to attend upon as many Buddha-heroes as there are grains of sand in the Ganges for many millions of eons, and another, with a mind weary of the household life, were to go forth from home— of these two, the latter is superior.
The Jinas, the supreme among men, are not served by means of food, drink, robes, flowers, perfumes, and ointments in the same way as they are when one has gone forth and practiced the Dharma.
But whoever, longing for awakening and weary of conditioned existence for the sake of sentient beings,
takes seven steps toward the forest— this person possesses merit far more distinguished than that.
Furthermore, young man, King Mahābala heard this very discourse concerning renunciation, set forth by the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One Ghoṣadatta.
Having heard it, he reflected: "As I understand the meaning of what the Blessed One has spoken,"
The Blessed One does not praise the perfection of giving, nor does he praise the perfection of ethical discipline;
he praises the ultimate consummation.
He praises ultimate purity,
the ultimate dwelling in the holy life,
and ultimate nirvāṇa.
This thought occurred to him: "It is not easy for one dwelling in the midst of a household to accomplish the practice of the unsurpassed Dharma or to attain its goal.
I am falling away from the practice of the unsurpassed Dharma."
"What if I were to shave off my hair and beard, don saffron robes, and with perfect faith go forth from the home to the homeless life?
Thus, O Prince, King Mahābala, surrounded and escorted by eight million brahmins and householders, approached the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Ghoṣadatta.
Having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, circumambulated him three times, and stood to one side.
Then, young man, the Blessed One Ghoṣadatta, knowing the resolute intention of King Mahābala, taught this samādhi called "The Manifestation of the Equality of the Essential Nature of All Dharmas.
Then, young man, having heard this samādhi, King Mahābala was satisfied, elated, and joyful; he shaved off his hair and beard, donned saffron robes, and with perfect faith—
He went forth from the home life into homelessness.
Having thus gone forth, he took up this samādhi;
having taken it up, mastered it, retained it, and recited it, he dwelt devoted to the practice of its cultivation.
By that very root of merit, he never fell into the miserable states of rebirth for ten billion eons,
and he propitiated twenty billion Buddhas;
in the presence of those Tathāgatas, he heard this samādhi.
Having heard it from those Buddhas, he took it up, mastered it, retained it, recited it, and dwelt devotedly engaged in the practice of its cultivation.
Thereafter, by that very root of merit, after the passing of ten billion eons and a full hundred thousand eons, he fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
Having accomplished the welfare of immeasurable sentient beings, he subsequently passed away into the final nirvana of a Buddha.

In that regard, young man, those eighty thousand living beings who, together with King Mahābala, had approached the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Ghoṣadatta— they too, having heard this samādhi, were satisfied, elated, joyful, and full of gladness.
Filled with joy and gladness, they shaved off their hair and beards, donned saffron-colored robes, and with perfect faith went forth from the home to the homeless life.

Having thus gone forth, they took up this samādhi, mastered it, retained it, recited it, and dwelt devoted to the practice of its cultivation. By that very root of merit, for twenty billion kalpas, they never fell into the miserable states of existence.
In every single eon, he propitiated millions upon millions of Buddhas.

In the presence of all those Tathāgatas, having heard, taken up, mastered, retained, and recited this samādhi, and having dwelt devoted to the practice of its cultivation, by virtue of that very same former root of merit, [he attained] twenty...

After the passing of ten million eons, and subsequently after ten thousand full eons, Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas named Dṛḍhaśūra appeared in the world, having awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. They too, having brought immeasurable and incalculable beings to maturity and having accomplished their welfare, passed into the final nirvāṇa of a Buddha.

Therefore, young man, by this method as well, it should be understood that this samādhi is of great benefit for bodhisattva mahāsattvas, as it conduces to the attainment of unsurpassed, all-knowing gnosis.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One further revealed this very chapter on the former connection to Candraprabha, the prince, in great detail by means of singing these verses:
"I remember in the past, in an inconceivable eon of the past, there was one supreme among men."
The Great Seer who arose for the sake of the world was called by the name Ghoṣadatta.
His first assembly of disciples was a full eighty million;
the second was a full seventy million, and the third consisted of sixty million arhats.
All had exhausted their outflows and were free from defilements; all had reached the perfection of the power of supernatural faculties.
Their lifespan was twenty-two thousand years, and their field was pure and beautiful.
Having received consecration for the immeasurable benefit of others, and being well-established in the masteries and the stages,
those protecting Bodhisattvas who existed then were close to awakening to enlightenment beneath the excellent tree.
In this Jambudvīpa there was a king named Dṛḍhabala, who possessed great strength;
he enjoyed half of the kingdom, while a second king ruled over the other half.
In the realm of Mahābala, a Buddha appeared who was honored by gods and humans;
having gained faith in the Sugata, the king attended upon him for a full thousand years.
Following his example, many other beings performed honors for the Tathāgata;
indeed, through both worldly offerings and the worship of the Dharma, there arose an incomparable abundance of merit for him and his disciples.
The thought arose in the Supreme among Men: "I shall teach this Dharma to those who desire the Dharma;
let them all abandon sensual pleasures here and go forth into homelessness within my teaching."

That supreme among men spoke these verses concerning the dharma of austerity, the training of the Sugatas, the faults of living at home, and the infinite sufferings; [he taught that] practice in accordance with the dharmas here is the true worship of the Dharma. (SRS 5.20)
Having heard that verse, the king, the lord of men, then reflected alone in seclusion:
"It is not possible, while remaining in the household life, to practice all these supreme offerings to the Dharma."
Having abandoned his kingdom like a lump of spittle, together with eighty thousand living beings, he approached the presence of that Jina; having bowed at his feet, he stood before him.
Knowing their intention, the Jina taught this peaceful samādhi so difficult to perceive;
gladdened by the happiness of joy and rapture, satisfied, elated, they then went forth into homelessness.
Having gone forth and having maintained, recited, and mastered this samādhi,
they shall never go to a state of ruin or an evil destiny for twenty full ten million eons.
By that wholesome karma, they all beheld thousands of millions of Buddhas;
and under the teachings of all those Jinas, having gone forth into homelessness, they cultivated this samādhi.
In a later time, they became Buddhas named Dṛḍhaśūra, possessed of infinite vigor;
having accomplished the welfare of many millions of living beings, they entered parinirvāṇa in that final age like a flame going out.
The king Mahābala who existed in the past became the Buddha Jñānaśūra in the world;
having established many thousands of millions of living beings in enlightenment, he later entered parinirvāṇa.
Therefore, having heard this at a later time, you should uphold this sutra praised by the Buddha.
By upholding such a treasury of Dharma as this, you will quickly become the most excellent among men.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "Ghoṣadatta," in the *Śrī-Samādhirāja*.
(Vaidya 30) Chapter Six: On Samādhi.
Thereupon, the Blessed One again addressed the youth Candraprabha: "Therefore then, O youth..."
A bodhisattva mahāsattva who desires this samādhi and wishes to quickly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment must perform the preparation for samādhi.
In this regard, young man, what is the preparation for samādhi?

In this regard, young man, a bodhisattva, with a mind set forth through great compassion, becomes intent upon performing acts of worship for Tathāgatas—whether they are currently residing or have passed into parinirvāṇa—namely, by means of robes, alms-food, bedding and seats, and medicinal requisites for the sick; and by means of flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, garments, umbrellas, banners, and flags, as well as musical instruments, cymbals, and victory banners.
And he dedicates that root of virtue toward the attainment of meditative concentration.

Desiring no phenomenon whatsoever, he honors the Tathāgata—not for the sake of form, nor desires, nor enjoyments, nor heavens, nor retinues; rather, he is one whose mind is fixed on the Dharma. Even when seeking him, he does not perceive the Tathāgata even as the Dharma-body.
How much less, then, could he be apprehended by means of a form-body?

Therefore, O youth, the worship of these Tathāgatas consists in this: namely, the non-seeing of the Tathāgata, the non-apprehension of a self, and the absence of expectation for the ripening of karma.

By worshipping the Tathāgata with this worship purified in the three spheres, O youth, a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains this samādhi and quickly awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One further elucidated this very instruction on the preparation for meditative concentration for the youth Candraprabha in detail by means of singing verses:
"By giving perfumes to one of infinite wisdom, one becomes a person of infinite fragrance."
For ten million eons they do not go to an evil destiny, nor does any foul odor ever arise from them.
Having practiced the conduct for tens of millions of eons and having made offerings to thousands of millions of Buddhas,
they become Buddhas who possess the fragrance of supreme morality through the well-arisen scent of wisdom.
If, moreover, one knows that there is no sentient being who gives the fragrance, nor anyone to whom it is given,
yet one gives the fragrance with such a mind— this is his soft, conformable patience.

If a person who practices this supreme patience is cut into pieces as small as a cowrie shell for as many millions of eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, his mind will not turn back from it.
For what reason is it called "patience," and how again is it called "conformable"?
For what cause is one called "irreversible," and how again is one called a "bodhisattva"?
I am patient regarding this dharma, which is by nature selfless; for one who possesses the perception of selflessness, there are no afflictions.
Just as he knows all phenomena to be like space, so here, what indeed could be called "patience"?
Training in accordance with the instruction of all the Victors, the wise one practices without [clinging to] any phenomenon;
he does not give rise to doubts regarding the qualities of a Buddha—this is the patient acceptance that conforms to reality.

While he is practicing in this way, whatever Māras in the world might speak these words in the form of a Buddha—"Awakening is very difficult to attain; become a Śrāvaka"—he does not accept their speech, nor does he turn back from his path.
He awakens beings from erroneous views, saying, "This is not the path for attaining the deathless";
by describing the wrong path and establishing them on the true path, for that reason he is called a bodhisattva.
For one who stands on the path that accords with patience, awakened to the attachment to selflessness,
there never arises— even in a dream— the thought that "there is a man, a person, a soul, or a sentient being."

Even if tens of millions of Māras, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, were to approach in the form of Buddhas and say: "There is an internal life-principle within your body; tell me that it does not exist, and you shall not be Buddhas. (SRS 6.11)
Through wisdom I know the aggregates to be empty; having known this, I do not dwell with the afflictions.
I converse by means of mere verbal expression, and though utterly extinguished, I move through this world.
Just as, my son, when a man is born, a name is given to him—
yet that name is not found by searching through the directions, and thus his name has come from nowhere at all.
In that very way, the Bodhisattva has a name, yet that name cannot be found by searching through the directions;
even while searching, this Bodhisattva knows: "He who is this is the Bodhisattva."
Even in the midst of the ocean fire might blaze, yet the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) does not exist for the Bodhisattva;
for from the very moment his mind has arisen for enlightenment, the view of a living soul (jīvadṛṣṭi) no longer exists within him.
For here no one has been born, nor has anyone died; no sentient being, human, or person has arisen.
All phenomena are like an illusion, empty of intrinsic nature, and cannot be understood by those of non-Buddhist schools.
Nor can this awakening of a Buddha be known by those who are infatuated with food, or who are greedy and craving for robes and alms bowls, nor by those who are agitated or conceited.
Those who are overcome by sloth and torpor, who are indolent, stubborn, arrogant, and shameless—
those who have no faith in the Buddha are unable to understand this supreme enlightenment. (SRS 6.18)
Those ordinary persons of broken conduct who have no faith in the Dharma,
and who lack respect for their fellow practitioners of the holy life, are unable to realize supreme enlightenment.
Those whose conduct is unbroken, who possess a sense of shame and modesty, and who have love for the Buddha as well as for the Dharma,
and who have intense reverence for their fellow practitioners of the holy life— they attain the supreme, excellent enlightenment.
Those whose sphere of activity here is the foundations of mindfulness, for whom joy and rapture are spread as a bed,
whose food is the meditative absorptions and whose drink is concentration— they too awaken to the supreme, excellent enlightenment.
The perception of selflessness, dwelling in the daytime, mindfulness, and the practice of walking while in a state of emptiness—
these fragrant and delightful flowers of the factors of enlightenment lead one who applies themselves to them to attain supreme awakening.
The conduct of the wise Bodhisattvas is not the domain of other people, nor that of Pratyekabuddhas or Śrāvakas; what person of discernment would not conceive a longing for it?
Even if my lifespan were to last for as many millions of eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges,
one could not reach the end of describing the qualities of even a single hair [of the Buddha] by means of the wisdom of a Buddha.
Therefore, having heard these benefits taught by the unconquered Jina, one should quickly expound this samādhi; then supreme enlightenment will not be difficult to attain.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Chapter on Samādhi," in the *Śrī-Samādhirāja*.
(Vaidya 35) Chapter 7: The Entrance into the Three Patiences.
Thereupon, the Blessed One addressed the youth Candraprabha once again: "Therefore, O youth..."

A bodhisattva mahāsattva who desires this samādhi and wishes to quickly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment must become skilled in the knowledge of the three patiences (*kṣānti*).
By him, the first patience must be understood.
The second patience is to be understood;
the third patience is to be understood.
One should become skilled in the distinctions between the three patiences, and skilled in the distinctions between the knowledge of the three patiences.
For what reason?

Because, young man, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva becomes skilled in the excellence of the three patiences and becomes skilled in the excellence of the knowledge of the three patiences, then, young man, this bodhisattva mahāsattva quickly attains samādhi.
And he swiftly awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Therefore, O youth, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who desires to swiftly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment should take up this Dharma discourse on the entry into the three patiences;
having taken it up, he should proclaim it in detail to others.
That will be for the benefit of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, and for the welfare, benefit, and happiness of the great multitude of gods and humans.
Then the Blessed One, by means of chanting verses, extensively proclaimed this Dharma discourse on the entry into the three kinds of patience to the youth Candraprabha:
"One does not engage in dispute with anyone, nor does one utter speech that is unbeneficial;
always established in the true meaning and the Dharma, one is said to possess the first patience. (SRS 7.1)
One knows all phenomena to be like an illusion, yet one does not dwell within the sphere of signs;
one does not fall away from the stage of the increase of knowledge—these are the distinctive qualities of the first patience.
Skilled in the systems of all the sūtras, wise in his conviction regarding this well-spoken teaching,
