and possessing infinite knowledge regarding the wisdom of the Sugatas— these are the distinctive qualities of the first patience.
Whoever hears the well-spoken Dharma and does not doubt what has been spoken by the Buddhas,
and who has conviction in the true nature (dharmatā) of all the Victors— these are the specific qualities of the first patience (kṣānti).
He understands the distinction of the sūtras of definitive meaning, namely emptiness as it was taught by the Sugata;
furthermore, he understands that all phenomena in which there is no person, being, or individual are of interpretable meaning. (SRS 7.5)
Those many other non-Buddhist teachers who exist in this world—his mind is not obstructed by them;
he establishes compassion toward them. These are the specific qualities of the first patience.
The dhāraṇī appears to him, and once it has appeared, he never wavers;
he speaks words that follow the truth—these are the specific qualities of the first patience.

Even if there were a transformation of the four elements—wind, water, fire, and earth—one would not turn back from the awakening of a Buddha; these are the specific qualities of the first patience (kṣānti).
Whatever various fields of craftsmanship exist in the world, the Bodhisattva has trained in them all;
yet he perceives nothing superior to himself—these are the distinctive qualities of the first patience.
Through the power of tranquility he becomes unshakable, and through insight he becomes like a mountain;
he cannot be disturbed by any sentient beings—this is described as the second patience.
He remains in meditative concentration and speaks while in concentration; he walks and sits in concentration.
Having reached the perfection of concentration, the wise one possesses these distinctions of the second patience.
Concentrated in meditative absorption, the teacher of Dharma attains the five superknowledges and travels to hundreds of fields;
yet he does not decline from the power of his supernormal faculties— these are the distinctions of the second patience.
He seeks such a peaceful concentration that, for one thus composed, there is no sentient being who could grasp the measure of his mind; these are the distinctions of the second patience.

Whatever beings there may be here in the world-systems, if they were to teach the Dharmas through the wisdom of a Buddha, one would grasp it all as it was spoken; these are the specific qualities of the second patience.
In the east, north, south, west, as well as below, above, and in the intermediate directions—everywhere he beholds the Lords of the World; this is described as the third patience.
Having manifested inconceivable emanations with bodies of golden hue, he teaches the Dharma to many millions of living beings; these are the specific qualities of the third patience.
That bodhisattva is seen everywhere throughout this Jambudvīpa buddha-field;
he becomes renowned in the world including the gods and asuras—these are the distinctions of the third patience.

The conduct of the Buddhas, as well as their spheres of activity and the manner of deportment of the Leaders—in all these things that wise one becomes trained; these are the distinctions of the third patience.
If all the beings whatsoever in the world-systems here were to speak the praises of that bodhisattva,
yet his mind is not attached to them, he is said to be trained in the wisdom of the Buddha. (SRS 7.19)
If all the beings who exist here in these world-systems were to speak the praises of that bodhisattva,
yet his mind were still provoked by resentment toward them, he has not yet been trained in the wisdom of the Buddha.
He does not become elated when wealth is gained, nor does he become dejected when it is lost;
his mind is always established like a mountain—this is the distinction of the third patience.

This patience that follows after sounds is said to be born of reflection and conformable to cultivation; that which is born of hearing is the patience of non-arising, and the training therein is likewise the path to enlightenment.
When that bodhisattva has attained all three unsurpassed patiences,
the Sugatas, the supreme among men, having seen him, then grant him the prophecy for stainless awakening.
Then, having heard that prophecy of his, the earth shook in six ways;
the field became radiant with light, and tens of millions of gods rained down flowers.
And having heard that prophecy of his, inconceivable millions of billions of beings conceived the thought for supreme, foremost enlightenment: "We too shall become Jinas, the noble ones."
When these three unsurpassed patiences have been attained by the Bodhisattva, he is neither born nor does he die; he neither passes away nor is he reborn.

When these three unsurpassed patiences have been attained by the Bodhisattva, he no longer perceives one who is born or one who dies; he perceives all phenomena as the established nature of reality. (SRS 7.27)
For thus he has known them to be unreal, like an illusion, with a nature empty of intrinsic being;
emptiness is neither born nor does it die, for all these phenomena are empty of intrinsic being.
When he is honored by someone, attended upon, respected, worshipped, and revered, his mind does not become attached to that; he knows the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of phenomena.
When reviled by sentient beings, struck, or threatened, he feels neither anger nor pride toward them;
rather, he generates firm loving-kindness toward them for the very purpose of liberating all beings.
Though being struck with clods of earth and sticks, the wise one does not harbor resentment toward them;
for one established in the patient acceptance of selflessness, there exists neither the stubbornness of anger nor pride.
For thus he has known them to be unreal, like an illusion, and empty of intrinsic nature;
established in such a system of dharmas, he becomes well-honored in the world including the gods.
Even when beings with raised weapons might cut his various limbs one by one,
his mind is not provoked toward them, nor do his loving-kindness and compassion ever diminish.
And thus he generates this thought therein: "For they are cutting my limbs and members one by one;
even so, there shall be no auspicious peace or nirvāṇa for me until I am established in this supreme enlightenment. (SRS 7.34)

For such bodhisattvas of great renown, who dwell in the equanimity of the patience of selflessness within this unsurpassed power of patience, tens of millions of eons have been constantly and thoroughly cultivated.

Even if one were to travel for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, enlightenment would not yet be touched here by those who do not apply themselves to the work of the Buddha’s wisdom; how much less so, then, regarding the wisdom of the Tathāgatas?
It would be impossible to exhaust their praise even if one were to speak for inconceivable hundreds of eons,
for those of infinite renown and great glory who are established in the patience of selflessness.

Therefore, whoever desires to awaken to that supreme and unsurpassed aggregate of wisdom, let them cultivate the patience praised by the Jina; then this excellent awakening will not be difficult to attain.
Thus ends the seventh chapter of the *Śrīsamādhirāja*, titled "The Entrance into the Three Patiences."
Chapter 8: The Emergence from Non-existence.
Thereupon, the Blessed One again addressed the youth Candraprabha: "In the past, O youth..."

In the past, during an age that was incalculable, more than incalculable, vast, immeasurable, inconceivable, and limitless kalpas ago— at that time, at that moment— a Tathāgata named Abhāvasamudgata arose in the world: an Arhat, a perfectly awakened Buddha,
endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and [humans].
and for humans as well—O Prince, what do you think: for what reason is that Tathāgata called Abhāvasamudgata?
Furthermore, O Prince, as soon as that Tathāgata was born, he rose into the air to the height of seven palm trees.
Having taken seven steps, he spoke these words: "All phenomena have arisen from non-existence;
all phenomena have arisen from non-existence.
And by that sound, O youth, the triple-thousand great-thousandfold world system was made aware by his voice.

There, starting from the gods of the earth up to the Brahma-world, they raised their voices in succession and proclaimed this sound: "Ah! This Tathāgata will indeed be Abhāvasamudgata (Arisen from Non-existence), he who, as soon as he was born, rose into the air to the height of seven palm trees, took seven steps, and uttered the word 'non-existence'.
Thus, the name "Abhāvasamudgata, Abhāvasamudgata" arose for that Tathāgata.

And when that Blessed One had attained awakening, from all the leaves of every tree, from all the grasses, shrubs, herbs, and forest giants, and from all the mountain peaks, there issued forth the sound "arisen from non-existence" (*abhāvasamudgata*);
and whatever designations of sound existed within that world-system, everywhere there issued forth the sound of the communication "arisen from non-existence.
And at that time, O youth, during that period, of that Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Abhāvasamudgata...
In the teaching of the Perfectly Enlightened One, there was a prince named Mahākaruṇācintī, who was handsome, pleasing, and beautiful to behold,

endowed with the most excellent and abundant complexion. Then, indeed, that prince named Mahākaruṇācintī approached the place where the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Perfectly Enlightened One Abhāvasamudgata was staying.
Having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, circumambulated the Blessed One three times, and stood to one side.
Then, young man, that Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Abhāvasamudgata, having understood the resolute intention of the prince Mahākaruṇācintin, taught this samādhi.
Then, young man, having heard this samādhi, the prince Mahākaruṇācintin was satisfied, elated, joyful, delighted, and filled with gladness and happiness; he became serene.
With a serene mind, he shaved off his hair and beard, donned saffron-colored robes, and with perfect faith went forth from the home to the homeless life.
Having gone forth, he mastered this samādhi;
having mastered, fully understood, retained, and recited it, he dwelt devoted to the practice of its cultivation.
By that very root of merit, he did not fall into an evil rebirth for twenty billion eons;
at the conclusion of those twenty eons, he fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
A Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha named Suvicintitārtha appeared in the world.
And throughout all those eons, he propitiated twenty koṭis of Buddhas.
Behold, O youth, how this samādhi is of great benefit for Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, as it leads to the fulfillment of unsurpassed Buddha-knowledge.

Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses: "I remember in the past, in an inconceivable eon, there arose a Great Sage, the supreme among men, who acted for the benefit of the world; his name was Abhāvasamudgata."
As soon as he was born, standing in the sky, he taught the non-existence of all phenomena;
accordingly, his name was established, and by that sound, the entire trichiliocosm was made aware.
All the gods also raised a cry: "He shall be a Jina by the name of Abhāva," for as soon as he was born, the Leader took seven steps and declared that all phenomena are non-existent.
When the Buddha becomes the King of Dharma, the Sage who reveals all phenomena,
the sound "all phenomena are non-existent" will resound throughout the grasses, trees, shrubs, herbs, rocks, and mountains.
However many sounds there are in that world-system, all of which are indeed non-existent and not any existent thing at all—
just so many voices issue forth from that Tathāgata, the Guide of the World.
And at that time, there was a prince named Karuṇāvicintin, who was handsome, gracious, and pleasing to behold; he approached the presence of that Jina.
Having bowed at the feet of the Bull among Sages and having circumambulated him with reverence,
he sat down there with a serene mind to hear the stainless, unsurpassed Dharma. (SRS 8.7)
That wise Victor, having understood his intention, revealed this samādhi;
and having heard of this stainless samādhi, he quickly went forth into homelessness in the teaching of the Supreme Victor.
Having gone forth and having maintained, recited, and mastered this samādhi,
for twenty full ten-million eons, he shall never go to a state of ruin.
By that very same wholesome karma, he pleased twenty billion Buddhas;
and in the presence of all those Victors, he cultivated this supreme, peaceful samādhi.
In a later time, he became a Buddha in the world named Sadanāmadheya, whose purpose was well-considered;
having accomplished the welfare of many millions of living beings, he entered parinirvāṇa like a fire at the end of time.

Therefore, whoever desires to awaken to enlightenment and to ferry sentient beings across the ocean of existence should uphold this sūtra praised by the Buddhas; for them, that supreme enlightenment will not be difficult to attain.
Thus ends the eighth chapter of the *Śrī Samādhirāja*, titled "The Chapter on the Emergence from Non-existence."
(Vaidya 44) Chapter 9: On the Receptivity to the Profound Dharma.
Thereupon, the Blessed One again addressed the youth Candraprabha: "Therefore, O youth..."
A bodhisattva mahāsattva who desires this samādhi and wishes to quickly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment must become skilled in the patient acceptance of profound dharmas.
And how, young man, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva become skilled in the patient acceptance of profound dharmas?
In this regard, young man, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should understand all phenomena as they truly are to be like an illusion.

All phenomena should be understood as being like a dream, like a mirage, like an echo, like an optical illusion, like the moon reflected in water, like a magical creation, like a reflection, and like space.
And when, young man, all phenomena have been fully understood by a bodhisattva mahāsattva to be like an illusion, [he attains non-attachment].

When all phenomena are thoroughly understood as they truly are— as being like a dream, like a mirage, like an echo, like an optical illusion, like the moon reflected in water, like a magical creation, like a reflection, and like space— then, O youth, this bodhisattva mahāsattva is said to be skilled in the patience regarding profound dharmas.

Endowed with profound patience toward the Dharma, he is not attached to things that provoke attachment, he is not repelled by things that provoke aversion, and he is not deluded by things that provoke delusion.
For what reason?
Because he does not perceive that phenomenon,
nor does he apprehend that phenomenon.
Whoever might be attached, or that in which one might be attached,
or that by which one might be attached;
whoever might be hostile, or that in which one might be hostile.
Or that by which one might become corrupted;
or he who might be deluded, or that in which one might be deluded,
or that by which one might be deluded.
He does not perceive that phenomenon, nor does he apprehend that phenomenon.
Not perceiving and not apprehending that phenomenon, he is without attachment, without aversion, without delusion, and with a mind free from inversion; thus he is said to be "composed."
Free from conceptual proliferation;
having crossed over, gone to the further shore;
having reached firm ground.
One who has attained security;
one who has attained the formless;
one who possesses ethical discipline.
Possessing knowledge, possessing wisdom, possessing merit.
Possessed of supernormal power... / possessed of mindfulness...
/ possessed of intelligence...
Possessed of skillful means, possessed of a sense of shame, ... possessed of steadfastness.
Possessed of virtuous conduct, endowed with the ascetic practices and the refinement of austerity, and free from blemish.
Possessing nothing;
an Arhat; one whose outflows are exhausted.

He is a śramaṇa who is free from afflictions, has attained mastery, is well-liberated in mind, is well-liberated in wisdom, is a noble thoroughbred, a great elephant, has accomplished what was to be done, has performed his task, has laid down the burden, has attained his own goal, has utterly exhausted the fetters of existence, is well-liberated in mind through right knowledge, and has reached the supreme perfection of mastery over all mental states.
A Brāhmaṇa who is a *snātaka*, one who has mastered the Vedas, a knower of the Vedas, a *śrotriya*,
and a son of the Buddha.
The son of the Śākyas,
who has crushed the thorns and cast away the moat.
One who has crossed over the moat,
one from whom the arrow has been extracted,
and one who is free from decay.
A monk;
one who is not clothed;
a man.
A true person; a supreme person;
a great person.
A lion among men,
an elephant among men,
a thoroughbred among men.
The preeminent among men, the hero among men,
the champion among men,
the flower among men.
A lotus among men; a white lotus among men;
a tamer of men.
He is called the moon among men,
the non-base man,
and the man untainted by worldly things.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
"When the world-system does not evolve, this entire world becomes space."
Just as it was before, so it is after; know all phenomena to be like that.
Whatever exists in this world, as far as it extends, has sunk below and become a mass of water;
just as it is below, so it is above—know all phenomena to be like that.
Just as there is no cloud whatsoever in the sky, yet in an instant a circle of clouds appears,
and one might wonder from where it was previously produced— know all phenomena to be like that.
Just as when the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa, his reflection is seen by those who bring him to mind;
just as it was before, so it is after—know all phenomena to be like that simile.
Just as a person might observe a large mass of foam being swept away by a current,
and having observed it, finds no essence therein— know all phenomena to be like that.
Just as when the god sends down rain in thick drops, individual bubbles arise;
once they have arisen, they are broken and do not exist—know all phenomena to be like these bubbles.
Just as various auspicious and inauspicious actions proceed from seeing a letter in another village,
yet no transfer of the letter exists through speech, so should you understand all phenomena to be like that.
Just as a man deluded by the intoxication of pride wanders about, perceiving this earth to be moving,
yet the great earth neither shifts nor trembles— know all phenomena to be like that.
Just as a woman gazes at her well-adorned face in the surface of a mirror or in a vessel of oil,
that foolish girl, having conceived passion for it, runs about in search of desire.
When no reflection of a face exists, a face is never actually found in the mirror;
just as a fool might conceive a passion for it, know all phenomena to be like that.
Just as a city of Gandharvas, just as a mirage, just as a magical illusion, and just as a dream— know all phenomena to be like these, empty of intrinsic nature, being merely the cultivation of signs.
Just as the reflection of the moon is seen in a clear lake within a pure sky,
yet no actual transfer of the moon into the water occurs— know all phenomena to have that same characteristic.
Just as a man standing amidst mountains and forests might speak, sing, laugh, or weep,
and an echo is heard but not seen— know all phenomena to be like that.
Just as an echo arises in dependence upon singing, instrumental music, or likewise weeping,
yet no sound ever exists within the mountain— know all phenomena to be like that.
Just as a person who has awakened does not see the desires they experienced while dreaming,
so too should you understand all phenomena to be like that— those fools who are excessively greedy for desires.
Just as a magician creates various forms such as elephant-carts, chariots of horses,
and chariots of men, yet no cart is actually seen there— know all phenomena to be like that. (SRS 9.16)
Just as a maiden in a dream sees a son born and then dead—
exceedingly joyful at his birth and dejected at his death— know all phenomena to be like that.
Just as one might weep with loud cries in a dream for a deceased mother or son,
yet neither the mother nor the son has actually died— know all phenomena to be like that.
Just as the moon in the water is seen at night in clear, undisturbed water— ungraspable, insubstantial, and empty— so too should you know all phenomena to be like that.
Just as a man, tormented by thirst, might travel at midday during the summer heat and see a mirage as a mass of water, so should you understand all phenomena to be like that.
In a mirage, water does not exist, yet that deluded being desires to drink it;
it is impossible to drink water that is unreal—know all phenomena to be like that.
Just as a person seeking the core might split open the moist trunk of a plantain tree,
yet find no core either outside or within— know all phenomena to be like that.
The eye is not a valid authority, nor are the ear or nose; the tongue is not a valid authority, nor are the body or mind.
If these sense faculties were valid authorities, what need would there be for the Noble Path?
Since these sense-faculties are immeasurable, insentient by nature, and indeterminate,
therefore, whoever seeks the path to nirvāṇa should perform their task by means of the Noble Path. (SRS 9.24)
When one observes the prior limit of the body, there is neither body here nor the perception of a body;
where there is neither body nor the perception of a body—that is called the unconditioned lineage.
For those whose nature is cessation, there is no phenomenon by which they might exist; thus, for them, existence never exists.
For those who possess such conceptualizations as "it exists" or "it does not exist," suffering is not stilled as they wander in this way.
"It exists" and "it does not exist" are both extremes; "purity" and "impurity"—these too are extremes.
Therefore, having avoided both extremes, the wise person does not take a stand even in the middle.
"It exists" and "it does not exist"—this is a dispute; "purity" and "impurity"—this is a dispute.
For those who have fallen into dispute, suffering is not stilled; for those who have reached the state beyond dispute, suffering ceases.
Having spoken on the discourse of the foundations of mindfulness, fools think, "We are body-witnesses.
Yet for one who is a body-witness there is no conceit; all his manifold conceits have been abandoned.
Having spoken about the four meditative concentrations, the foolish say, "We are the ones whose domain is meditation.
They do not meditate on the afflictions, nor is there any conceit; yet, having understood through knowledge, pride is abandoned.
Having spoken to four beings, fools say, "We are seers of truth.
Yet for one who sees the truth, there is no conceit; the Jina has taught that truth is non-conceit.

One should guard moral conduct, yet not be conceited because of it; one should listen to the Dharma, yet not be conceited because of it. For whatever that person of little wisdom is conceited about, suffering increases for him on that very basis.
Pride is shown by the Omniscient One, the Guide of the World, to be the root of suffering.
For those intoxicated by pride, suffering increases; for those who are free from such conceit, suffering ceases.

How many dharma-discourses one might master, if one does not guard moral discipline and is intoxicated by learning— by such great learning he cannot be saved, for one who is immoral goes to an evil rebirth.
But if, intoxicated by the pride of ethical discipline, he does not apply himself to great learning,
he will exhaust the fruit of his discipline without remainder and once again experience suffering.
Even if one should cultivate meditative concentration in the world, yet does not eliminate the perception of a self,
his afflictions will flare up again, just like Udraka’s cultivation of concentration in this world.

If one discerns the dharmas as being without self, and having discerned them, if one should cultivate that [insight], it is the cause for attaining the fruit of nirvāṇa; any other cause does not lead to peace.

Just as a man, harassed by a band of thieves and seeking to escape for the sake of his life, finds that his feet have no power to move, and is slain there by those thieves who seize him; so it is with one who has fallen into the hands of Māra.
In this way, a foolish man devoid of ethical discipline desires to flee from the conditioned;
yet, being lacking in discipline, he is unable to go, for he is struck down by old age, sickness, and death. (SRS 9.39)
Just as many thousands of thieves commit evil through various means,
so too do the afflictions through their diverse modes, just as a thief destroys one who belongs to the side of purity.
One who has thoroughly realized that the aggregates are selfless does not become agitated when reviled or abused;
such a person does not fall under the power of the Māra of the afflictions, for he who knows emptiness does not give way to anger.
Many people speak of the emptiness of the aggregates, yet they do not understand how they are selfless.
Not understanding this, when challenged by others, they are overcome by anger and speak harshly.
Just as a man who is ill and afflicted by bodily suffering is never released for many years,
being oppressed by the misery of long-term disease, he seeks out a physician, desiring medical treatment.
Seeking him again and again, he found a physician who was wise and discerning; having established compassion for him, the physician prescribed: "Let this medicine be used."

If a patient, having received extensive and excellent medicines, does not take them by which he might be freed from illness, it is neither the fault of the physician nor of the medicines; rather, the fault belongs to that patient alone.
Having thus gone forth in this teaching and mastered the powers, meditations, and faculties, they do not apply themselves to cultivation; for those whose yoga is unapplied, how can there be nirvāṇa?
All phenomena are always empty of intrinsic nature; the sons of the Victors discern their reality as such.
Existence is entirely and in every way empty; the emptiness of the non-Buddhist outsiders is merely partial.
The wise do not engage in conflict with fools; they treat fools with respect and avoid them.
Even when those with malicious minds come before them, they do not cultivate intimacy through the ways of fools.
The wise do not cultivate intimacy with fools, having understood the continuous nature of fools' character;
however long a fool may be well-served, they once again become like enemies.
The wise do not place their trust in fools here, having understood the nature of the character of fools;
for fools are by nature alienated, and among ordinary persons there is no such thing as a friend.

When addressed with words consistent with the Dharma, they manifest anger, malice, and lack of confidence; these are the traits of fools, for having understood this matter, they do not place their trust [in it].
For fools associate with fools, just as filth mingles with filth; but the wise associate with wise people, just as clarified butter blends with the cream of ghee.
Because they do not reflect upon the defects of saṃsāra and do not understand the ripening of karma,
these fools, lacking faith in the words of the Buddhas, wander in a state of being cut and pierced.
Having obtained this human birth, which is so very difficult to find, they do not become skilled in the various arts and crafts;
having become impoverished and possessing no wealth, they go forth into homelessness while still unable to earn a living.
Having gone forth in this teaching of the Buddha, they become attached to robes and alms bowls;
taken hold of by evil friends, they do not practice the training of the Sugatas.
Not perceiving their own moral conduct, those fools find no stability of mind;
day and night they are unapplied in yoga, and they feel no revulsion toward evil deeds.
For those who are unrestrained in body and mind, nothing at all should be spoken by way of speech;
they are always seeking the faults of others, thinking, "What has he done wrong, and with what shall I reproach him? (SRS 9.57)
Fools dwell upon their food and lack moderation in eating;
though they obtain food through the merit of the Buddha, those fools remain ungrateful for it.
Having obtained food that is delicious, flavorful, and excellent, they eat it while lacking application to yoga;
for them, that food leads to their destruction, just as unwashed lotus stalks do for young elephant calves.

Moreover, though he be wise, intelligent, and discerning, and may eat pure and excellent food, he does not become attached to it; free from greed, that practitioner of yoga eats with proper mindfulness.
Moreover, even though he is wise, intelligent, and discerning, he addresses a fool, saying, "From where have you come? Welcome!
Thus, having embraced them with pleasant speech, he establishes compassion toward them.
Those who are compassionate and wish for the welfare of fools are, in turn, delighted by the misfortune of those very fools.
Because of this fault, one should abandon fools and dwell alone in the forest like a deer.
Having recognized such faults as these, the wise person never forms an association with fools.
For one who serves those deficient in wisdom, there is a fall from heaven; how then shall they attain awakening?
The wise dwell in loving-kindness, they dwell in compassion, they dwell in sympathetic joy;
being always equanimous toward all states of existence, and having cultivated meditative concentration, they touch enlightenment.
Having awakened to that auspicious and sorrowless enlightenment, and having perceived sentient beings oppressed by the diseases of worldly existence,
they establish compassion toward them and deliver discourses endowed with the ultimate truth.
Those who understand that nature of the Dharma of the Victors, the ineffable truth of the Sugatas— they,
having heard such a Dharma as this, will attain this noble, disinterested patience.
Thus ends the ninth chapter of the *Śrī-Samādhirāja*, titled "The Chapter on Profound Patience toward the Dharma."
(Vaidya 54) Chapter Ten: The Entrance into the City.
Thereupon, the Blessed One again addressed the youth Candraprabha: "Therefore, O youth, you should always train yourself in this way: 'I shall make practice the very essence.'"
For what reason?
Because, O youth, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva whose essence is practice, unsurpassed perfect enlightenment is not difficult to attain, let alone this samādhi.

Then the youth Candraprabha rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ground, and bowing with palms joined toward the Blessed One, addressed the Blessed One as follows: "It is marvelous, Blessed One, how well-spoken is this instruction and admonition for the bodhisattva mahāsattvas by the Blessed One."
All the training of the bodhisattvas has been taught, well-proclaimed, and well-established.

This, O Blessed One, is the domain of all the Tathāgatas, wherein there is no ground for any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, let alone for those of other sects. O Blessed One, we shall make practice our essence; becoming indifferent toward body and life, we will train ourselves in accordance with the Tathāgata.
For what reason?
Blessed One, we desire to train in the way of the Tathāgata; Blessed One, we desire to fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
“Blessed One, we are seekers of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. Blessed One, we desire to shatter Māra, the Evil One.
Blessed One, we desire to liberate all sentient beings from all fears and all sufferings.”
"May the Blessed One, out of compassion, consent to take his meal tomorrow at my house together with the assembly of Bodhisattvas and the community of monks.

The Blessed One consented to Candraprabha Kumārabhūta’s request by remaining silent, accepting the meal for tomorrow at his house together with the assembly of Bodhisattvas and the community of monks,
out of compassion.
Then, the youth Candraprabha, perceiving the Blessed One’s acquiescence through his silence, rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder,
bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, circumambulated the Blessed One three times, and departed from the presence of the Blessed One.
Then the youth Candraprabha proceeded toward the great city of Rājagṛha and toward his own residence.
Having arrived, Candraprabha entered his home;
having entered, he had abundant, exquisite, and delicious hard foods, soft foods, and delicacies prepared that very night.

Having prepared food of a hundred flavors, at the end of that very night, he had the great city of Rājagṛha well-sprinkled and well-swept, strewn with loose flowers, perfumed by incense burners, with umbrellas, banners, and flags raised high; it was fumigated with incense, covered with canopies, and draped with bundles of silk ribbons and cords; and the streets and marketplaces were cleared of stones, gravel, and potsherds.

He had the city strewn with various flowers and sprinkled with sandalwood powder; it was adorned with windows, archways, turrets, balconies, lattices, and crescent-shaped ornaments, and was anointed with sandalwood paste.
He had the entire city covered with scattered blue lotuses, water lilies, red lotuses, and white lotuses.
He also caused his own house to be adorned with every kind of ornament.

Then, Prince Candraprabha, having thus decorated these arrays of the city, the arrays of the house, and the arrays of food, departed from the great city of Rājagṛha and approached Vulture Peak Mountain, where the Blessed One was staying.
Having approached and circumambulated the Blessed One three times, he stood to one side.
Standing to one side, the youthful Candraprabha announced the time to the Blessed One: "It is time, Blessed One;
it is time, Sugata."
"The meal is ready; now, do as you deem the time appropriate.

Then the Blessed One rose from his seat, dressed early in the morning, took his bowl and robe, and set out surrounded by a great community of monks—fully one hundred thousand monks—and accompanied by a vast multitude of Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas.
Honored and attended by many hundreds of thousands of gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans,
he was being worshipped and praised with the great majesty of a Buddha, the great miraculous power of a Buddha, and the great deportment of a Buddha,

while hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of light rays issued forth, accompanied by hundreds of thousands of various musical instruments and offerings of flowers, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, and robes.
Showering down [rain], he proceeded toward the great city of Rājagṛha.
The Blessed One placed his right foot-jewel, adorned with the wheel-treasure and accumulated through immeasurable merit, upon the threshold at the residence of the youth Candraprabha;
and immediately, many wonderful and marvelous miracles were manifested in that great city.
This is the natural law in this regard.
Concerning this, it is said:
When the Leader enters the excellent city, his noble foot is placed upon the threshold of Indra’s pillar.
The earth trembles at his splendor, and the beings in that supreme city become overjoyed.
Those men who were hungry or thirsty—none experienced hunger at that time;
hunger and thirst vanished when the Jina set his foot upon the threshold of Indra’s gate.
Furthermore, those men who are blind, deprived of hearing, destitute, and of little merit—
all of them regain their sight and hearing when the Jina places his foot upon the threshold of Indra’s pillar.
Whatever hungry ghosts there may be in the realm of Yama, suffering greatly and longing for food such as spittle and snot—
all of them become happy when the Victor sets his foot upon the threshold of Indra’s palace.
The mountain peaks, summits, and mountains, as well as the excellent trees, śālas, and karṇikāras—
all bow down toward where the Buddha is when the Jina plants his foot upon the threshold of Indra’s palace.

When the Jina set his foot upon the threshold of Indra’s palace, the entire earth, including its cities and towns and extending to the edge of the ocean, trembled in six ways; yet no one here experienced any distress.
Gods, humans, kumbhāṇḍas, and rākṣasas, standing in the sky with uplifted minds, were filled with joy;
holding up a parasol for the Leader of the World, they generated the aspiration for awakening with supreme delight.
And the delightful sound of musical instruments is heard as thousands of drums resound without being struck;
at that time, all sentient beings become overjoyed when the Jina sets his foot upon the threshold of the city.
Hundreds of thousands of trees all bowed down and came into full bloom at that time;
hundreds of thousands of gods in the sky performed superhuman worship for the Jina.
Then the bull-herds bellowed with joy, as did the lords of horses and elephants with their bodies fully grown;
and the lions roared their lion’s roar when the Jina set his foot upon the threshold of Indra’s gate.
Whatever lords of the earth, protectors of the land, have come from every direction and sub-direction,
they fall upon the surface of the ground with joyful hearts, having beheld such splendor as this of the Jina.
Others praise the Lord of the World, while others scatter a rain of flowers over the Jina;
others, having joined their ten fingers in palms-pressed reverence, exclaim these words: "O, how compassionate is the Jina!"
Some, having conceived joy, cast forth excellent pearl necklaces and various kinds of ornaments;
others cast forth robes and jewels, [dedicating] the incomparable and supreme mind of enlightenment for the state of a Jina.
Some cast down excellent nets of gold, while others cast down mukhaphullaka ornaments;
some cast down excellent golden neck-ornaments, and likewise others cast down bracelets.
Some there cast excellent bracelets, others cast armlets variegated with jewels;
others cast garments and flowers, having generated the thought: "May we too become Buddhas."
Other men, with serene minds, cast forth golden ornaments as well as excellent strings of jewels;
and some cast forth nets of gems when the Lord of the World stands at the gate.
Those beings who are in extreme suffering, afflicted by many kinds of calamities and the thorn of grief,
all become endowed with happiness through the glory of the Leader, the Best of Men.
Cuckoos, parrots, mynas, and peacocks, as well as cranes, blue jays, swans, and curlews—
all these flocks of birds, stationed in the sky, utter most enchanting cries.
Then the flocks of birds become overjoyed, emitting sweet and pleasing sounds;
likewise, those who hear the charming voices of the birds have their passion, hatred, and delusion stilled.
Having heard these delightful words, millions of beings all attain the patient acceptance that accords with reality;
and the Sugata prophesies for them all: "In the future, you shall all become Jinas."
At that time, no afflictions arise; all become full of reverence for the King of Dharma.
With the nets of fear, fault, and delusion removed, they prostrate themselves and praise the Sugata.
Beholding the form of the Leader at that time, they conceived a longing for the supreme Buddha-knowledge;
"When shall we obtain such knowledge as this?"—knowing their aspiration, the Jina gave them a prophecy.
From each single pore of the Sugata, hundreds of thousands of light rays stream forth;
they exceed even the sands of the Ganges in number, and it is impossible to grasp their signs.
At that time, O Sūryaprabha, neither the sun shone, nor did the jewels, nor the fire, nor the radiance of all the deities;
at that time, when the Buddha entered the city, all other lights ceased to shine.
Hundreds of thousands of pure lotuses with millions of petals appeared upon the earth,
whereon the Sugata, the One Possessing Ten Powers, set his foot as he traveled along the road with a great retinue.
At that time, when the Leader enters the excellent city, there are no impurities or stains;
the entire city becomes fragrant with incense, and a delightful scent wafts everywhere.
Then that entire city becomes free of clods of earth and gravel, sprinkled with perfumes;
such is the merit of one who possesses the ten powers, for various loose flowers are strewn about.

Having seen the Buddha, the Lord of Men, who resembles gold, those hundreds of thousands of yakṣas with fierce minds conceived vast love for the Guide and went for refuge to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.

And hundreds of thousands of millions of gods, all having approached to behold the Lord of Men, rained down a shower of flowers upon the Sugata; and those released flowers remained suspended in the sky.
Those humans who scatter flowers for the Jina find that they become a flower-parasol in the expanse of the sky;
furthermore, those gods who scatter flowers find that divine blossoms are spread across the surface of the earth.
Never do the gods, humans, kumbhāṇḍas, and rākṣasas reach satiety upon seeing him;
when they behold the Lord of the World, the One Possessing the Ten Powers, they become joyful, exultant, and of virtuous mind.
At that time, celestial flowers do not even enter their minds, nor does any sense of wonder arise there;
yet when they behold the body of the Best of Men, all sentient beings become joyful and uplifted.
To the right of the One Possessing the Ten Powers was Brahmā, and likewise to his left was Śakra, the king of the gods;
many millions of gods stationed in the expanse of the sky produced a feeling of reverence for the Best of Men.
Surrounded by gods and dānavas, having eclipsed all the glory of gods, humans, and men,
the Blessed One entered the city for the invitation, making the earth beautiful with the soles of his feet.
With his body adorned with the secondary marks of excellence, like the sky filled with stars,
the Buddha shines resplendent upon the royal road, just like the full moon situated in the heavens on the night of the full moon.
Just as a jewel, most excellent and pure, free from defects and impurities,
radiates a clear light in every direction and intermediate direction, so too does the Jina illuminate all world-systems.
Surrounded by gods and dānavas, the Jina, the best of men, entered Rājagṛha;
the Buddha entered the house of Candraprabha, adorning the earth with the soles of his feet.
The excellent city was adorned on all sides, with many thousands of millions of banners raised up there;
the entire ground was smeared with the finest perfumes and likewise strewn with *sumana* and *vārṣika* flowers.
When the Sugata, the Protector, out of compassion for humanity, delivers a discourse while standing in the street,
the Jina creates an emanation there and bestows upon them the sublime Buddha-dharmas.
Ten million emanated Jinas, resembling gold, handsome and beautiful to behold,
surrounded the Victorious Buddha as he bestowed the peaceful awakening of a Buddha, which is emptiness.

Hearing this, hundreds of thousands of living beings set their minds upon the supreme, foremost wisdom of a Buddha, thinking, "When shall we attain such wisdom as this? Knowing his intention, the Jina gave him a prophecy.
At that time, some conceived a longing for it, having obtained a most inconceivable gain:
those by whom the Jina, the Lord of Men, was invited; and there is no limit to the merit of their offerings. (SRS 10.42)

Some, moreover, conceived a pure thought: "Tomorrow we shall invite the Compassionate One, who acts for the benefit of beings and is compassionate toward all creatures—he whose sight is so very difficult to obtain throughout the realms of existence."
Some, standing upon the beautiful, well-adorned turrets of the gateways, lovely to behold,
scattered divine flowers before the One Possessing the Ten Powers, having generated the mind of awakening.
Some cast beautiful garlands of excellent campaka flowers, as well as showers of fragrant atimuktaka blossoms;
others, moreover, cast silk ribbons, having generated a supreme and unsurpassed state of mind.
Some, staying at home with flowers in their hands and bodies adorned with supreme robes,
took various flowers and silk garlands and rained them down upon the Jina of great majesty.
Some scatter lotuses, water-lilies, and blue lotuses; others scatter exquisite golden flowers.
Some scatter precious jewels upon him, while others scatter powdered sandalwood.
Immeasurable were the wonders, incomparable and impossible to describe;
as the Leader entered the excellent city, many millions of beings became established in the wisdom of a Buddha.
The Abṛha and Atapa gods, those who have seen the Truth, the Sudṛśas and Sudarśanas, and whatever other gods there are,
as well as the Akaniṣṭhas free from passion— all have approached to behold the Lord of Men.
Likewise, immeasurable and boundless Śubhamaruts with uplifted minds,
and immeasurable millions of Śubhakṛtsnas, have approached to behold the Guide, the Great Sage.
Those of immeasurable and likewise measureless radiance, as well as the gods of limited radiance,
and many millions of those from the Ābhāsvara realm, all approached there to behold the Lord of the World.
Many hundreds of thousands of Brahma-purohita attendants, likewise full of faith,
and many hundreds of Brahma-kāyika deities— all of them approached to behold the Leader.
Furthermore, the gods of the Heaven of Others' Emanations, as well as the gods who Delight in Emanations and the pure beings,
the gods of the Joyful Heaven, the Tuṣita heaven, and the Yāma gods— all approached, paying homage to the Buddha.
And Śakra, the king of the gods of the thirty-three, arrived there together with hundreds of millions of apsarases;
raining down a shower of excellent flowers, he approached to behold the Buddha, the Lord of Munis.
The four world-protectors in the four directions— Vaiśravaṇa, Dhṛtarāṣṭra the king of nāgas,
Virūḍhaka, and Virūpākṣa— all approached with joyful minds and praised that Lord of Men.
The powerful King of Yakṣas, Aiḷavila, surrounded by hundreds of yakṣas and filled with affection,
stood in the expanse of the sky with a joyful heart and rained down many various kinds of flowers.
Furthermore, others, infinite in number and wearing garlands, taking up various and manifold flowers and perfumes,
all with joyful hearts and accompanied by their retinues, performed worship there for the Best of Men.
Many hundreds of *karoṭapāṇi* yakṣas, as well as the beautifully adorned yakṣa maidens,
perform worship of the Buddha with hundreds of musical instruments and most sweet, pleasing yakṣa melodies.
Accompanied by thousands of kinnarīs who were highly skilled in charming and sweet singing and instrumental music,
Druma came from Mount Gandhamādana and paid homage to the supreme Jina.
Śambara, Bala, Vemacitra, Rāhu, and the thousands of Dānava maidens with their retinues,
as well as other hosts of Asuras of great supernatural power, approached while raining down jewels.
Hundreds of niyutas of infinite rākṣasas, being attended by hundreds of millions of rākṣasas, out of reverence scatter broad, various, and wonderful loose flowers upon the Best of Men. //61//
Moreover, the Naga king Anavatapta and highly trained Naga maidens approached there to worship the Lord of the World, sounding hundreds of thousands of musical instruments.
The five hundred sons of Anavatapta, seeking vast and unsurpassed wisdom,
surrounded by their own kin and filled with exultation, approached in person to worship the Self-Existent One.
And yet, the Naga king Apalāla, having bowed with palms joined to the Best of Men,
took beautiful *nāgapuṣpa* flowers and stood in the sky, honoring the King of Sages.
And yet, the Naga King Mucilinda, with a joyful mind, thoroughly satisfied and filled with rapture,
took various jewels and pearls and approached the Leader there to scatter them over him.
And yet, even Kālika, the Naga king, approached the presence of the Tathāgata with a joyful heart;
taking beautiful and exquisite strings of jewels, he performed the most excellent worship for the Supreme Man.
Having conceived the highest reverence and recollecting the qualities of the Tathāgata, he,
surrounded by his own kin and accompanied by a host of nāgas, spoke many kinds of praises for the Leader.
The nāga kings Nanda and Upananda, as well as Takṣaka, Kṛṣṇa, and Gautama, approached the Jina while paying him homage; they prostrated themselves at the feet of the Sugata.
The Naga king Elapatra, resplendent and surrounded by hundreds of nagas, approached;
remembering Kāśyapa, the supreme Sage and Jina, he beheld his own rebirth among the inopportune states.
Alas! Formerly I was full of longing; once in the past I plucked a single small leaf from the *elāpatra* tree.
Because of that, I was reborn in an unfavorable state where it is not easy to understand the Dharma of the Victor.
May I quickly abandon this most loathsome body of a being, this birth as a nāga;
may I realize the Dharma, the state of peace, which the Supreme among Men realized at the seat of awakening.
Sāgara, the universal monarch of the serpent kings, surrounded by thirty million nāgas,
and Varuṇa, the wise one, having taken pearl necklaces, approached the Blessed One for the sake of worship.
At that time, Kimpila, the yakṣa of Rājagṛha, who was staying in the sky, caught the stone thrown at the Jina; out of reverence for the Sugata, he stood before him.
The entire capital city of Alakavatī became empty; not a single yakṣa remained there. Having performed all their duties for one another, they all gathered to behold the Lord of the World.
Moreover, Kharakarṇa, Sūciroma, the forest-dwelling Yakṣa Bheṣaka,
Haimavata, Śatagiri, and the Yakṣa Gardabhaka approached the Jina, the Self-Existent One.
Indraketu, Vikaṭa, Surūpa, Vakkula, Pañcika, and Śākyapravṛddha—
these and other lords of yakṣas, by the thousands, approached carrying incense jars.
At that time, many hundreds of thousands of yakṣas approached there, having taken flowers; their bodies were deformed, ill-proportioned, and of various forms, with their ornaments fallen away.
The Suparṇas who dwell in the ocean, having assumed the guise of brahmins,
stand in the sky wearing various beautiful crowns, paying homage to the Sugata.
Whatever city-deities there are in the hundreds of cities throughout Jambudvīpa, and whatever deities dwell in the forest hermitages—
all those city-deities together have approached to perform worship for the Guide.
Infinite forest deities, as well as all the mountain deities,
and likewise all the river deities together, approached to perform worship for the Leader.
Hundreds of deities in the wilderness forests, all the deities upon the mountain peaks,
the deities of springs and lakes, and the deities of the ocean have approached the Buddha.
The hosts of gods, asuras, nāgas, and yakṣas, the garuḍas, mahoragas, and kinnaras, as well as the kumbhāṇḍas,
and likewise many pretas and pūtanas, pay homage to the Best of Men.
And having performed worship to the Supreme Victor, when the Leader enters the excellent city,
the kings of gods, asuras, nāgas,
and yakṣas never tire of beholding him.

Just as the Lord of the World performed the most excellent worship toward the previous Victors in his former lives, such is the ripening of the fruit of that merit; yet, O Lord of Men, he never grew weary while beholding it.
Mount Meru, as well as Sumeru, the Cakravāla mountains, the Himavat, and Gandhamādana—
these do not become obstructions for the Jina when the Jina releases his light into the Buddha-field.
And those who are here in this ocean-like buddha-field, they too then become level with the earth;
this entire universal buddha-field becomes level, strewn everywhere with flowers.
The King of Dharma scatters immeasurable hundreds of thousands of rays from the soles of his feet;
all the hells become cool, and those brought to the suffering of the Dharma experience happiness.
When the Dharma is proclaimed by the One Possessing the Ten Powers, the eye of gods and humans there becomes purified;
hundreds of thousands of immeasurable beings all become destined for the wisdom of a Buddha.
These many miracles of the Sugata could not easily be told even in ten million eons;
when the Guide enters the supreme city, the entire world rejoices at the Jina’s arrival.
These immeasurable qualities belong to the Sugata, the bull among men, who has reached the further shore of the supreme qualities;
he has reached the further shore of all distinguished qualities—bow your heads in homage to the Buddha, the field of merit.
Thus ends the tenth chapter of the *Śrīsamādhirāja*, titled "The Entry into the City."
(68) Chapter Eleven: The Retention of the Sūtra.
Then the Blessed One, entering the street where the residence of the youth Candraprabha was located, entered the residence of the youth Candraprabha.
Having entered, he sat down upon the very seat that had been prepared;
and the assembly of bodhisattvas and the assembly of monks sat down upon their respective seats.
Then, the youth Candraprabha [addressed] the Blessed One, the assembly of bodhisattvas, and the assembly of monks.

Having perceived that [the Blessed One] was seated, he himself satisfied and served the Blessed One with abundant, excellent food of a hundred flavors— consisting of solid foods, soft foods, foods to be licked, foods to be sucked, and foods to be drunk— and having understood that the Blessed One had finished eating and had withdrawn his washed hands, [he presented him] with a pair of divine garments worth nine hundred and ninety billion.
He covered the Blessed One [with robes] and gave three robes to each of those bodhisattvas and to each member of the community of monks.

Then the youth Candraprabha, having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder and placed his right knee upon the ground, bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One; then, extending his joined palms toward the Blessed One, he questioned the Blessed One with a song in verse:
How does the wise Bodhisattva, while practicing, always understand the intrinsic nature of phenomena?
How does the discerning one perform his activity? O Leader, tell us how he performs that activity.
And how, O Leader, does one become a rememberer of past births, and how is it that one is not reborn from a womb?
How may one’s retinue be indivisible, and how does one possess infinite eloquence here in this world?
You understand the conduct of all sentient beings; your knowledge operates regarding all phenomena. Unconquered, supreme among bipeds, I ask you a question: please explain it to me.
You know that the intrinsic nature of phenomena is non-existence, yet you utter speech that is inexpressible;
just as all jackals are overcome by a lion, so too are the followers of other sects here surpassed by the Buddha.
You understand the conduct of all sentient beings; your wisdom follows after all phenomena.
Possessing unimpeded knowledge and a perfectly pure sphere of activity, O Lord of Dharma, grant me a prophecy.
You know the past as well as the future, and that which exists here in the present; your knowledge of the three times proceeds without attachment. Therefore, I ask the Lion of the Śākyas here.

O King of Dharma, you know the true nature of the Victors who are joined with the three times; you are a self-arisen one skilled in the intrinsic nature of phenomena. Therefore, I ask here of you, an ocean of wisdom.
Since there is no dharma whatsoever in which you have stumbled, your mind is entirely free from defilement.
Having abandoned the knots and the delusions that cause barrenness, O Lord of Men, teach me the conduct of awakening.
Reveal to me the characteristics of those dharmas which have been realized by the Victorious One;
having understood those characteristics of the dharmas, I shall practice the conduct of awakening according to those very characteristics.
How do those who practice the infinite and diverse conduct of sentient beings transcend that very conduct?
Teach me yourself the entry into such conduct; having heard it, may I understand the conduct of sentient beings.
The characteristic of the intrinsic nature of phenomena is devoid of characteristics, empty of intrinsic nature, and naturally secluded.
How do bodhisattvas perceive this directly? Explain to me the guidance of the Buddhas.
Having reached the perfection in all phenomena here, and having trained in all the words of instruction,
you who are free from doubt and the cutter of the longing for doubt— reveal to me the enlightenment of a Buddha.
Then the Blessed One, knowing with his own mind the reflection in the mind of the youth Candraprabha,
addressed the youth Candraprabha: "Young man, a bodhisattva mahāsattva endowed with a single quality attains these virtues."
And he swiftly awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
By what single dharma, young man, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva here understand the intrinsic nature of all phenomena as it truly is?
And how, young man, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva know the intrinsic nature of all phenomena?

In this regard, young man, a bodhisattva mahāsattva understands all phenomena to be nameless and devoid of names; they are devoid of sound, devoid of the path of speech, devoid of syllables, devoid of arising, and devoid of cessation. They are characterized by the absence of causes, characterized by the absence of conditions, characterized by maturation, characterized by the absence of a basis, and characterized by solitude. They possess a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of being without characteristics.
He understands all phenomena as they truly are: as devoid of signs, inconceivable, beyond thought, and beyond the reach of the mind.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses: There is but one teaching regarding phenomena: all phenomena are without characteristics.
It was taught by the one of excellent wisdom who understands things as they truly are.
The bodhisattva who understands this teaching of the Dharma in such a way experiences no obstruction while proclaiming ten million sūtras.
For the Leader, being empowered, understands the limit of reality;
he understands that limit, yet herein nothing at all has been spoken.
With one [knowledge] he knows all; with one [vision] he sees all.
No matter how much he speaks, no weariness arises within him.
Thus his mind is thoroughly concentrated: all phenomena are nameless;
trained in the designation of names, he speaks words that are true.
Whatever sound one hears, one knows its prior limit;
having known the prior limit of the sound, one is not carried away by that sound.
Just as the prior limit of an echo, such is the characteristic of phenomena;
one who understands phenomena in this way is not reborn in wombs.
One understands the non-arising of all phenomena as their non-origination;
understanding this teaching on arising, one shall always be a rememberer of past births.
When one becomes a rememberer of past lives, then one practices the proper conduct;
for one who is devoted to such conduct, the retinue is not divided.
When a bodhisattva understands all phenomena to be thus empty,
there is nothing whatsoever unknown to him; this is the limit where nothing exists.
For within the limit of nothingness, something has been conceptualized by the foolish,
because of which they wander again and again through tens of millions of eons.
If they were to know the eons as the Leader knows them,
no suffering would arise for them, nor would they go to an evil destiny.
Thus all ordinary beings, not understanding this principle,
reject such teachings wherein suffering is brought to cessation.
The non-apprehension of all phenomena gives rise to the notion of "phenomena";
understand that such a kind of notion is nothing but a notion itself.
Discernment and perception—this is what is conceptualized by the foolish;
regarding these conceptually constructed phenomena, the wise are not deluded.
This is the domain of the wise; it is not the sphere of activity for the foolish.
It is the range of the sons of the Buddha: empty phenomena, free from turbidity.
This is the stage of the bodhisattvas, this is the conduct of the sons of the Buddha; it is the ornament of the Buddha-qualities, the peaceful emptiness that has been taught.
And when the latent predispositions of the bodhisattvas have been abandoned,
they are not led astray by forms, for they are established in the lineage of the Buddhas.
All phenomena are without location; no location for them exists.
For one who understands location in this way, awakening is not difficult to attain.
Having cultivated generosity, ethical discipline, learning, and patience with virtuous friends,
and understanding this practice, that person quickly awakens to enlightenment.
Gods, nāgas, gandharvas, yakṣas, asuras, and mahoragas always honor him;
all kings, garuḍas, kinnaras, and night-stalkers likewise pay him worship.
Tens of millions of Buddhas, providing their empowerment even for many tens of millions of eons, proclaim his fame;
as he reveals the Dharma, its excellence is such that its limit cannot be exhausted.
The bodhisattva who understands emptiness accomplishes the welfare of many millions of living beings;
he teaches the Dharma through various discourses, and having heard it, they conceive love and reverence for him.
And vast knowledge arises within them by which they behold the Jinas, the supreme among men;
they behold the beautiful array of the field, and those Lords of the World teach the Dharma.
Know all phenomena to be like an illusion, empty by nature like the sky;
knowing their nature to be just such, one who practices in this way does not cling anywhere.
Moving through the world while practicing the supreme conduct of awakening, he accomplishes his purpose with unattached wisdom;
having perceived all phenomena through wisdom, he sends forth emanations to other realms.
Having performed the work of a Buddha, those emanations return to their original nature just like the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
And those persons who are established in the thought of awakening (bodhicitta) obtain their goal according to their intention.
He is always grateful to the Buddhas who applies himself to the stability of the lineage of the Buddhas;
with a radiant physical form, thirty-two marks appear upon his body.
One practicing this supreme samādhi will obtain many other infinite benefits:
one becomes always possessed of great strength and unshakable; even kings cannot withstand one's splendor.
He becomes gracious, a great physician, exalted by merit, splendor, and glory;
even the gods cannot withstand the brilliance of that wise one who courses in the Buddha-dharmas. (SRS 11.42)
He who is firmly established in the thought of awakening (bodhicitta) is always a friend to all living beings;
for him there is never any darkness, as he illuminates the awakening of the Buddhas.
Free from the path of speech and words, inexpressible like space, such is the nature of phenomena;
knowing this supreme state, his eloquence likewise becomes inexhaustible.
Speaking hundreds of thousands of sūtras, he understands their subtle, prior limit;
the wise one is always possessed of unimpeded speech, knowing the extremely subtle intrinsic nature of phenomena.

They are always skilled in hundreds of methods, proficient in various sounds and etymologies, and certain regarding the differentiation of karma and its fruit; such are their distinguished and superior qualities.
The wise and high-minded son of the One Possessing Ten Powers wears complete attire;
his mindfulness is always pure as he knows the extremely subtle nature of phenomena.
He never hears unpleasant sounds; he always hears sublime and agreeable sounds.
His speech is forever pleasing, as he understands the extremely subtle nature of phenomena.
He becomes possessed of mindfulness, intelligence, comprehension, and wisdom; likewise, his mind is untroubled and serene.
Knowing the extremely subtle nature of phenomena, he speaks many hundreds of thousands of sūtras.

Skilled in the distinctions of syllables and words, he understands many various languages; he becomes proficient in both the meaning and the phrasing, knowing these qualities as the very nature of phenomena.
Among gods, humans, nāgas, and rākṣasas, asuras, mahoragas, and kinnaras,
he is always dear and pleasing, knowing the extremely subtle intrinsic nature of phenomena.
The hosts of bhūtas, piśācas, and rākṣasas, as well as those flesh-eaters who are most exceedingly cruel—
none of them ever cause him fear, for he knows the extremely subtle intrinsic nature of phenomena.
Having heard the vast discourse of the wise, a great thrill of horripilation arises within them;
they then generate vast love for the Buddha, and an inconceivable benefit accrues to them in abundance.
The power of their merit cannot be told, even by speaking for many thousands of eons,
by those who uphold this immeasurable, infinite, and unfathomable treasury of Dharma of the Sugatas.
Those Victors of the past have all been honored by them, as well as the immeasurable Buddhas yet to come;
and those Buddhas who currently abide in the ten directions [have been honored] by maintaining this supreme, peaceful samādhi.
Suppose some person here, desiring merit, were to attend upon the compassionate Ones of Ten Powers for immeasurable and infinite millions of eons, and were to generate toward them immeasurable love.

Suppose there were a second person desiring merit who, during this final age, should uphold even a single verse from this method of the ultimate truth; the former's merit would not equal even a fraction of that person's merit. (SRS 11.57)
This is the supreme and distinguished worship of the Buddha when the final, terrible age has arrived:
by hearing and retaining even a single four-line verse, one thereby worships all the Buddhas.
The greatest gain has always been well-obtained by them; they have always most excellently enjoyed the alms of the kingdom.
They are the supreme eldest sons of the One Possessing the Ten Powers; for a long time, they have honored many Victors.
I too was seen here on Gṛdhrakūṭa, and thus I was prophesied by you for the wisdom of a Buddha;
furthermore, Maitreya, I was tested so that I might receive another prophecy at that time.
Furthermore, Amitāyus, there the Buddha speaks of many benefits for them:
that all these have entered Sukhāvatī, and having gone to Abhirati, they shall see the Buddha Akṣobhya.
For immeasurable hundreds of thousands of eons, there is never any fear of falling into the lower realms;
for one who practices this excellent conduct of awakening, they indeed experience constant mental well-being.
For one who trains in accordance with my practice, these distinguished and such-like supreme benefits have been proclaimed; they shall uphold this sūtra in the final age.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter of the Śrī-Samādhirāja, titled "The Chapter on Upholding the Sūtra."
Chapter Twelve: Training in Concentration.
In this regard, young man, that bodhisattva mahāsattva who thoroughly understands the intrinsic nature of all phenomena,

For him, there are these very qualities and benefits: he speaks of the true praise of the virtues of the Tathāgatas, and he does not misrepresent the Tathāgatas with what is false or unreal. Why is that?
He understands, as it truly is, that very nature of phenomena by which the Tathāgata is manifested;
he understands the infinite qualities of a Buddha.
For what reason?
Because, young man, the qualities of a Buddha are infinite, inconceivable, and beyond thought; therefore, it is impossible to conceive of them or to measure them.
For what reason?
Because, young man, the mind is without intrinsic nature, formless, and invisible.
Thus, young man, whatever is the intrinsic nature of the mind, that is the intrinsic nature of the qualities of a Buddha.
Whatever is the intrinsic nature of the qualities of a Buddha, that is the intrinsic nature of the Tathāgatas;
that is the intrinsic nature of all phenomena.
Young man, the bodhisattva mahāsattva who understands this teaching on the intrinsic nature of all qualities as it truly is—
Young man, this bodhisattva mahāsattva is said to be one whose mind is deeply resolved,
skilled in renunciation,
and who understands, as it truly is, the renunciation of the triple world.
He sees things as they truly are, speaks without falsehood, and does not speak otherwise than he intends;
he acts exactly as he speaks,
is unattached to the triple world, and has transcended the triple world.
He has completely transcended the realm of desire, the realm of form, the formless realm, the realm of afflictions, the realm of names, and the realm of sounds.
He is skilled in the methods of syllables and phrases;
his knowledge is fully cultivated through syllables.
He is skilled in the ineffable Dharma;
he knows syllables;
he is proficient in syllables.
He is skilled in the knowledge of the distinctions between syllables and words;
he is skilled in the knowledge of the extensive expansion of the distinctions between syllables and words;
he is skilled in the distinctions between the words of all phenomena.
He is skilled in the detailed analysis of the distinctions between the words of all dharmas;
he is skilled in the knowledge that establishes all dharmas;
he is endowed with a resolute intellect, and he is unsurpassed by any of the Māras, the Evil Ones, or the deities belonging to the host of Māra.

Furthermore, while this Dharma discourse was being spoken, ninety-eight million beings among the host of gods and humans who had performed prior preparations attained the dhāraṇī called "The Hundred Thousand Million Revolutions," as well as the patient acceptance of unobstructed insight into the Dharma.

And all of them were prophesied by the Blessed One that, after forty-eight hundred thousand incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), they shall fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
All of them, having different names but identical lifespans, shall fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment in various Buddha-fields.
Regarding this, it is said:
The wise Bodhisattva who attains supreme and excellent enlightenment is skilled in both the meaning and the Dharma, and he practices within the very nature of phenomena.
He speaks words that are not false regarding the specific qualities of the Buddhas;
for that hero, free from doubt, knows that Dharma of the Jinas.
He understands all phenomena as having a single meaning and as emptiness;
they have no diverse meanings, for he is trained in that single meaning.
The wise one knows them to be without conceptualization, without discursive thought, and without apprehension;
his perception of "perishing" or "imperishable" is abandoned entirely without remainder. (SRS 12.4)
For he does not see the Ten-Powered Ones by way of form, those lions among men who possess the Dharma-body;
nor does he see them by their marks, for all his inversions have been abandoned.
These phenomena are inconceivable, free from thought, and by nature quiescent;
one who understands them thus beholds the Buddhas, the supreme among bipeds.
Just as one has understood the notion of a self, so too has the intellect been directed toward all things;
all phenomena are of that same nature—pure and like the sky.
For once he has known the departure from all phenomena within his mind,
no aspiration for liberation within the triple world arises in him.
He becomes one who sees things as they truly are, whose speech is not false, and who speaks without deviation;
and every word of his issues forth through the power of the Victors.
Having transcended the realm of desire, the realm of afflictions, and the realms of form and formlessness,
he whose mind is unattached to phenomena wanders joyfully for the benefit of the world.
Having transcended the stage of names, sound is by its very nature accumulative;
even if one speaks for as long as it takes, no basis for it is found.
The activity of perception does not exist; the perversion of views has been entirely exhausted.
Your intellect is perfectly certain, and your wisdom is as steadfast as space.
Even if there were tens of millions of billions of monasteries for the purpose of distracting the mind,
one overcomes all Māras and does not fall under their power.
May they all abandon the net of Māra— being pure in conduct, free from affliction,
devoted to the bliss of meditative concentration, and realizing that the world is empty.
The worlds are said to be the aggregates, and he understands them to be empty;
all phenomena are without arising or cessation, comparable to space.
He does not abandon himself nor the training heard from the One of Ten Powers;
having reached the perfection of ethical conduct, he is reborn wherever he makes his vow.
They travel through the Buddha-fields and behold millions of billions of Buddhas;
yet they do not long for heaven, nor are they liberated by mere aspiration.
Practicing the Dharma, he does not let his vigor falter for even a single moment;
and he is praised by the Buddhas throughout the worlds of the ten directions. (SRS 12.18)
Therefore, O youth, having heard these teachings within this samādhi,
abandon the gain of fame and proclaim the Dharma to the great multitude.
Whoever desires to become a self-arisen Buddha, endowed with great qualities—
having trained here, that skillful one becomes a Buddha who possesses the ten powers.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter of the *Śrīsamādhirāja*, titled "Instruction on the Samādhi."
(Vaidya 79) Chapter 13: The Exposition of Samādhi.
Thereupon, the Blessed One addressed the youth Candraprabha once again: "Therefore, then..."
Young man, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who desires to fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment must be skilled in the exposition of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
In this regard, young man, what is the exposition of meditative concentration?
It is the suchness of all phenomena, their equality, and their non-inequality.
Non-conceptualization, non-discrimination; non-formation, non-arousal;
non-arising, non-ceasing.
The complete cutting off of conceptualization, discursive thought, and mental construction;
the state of the mind having no objective support; and non-attention.
The complete cutting off of designations; the complete cutting off of discursive thought and conceptualization;
the complete cutting off of attachment, aversion, and delusion.
It is the mental attention that is neither finite nor infinite;
it is the total cessation of mental attention;
it is the knowledge of the intrinsic nature of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases.
It is the locus for the practice of mindfulness, intelligence, comprehension, modesty, fortitude, conduct, and proper behavior;
it is the ground of freedom from strife and the ground of peace.
The complete cutting off of all conceptual proliferation;
the training of all bodhisattvas;
the sphere of activity of all tathāgatas.
The complete perfection of all qualities—
this, young man, is called the exposition of samādhi.
Established in this exposition of samādhi, a bodhisattva mahāsattva remains never separated from samādhi.
He possesses an undeluded mind,
is endowed with great compassion, and works for the benefit of immeasurable sentient beings.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
"The stage of samādhi is level, peaceful, subtle, and very difficult to see;
because it is the complete eradication of all perceptions, it is called 'samādhi'."
Neither conceptualizing nor discursive, ungraspable and non-demonstrable,
the non-apprehension of the mind is therefore called "samādhi."
When one is concentrated, one does not conceive of any phenomena;
this non-conception, as it truly is, is designated by the term "samādhi."
In phenomena there is not even a particle of dust, nor is any dust found;
because phenomena are non-apprehendable, it is therefore called "samādhi."
The non-apprehension of the mind is indeed called conceptual construction;
know that those phenomena which are free from conceptual construction are this samādhi.
For the object indicated by a word is itself without substantial reality;
the word is like an echo, just as the sky is like space.
For these phenomena are not established; no stability is found in them.
Non-stability is not to be found by way of intrinsic nature even under the designation "stability."
"It passes away" means that no such going exists;
thus, the concentration is proclaimed by the term "non-going."
"To be 'unconcentrated' is called a conceit; to be 'concentrated' is a second conceit.
Those who move about without conceiving [of such states] proceed toward awakening; without conceiving, they touch supreme awakening. (SRS 13.9)
This level of peace is both even and uneven; it has the signs of calm abiding and insight.
Having cultivated this peaceful awakening of the Buddha, one is here engaged in the cultivation of meditative concentration.
Furthermore, this entry into the course of meaning cannot be accomplished by means of syllables;
having abandoned all sounds of speech and vocal expression, one becomes composed, yet there is no conceit in him.
And whichever bodhisattva here, being disciplined, should abide in this samādhi exactly as it has been taught—
if there were a conflagration at the end of an eon in this field, the fire would not burn him even if he were in the midst of the highest mountain.
Just as the sky has never before been burned, even when scorched for many hundreds of eons,
so too one who understands that all phenomena are equal to space is never burned, even in the midst of fire.
Furthermore, if one makes a vow while remaining in meditative concentration within a blazing buddha-field:
"May this fire be extinguished without remainder, and may the earth not suffer destruction," then there shall be no alteration of that [vow].
His power of supernatural transformation becomes infinite; he travels through the path of the sky without obstruction.
A bodhisattva experiences these qualities by remaining established in the samādhi as it has been taught.
One is neither born nor does one pass away, for there is neither birth nor death for one who possesses this understanding; for such a person, this samādhi is not difficult to attain.
Neither passing away nor birth has been taught by the Lord of the World;
having understood the Lord of the World in this way, you should therefore know this samādhi.
Unstained by the world, he does not cling to worldly dharmas;
being unattached, he travels to the Buddha-fields with his body.
He constantly beholds the perfectly awakened ones, the leaders of the world, within the fields;
and there, in those buddha-fields, he hears the Dharma being proclaimed.

He never possesses ignorance, yet he speaks of the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu); knowing the course of all things, he is ever established in the Dharma, for he is composed of the realm of phenomena.
Even as he speaks for tens of millions of eons, his eloquence does not diminish;
