the wise one manifests many other bodhisattvas.
The emanations of the bodhisattvas go from field to field,
seated cross-legged upon thousand-petaled lotuses.
They proclaim the awakening of the Buddhas, beautified by the dhāraṇīs and sūtras,
as well as other millions of sūtras, while cultivating peaceful samādhi.
They establish many inconceivable beings on the path of non-retrogression;
their eloquence never fails as they proclaim the enlightenment of the Buddhas.
Indeed, they go to the gabled pavilions adorned with various jewels,
and they scatter fragrant flowers over the Guide.
And they sprinkle fragrant powders upon the Guide;
all of them perform extensive worship for the sake of awakening.
These qualities of the Bodhisattvas, the protectors, are immeasurable;
when they become free from defilements, then they attain supernatural power.
Free from the arising of afflictions, limpid, pure, and luminous, unconditioned and immovable— such are the spheres of activity of the bodhisattvas.
They are tranquil and thoroughly calmed, free from defilements and without blemish;
they are beyond conceptual proliferation, devoid of proliferation, having transcended all proliferation.
The non-functioning of syllables is the characteristic of all phenomena;
because it is difficult to be discerned by means of sound, it is therefore called "samādhi."
Inexhaustible, tranquil, effortless, and invisible,
it is the range of all Buddhas, the unstained limit of reality.
This training is that which all Buddhas have relied upon: the intrinsic nature of all phenomena.
Having trained in this, the Perfectly Awakened Ones have reached the perfection of all virtues.
Neither this shore nor the further shore, nor the prior limit, have been conceptualized;
therefore, all those perfectly awakened ones have reached the perfection of all virtues.
Having known, by their very nature, that phenomena have neither future nor destination—
being free from conceptual proliferation and effortless— you have reached the perfection therein.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter of the *Śrīsamādhirāja*, titled "The Exposition of Samādhi."
(Vaidya 83) Chapter 14: The Manifestation of a Smile.
Then, the youth Candraprabha rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, and [placed his right knee] on the ground.
Placing his knees upon the ground and bowing with palms joined toward the Blessed One, he addressed the Blessed One as follows:

"It is marvelous, Blessed One, how well-spoken is this teaching by the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, concerning the equality of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena and the instruction on the meditative absorptions that constitute the training for all bodhisattvas."
Just as it is, Blessed One, having trained in this for a long time, I have attained realization in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
It occurs to me, Blessed One; it occurs to me, Sugata.
The Blessed One said, "May it be inspired in you, O youth, as you deem it now the right time.
Then, having been granted leave by the Blessed One, the youth Candraprabha praised the Blessed One to his face with these appropriate verses:
"Having seen beings afflicted and oppressed, always overcome by passion and hatred..."
You have generated the mind for the sake of awakening with the thought, "May I become a Buddha, a liberator of beings."
For many millions of eons you have practiced with vigor; you were constantly trained in generosity, self-restraint, and self-control.
You were untiring in ethical discipline, patience, and likewise vigor, and you gave vast and infinite gifts.
Yet your mind was never once weary, even as you gave up your hands, feet, and life;
having become free from attachment, you renounced gold and silver, as well as children, wife, and the kingdom.
Your morality is clear, stainless, and pure; you have renounced yourself, yet your morality has not been impaired.
Well-restrained in body, speech, and mind, with a perfectly tamed heart—O Sugata, homage be to you!
Delighting in patience, established on the path of forbearance, you do not become angry even when your body is cut to pieces;
from that, the milk of the cultivation of loving-kindness flows forth—O Sugata, you who are truly marvelous, homage be to you!
Endowed with the ten powers, you abide in unimpeded knowledge and have realized all phenomena.
O Compassionate Lord of Dharma who brings benefit to the world, you take pity upon these beings, desiring their welfare. (SRS 14.6)

Knowledge is empty, and yet there is no sentient being here; having seen the world thus as one whose path is lost, they were awakened to the phenomena that are by nature selfless. They became born into liberation, yet that liberation is nowhere to be found.
Always abandon heedlessness, and having conquered Māra along with his power and infinite army,
having awakened to vast enlightenment and infinite wisdom, teach the Dharma that is supremely pure and peaceful.
The sky might fall along with the moon and stars; the earth, together with its cities and mountain ranges, might perish;
and even the realm of space might undergo change—but your words would never be otherwise than true.
Having seen sentient beings who are suffering— creatures who delight in apprehension—
you taught the non-apprehension of the profound, peaceful emptiness.
O Great Hero, you have been trained for inconceivable tens of millions of eons;
in the training of non-apprehension, no lapse is found in you.
In whatever Dharma you have been trained, such is the Dharma you proclaim;
this is not the domain of fools or of any of the other non-Buddhist teachers.
Those who abide in the notion of a self stumble because they lack wisdom;
having realized the selflessness of all phenomena, no stumbling occurs for them.
O Great Hero, speaker of reality, established in the true nature of phenomena; O Protector, abiding in reality and truth, you utter words that are real.
Your conduct has become exactly as your vow was made;
as the natural outflow of that reality, you speak words that are true.
Perfected in true conduct, well-trained in the limit of reality,
possessing a true intention, true practice, and true wisdom— homage be to you!
O Proclaimer of Knowledge, Radiant One, there is nothing that is not encompassed by your wisdom;
having attained excellence in knowledge, homage be to you, O Proclaimer of Knowledge! (SRS 14.17)
You are a friend to all sentient beings; your loving-kindness is well-cultivated.
You are unshakable like Mount Meru, immovable and firmly established.
Within the vast assembly, you draw the followers of the Teacher toward you;
O Sugata of profound wisdom, you roar as you enter the gathering.
The Buddha, whose stride has the prowess of a lion, roars the lion’s roar;
all those heretics have been conquered by him, just as jackals are by a lion.
O Hero, tamer of the untamed, the untamed have been tamed by you;
they become steadfast friends, indestructible and well-established.
Having seen sentient beings who are suffering and rely upon the view of a self,
I teach the Dharma of selflessness, wherein there is neither the pleasant nor the unpleasant.
To the untrained, the foolish, who wander upon the paths of evil ways,
you clearly reveal the path by which the Leaders go.
Those who abide in the notion of a self are well-established in suffering;
they do not know selflessness, wherein suffering does not exist.
You are the teacher of the dharma of all words without exception; O Lord of the World, no stumbling is found in you.
You speak with speech that is never false; homage to you, O Protector who brings liberation from suffering!
Many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of vast numbers of gods, nāgas, and yakṣas, stationed in the sky,
all conceived a longing for the Leader upon hearing the meaningful words of the Blessed One.
His speech is smooth, gentle, pleasing, and timely; it is exceedingly sweet, sublime, and affectionate.
Endowed with immeasurable qualities of sound, it brings benefit and liberation to many people.
Immeasurable hundreds of thousands of lutes, perfectly sweet and played simultaneously,
with divine sounds, distinguished and lovely, are all surpassed by a single word of the Sugata.
The sweet warbling of flocks of birds and kalaviṅkas, the most beautiful and lovely sounds of well-sung songs,
and the sounds of conchs, kettledrums, drums, and lutes do not attain even a fraction of the splendor of the sound of the Buddha.
The sounds of cuckoos, parrots, and mynas, as well as those of cranes, peacocks, and kinnaras—
whatever lovely cries there may be, they do not equal even a fraction of the Buddha’s voice.

All these words—lovely, sweet, charming, and endearing; uttered with most sweet and peaceful voices, and worthy of praise—are applied at one and the same time as the most excellent speech that gladdens the Tathāgata.
Whatever beings there are among the gods, humans, kings, and dānavas throughout all existence in the three worlds,
the single ray of the Sugata surpasses the radiance of all those who produce light.
The body of the Sugata is blossomed and adorned with all the various marks;
produced from a hundred merits, clear and pure, the body of the Jina shines forth throughout the entire world.
The sound of conchs, paṇavas, and sughoṣakas, the sound of kettledrums as well as that of kimpalas—
all these sounds, though sweet and lovely, do not equal even a hundredth part of the Buddha’s voice.
The sounds of hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of musical instruments— delicious, very sweet, and like those of the gods,
bringing great joy to the hosts of Maruts and Apsarases— are not worth even a hundredth part of the sound of the Buddha.

The cranes, peacocks, cuckoos, ruddy geese, swans, and kunālas— the various flocks of birds that utter their sounds so sweetly at once— do not equal even a hundredth part of the Buddha’s voice. (SRS 14.36)
The sounds of the nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, mahoragas, and the lords of the gods, Brahmās, and the rulers of the maruts—
all the charming and lovely sounds that exist within the three worlds— do not equal even a fraction of the Buddha’s voice.
Whatever light belongs to Brahmā or the Lord of Maruts, whatever is the light of the luminous jewel-gems—
all those lights of various and manifold forms— the single ray of the Buddha outshines them all.
Pure in body, speech, and mind, pure in wisdom, he is unstained by the three realms of existence;
a mass of the essence of virtues, a jewel of qualities, a lord of men, the self-arisen one who is unequaled in all virtues.
Having thus praised the Ten-Powered One who speaks the truth, the prince, with a joyful mind, uttered these words:
"Having honored the Buddha, who is incomparable and immeasurable, may I become a Buddha just like the Lion of the Śākyas."
Having understood his distinguished conduct, the Sugata, the Lord of Men, who possesses unimpeded knowledge, manifested a smile.
Maitreya questioned the eldest son of the One Possessing the Ten Powers: "For whose sake has this smile been made by the Leader?"

The earth shook in six ways, and the gods and nāgas dwelling in the sky were uplifted; with joyful and thrilled hearts, they gazed upon the Buddha. "O Sugata, unconquered one, please grant him a prophecy! SRS_14.42.
“I am not the ground for the disciples of the Blessed One, wherein the wisdom of the Best of Men has proceeded.
O Jina, possessor of perfectly pure wisdom and incomparable insight, you have displayed a smile; for what purpose was it done? (SRS 14.43)

I ask the One of Ten Powers, the Guide, the Lion of the Śākyas, the supreme among bipeds; the light-maker who has reached the perfection of wisdom, the one who brings an end to passion, hatred, stubbornness, and delusion. (SRS 14.44)

O Leader, for more than as many tens of millions of eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, you have practiced while seeking supreme, excellent enlightenment; for what purpose has this smile been displayed?
Having had his hands and feet cut off by the Teacher, along with his sons, wife, dear kinsmen, and relatives,
while seeking supreme and noble knowledge— what indeed, O Sage, is the cause for this display of a smile?
Horses, elephants, chariots, and infantry; male and female slaves, jewels, gems, and silver—there is no material wealth that could not be relinquished by you while practicing your course.
Your supreme knowledge transcends the three worlds; you thoroughly understand the conduct of all sentient beings.
You are skilled in knowing the elements, the mind, and the inclinations—on whose account has this smile been shown?
By whom have these supreme among men been honored? Whose vast purpose will be fulfilled?
Who is the one who will grasp this conduct? For whose sake, O Sage, was this smile displayed?
The earth shook in six ways, and ten million lotuses rose from the ground—
possessing millions of petals, radiant, golden-hued, beautiful, and delightful.
Where these heart-sons of the Jina, supreme Bodhisattvas of great supernatural power,
and many Dharma-preachers have assembled— to them, O Compassionate One, you questioned the Leader.
Drums, conchs, flutes, and *sughoṣaka* lutes— millions of billions of musical instruments were played;
yet their sound was heard in the sky only as the inconceivable voice of the Sugata.
Swans, cranes, sparrows, cuckoos, and many other flocks of birds have gathered together;
though they let out a most brilliant sound, it does not equal even a fraction of the Buddha’s voice.
By whom were giving, self-control, and restraint practiced for many millions of eons in the past?
By whom were the supreme among men worshipped? For whose sake has this smile been displayed? (SRS 14.54)
Who was it that formerly questioned the Lord of Bipeds, having generated supreme reverence? How is this awakening of a Buddha attained? For what purpose has this smile been displayed?

As many as are the Possessors of the Ten Powers who have passed away, the Sugatas of the present, and those yet to come—you know them all, O Supreme among Men; therefore I ask you for the sake of all living beings.
They know the mental continuums of all living beings, whose range is infinite;
according to whatever disposition each person possesses, I ask this of the Supreme among Men.
Those who practice the unsurpassed conduct and are skilled in causes, reasoning, and discipline—O Lord of Men, I ask this for the sake of those who desire: how is the wisdom of a Buddha obtained?
For those dharmas which are subtle, extremely difficult to see, empty, peaceful, incomparable, and inconceivable—
the domain of those who possess the ten powers— I ask the Guide for their meaning.

Those who have cultivated inconceivable loving-kindness and compassion toward all living beings in the world, and in whom no notion of a "sentient being" occurs— to them, the Lord of Bipeds, I address my inquiry. (SRS 14.60)
For those whose wisdom is incomparable and inconceivable, nothing whatsoever exists that can be grasped;
having reached the perfection of the sphere of the mind, O Protector, it is for their sake that I ask you this.
Having reached the perfection of the qualities of morality and knowledge, you turn toward incomparable wisdom regarding the three times;
not even a single lapse is found in you— for whose sake has this smile been displayed?
Śāriputra, Aniruddha, Kolita, and whatever other disciples of the Sugata there may be—their knowledge does not even function here; this domain of the Buddha is unsurpassed.
Having reached the perfection of mastery over all phenomena and having risen above all training and conduct, O Leaders,
skilled in the ultimate truth, arouse compassion and let forth your voice!

Those who for many millions of eons in the past have thus reflected and questioned the Lord of Bipeds— O Leader, tell us today the fruit of that supreme refuge and ultimate resort which they proclaimed.
Yakṣas, rākṣasas, kumbhāṇḍas, and guhyakas gazed upon the Supreme among Men;
all stood with palms joined in reverence, desiring to hear the prophecy concerning the Foremost of Beings.
Many Bodhisattvas endowed with supernatural powers have arrived today from many millions of fields;
they are the eldest sons of the Sugata, born from his heart, all standing with palms joined in reverence.
The Gandhahastin, who has gone to the eastern direction, is world-renowned in the realm of Akṣobhya;
surrounded by millions of bodhisattvas, he comes to inquire after the Lion of the Śākyas, the Lord of Men.
From the excellent world-system of Sukhāvatī, Avalokiteśvara, who has attained great power,
accompanied by millions of bodhisattvas, came to inquire after Śākyasiṃha, the lord of bipeds.
By whom, in former times, for many millions of incalculable eons, Sugatas as numerous as all the grains of sand in the oceans were served, while seeking the supreme, most excellent wisdom.
Praised and extolled by all the Buddhas, having reached the perfection of the qualities of all dharmas,
Mañjughoṣa, renowned throughout all the directions of the world, stood with palms joined in reverence.
Having traveled through millions of Buddha-fields, they have rarely seen such as these;
all the sons of the Buddha, virtuous and well-trained, stand with palms joined in reverence.
There is no one else here in this world who is such a worthy vessel as these gentle ones;
O Leaders, you who hold the Dharma-treasury of all the Teachers, release your words of affectionate intent.

For the Jinas, the Leaders, the supreme persons, do not display a smile without a cause. O you with the excellent voice like the sound of a drum, for what purpose has this smile been shown? SRS_14.74.
The cries of swans, cuckoos, peacocks, and cranes, and the thundering roars of bulls;
the sweet sounds of celestial instruments being played—proclaim your voice that liberates all beings! (SRS 14.75)
It generates loving-kindness, increases affection, reveals knowledge and vision, and casts out ignorance;
it discerns the true meaning, increases wisdom, and purifies [the mind] for hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons.
It demonstrates the meaning of the cessation of suffering as clearly realized through the certainty of its nature;
it destroys the doctrines of all false teachers and reveals that things are empty, devoid of a person, and devoid of a life-principle.
Adorned with hundreds of thousands of merits, having practiced here under hundreds of thousands of Buddhas,
he is well-praised by hundreds of thousands of gods and saluted by hundreds of thousands of Brahmās.
Bringer of grace to rākṣasas, yakṣas, and kumbhāṇḍas; liberator of nāgas, suparṇas, and mahoragas;
you who always utter [the Dharma] with unimpeded application, arisen through auspicious fruits of karma.
Whosoever are the Jinas who have attained final nirvāṇa, those yet to come, and those currently abiding—all these you know; you have no attachment, O Leader, arisen through all virtuous qualities.
The entire earth, the sustainer of beings, including its oceans and mountains, shook in six ways;
hosts of gods scattered flowers from the sky, and a divine, delightful fragrance wafted forth.
Having destroyed the darkness of passion and hatred, with entirely pure conduct and a completely purified mind,
you who delight in tranquility, emptiness, and the signless— O compassionate one, roar the lion’s roar! SRS_14.82.

O Victors, possessed of eloquence, of most extensive fame, whose wisdom is perfectly complete and who possess knowledge of reality as it is—there is no one equal to you in the world, O Compassionate One; tell us for what purpose you display this smile.
The calls of the kalaviṅka, the cuckoo, and the peacock, as well as the delightful songs of the jīvaṃjīvaka and the jīvaka birds—
all such enchanting sounds on earth in a single moment become but a fraction of the Sugata’s voice.
Kettledrums, clay drums, and small drums, as well as conchs, flutes, and lutes—
even if thousands of musical instruments were to sound as one, they could not equal a fraction of the Sugata’s voice.
The sounds of thousands of excellent celestial instruments, the enchanting songs of the apsarases,
and the delightful music produced by beautiful singing— all these are not even a fraction of the sound of the Sugata’s voice.
Your voice for the benefit of the world is indeed of a single sound, yet it issues forth according to the diverse inclinations [of beings].
Each individual thinks, "The Jina is speaking to me. Tell us, for what reason has this smile been made?
The voices of the gods, the cries of the nagas, and even the sweet songs of the kinnaras—
these may at times pacify the afflictions, but the voice of the Buddha always dispels the afflictions.
It generates joy but not the delight of passion; it generates loving-kindness but not a mind of hatred;
it generates wisdom but not the delight of delusion—such is the voice of the Buddhas, which destroys all stains.
The sound of the Sage does not go outside the assembly, yet it cuts through the hundreds of doubts of all beings;
it is neither low nor high, for the voice of the Muni reveals equal happiness to all.
This earth with its mountains and forests might break apart, and the waters of the ocean might dry up;
the moon and the sun might even fall to the ground—but the Jina would never speak his word otherwise.
O Sugata, whose speech is pure in every limb and phrase, who possesses the voice of a lion and sweet, charming tones,
who has the voice of Brahmā and is compassionate— tell us for what purpose you display this smile.

You are skilled in knowing the mental conduct of all beings throughout this entire world—those of the past, those of the future, and those of the present. Tell us, for whose sake do you display this smile?
However many compassionate Victors there may be, they have all attained mastery and perfection in wisdom;
yet those Victors with faces like the stainless moon do not ever display a smile without a cause.

Even if one were to speak for ten million eons, as incomparable as the sands of the Ganges, it would still be impossible to fully proclaim the measure of your virtues; tell us, for whose sake do you show this smile?
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter of the *Śrīsamādhirāja*, titled "The Manifestation of the Smile."
Chapter 15: The Prediction through a Smile.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya with these appropriate verses:
This youth Candraprabha, having praised the Buddha with incomparable joy and having spoken the most excellent praise of the Buddhas,
shall always be worthy of commendation.
And even here in Rājagṛha, in the past, he beheld thousands of millions of Buddhas;
and in the presence of all those Victors, he inquired about this supreme, peaceful samādhi.
And everywhere he was my son, practicing this supreme conduct of awakening;
everywhere he possessed eloquence, and everywhere he was always a practitioner of celibacy.
In the future time, when it is most terrifying, you alone, O Ajitā, shall be my witness here;
for having always remained established in pure celibacy, you will cause this samādhi to be widely propagated.
May they seek this sublime samādhi; by means of this path, he shall attain awakening.
Upheld by many millions of Buddhas, he shall offer excellent worship to the Leaders.
Abiding in wisdom, I prophesy the distinguished conduct of Candraprabha:
in his future time, there shall be no obstacle to his holy life nor to his existence.
Just as one clearly perceives five myrobalan fruits in the palm of the hand, so too does one perceive thousands of millions of Buddhas;
and beyond that, as many as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, for whom this worship is performed in the future.
Eighty koṭis of gods, eighty koṭis of nāgas, and seventy thousand koṭis of yakṣas will feel a sense of longing in the future time, performing worship for the Supreme among Men.
Having performed worship for those supreme among bipeds, he practiced this unsurpassed knowledge;
in his final existence, he will become a Lord of the World, a Jina named Vimalaprabha.

Having heard this prophecy concerning himself, the youth Candraprabha was suffused with joy; rising seven palm trees' height into the air and remaining there, he uttered this inspired utterance: SRS_15.10: "Having heard this prophecy concerning himself, the youth Candraprabha was suffused with joy; rising seven palm trees' height into the air and remaining there, he uttered this inspired utterance."

Oh, Victors, teachers of the supreme Dharma, established in the power of the knowledge of liberation! You abide in well-ascertained, supreme wisdom; you are unsurpassed by any proponents of other doctrines.
Free from attachment, you have touched liberation; having contemplated the nature of things, you do not cling to existence.
All conceptual proliferations cease for you entirely, and your unattached gnosis prevails throughout the three realms of existence.
Unstained by all conceptual proliferations, all views have been completely abandoned;
the path is well-cultivated and free from any fixed abode, unconquered and unopposed by anyone.
You have no abode within the triple world; all floods and knots have been abandoned.
All bonds of the creeper of craving are severed; existence is relinquished, and the mass of becoming no longer exists.
You know the intrinsic nature of phenomena to be non-existence, yet you proclaim words that are ineffable;
like a lion who destroys the jackals of the heretics, you have vanquished those ignorant ones who abide in perversions.

Today I have obtained the most excellent treasure within me—the treasure of Dharma taught by the Sugata. All states of ruin and miserable rebirths have been abandoned; I have no further doubt that I shall become a Leader.
Having placed his hand— golden-colored, beautiful, and radiant—
upon my head, O Bull among Men, consecrate me for enlightenment, setting the world with its gods as witnesses.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter of the *Śrī-Samādhirāja*, titled "The Prediction Concerning the Smile."
Chapter 16: The Previous Life Story.
I remember that in the past, while practicing my conduct under the teaching of the Sugata Siṃhadhvaja, I was once a king.
There was a wise monk, a preacher of the Dharma, who was called by the name Brahmadatta.
At that time, I was the prince Matisāra, severely afflicted, gravely ill, and suffering;
and Brahmadatta, the preacher of the Dharma, was then my teacher.
No fewer than five hundred physicians, with diligent minds, treated my illness;
yet they were unable to cure my disease, and all my kinsmen became distressed.
Having heard that I was ill, that monk came into my presence to inquire after my health;
having conceived compassion for me, Brahmadatta then taught this supreme samādhi.
Having heard of this samādhi of mine, a noble, non-material joy arose within me; understanding the intrinsic nature of phenomena, I sighed deeply at that time, thinking, "The disease has been cured."
While Dīpaṃkara was practicing his conduct, he became a wise monk, a preacher of the Dharma;
and I was then the prince Matirāja, who was indeed liberated from illness through meditative concentration and wisdom.
Therefore, young men, remembering this decline over much of the past time, you should endure the ill-spoken words of fools; you should uphold and recite this samādhi.
In the future time, there will be many monks who are greedy, wicked, and unrestrained;
having evil desires and being deeply attached to their bowls and robes, they will reject this samādhi. (SRS 16.8)

Envious, arrogant, with unrestrained senses, and dwelling among families out of desire for gain; constantly relying on the praise of those engaged in worldly application—they will reject this samādhi.
With their hands and feet thus displayed, always engaged in laughter and dance,
embracing one another by the neck, they will wander through villages and on the paths of travel.
These are the characteristics of those engaged in improper yoga: they are constantly obsessed with the daughters of others;
attached to physical beauty and bound by it, they wander through villages, towns, and kingdoms.
They are always intent on food and drink, as well as on dancing, singing, and instrumental music;
they are constantly eager for buying and selling, and being addicted to drinking, they have lost all sense of shame.

Those who apply themselves improperly will grind away at their writing; having abandoned ethical discipline and the proper deportment, they break the boundaries of conduct and, being of corrupt behavior, are established in falsehood.
Those who always avoid the deeds practiced by the Buddhas, yet are constantly engaged in cheating with scales and measures—
having performed such defiled and evil actions, those of inferior conduct will go to the states of woe.
Having abandoned abundant wealth— jewels, gold, and conch shells— as well as their homes and kinsmen, they go forth into homelessness; yet,
having gone forth here in the teaching of the Buddha, they constantly commit evil deeds.
Regarding wealth and grain, they perceive them as essential; they prepare cows, cattle, and wagons.
For what purpose have these hairs been shorn by those who lack the practice of the training?
Having practiced the conduct in the past and performed what is extremely difficult for a thousand eons, I have sought this peaceful samādhi; when they hear of it, they will then fall into derision.
For a long time, those who speak falsehoods, who do not live the holy life, who are inclined toward the lower realms, and who are always greedy for sensual gains,
will take up the banner of those who practice the holy life and say, "This is not the Dharma," while being themselves of immoral conduct.
Seeking gain through improper means, they will stand in mutual opposition for the sake of division;
having spoken dispraise of one another, they will fall and go to the realms of misery.
Among hundreds of thousands, those in whom the power of patience will then exist are very difficult to find;
far more numerous are those who are eager for quarrels and, having abandoned patience, will engage in conceptual proliferation.
They will say with their voices, "We are bodhisattvas," yet even their sound will spread from place to place;
intoxicated by the pride of false speech, how can there be awakening for those whose ethical discipline has failed?
I have never heard of, nor have I ever seen, one whose resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*) is not pure;
and he who lacks patience regarding these teachings will attain awakening only after having rejected the Dharma.
Frightened and terrified, they abandon their homes; though they become even more firm in their resolve to go forth,
those who desire distinction meet with ruin by rejecting the vehicle of the Supreme Men.
Those of inferior wisdom, devoid of virtue, will always speak of faults in the supreme vehicle;
and they speak hundreds of faults even regarding that very refuge to which they have themselves gone for protection.
Those Ājīvikas who have gone forth in great numbers but lack the desire for the awakening of all the Buddhas—
those fools, remaining fixed in the view of a self, will become terrified upon hearing of emptiness.
Having built monasteries for one another, yet having generated malice, hatred, and stubbornness,
and having cast aspersions upon each other, they will find no joy, having committed evil.
He who shall be virtuous and endowed with qualities, dwelling always in loving-kindness and skilled in patience,
well-restrained, gentle, and amiable— he shall be held in contempt at that time.
Furthermore, whoever at that time shall be evil-minded, extremely cruel, fierce, and a performer of most base deeds—
one who practices unrighteousness and delights in quarreling— that person will be honored at that time.
I declare and I make known: if you, young man, have faith in me, then remembering this instruction of the Sugata, never place your trust in them.
They possess intense passion, as well as intense hatred; they possess intense delusion and are always intoxicated by pride.
With bodies unsubdued, speech unsubdued, and minds unsubdued, they are inclined toward the lower realms.
Even if I were to speak the praises of virtues, yet a monk should not practice those virtues;
enlightenment is not attained by mere sound alone—for those whose essence is practice, enlightenment is not difficult to find.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter of the *Śrīsamādhirāja*, titled "The Chapter on Previous Connections."
(Vaidya 103) Chapter 17: The Entrance to the Samādhi of the Manifestation of Many Buddhas.
Then the Blessed One, having instructed, inspired, gladdened, and incited that great assembly which was like the ocean with a discourse on the Dharma, rose from his seat and departed.
He approached the Vulture Peak, the king of mountains, and having arrived,
sat down upon the seat that had been prepared.

Surrounded by the community of monks and honored by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans, he taught the Dharma to the assembly, which was like the ocean.

Then, indeed, the youth Candraprabha, perceiving that the Blessed One had departed, took up flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, and ointments; accompanied by eight billion living beings— all of whom had become gods— and together with many millions of bodhisattva mahāsattvas who had come from other world-systems, he set out while hundreds of musical instruments were being played and as parasols, banners, bells, and flags were raised on high.
Taking with him a great array of garlands for the purpose of worshipping the Blessed One, he went toward Vulture Peak Mountain and approached the Blessed One.
Having arrived, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, circumambulated the Blessed One three times,
and performed a grand worship by offering those flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, and ointments, while musical instruments, cymbals, and drums were being played.
He sat down to one side with reverence and respect, desiring to inquire about the Dharma.
Then the youth Candraprabha said this to the Blessed One: "I would like to ask the Blessed One,
the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, about a certain point, if the Blessed One would grant me the opportunity to have my question answered."
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the youth Candraprabha: "Ask, O youth, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened one, whatever you desire.
For you, O youth, the Tathāgata has always granted the opportunity.
When this had been said, the youth Candraprabha spoke thus to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, endowed with how many qualities does a bodhisattva [attain] this *Sarvadharmasvabhāvasamatāvipañcita*..."
"How does one attain this samādhi?

When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the youth Candraprabha: "Young man, a bodhisattva endowed with four qualities attains this samādhi called 'The Manifestation of the Equality of the Essential Nature of All Phenomena'."
What are the four?
Here, young man, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is gentle, pleasant to dwell with, self-controlled, and has attained the stage of self-control.

When reviled or abused by others, he is patient toward ill-spoken words and paths of harsh speech; he is by nature enduring, perceives [the ripening of] karma, has subdued pride, and desires the Dharma.
By this first quality, O youth, a bodhisattva mahāsattva endowed with it attains this samādhi.
Furthermore, O youth, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is possessed of ethical discipline;
he is one whose ethical discipline is completely pure.

With unbroken morality, flawless morality, unstained morality, untarnished morality, unfailing morality, unperturbed morality, irreproachable morality, exalted morality, non-reliant morality, unadulterated morality, morality beyond apprehension, morality praised by the noble ones, and morality praised by the wise—
by being endowed with this second quality, O youth, a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains this samādhi.

Furthermore, young man, a bodhisattva mahāsattva has a mind that is terrified of the triple world, a mind that is thoroughly alarmed, a mind that is weary of it, and a mind that seeks its transcendence.
He is without desire for it, finds no delight in it, is not attached to it, and is not bound by it;
his mind is agitated toward the entire triple world.

Exerting himself with the thought, "I shall liberate sentient beings from the three realms," he realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Young man, endowed with this third quality, a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains this samādhi.
Furthermore, young man, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is endowed with faith; he is insatiable in his search for the Dharma;
and he is one who has heard much.
He becomes confident;
he loves the Dharma and honors the Dharma,
rather than honoring gain, honor, and fame.
He does not hold knowledge as a heavy burden;

rather, he teaches and elucidates in detail for others those teachings exactly as they were heard and mastered, with a mind preceded by the intent to benefit, and not out of a desire to gain a reputation for being wise.
On the contrary, his thought is: "How might these beings, having heard these teachings, become irreversible from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"
Young man, endowed with this fourth quality, a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains this samādhi.

Young man, endowed with these four qualities, a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains this samādhi, which is manifested as the equality of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena, and swiftly awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Therefore, young man, by this very method you should understand that this samādhi has been taught by many buddhas, praised by many buddhas, revealed by many buddhas, and investigated by many buddhas.

Having gone forth into homelessness in the presence of many Blessed Buddhas, O youth, I have heard, mastered, questioned, retained, recited, promulgated, cultivated through the meditation on non-conflict, repeatedly practiced, and extensively elucidated for others this samādhi called "The Manifestation of the Equality of the Essential Nature of All Phenomena."

Then, at that time, the Blessed One further expounded this very entrance into the samādhi of the accomplishment of many Buddhas— the narrative of past connections— in detail for the youth Candraprabha by singing it in verses:
I recall that in an incomparable and immeasurable eon, there was a Jina named Svarāṅgaghoṣa;
the lifespan of that Tathāgata Svarāṅgaghoṣa was sixty hundred years.
After him, there was a Buddha named Jñāneśvara, the supreme among men;
the lifespan of that Jñāneśvara, the best of bipeds, was twelve thousand years.
After Jñāneśvara, there was another Victor named Tejeśvara.
The lifespan of that supreme among bipeds, Tejeśvara, was seventy-six thousand years. (SRS 17.3)
After Tejeśvara had passed away, there was a Jina named Matiśvara;
the lifespan of that supreme among bipeds, Matiśvara, was a full ten million years.
After the passing of Matiśvara, there was a Jina named Buddhabrahmeśvara;
the lifespan of that supreme among bipeds, Brahmeśvara, was fourteen thousand years.
After the passing of Brahmeśvara, there was a Buddha, a Jina named Agnīśvara;
the lifespan of that Agnīśvara, the supreme among bipeds, was then sixty thousand years.
After the passing of Agnīśvara, there was a Buddha, a Jina named Brahmānana;
the lifespan of that supreme among bipeds, Brahmānana, was seven days and nights.
After the passing of Brahmānana, there was a Jina named Gaṇeśvara;
the lifespan of that supreme among bipeds, Gaṇeśvara, was a full sixty million years.
Upon the passing of Gaṇeśvara, there was a Jina named Ghoṣeśvara;
the lifespan of that supreme among bipeds, Ghoṣeśvara, was a full nine hundred million years.
After the passing of Ghoṣeśvara, there was a Jina named Buddha Ghoṣānana;
the lifespan of that supreme among bipeds, Ghoṣānana, was a full ten billion years.
After Ghoṣānana had passed away, there was a Buddha, a Jina named Candrānana.
The lifespan of that supreme among bipeds, Candrānana, lasted for one day and night. (SRS 17.11)
After the passing of Candrānana, there was a Buddha, a Jina named Sūryānana;
the lifespan of that Sūryānana, the supreme among bipeds, was eighteen thousand years.
After the passing of Sūryānana, there was a Buddha, a Jina named Brahmānana;
the lifespan of that supreme among bipeds, Brahmānana, was twenty-three thousand years.
After the passing of Brahmānana, there was a Jina named Buddha Brahmaśrava;
the lifespan of that supreme among bipeds, Brahmaśrava, was eighteen thousand years.
In a single eon, these two hundred leaders of the world have appeared;
listen, for I shall here proclaim the names of those unconquered Tathāgatas.
Anantaghoṣa and Vighuṣṭaghoṣa, Vighuṣṭatejas and Vighuṣṭaśabda; Svarāvighuṣṭa and Svarārcita, Svarāṅgaśūra and Svarāṅgaśabda.
Jñānābala, Jñānaviśeṣaga, Jñānābhibhū, and Jñānasamudgata;
Jñānārcimat, Jñānābhyudgata, Vighuṣṭajñāna, and likewise Jñānaśūra.
Brahmābala, Brahmavasu, Subrahma, and the god Brahmā, as well as Brahmaghoṣa;
Brahmeśvara, Brahmanarendranetra, Brahmasvarāṅga, and Svarabrahmadatta.
Tejobala, Tejavatī, Sutejas, Tejeśvara, Tejasamudrata, Tejovibhu, Tejaviniścita,
Tejasvarendra, and Suvighuṣṭatejas.
Bhīṣma, Bala, Bhīṣmamati, Subhīṣma, Bhīṣmānana, and Bhīṣmasamudrata;
Bhīṣmārcis, Bhīṣmottara, and Bhīṣmaghoṣa—these were the Jinas, the leaders of the world.
Gambhīraghoṣa, Śrīdhāraṇa, Viśuddhaghoṣeśvara, Śuddhaghoṣa, Anantaghoṣa, Suvimuktaghoṣa, Māra, Bala, and Māravitrāsana.
Sunetra, Śuddhānana, Netraśuddha, Viśuddhanetra, Anantanetra, Samantanetra, Vighuṣṭanetra, Netrābhibhū, and Aninditanetra.
Supremely tamed, tamed, with a well-tamed mind; well-tamed, with senses stilled and a peaceful heart;
supremely peaceful, with peaceful splendor, utterly tranquil; having reached the further shore of peace, a hero of peace.
Established in the supreme, his mind is peaceful and well-subdued; his senses are thoroughly tamed, his intellect is tranquil.
He is preeminent in peace, blazing with the glory of peace; he is the Lord of peace and perfect stillness, a hero of peace.
Lord of the hosts, chief of the hosts, sovereign of the hosts, the conqueror of the hosts, the best of the hosts, the possessor of pure knowledge;
the great lord of the hosts, the hero among the lords of the hosts, and yet another, the best of the hosts, the liberator.
Dharmadhvaja and likewise Dharmaketu, Dharmottara, and the exalted Dharmasvabhāva;
Dharmabala and Sudharmaśūra, and Svabhāvadharmottaraniścita as well. (SRS 17.26)
Eighty koṭis of leaders, all bearing the same name Svabhāvadharmottaraniścita, appeared in the second eon; for the sake of awakening, I made offerings to them.
Whoever hears the name of the Jina, who is certain in the supreme dharma of intrinsic nature,
and having heard it, retains that proclaimed name, will quickly attain this samādhi.
Beyond these Buddhas, in another inconceivable and immeasurable eon,
there was a Buddha honored by humans and gods, named Narendraghoṣa.
The lifespan of the Tathāgata Narendraghoṣa was seventy-six thousand years;
his first assembly of disciples consisted of three hundred koṭis.

At that time, the Saṅgha of Prabhākara consisted of those possessing the six superknowledges and the three insights, who had conquered their senses, were of great majesty and great supernatural power, whose outflows were exhausted, and who bore their final bodies.
There was a host of eighty thousand billion nayutas of bodhisattvas,
possessed of profound intelligence, confident, of great majesty, and endowed with great supernatural power.
Having attained the superknowledges, possessed of eloquence, and having reached the mastery of all emptiness,
they travel by means of miraculous power to millions of fields, and even beyond that, as many as the sands of the Ganges.
Having asked questions of the unsurpassed among two-legged beings, they return once more into the presence of that very Jina;
skilled in the extraction and interpretation of the sūtras, they wander the earth as embodiments of light. (SRS 17.34)
For the sake of sentient beings, the sons of the Sugata, possessed of great majesty, carry out their course of conduct;
they do not commit evil for the sake of sensual desires, and even the gods conceive a longing for them.

Having no desire for the realms of existence, they are not dependent [on them]; being concentrated, their sphere of activity is the dwelling in meditative absorption; having ascertained the meaning, they are confident, free from the scent of impurity, and always practitioners of the holy life.
With invincible speech and inspired eloquence, they are experts in etymology, exposition, and the meaning of words;
these sons of the Buddha demonstrate everything, having been sustained by wholesome karma.

For infinite eons they have risen through their conduct; they are praised and extolled by the Leaders at all times. They are teachers of the words concerning the reality of liberation, undefiled and possessed of perfectly pure ethical discipline.
Unstained like a lotus by water, liberated from the three realms and heedful,
they are unstained by the eight worldly dharmas, possessing purified bodies and perfectly pure actions.
With few desires, contented, and of great majesty, you are free from greed; the qualities of a Buddha are firmly established in you.
You are the refuge and the ultimate resort for all sentient beings, and your practice does not consist merely in the sound of words.
Wherever they abide, they teach that [Dharma] to others; they are embraced by all the Buddhas.
They are the trusted confidants who hold the treasury of the Jinas; their minds are terrified of the triple world.
With minds always tranquil, dwelling in forest retreats and sustained by the Guides of the World, they speak billions of sūtras; and whatever they speak is praised by the Buddhas.
They have abandoned all worldly states, are resolved upon emptiness, and teach the ultimate truth;
they possess infinite praise, are like oceans of virtue, and are deeply learned, wise, and discerning.
Even if the Prince were to remain empowered for many millions of eons and speak of his qualities,
that which would be proclaimed would be but a small portion, like a single drop of water from the ocean.
And at that time, that King of Men’s Voice taught this peaceful samādhi so difficult to perceive;
the great trichiliocosm was filled with devas and nāgas.
As he was teaching this peaceful samādhi, the earth shook in six ways;
gods and humans, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, became established in the irreversible state of Buddha-knowledge.
There, a king was the lord of men, named Śirībala, possessed of great majesty;
he had five hundred sons who were handsome, pleasing, and beautiful to behold.
That king had an inner court of one hundred billion women;
that king had fourteen thousand million daughters in full.
Then, on the full moon day of the month of Kārttika, having undertaken the eightfold poṣadha vow,
he approached the presence of the Teacher of the World together with eighty quadrillion followers.
Having bowed at the feet of the Best of Bipeds, the king sat down before the Jina;
knowing the king’s resolute intention, the Lord of Bipeds taught him this samādhi.
Having heard this meditative concentration, that king abandoned his kingdom like a lump of spittle;
having renounced his dear kinsmen and relatives, he went forth into homelessness under the teaching of that Jina.
Fifty sons went forth into homelessness, as did the women of the inner apartments and likewise the daughters;
and there were others there—sons, kinsmen, and relatives—amounting to seventy-six nayutas and three koṭis.

Having gone forth here together with his son and wife, and having set aside the ground for obtaining food, he practiced walking meditation for eight years under a supernatural empowerment; while remaining on that walking path, he passed away.
Having passed away then, that elephant among kings, whose mind was always perfectly concentrated in meditative absorption,
was reborn right there in the royal family by spontaneous birth, unstained by the impurities of the womb.
His father was named Dṛḍhabala, and his mother was named Mahāmatī.
As soon as he was born, the prince said: "Does that Protector of the World still abide?"
The Lord of the World knows my intention, by which he has taught me this peaceful samādhi;
it is without conditions and free from conditions, the single teaching regarding the destinies of beings.
Is the Jina teaching that samādhi, which is the seal of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena, which is the source of millions of billions of sūtras,
and which is the unsurpassed wealth of the bodhisattvas?
Purity of body, purity of speech, purity of mind, and likewise purity of view—the transcendence of all objective referents: does the Jina teach that as this samādhi?
The non-perishing of karma, the vision of the nature of its fruit, the cultivation of the supreme eightfold path,
meeting with the Tathāgatas, sharp wisdom, entry into the truths, and constant knowledge of the Dharma.
The full comprehension of the aggregates, the equality of the elements, and the complete removal of the sense-bases;
the entry [into the path] through the direct realization of non-arising—does the Jina teach that samādhi?
Through analytical knowledge, there is the wisdom that enters into peace and the wisdom that discerns the distinctions of all syllables;
that which is the transcendence of settling upon entities—that is the samādhi which the Jina speaks of.
Thorough knowledge of sounds, the attainment of joy, and the arising of rapture through praising the Sugatas;
the noble state, gentleness, and uprightness—does the Jina speak of that samādhi?
That gentle one shall never knit his brow; his face shall be friendly, sweet, and smiling.
Upon seeing sentient beings, he addresses them first, asking: "Does the Jina speak of that samādhi?"
Freedom from laziness, reverence for teachers, service to them, salutation, and looking upon them with love;
contentment with one's rebirth and purity—does the Jina speak of that samādhi? (SRS 17.64)
Purity of livelihood, dwelling in the forest, abiding in the dhūtas, non-forgetfulness of mindfulness,
skill in the aggregates and likewise in the elements— does the Jina teach that samādhi?
Skill in the sense bases, the knowledge of supernormal powers, the removal of afflictions, and the stage of the tamed;
the severance of all extensive mantras—does the Jina teach that samādhi?
The transcending of all states of existence, the recollection of past births, freedom from doubt regarding the Dharma,
a mind fixed on the Dharma, and the seeking of what has been heard— does the Jina speak of that samādhi?

One who always advances toward distinction, delights in cultivation, and abides in skillfulness regarding transgressions and their transcendence—does the Jina teach that samādhi by which, when one abides therein, one abandons all latent tendencies? SRS_17.68.
Since there is the arrival of the supreme, sharp knowledge, whereby one is immovable like a mountain and unshakable—
does the Jina teach that samādhi, which has the characteristic of non-retrogression and is the gateway to dhāraṇī?
The constant seeking of pure qualities and the constant avoidance of unwholesome qualities,
and the constant practice regarding the side of affliction— does the Jina ever speak of that samādhi?
Having mastered all the trainings and attained mastery over the states of meditative concentration,
the wise one, knowing the inclinations of sentient beings, exhorts them and teaches the Dharma for the sake of the supreme enlightenment of a Buddha.

Does the Jina speak of that samādhi which is the knowledge of distinctions, the knowledge of rebirth, infinite knowledge, perfectly complete knowledge, and the knowledge of the reconnection of all states of existence? SRS_17.72 //

Having renounced the household life, the supreme among bipeds teaches the Dharma: the mind set on going forth, lack of delight in the three realms, absence of attachment, and the joyful mastery of the mind.

The Protector, the supreme among bipeds, teaches the Dharma that consists of non-attachment to phenomena and constant embracing of the sublime Dharma, as well as firm conviction in the ripening of karma.

The Supreme among Humans teaches the Dharma: skill in the Vinaya, knowledge of the ripening of karma, the pacification of quarrels and disputes, as well as non-contention and the ground of non-dispute.

Having generated compassion, he teaches the Dharma— consisting of the undertaking of patience, abiding in non-anger, certainty regarding the Dharma, and constant skillfulness, as well as the vision of knowledge regarding the distinctions between words.

Knowledge of the past limit, knowledge of the future limit, and the equality of the three times—this is declared to be the discernment of the three spheres within the teaching of the Sugatas; thus does the Jina, the Lord of Dharma, teach.
The stabilization of the mind and one-pointedness, the stabilization of the body according to the noble stages,
and the constant protection while abiding in the modes of conduct— the Sage, the Bull among Men, teaches this Dharma.

Possessing a sense of shame and dread of blame, and being graceful, he speaks words that are appropriate and possess knowledge of the world; he teaches the Dharma of active engagement and the nature of living beings, the Dharma for the sake of supreme and foremost enlightenment.
Bestowing favor, as well as a sense of shame and dread of blame, and the loathing of unwholesome states of mind;
through not abandoning the ascetic practices, the Supreme among Bipeds teaches the Dharma regarding the practice of alms-gathering.
One should always practice shame and dread of blame, greeting and rising for one's teachers, and the suppression of pride from the very beginning; thus the Jina, the Lord of Dharma, has taught.
Through the origination of the mind, the health of the mind, the penetration of knowledge, and likewise through such awakening,
and by always avoiding the side of ignorance, he teaches the Dharma of the supreme awakening of a Buddha.
The entrance into the mind, knowledge of sounds, abiding in etymological interpretation with certain meaning,
and the constant avoidance of all that is unbeneficial— thus the Jina, the Lord of Dharma, has taught.
Constant association with virtuous persons and the avoidance of base individuals,
as well as always maintaining faith and affection for the Jina— thus the Jina taught this supreme Dharma.

The Victor taught this supreme Dharma: that conventions, designations, and verbal expressions are merely such; that one should always avoid the sufferings of saṃsāra; and that even when obtaining gain, one should remain in a state of non-attachment. SRS_17.85 //

Having received honor, one should not be conceited; even when treated with disrespect, one should remain equanimous. One should never rejoice even when praised. Such is this teaching of the Benefactor of the World.

One should endure all abuse and disparagement, and avoid intimacy with householders; one should maintain association only with those who have gone forth—thus has the Jina, the Lord of Dharma, taught. (SRS 17.87)
Well-established in the range of the Buddhas, having completely avoided what is not their range,
perfected in conduct with a well-tamed mind— this is the guidance of the Dharma taught by the Sugata.
One should always avoid those qualities of the foolish and avoid everything that brings disgrace to one's family;
the teaching of the Buddha must always be protected—thus has the Jina, the Lord of Dharma, taught.
Speaking little, yet sweetly and appropriately, with words that are auspicious and gentle toward others; subduing adversaries through the Dharma—such is the instruction of the Jina.
One should practice at the proper time and not at the improper time; one should place no trust in any ordinary worldlings.
When touched by suffering, one should not become dejected—this is the instruction of the Jina.
Seeing one who is poor, one should provide them with wealth; seeing one who is immoral, one should show compassion.
One should always exhort them toward what is beneficial—this, O Conqueror, is such an instruction.
One should assist sentient beings through the Dharma and always practice the renunciation of worldly material things;
one should neither make hoards nor accumulate stores—such is the instruction of the Jina.
Praise of ethical discipline and censure of immorality, freedom from deceit, and attending upon those possessed of virtue;
relinquishing all one's possessions and not being dependent even on wealth—such is this instruction of the Victor.
With a profound resolve, one should offer invitations to the Guru; I shall do everything exactly as I have spoken.
One should constantly attend upon the Dharma-preacher—this is the instruction of the Jina.
One should always be respectful and joyful in mind, and should always remain established in a gentle gaze;
always being well-resolved regarding former practices—this is such an instruction of the Jina.
Always taking skillful means as the precursor for abandoning signs,
and likewise for the reversal of perceptions and the characteristics of entities— such is this instruction of the Jina.
Skill in the words that bring forth the sūtras, certainty regarding the words that teach the truths,
and the direct realization of the knowledge of liberation— such is this instruction from the Jina.

One should always cultivate the empty dharmas, being confident and established in the power of ethical discipline; one should cross over by means of the station of samādhi—such is this instruction of the Jina.
One should never proclaim the gain of reputation, nor should one practice hypocrisy of mind;
one should avoid all views that have been formed—such is the instruction of the Jina.
Supreme eloquence, excellent dhāraṇīs, and the infinite radiance of knowledge;
this empowerment, mantra, and application of eloquence—such is the instruction of the Jina.
This is the gateway of ethical discipline, the cultivation of the path, the practice, and the auspicious method of instruction;
having practiced the teaching herein, such is this instruction from the Victor.
The concordant patience praised by the Buddhas—abiding in patience, one should abandon faults;
abiding in knowledge, one should abandon ignorance. Such is this instruction of the Jina.
The foundation of knowledge, as well as the stages of yoga, and the mastery of yoga for those set out toward awakening;
constant attendance upon holy persons—such is this instruction from the Jina.
The Tathāgatas have taught that the Buddha-ground consists in always avoiding those who practice improperly; this has been rejoiced in by all the wise. Such is this instruction of the Jina.
Rejected by the ignorant, the unlearned, and the immature, yet embraced here by the many śrāvakas and always by the bodhisattvas— such is this instruction of the Jina.
This has been realized by the Tathāgatas and honored and worshipped by the gods;
it is rejoiced in by billions of Brahmās—does the Jina speak of that samādhi?
Always well-honored by thousands of nāgas, as well as by suparṇas, yakṣas, and kinnaras—
does the Jina now teach that very samādhi which was spoken by the Jinas as the supreme enlightenment?

Is it that the Victorious One teaches this samādhi— the supreme, unsurpassed, and spiritual medicine of knowledge— which the wise have always deemed sufficient, excellent, and most excellently attained?
The treasury of knowledge, inexhaustible inspired eloquence, and this entry into millions of sūtras;
the thorough understanding of the three realms and the knowledge of reality—does the Jina speak of that samādhi?
This boat has been taught for those who wish to go to the further shore, and it is also a ship for those caught in the flood;
fame, renown, and garlands of praise increase for those to whom this peaceful samādhi has been taught.
This is the praise of the Tathāgatas and the hymn of those bulls among men;
it is the hymn of the Bodhisattvas and the inexhaustible method by which this peaceful samādhi has been taught.

This loving-kindness is revealed for the pacification of faults; equanimity is the ground of the compassionate ones. This is the consolation of those of great resolve, for whose sake this samādhi has been taught.
This is the arrival of the supreme Buddha-knowledge taught by the Lions among Men;
this samādhi, the seal of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena, has been taught by the Leaders.
This practice, which brings forth the wisdom of the omniscient one for those set out toward enlightenment,
and which also terrifies the army of Māra, is this peaceful samādhi taught by the Jina.

This knowledge is the supreme protection for the Protectors who abide in the Dharma, even in the midst of enemies; it is the subduing of adversaries through the Dharma itself. This peaceful samādhi was taught by the Jina.
This stage of inspired eloquence has been fully revealed: the powers, the liberations, as well as the faculties;
the eighteen distinguished qualities of a Buddha, while practicing these peaceful meditative absorptions.
The ten powers have been truly sought after, as has the precursor sign for the Buddha-knowledge;
these are the Buddha-qualities revealed by the Supreme among Men, who out of compassion seeks the welfare of the world.
This has been established by the sons of the Buddhas; this path leading to liberation has been taught for those who desire release.
And there is joy for the sons of the Sugata upon hearing this peaceful samādhi so difficult to perceive.
The wise Bodhisattva who desires the complete fulfillment of the Buddha-knowledge—
pure in mind, clean, and free from defilements— should practice this peaceful samādhi.
His body is completely purified, like the liberation-knowledge and the vision of liberation of the Victors;
always untainted by the bonds of passion, one should practice this auspicious samādhi.
For one who desires liberation, there is no ground for hatred and the departure from delusion, as well as the arrival of knowledge;
through the arising of true insight which destroys ignorance, one should practice this peaceful samādhi.
This satisfaction is declared to be the essence of liberation; this peaceful samādhi has been taught for those who meditate.
One should cultivate this peaceful samādhi, which is the eye of the irreproachable Buddhas.
This supernormal knowledge has been displayed across many fields, and the infinite miraculous powers of the Buddhas have been shown;
moreover, for one who cultivates this samādhi, even that dhāraṇī will not be difficult to obtain.
For one whose senses are tranquil and who stands here for the sake of awakening, this empowerment has been shown by the Infinite One;
it belongs to one who cultivates this samādhi— subtle, vast, and pure knowledge.
This turning back of all syllables is not easily understood by those whose yoga is unapplied;
it cannot be known through sound by one who has not heard this peaceful samādhi.
But this has been understood by wise Bodhisattvas, just as it was taught by the Lord of Dharma;
they have awakened through peaceful and blameless means while practicing this samādhi.
By those who have initiated vigor, it has been fully grasped and maintained;
and by those who practice this samādhi, the exhaustion of suffering and the knowledge of the cessation of birth are always well-sustained.
The non-arising of all phenomena has been taught, as it is in all states of existence;
does the Jina now speak of that samādhi, the supreme knowledge of the Buddhas of great resolve?

While that prince was reciting these verses, eighty-eight thousand full *niyuta*s attained the patience that follows the sound (*ghoṣānugā-kṣānti*), and there they became established in the irreversible state of the Buddha-knowledge.
Dṛḍhabala said to that boy: "Even today that Lord of the World remains.
Boy, I ask you about this matter: from whom did you hear of this samādhi?"
The prince said, "O King, listen! I have seen billions of Jinas;
in a single eon, they were all honored by me, and this peaceful samādhi was requested from them."
For ninety-four kalpas, and for thousands of millions of billions of other kalpas,
I was one who remembered my past births in each of those places, and I was never again conceived in a womb.
Then this samādhi was cultivated by me, having heard it in its purity as those Jinas were speaking;
and having heard and taught it, having generated aspiration and attained freedom from doubt, I shall touch enlightenment.
To those monks who questioned me while they were mastering this samādhi,
I established there a sense of reverence just as if they were in the presence of those who act for the sake of the world.

Those from whom I have received even a single verse while practicing the conduct that is in accordance with the Dharma—I honor them as peaceful ones; I maintain toward them the same reverence as for a Buddha.
Furthermore, if anyone should come to question me as I am mastering this sublime samādhi, even in my dreams I have no doubt: "I shall not fail to become a Jina, a Leader of the World."
Toward monks who are senior, those of middle standing, and those who are new, I am respectful and well-pleased.
For me, being full of respect, my fame, merit, renown, and likewise my virtues increase.
I am not eager for disputes in the Kali age; at that time, I shall have little concern for them.
One destiny awaits those who have committed evil, and another destiny awaits those who have performed what is auspicious.
Having heard the unpleasant words of those who are unrestrained and engaged in improper yoga, I thought at that time:
"I am the owner of my own karma; there is no destruction of the action that has been performed. (SRS 17.140)
For in this matter, O Bhagavat, anger is not the final resort; rather, take up the power of patience as praised by the Buddhas.
Patience has always been extolled by the Leaders; having cultivated patience, enlightenment is not difficult to attain.
I am always possessed of ethical discipline, and I establish others in ethical discipline as well;
I always speak in praise of ethical discipline, and my words there are held in high esteem.
I always speak in praise of the forest life and am ever established in moral discipline;
I encourage others in the observance of the *poṣadha* and likewise urge them toward awakening.
I also encourage them in the holy life and establish them in the goal and the Dharma;
and for them I reveal the path to awakening, upon which these infinite attachments cease.
I remember a past eon on the path when there was a Jina named Svarāṅgaghoṣa;
in his presence I made this vow: "May I always be one whose strength is patience."
Having made that vow and remained steadfast there for eighty-four million years,
though I was reviled and insulted by Māra, my mind was never once disturbed.
Having investigated him there and recognized my firm patience and loving-kindness, Māra, with a serene mind, prostrated at my feet; five hundred [of his followers] set out for supreme enlightenment.
I am always free from envy and constantly speak in praise of renunciation;
I am wealthy, possessed of riches, and a great-souled being, and during times of famine, I am a generous donor.
Those monks who maintain this samādhi, those who recite it, and those who teach it—to them I shall perform service; and they all shall become the most excellent among men.
By that unsurpassed karma, I behold many Buddhas, the protectors of the world;
having obtained the going forth in the teaching of the Jinas, I shall always be a wise Dharma-preacher.
I am always devoted to the ascetic practices (dhūta), constantly dwelling in forests and wildernesses;
I do not practice hypocrisy for the sake of food, and I am content with whatever comes my way.
I am always free from envy, and I do not become dependent upon families;
for envy increases in one who is attached to families, but being free from envy, I find contentment in the forests.
I have always dwelt in loving-kindness; even when reviled, I do not give rise to anger. Dwelling in loving-kindness, gentle and serene, a garland of praise spreads in the four directions.

I am always one of few desires and contented, dwelling in the forest and devoted to the ascetic practices (*dhuta*). I do not abandon the practice of alms-gathering, and I find firm stability in the ascetic virtues.
I am faithful and have clarity of mind; I possess great serenity always within the Buddha’s teaching.
Through this serenity, I shall obtain many benefits: I become pleasing to behold, with faculties that are never deficient.
And wherever I speak, there I abide; I am always one for whom practice is the essence.
For those who take practice as their essence, these gods and nāgas, with hearts full of faith, rise up to serve them.
These virtues have been proclaimed by me as far as they extend, as well as these others, many and manifold,
which should always be practiced by the wise person who desires to awaken to the enlightenment of a Buddha.
I remember the many more difficult deeds that were performed by me in previous eons;
though it would take a long time to speak of them now, I shall go for a while into the presence of the Sugata.
The wise Bodhisattva, possessed of extremely sharp wisdom, at that very moment attained the five superknowledges;
by means of his miraculous power, he went into the presence of the Jina together with eighty koṭis of living beings.
At that time, Dṛḍhabala was exceedingly exalted; together with six billion followers, he approached the presence of the Tathāgata, and having bowed at his feet, sat down before him.
Having understood the king’s resolute intention, the Lord of Men taught him this samādhi;
and having heard this samādhi, the monarch, casting aside his kingdom without regret, went forth into homelessness.
Having gone forth, he cultivated this samādhi, recited it, and proclaimed it;
after sixty thousand eons, he became the Victor named Padmottara.
At that time, no fewer than sixty hundred million [beings] who had approached the Jinas together with the king—
having heard this very samādhi— they too became joyful and elated, and then went forth into homelessness.
Having gone forth, they upheld, recited, and proclaimed this samādhi;
after the passing of sixty nayutas of kalpas, they touched supreme enlightenment in a single kalpa.
There were Buddhas named Anantajñānottara, honored by humans and gods;
each one of those supreme among bipeds liberated beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
I was King Śirībala while practicing this supreme conduct of awakening;
those who were my five hundred sons are these very ones who protect the true Dharma.
Thus, for thousands of millions of eons, with diligence undertaken and without weariness,
I have sought this pure samādhi, thereby attaining that supreme enlightenment.
Therefore, O Prince, those bodhisattvas who desire to seek this samādhi should always train themselves in accordance with me, O Prince, being diligent in effort and indifferent toward life.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter of the *Śrī-Samādhirāja*, titled "The Entrance to the Samādhi of the Manifestation of Many Buddhas."
(Vaidya 127) Chapter 18: The Entrustment of the Samādhi.
Then the Blessed One addressed the youth Candraprabha: "Therefore, O youth, whichever bodhisattva..."
A mahāsattva will take up this samādhi, master it, retain it, recite it, propagate it, explain it, study it, and reveal it in detail to others;
furthermore, he must be devoted to the practice of its cultivation.
For one who practices this, four benefits and advantages are to be expected.
What are the four?
Namely, that he will be unsurpassed in terms of merit.
He will be invincible by adversaries;
he will be immeasurable in wisdom;
and he will be infinite in eloquence.
For any young man, O Kumāra, who shall take up this samādhi, master it, retain it, recite it, propagate it, teach it, study it, and reveal it in detail to others,
these four qualities and benefits are to be expected for him.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
"Through merits, he shall always be unsurpassed;
through the state of tranquility, he will attain the samādhi that is the domain of all Buddhas."
Protected by merits, that hero shall always remain so as he practices the supreme, pure, and distinguished conduct of awakening.
No adversary shall ever cause him harm;
he will be constantly sustained by the Buddhas.
And they shall be immeasurable in wisdom at all times;
being infinite in eloquence, they will uphold the peaceful state.
One will possess a mass of merit that is forever unsurpassed and will practice the supreme conduct of awakening;
having maintained this excellent, peaceful samādhi, one will not be overcome by adversaries.
His knowledge shall become vast and sharp, as shall his eloquence; his vision will be infinite and pure.
That wise one will always possess the power of mindfulness and the power of dhāraṇī.

Speaking words of meaning that are most dear and pleasing to the wise, the one possessed of wisdom will become renowned among many people while proclaiming this excellent, peaceful samādhi. (SRS 18.7)
One who maintains this excellent, peaceful samādhi will become delicate and beautiful to behold, and shall obtain the most superior robes, invitations for lodging, and food and drink. SRS_18.8 //
He will behold many Buddhas, the Lords of the World, and he will perform incomparable worship for those Leaders;
indeed, there shall be no obstacle for him as he seeks this excellent, peaceful samādhi.
Standing before the Lords of the World, with a joyful heart, he will speak with hundreds of most beautiful verses;
and for him who maintains this excellent, peaceful samādhi, there shall never be any decline.
The Lord of the World will stand before him with a body adorned with beautiful primary and secondary marks;
and there shall be no loss of his wisdom once he has maintained this excellent, peaceful samādhi.
Having maintained this excellent, peaceful samādhi, he will never have a depressed mind; he will always be wealthy and never poor, nor will his mind ever become arrogant.
Nor shall he ever be born in the inopportune states, O Lord of the Earth; he shall become a universal monarch (cakravartin).
His kingdom shall always be secure once he has maintained this excellent and peaceful samādhi.
There is no doubt that his wisdom is vast, even if it were to be spoken for hundreds of eons;
having heard this samādhi, the ground of peace, the wise one should abide exactly as it has been taught. (SRS 18.14)
O Daśabala, even if one were to speak of his merits for immeasurable and infinite millions of eons,
it would not constitute even a fraction of what has been proclaimed, just as a drop of water taken from the ocean.

At that time, the prince was filled with joy; rising with palms joined in reverence, he stood facing the One of Ten Powers, uplifted, and uttered these sublime words: SRS_18.16: "At that time, the prince was filled with joy; rising with palms joined in reverence, he stood facing the One of Ten Powers, uplifted, and uttered these sublime words."
Inconceivable is the Great Hero, the Lord of the World, the Illuminator;
such are the benefits as they have been proclaimed by this Lord of Men.
Tell me, O Great Hero, you who desire our welfare and are compassionate:
who indeed will hear this sūtra in the final age?
Then the Teacher, the Blessed One, whose voice is like the song of the kalaviṅka bird and who possesses unimpeded knowledge, spoke these words:
"O Kumāra, listen; I shall speak of the unsurpassed practice:
whoever, training in accordance with the Dharma, shall hear this sūtra."
Performing worship of the Lords of Jinas and seeking the wisdom of a Buddha,
one who cultivates a mind of loving-kindness shall hear this sūtra.
Having cultivated the ascetic virtues (dhūtaguṇa), the qualities of austerity (saṃlekha), and the most excellent qualities,
and having remained steadfast in correct practice, he shall hear this sutra.
This sutra will not be heard from the hands of evildoers,
nor by those who have violated their moral discipline in the presence of the Lords of the World.
From the hands of those who are celibate, heroic, whose minds are free from craving,
and who are sustained by the Buddhas, one shall hear it.
For those former Buddhas, the protectors of the world, whom he served, from their hands he shall hear this sūtra in a future time.
But those who in previous births were followers of other sects,
upon hearing this sūtra, will find no joy.
Having gone forth here in my teaching for the sake of a livelihood,
those overcome by gain and honor will revile one another. (SRS 18.27)
Those who are deeply attached to the wives of others, monks who are unrestrained,
desirous of gain, and of immoral conduct— these will not have faith in this sūtra.
Having attained merit under the Buddhas, yet being indifferent even to the attainment of meditative concentration,
and remaining dependent on the notion of a self— they do not have faith in this sutra.
In the final age, perceiving the fruit of worldly meditation,
they will consume the alms-food of Arhats and reject the awakening of a Buddha.
Whether one were to destroy all the reliquaries in Jambudvīpa,
or whether one were to reject this sūtra— the latter evil is more significant.
And whoever should kill as many Arhats as there are grains of sand in the Ganges,
the evil of one who rejects this sutra is more serious than that.
Who among you has the courage, in the dreadful final age when the true Dharma still persists in the world, to proclaim this sūtra?
Rising up there while weeping, the prince spoke to the Jina;
thus did the Buddha’s own son let out a lion’s roar.
When the Perfectly Awakened One has entered parinirvāṇa, during the terrible final age, I shall propagate this sūtra, even at the cost of my body and life.
"O Leader, I shall endure here the insults of fools;
I shall tolerate their abuse and their threats."
May I exhaust this evil karma which was committed by me in the past,
for I gave rise to malice toward other bodhisattvas.
Placing his hand, which resembled gold, upon the head [of Candraprabha],
the Teacher, the Tathāgata Mañjughoṣa Buddha, spoke to Candraprabha.
I grant you my empowerment, O youth, in this final age;
there shall be no obstacle to your celibate life nor to your lifespan.
And eight hundred others have arisen here as upholders of the Dharma;
for we are the upholders of this sūtra in the final age.
Eighty koṭis of devas, nāgas, and yakṣas have gathered;
and sixty nayutas of others pay homage to the Leader of the World.
O Leader, we shall provide protection for these monks who have arisen today, and also during that final age.
In this sutra, the Buddha-fields are proclaimed to be shaken by the power of the Teacher, like the sands of the Ganges.
And all those fields that were shaken, in which emanations of the Buddha appeared—
those very dharmas that were proclaimed by the Lord of the World were sent forth.
And from each single field, inconceivable millions of beings,
having heard the Dharma at that time, were established in the wisdom of a Buddha.
Moreover, from this buddha-field, ninety million devas,
having generated the mind set on awakening, scattered flowers over the Buddha.
