They have been prophesied by the Lord of Men that, after eighty koṭis of eons,
they shall all become guides in this very same single eon.
Monks and nuns, as well as laymen and laywomen— seventy-six koṭis of living beings by whom this sūtra was heard.
They too have been prophesied by the Buddha; practicing the conduct of awakening, they shall behold the leaders of the world, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Seeking the wisdom of a Buddha, they will perform worship to all [the Buddhas] and will hear this unsurpassed sūtra in various places.
With eighty koṭis of auspicious eons, they shall all become leaders of the world in this single kalpa, seeking the welfare [of beings] and full of compassion.
Having performed unsurpassed worship of the Buddha Maitreya and having upheld the supreme True Dharma, they will go to Sukhāvatī.
There, they will perform worship to that stainless Buddha, the Tathāgata Amitāyus, for the sake of supreme enlightenment.
For seventy-three incalculable eons, both those that have passed and those yet to come,
they shall not go to an evil rebirth after hearing this supreme sūtra.
Whoever shall hear this supreme sūtra in the future time and shed tears, by all of them indeed am I honored.
I announce to all of you who stand before me:
I entrust this awakening, which I have attained with great hardship.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter of the *Śrīsamādhirāja*, titled "The Entrustment of the Samādhi.
19. The Chapter on the Teaching of the Inconceivable Qualities of a Buddha.

Therefore, young man, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who desires this samādhi should become skilled in the teaching of the inconceivable qualities of a buddha; he should be of a nature that inquires about the inconceivable qualities of a buddha;
and he should have faith and resolve in the inconceivable qualities of a buddha.
One should be skilled in seeking the inconceivable qualities of a Buddha;
and having heard of those inconceivable qualities of a Buddha, one should not be startled, should not be terrified, and should not fall into fear.

When this was said, the youth Candraprabha addressed the Blessed One: "In what way, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva become skilled in the teaching of the inconceivable qualities of a Buddha?"
He is skilled in inquiring about the inconceivable qualities of a Buddha,
he has resolute faith in the inconceivable qualities of a Buddha,
and he is skilled in seeking the inconceivable qualities of a Buddha.
"And having heard of the inconceivable qualities of a Buddha, he does not tremble, does not become terrified, and does not fall into fear?
At that very time, a son of the gandharvas named Pañcaśikha, accompanied by five hundred musical instruments, descended from the sky and stood before the Blessed One to attend upon him and serve him.

Then, this thought occurred to Pañcaśikha, the son of the gandharvas: "What if I were to [perform] for the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven and for Śakra, the lord of the gods, in the Sudharmā hall..."
Just as I perform attendance and service in the assembly hall of the gods and provide musical performances there,
so too today might I provide musical performances for the worship of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the God beyond gods.

Then Pañcaśikha, the son of the Gandharvas, together with those five hundred musical instruments and those five hundred sons of the Gandharvas, using musical performances joined in a single harmony, took up a lute with a stem of lapis lazuli and played it before the Blessed One.
Then this thought occurred to the Blessed One: "What if I were now to perform such a feat of supernatural power (ṛddhyabhisaṃskāra)..."
By means of such a performance of supernatural power (*ṛddhyabhisaṃskāra*), may the youth Candraprabha attain skill in the profound contemplation of the inconceivable qualities of a Buddha,
and may he not waver from the samādhi manifested by the equality of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena;
and may I instruct Pañcaśikha, the son of the Gandharvas, in his skill regarding the sounds of lute strings and the melodies of song.

Then the Blessed One performed such a feat of supernatural power that from those five hundred musical instruments, when they were played together, there issued forth a sound like that drawn from a water-jar, associated with the Dharma;
and by the power of the Buddha, these verses of realization regarding the qualities of a Buddha resounded:
In a single hair-pore there are many Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges;
so many are the fields of those Jinas, and they are diverse and distinct from one another.
Those who have gone into the five realms within the path of fools— the denizens of hell and those in the animal realm,
those in the world of Yama, gods, and humans— there is neither confusion nor oppression among them.

In that place, there are lakes together with oceans, as well as all rivers, springs, and ponds; yet there is neither confusion nor crowding—such is the inconceivable nature of the dharmas of the Victors.
And there, O Parvata, were many mountains— Cakravāla, Meru, Sumeru,
Mucilinda, Mahāmucilinda, Vindhya, Gṛdhrakūṭa, and Himavat.
In that place there are most terrifying hells— Tapana, Pratāpana, and others that are unpleasant—
and those who are born in those hells experience painful sensations as well.
And there, even on that ground, are twelve yojanas of delightful celestial palaces;
within them, many thousands of gods experience pleasures through divine delights.
And therein occurs the arising of Buddhas, who kindle the teaching of the Knower of the World;
yet one devoid of wisdom does not see it, because their pure conduct has not been purified.
In that place, even though the Dharma has ceased and the Leader has entered nirvāṇa, the sound is heard;
and in that very place, some hear it as if the Leader were still present, preaching the Dharma.
In that state, for some, an inconceivable lifespan of years persists;
yet in that same state, they may pass away, and the sound is heard: "He does not live long."
And in that very place, some perceived the designation "Tathāgata" and honored the Buddha;
they satisfied their minds by grasping at that designation, yet he was not truly honored, nor did he arise [from it].

Just as a man in his own house, having experienced delights in the qualities of sensual pleasure while dreaming, does not see those sensual pleasures upon waking and realizes that it was a dream; so too [should one understand this].
Whatever has been thus seen, heard, thought, or known—all this is false, like a dream;
but he who has attained this samādhi understands the intrinsic nature of all phenomena.
Those people in the world who are always well-happened, for whom there is nothing whatsoever pleasant or unpleasant,
and who delight in forest caves, experience the supreme happiness of the ascetic life.
But those for whom even "mine" does not exist anywhere, and for whom there is no grasping at all—
moving through the world like rhinoceroses, they proceed like the wind in the sky.
The path has been cultivated and wisdom set in motion; all phenomena are empty and without self.
For one by whom these phenomena have been thus discerned, there shall be infinite eloquence.
Truly happy are those people in the world whose minds do not cling to the world;
their minds here are always like the wind, and they have no attachment to what is pleasant or unpleasant.
Dwelling with those who are unpleasant is suffering for those who love them, and separation from those who are pleasant is suffering;
having abandoned both of these extremes, those men who delight in the Dharma are happy. (SRS 19.17)

Those who are led astray upon hearing these teachings, and who are repelled upon hearing what is not the Dharma, are struck down by intoxication and pride; being perverted through the power of conceit, they experience suffering.
Those who are established in equanimity are always neither elated nor dejected;
being well-liberated from both the pleasant and the unpleasant, they dwell with minds forever free.
Those who are well-established in perfectly pure morality and always established in inconceivable meditation,
who delight in the peace of forest caves— for them, doubt never exists.
Furthermore, those fools who have entered upon the unreal and are always delighted by the qualities of sensual desire,
like vultures intent upon corpses, remain perpetually under the power of Namuci.
Furthermore, while this exposition of verses was being spoken, the youth Candraprabha attained skill in the profound contemplation and explanation of the inconceivable qualities of a Buddha,
and he obtained the illumination of the extraction of the sūtras.
And for Pañcaśikha, the son of the Gandharvas, there occurred the attainment of the patience that follows the sound.
The minds of immeasurable beings among the populations of gods and humans were set upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment;
and the welfare of immeasurable beings was accomplished.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter of the *Śrī-Samādhirāja*, titled "The Teaching on the Inconceivable Qualities of a Buddha."
Chapter 20: The Chapter on King Indraketudhvaja.
Then the Blessed One addressed the youth Candraprabha: "Therefore, young man, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should rely upon all roots of virtue, training, qualities, and dharmas;
and he should be one who frequently avoids worldly entanglement."

One who avoids evil friends, relies upon spiritual friends, is inquisitive by nature, insatiable in the search for the Dharma, abundant in joy, seeking the Dharma, desiring the Dharma, delighting in the Dharma, upholding the Dharma, and practicing the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma—
such a person should conceive the perception of the Teacher toward all bodhisattvas.
And from whomsoever one hears this Dharma-discourse, one should generate toward that person joy and reverence, as well as the perception of them as the Teacher.
Young man, the bodhisattva mahāsattva who proceeds by undertaking these dharmas—
He quickly becomes one who has emerged with an uninterrupted eloquence;
he becomes devoted to the inconceivable qualities of a Buddha,
and he attains deep realization regarding profound dharmas.
And he becomes a light for the world including its devas, by dispelling the darkness of doubt, uncertainty, and hesitation.

Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses: "In the past, many billions of eons ago— immeasurable, incomparable, and inconceivable— there was a leader, the supreme among bipeds, named Indraketudhvajarāja."
He taught this peaceful concentration, wherein there is no person, no life-force, and no individual;
all phenomena are like an illusion, a bubble, a mirage, lightning, and like the moon reflected in water.
No being or human is found who, having passed away, goes to the next world;
yet the karma performed does not perish, yielding fruit accordingly, whether dark or bright.

This gateway of the method of reasoning is auspicious, subtle, and difficult to perceive; it is the domain of the Jinas, wherein no syllable or word is found, yet the Blessed One fully knows the enlightenment of the Buddhas.
The dhāraṇī which is a vast accumulation of knowledge has emerged from millions of billions of sūtras;
the Blessed One proclaims this samādhi, which is the domain of millions of billions of Buddhas.
This is the liberator from disease for the sick, the wealth acquired by Bodhisattvas;
it is praised by all Buddhas, proclaimed [by them], and honored by millions of billions of gods.
Always avoided by non-Buddhists who incite all foolish people,
this supreme wealth of ethical discipline praised by the Buddhas is unsullied like lightning in the sky.
Those wise ones who have honored tens of millions of Jinas by practicing generosity and morality,
and who have avoided evil friends in the past, possess an unsurpassed paternal inheritance.
There stood a monk, a preacher of the Dharma, living the holy life as a true son of the Sugata;
having heard this conformable Dharma, he fixed his mind upon the Leader of the World.
The leader Indraketudhvajarāja addressed the Dharma-preacher:
"The state of being a monk is supreme, yet it is difficult; the resolve for the sake of excellent, supreme enlightenment is even more so."
Guard your ethical discipline like a precious jewel, and always attend upon favorable friends;
never associate with evil companions, and you will before long attain the wisdom of a Buddha.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter of the *Śrī-Samādhirāja*, titled "The Chapter on King Indraketudhvaja."
Chapter 21: The Previous Account.
Formerly, in this world called Jambudvīpa, there were two sons of a merchant who were heedful.
Having gone forth in the teaching of the Sugata, they became like rhinoceroses, dwelling in the forest groves.

Possessing supernatural powers, having attained the four dhyānas, skilled in poetry and treatises, and well-trained; conversant with the stages of the path in the intermediate space, they travel through the sky without attachment.
And there, in that cool, delightful forest grove filled with various flowers and frequented by flocks of various birds and winged creatures, they engaged one another in conversation.
While the king was wandering on a hunt, he heard a sound and approached that forest;
having seen the two Dharma-preachers there, the monarch conceived the highest affection for them.
Having engaged in a conversation that was in accordance with the truth with them, he sat down before the king;
an infinite army of that king, numbering sixty quintillion, arrived there.
One by one, those Dharma-preachers said to the king: "Listen, O Kṣatriya!
The state of Buddhahood is supreme and extremely difficult to attain; therefore, O Ruler, always remain heedful."
Life always passes away without staying, flowing swiftly like the water of a mountain river;
for you who are afflicted by disease, sorrow, and old age, there is no protection other than wholesome karma.
O elephant among kings, be a protector of the Dharma; guard this teaching of the One Possessed of the Ten Powers.
In this most dreadful and final age, O elephant among kings, remain on the side of the Dharma.
Thus did those wise ones advise the lord of men in many ways;
at that time, together with sixty million followers, the king then generated the mind of awakening.
Having heard the Dharma then as it was being spoken by all those gentle ones, that elephant among kings,
filled with joy, delighted, and uplifted, bowed his head at their feet and departed.
Many other monks, desiring gain, entered that family of the king;
having observed their conduct, which was not such [as he expected], the king did not show them the same respect.
And that teaching, its Teacher having passed away, exists in its final years;
in Jambudvīpa, the vessels [of disciples] are very few, and many who are unrestrained have appeared.
There were many monks there who were greedy and eager for gain, holding the view of objective existence;
having strayed from the teaching of the Sugata, they then largely induced the king to adopt their views.
"Kill both these Dharma-preachers, those heretics who proclaim annihilation! They incite people to a long wandering; they do not show anything of true extinction."
"Karma perishes, its ripening perishes; the aggregates do not exist"—thus say the deceivers.
O King, banish them from your realm, and in this way the Dharma will endure for a long time.
Having heard those words, the elephant among kings immediately felt a longing to seize them, thinking:
"I shall have these two preachers of the Dharma killed, lest they be neglected and some misfortune befall them."
A deity who had followed that king throughout his previous births and had practiced the holy life together with him—
a wise one who longed for his welfare— then spoke to the royal sovereign:
O Kṣatriya, do not give rise to such a thought at the word of an evil friend;
O Bhikṣu, do not, because of the word of an evil friend, cause these two Dharma-preachers to be killed.
"O Lord of Men, do you not remember anything that was spoken by them in the forest grove? At this time of exhaustion, most terrible, O elephant among kings, remain on the side of the Dharma!
Urged by these words of truth, the king did not neglect the teaching of the Jinas."
At that time, the king’s brother, who was cruel and lived on the border, was incited by them:
"O King, this wicked brother of yours never finds joy in life.
And those two monks, terrible practitioners of medicine, traveled through the sky by means of their magical spells.
Having heard this, we have all come to your presence; we now make this request of you:
quickly execute these terrible physicians, lest there be regret for you later.
Having thus armed himself, that elephant among kings set out at the word of his evil friend;
surrounded by his entire army, the monarch approached the forest where the monk resided.

Having recognized that the king was fierce and extremely cruel, the nāgas, yakṣas, and forest-dwellers who were stationed there caused a rain of stones to fall upon him; thus the king was slain along with his army.
Behold how, by the words of an evil friend, that king then met a terrible end; because he gave way to anger toward a Dharma-preacher, he went to the Avīci hell for sixty births.
Those many monks who were proponents of objective apprehension caused the Kṣatriya king to believe;
for hundreds of millions of births, inconceivable even, they experienced sensations within the hells.
By that deity by whom the Dharma-preachers were urged and protected,
Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges were seen and honored while they were practicing their course.
No fewer than sixty quintillion beings heard the Dharma together with the King;
they have all generated the supreme mind of awakening, and many Buddhas have appeared in the vast world-systems.
In those [lifetimes], their lifespan lasted for many millions of eons; their wisdom was incomparable and inconceivable.
Having taught this entire auspicious samādhi to them all, those moons among bipeds passed into nirvāṇa.
Having heard these unsurpassed words, which are a collection of virtue, the quality of purity, and wisdom, be heedful and untiring; before long, you shall attain the wisdom of a Buddha.

You shall behold the Tathāgatas in the ten directions, their minds peaceful, with eyes of compassion and loving-kindness; they are the refuge and ultimate resort for all the world, and you shall see them releasing the rain of Dharma upon the universe. (30)
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter of the *Śrīsamādhirāja*, titled "The Chapter on Previous Yogas."
Chapter 22: The Exposition on the Body of the Tathāgata.
Then the Blessed One addressed the youth Candraprabha: "Therefore, young man, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, being unattached to the body and unattached to life..."
One should be free from attachment.
For what reason?
Because, young man, it is due to the obsession with body and life that the formation of unwholesome dharmas occurs.
Therefore, young man, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not perceive the Tathāgata by means of the form-body (*rūpakāya*).
Why is that?
For the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*); they are manifested as the Dharma-body and not manifested as the form-body.
Therefore, young man, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who desires to seek the body of a Tathāgata and who desires to know the body of a Tathāgata should take up this samādhi, master it, retain it,
recite it, propagate it, explain it, study it, and have it read; he should be devoted to the practice of its cultivation and [teach it] to others.
It should be proclaimed in detail.

In this regard, young man, the body of the Tathāgata is produced by a wisdom born of a hundred merits; it is the manifestation of manifold meanings, born of the Dharma, signless, free from all signs, profound, immeasurable, possessing immeasurable qualities, and having the nature of the signless.
The *dharmakāya* is to be understood as that which is free from all signs, immovable, non-abiding, having the nature of absolute space, invisible, and transcending the path of the eye;
it is inconceivable, beyond the realm of the mind, unshakable by pleasure or pain, transcending all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), and inexpressible.

The dwelling of those who desire to seek the wisdom of a Buddha has been described as transcending the path of sound, yet possessing a core; as transcending passion; as being indivisible, having transcended the path of hatred; and as being firm, having transcended the path of delusion.
Through the teaching of emptiness, it is unborn, having transcended birth; it is untainted, having transcended karmic ripening; and it is eternal in its conventional expression.
And conventional practice is empty, indistinguishable from nirvana;
it is ceased by sound and stilled by resonance.
The conventional is established by means of convention;
convention is established by means of the ultimate truth; and the ultimate truth is established by means of true speech.
It is cool, free from burning anguish, signless, unthought, blameless, and non-proliferated— having few words in its description.
It is limitless in the description of its qualities,
born from the cultivation of the great superknowledges, and not far from the description of the cultivation of the great superknowledges due to its lack of recollection.
This, young man, is called the body of the Tathāgata.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
"If one wishes to know such a body as that of the Lord of the World,
one will come to know the body of the Buddha by cultivating this samādhi."
The Buddha’s body, born of merit, is pure and radiant;
it is equal to space, and no diversity can be found in it.
Just as is the awakening of the Buddha, so are his marks;
just as are his marks, so indeed is his body.
The body characterized by perfect enlightenment is indeed such a buddha-field;
the powers, the liberations, and the meditative concentrations—all these, too, possess a single characteristic.
Such is the manner of the arising of the Buddhas, the Lords of the World;
it can never be seen by anyone with the physical eye.
Many will speak thus: "I have seen the Leader of the World;
with his body the color of gold, he illuminates the entire world."
Through the empowerment of the Buddhas, by their majestic power and miraculous transformations,
that body is seen adorned with the various marks.
The body of the Buddha is shown in its height and circumference, yet no measure of the body can be found; therefore, he is inconceivable.
If the extent of the Buddha’s body could be measured,
the Teacher would be no different from gods or humans.
The maturation of the concentrated mind also possesses that same characteristic;
name-and-form, possessing that characteristic, becomes pure and luminous.
And this peaceful samādhi has never been cultivated by anyone else as it has been practiced here by the Lord of the World for ten million eons.
Although this samādhi has been produced by many pure qualities,
because of the vastness of this samādhi, my body is not seen.
Whatever kind of mind you have, such is your name-and-form;
for a mind that is devoid of intrinsic nature, name-and-form is without defining characteristics.
And for one in whom gross perception and so forth operate with respect to name-and-form,
a gross mind arises toward that which is of a different nature.
And for one whose perception regarding name-and-form is subtle,
the mind becomes luminous and free from greed toward name-and-form.
I remember throughout seven incalculable previous births;
at no time did the three evil perceptions ever arise within me.
For inconceivable millions of eons, my mind has been free from outflows;
I work for the benefit of sentient beings, yet my body is not seen.
And just as for one whose mind has become liberated from phenomena,
there is no further meeting with those phenomena.
My consciousness is liberated from all entities in every respect;
having known the intrinsic nature of the mind, knowledge proceeds further.
My emanations go to thousands of millions of fields and perform the welfare of sentient beings where no [physical] body is found.
Without characteristics and signless, just like the sky;
my body is inexpressible, shown to be difficult to comprehend.
The Great Hero is the Dharmakāya; his body is produced through the Dharma. The Jina can never be fully defined by means of a form-body (rūpakāya).
Upon hearing this exposition of the discourse, Māra the Evil One shall find no opportunity for entry into one who experiences joy.
And having heard the profound Dharma, he who shall have no fear will not,
for the sake of his own life, reject the awakening of a Buddha.
He will know the true teaching of thousands of millions of ultimate realities;
becoming a light for the worlds, wherever he goes, [he shall illuminate them].
In that regard, young man, the body of the Tathāgata cannot easily be known even by means of signs or actions;
it is not blue, nor blue-colored, nor blue-appearing, nor blue-shining; nor is it yellow, nor yellow-colored, nor yellow-appearing, nor yellow-shining.
Or red, or red-colored, or red in appearance, or red in luster; or white, or white-colored, or white in appearance, or white in luster;
or madder-red, or madder-red-colored, or madder-red in appearance, or madder-red in luster.
Or like crystal, or crystal-colored, or crystal-like in appearance, or crystal-like in luster; or like fire, or fire-colored, or fire-like in appearance, or fire-like in luster;
or like the surface of clarified butter, or clarified-butter-colored, or clarified-butter-like in appearance, or clarified-butter-like in luster.
Or golden, or gold-colored, or appearing as gold, or radiant as gold; or beryl, or beryl-colored, or appearing as beryl, or radiant as beryl;
or lightning, or lightning-colored, or appearing as lightning, or radiant as lightning.
Whether it be Brahmā or the color of Brahmā, or the appearance of Brahmā or the radiance of Brahmā;
whether it be a god or the color of a god, or the appearance of a god or the radiance of a god—
thus, O youth, the body of the Tathāgata is pure, inconceivable even by all signs, and its description is inconceivable through the perfection of its form-body.
It is not easy for the world, including the gods, to grasp the measure of his body; otherwise, it is inconceivable and immeasurable in all its aspects.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
"Whatever dust there is in the world-systems, which is perceived and designated as particles— "
Whatever water is in the springs, lakes, ponds, and oceans—no end to it can be found; such is the number of its atoms.
The water in the ocean might be possible to measure by means of tens of millions of hairs from a child's head;
yet no comparison equal to the Lord of the World has been revealed.
The drops of water are immeasurable, and likewise are the atoms.
I see that for a single sentient being, I am unable to know at one time the arising of their thoughts of resolute conviction, which are even more numerous than that.
The true colors of my physical form that I have displayed are such that all sentient beings, according to their inclinations, are unable to bear even a comparison with them.
And by the very act of taking signs, such an appearance of color is possible;
thus can the distinction of the Buddha be known as being such as mine.
The Buddhas are free from signs and are manifested as the Dharma-body;
they are profound and immeasurable, and for that reason the Buddhas are inconceivable.
The Buddha-body of the inconceivable Buddha is also inconceivable; for those bodies of his are manifested from the Dharma-body.
Even with the mind, it is not possible to conceive of the bodies of the Buddhas;
for indeed, no measure of that body can be apprehended.
For those immeasurable qualities were cultivated by me for tens of millions of eons;
therefore, this inconceivable and radiant body has been manifested by me.
Ungraspable by all sentient beings, it cannot be grasped by any means of measurement;
for the body of the Buddha is indeed immeasurable and inconceivable.
In immeasurable phenomena, a measure is conceptually constructed;
yet by means of phenomena that are beyond conceptual construction, even the Buddha is likewise beyond conceptual construction.
The conceptualized is said to be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), while the non-conceptualized is not a means of valid cognition.
Because he is non-conceptual, free from conceptualization, and thus inconceivable, the Buddha is beyond thought.
Just as space is immeasurable and cannot be measured by anyone,
so too is the body of the Buddha, exactly like space.
Those who thus understand the body of the Buddhas are the sons of the Victors;
they too shall become inconceivable Buddhas, protectors of the world.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter of the *Śrī-samādhirāja*, titled "The Exposition of the Tathāgata’s Body."
Chapter 23: The Exposition on the Inconceivability of the Tathāgata.
Therefore, O youth, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva should desire: "How might I personally realize the four analytical knowledges? [he should apply himself accordingly].
What are the four?

Namely, the analytical knowledge of meaning (arthapratisaṃvid), the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dharmapratisaṃvid), the analytical knowledge of expression (niruktipratisaṃvid), and the analytical knowledge of eloquence (pratibhānapratisaṃvid).
[He thinks: "May I directly realize these four analytical knowledges."
Therefore, young man, this samādhi must be taken up by the bodhisattva mahāsattva; it must be mastered, maintained, recited, promulgated, taught, studied, and extensively expounded to others.
Furthermore, he must be devoted to the practice of its cultivation.
In that regard, young man, what is the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*)?

Young man, a bodhisattva trains himself in this analytical knowledge of phenomena as follows: "As many as are the verbal expressions for form (*rūpa*), so many are the verbal expressions for the qualities of the Tathāgata;
and likewise for feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and mental formations (*saṃskāra*)."
"O youth, as many as are the expressions of consciousness, so many are the expressions of the Tathāgata’s physical form.
Thus, O youth, the expressions of the Tathāgata’s physical form and color are immeasurable, inconceivable, incalculable, incomparable, unquantifiable, and limitless.
Thus, O youth, the expressions of his physical form are boundless and infinite."
In this way, the verbal expressions of the Tathāgata’s form are inconceivable;
likewise are his feelings, perceptions, and mental formations.
Thus, indeed, the verbal expressions of consciousness are infinite, boundless, and inconceivable.
In this way, the verbal expressions of the Tathāgata’s qualities are inconceivable.
Thus, young man, the faults in the conditioned are immeasurable and incalculable;
the benefits in nirvāṇa are immeasurable and incalculable;
and the praises of the Tathāgata are incalculable.
Thus, O youth, as many as are the names for nirvāṇa, so many are the praises of the Tathāgata. Thus, O youth, the names for nirvāṇa are incalculable;
the praises of the Tathāgata are incalculable.
Young man, these four expressions of the Tathāgata’s praise are inconceivable and are inconceivable expressions.
What are the four?
Namely, the inconceivable expression regarding conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
The discourse on the vocal expression is inconceivable;
the discourse on affliction is inconceivable;
the discourse on purification is inconceivable.
Young man, these four expressions of the Tathāgata’s praise are inconceivable and are inconceivable expressions.
Young man, these four expressions of the Tathāgata’s praise are inconceivable and are inconceivable teachings;
they cannot easily be described by reaching their ultimate limit.
Which four?
This very same tetrad;
it should be explained in detail in this manner.
Namely: the four methods of the bodhisattvas, the four reasonings,
and the four doors.
There are four explanations,
four sounds,
and four paths of speech.
There are four modes of expression,
four types of communal discourse,
and four kinds of comprehension of names.
There are four ways of perceiving humans,
four types of responses,
and four gates.
There are four syllables,
four entries,
and four words.
There are four bases of accomplishment,
four phrases of the sūtras,
and four modes of conduct.
There are four inconceivable paths,
four equal paths,
and four infinite paths.
There are four paths that are limitless, four paths that are incalculable,
and four paths that are immeasurable.
There are four immeasurable paths,
four knowledges,
and four accumulations of knowledge.
There are four lineages of knowledge, four types of eloquence, and four accumulations of eloquence.
There are four lineages of eloquence,
four collections of discourses,
and four causes of eloquence.
There are four expositions of the sūtras,
four lineages of extensive learning,
and four treasures of the Buddha.
There are four trainings of a bodhisattva, four spheres of activity of a bodhisattva,
and four deeds of a bodhisattva.
There are four kinds of bodhisattva eloquence, four kinds of cultivation of the path,
and four kinds of abandonment of the afflictions.
The four abandonments of what is unwholesome, the four dispellings of non-knowledge, and the four relinquishings of ignorance.
There are four ways of pacifying suffering, four ways of abandoning mental distress,
and four ways of generating skillful means.
There are four abandonments of views,
four thorough knowledges of those reborn,
and four abandonments of the view of self.
There are four abandonments of the view of a sentient being, four abandonments of the view of a living soul,
and four abandonments of the view of a person.
There are four abandonments of the view of existence, four abandonments of entities,
and four abandonments of the view of apprehension.
It is not easy to describe them by defining their limits.
There are four dhāraṇīs.
What are the four?
Namely: the infinite discourse that explains all conditioned phenomena.
In that regard, the knowledge therein is this first dhāraṇī;
the infinite expression of vocal designations is the knowledge therein, which is this second dhāraṇī.
Infinite is the discourse on the censuring of afflictions;
the knowledge therein is this third dhāraṇī.
Infinite is the discourse on the qualities and benefits of purification.
In that regard, whatever knowledge there is, this is the fourth dhāraṇī.
These are the four dhāraṇīs.
Thus, O Youth, that which is dhāraṇī is knowledge; that is the Dharma.
Thus, through the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), there is the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dharmapratisaṃvid).
That which is the meaning within the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) is called the analytical knowledge of meaning (arthapratisaṃvid);
that which is the verbal expression within the knowledge of phenomena is [the analytical knowledge of dharma].

This is called the analytical knowledge of etymological interpretation (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*). Regarding the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), whatever teaching, declaration, designation, manifestation, establishment, investigation, analysis, elucidation, unimpeded speech, and non-stammering speech there is in conventional usage— this is called the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*).
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
"As great as is the knowledge of the Buddha, so great is the designation of form;
as far as there is the designation of form, so far is the verbal expression of form."
As many as there are verbal expressions for form, so many are the names for ethical discipline;
as many as there are names for ethical discipline, so many are the names for a Buddha.
As many as are the names of Buddhas and the names of sentient beings,
so many are the names of a single sentient being that I know.
The infinite expressions of names that were previously revealed by me—
those names of discipline, those names of Buddhas, and those names of sentient beings— are all equal.
As many as are the faults in the conditioned, so many are the virtues in nirvāṇa;
so many are the praises of the Buddha that have been revealed by me through similes.
As many as are the productions of thought shown by all sentient beings,
so many are the rays of light from a single hair-pore of the Lord of the World.
As many as are the names and inclinations of all sentient beings,
even more than those are the qualities of the tones of the Lord of Men that he utters.
Whatever names have been shown for all sentient beings are shown for a single sentient being;
those names of a single sentient being are shown for all sentient beings.
This crossing over by means of the analytical knowledges has been taught by the Buddha for the sake of the Bodhisattvas who possess infinite names and descriptions.
Whoever should wish to speak infinite millions of sūtras should,
having set forth this sūtra, proclaim it without shrinking back.
Unattached in the midst of the assembly, he proclaims millions of sūtras;
just as space is limitless, so does he speak the Dharma.
In the same way, for Bodhisattvas, those pure beings who are protectors,
by fully upholding this sūtra, there arise perfections of wisdom.
To the extent that one who has faith in this method explains it,
their wisdom increases like trees on the Himalayas.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter of the *Śrī-samādhirāja*, titled "The Exposition on the Inconceivability of the Tathāgata."
Chapter 24: The Entrance into the Analytical Knowledges (Pratisaṃvid).

In this regard, young man, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing in the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dharmapratisaṃvid), observing phenomena within phenomena, fully attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?

In this regard, young man, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, observing phenomena within phenomena, does not perceive awakening as something other than form; he does not practice for the sake of awakening apart from form;
he does not seek awakening apart from form.
One does not arrive at awakening through anything other than form; one does not cause sentient beings to undertake awakening through anything other than form;
and one does not perceive the Tathāgata through anything other than form.
One perceives the Tathāgata as the nature of the non-destruction of form;
one does not perceive it thus that form is one thing and the nature of form is another,
nor does one perceive it thus that the nature of form is one thing and the Tathāgata is another.

That which is the intrinsic nature of form and that which is the Tathāgata—this is the non-dual reality (*dharmatā*). Seeing thus, the bodhisattva mahāsattva courses in the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*).
In this way, he does not perceive awakening as being elsewhere than in feeling, nor elsewhere than in perception, nor elsewhere than in mental formations, nor elsewhere than in consciousness.
He does not practice for the sake of awakening apart from consciousness;
he does not seek awakening apart from consciousness;
he does not fully realize awakening apart from consciousness.
He does not exhort sentient beings toward awakening by means of anything other than consciousness;
he does not perceive the Tathāgata by means of anything other than consciousness.
He perceives the Tathāgata as the Tathāgata whose intrinsic nature is the indestructibility of consciousness.
One does not view consciousness as one thing and the intrinsic nature of consciousness as another;
nor does one view the intrinsic nature of consciousness as one thing and the Tathāgata as another.
That which is the intrinsic nature of consciousness and that which is the Tathāgata—this is the non-dual reality (dharmatā).
Seeing in this way, the bodhisattva mahāsattva courses in the analytical knowledge of phenomena.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
"Awakening was shown through form, and form was shown for the sake of awakening;
the supreme Dharma was taught by means of a dissimilar sound."
By means of sound, the subsequent form is profound by its very nature;
the form and awakening are equal, and no diversity is found in them.
Just as nirvāṇa is profound and not manifested by means of sound,
so too nirvāṇa is not attained, nor is that sound itself attained.
Sound and likewise nirvāṇa—neither of these two is found.
Thus, within empty phenomena, nirvāṇa is fully revealed.
Nirvāṇa is said to be cessation, yet nirvāṇa is not to be found;
through the very non-occurrence of phenomena, as it is afterwards, so it was before.
All phenomena are by their very nature equal to and like nirvāṇa,
as understood by those who are devoted to the essence of renunciation within the Buddha’s teaching.
Having seen the body of the Buddha, they will say, "The Guide has been seen";
yet I cannot be seen by anyone through the form-body (*rūpakāya*). (SRS 24.7)
The intrinsic nature of form has been understood, just as the characteristic of form is;
having realized the intrinsic nature of form, my body has been pointed out.
Thus, my knowledge of the five aggregates is the characteristic of phenomena;
having understood the intrinsic nature of phenomena, I am established in the Dharma-body.
I teach the Dharma to sentient beings, yet it does not issue forth from the Dharmakāya;
nor can the true nature of the Buddhas be expressed by means of speech.
Not understanding this method, upon hearing the word "Buddha," they will say,
by the mere sound of it, "I have seen the Leader of Men."
For one who has abandoned all perceptions, the perception of existence vanishes; for one who perceives sounds, there can never be a vision of the Teacher.
Whoever understands emptiness as having such a characteristic of form—
emptiness is not said to be one thing and the intrinsic nature of form another;
whoever understands form, he understands emptiness.
He who understands emptiness as having such a characteristic of form cannot be defeated again by millions of Māras.
For he who understands form understands emptiness;
he who understands emptiness understands nirvāṇa.
Not knowing this destination, those who grasp at objective referents are lost;
they perceive existence in non-existence and non-existence in existence.
Deceived by the gain of kinsmen, they have strayed from my teaching;
clinging to the notion of fruit while remaining in a state of stagnation, they are empty of the wealth of the ascetic life.
Lax and lacking in vigor, not established in the aggregate of ethical discipline, and being full of obstacles, they will say: "This is not the teaching of the Buddha."
Some will speak thus: "We have set out for enlightenment," yet they are untamed, undisciplined, and lacking mutual respect.
They will become seekers of fame and remain unestablished in the Dharma;
thus will that desire arise in the pursuit of reputation and gain.
Desirous of gain, they will indeed be preoccupied with congregations;
overcome by intoxication and negligence, they will seek after profit and honor.
Having emerged into gain and honor, seeking the profit of renown,
they will build stūpas and monasteries while being infatuated with women of good family.
Having emerged from objective perception and having emerged from the thirst for sensual desires,
they will nevertheless perform the work of householders while remaining within the domain of Māra.
They will teach householders that sensual desires are like the crest of a flame;
yet, having entered their homes, they will corrupt those families.
And among them there will be householders who regard [the monks] as teachers;
and when those [monks] have gone away, they will corrupt their wives and children.
Those who provide them with food and drink as an act of kindness will regard their wives and children as their own.
Householders will not be infatuated with their own wives as much as those who,
having gone forth, are infatuated with the wives of others.
The training in white robes that was shown to householders will not exist for those monks at that time.
They will offer me worship with kettledrums, conchs, and clay drums;
yet that which is the supreme worship—right practice—will not exist.
Being themselves of very poor conduct, when they see those established in morality, they will say to one another: "These people are just like us."
Having heard this praise of your ethical discipline, those of immoral conduct who dwell in evil spheres will become agitated and say, "This was certainly not spoken by the Buddha."
They will have no sense of shame; their spiritual wealth as renunciants will be lost.
Urged on by false speech, they will reject the awakening of a Buddha.
Having abandoned the teaching of the Buddha with malicious intent and having rejected the Dharma, their dwelling shall be in Avīci.
I have neither heard nor seen those established in the ways of fools who, while possessing such conduct, will attain the wisdom of a Buddha.
Whatever hypocrisy, deceit, or verbal pretension they may have therein, I know it all; my knowledge operates in this regard.
Even if I were to speak for an eon regarding their many transgressions,
I would only have proclaimed a mere fraction of the vows of those bodhisattvas.
"O Prince, there will be no evil that those [beings] will not commit;
you should not associate with them in the final age."
You should address them and converse with them, and you should show them respect;
without being disheartened, you should honor them for the sake of supreme enlightenment.
Having inquired about the number of years since their ordination, one who is senior to another should show him respect by bowing his head at his feet.
One should not look for the faults of those who behold the seat of awakening;
one should not give rise to resentment, but should always maintain a mind of loving-kindness.
If one should see a lapse in these [practitioners], one should not proclaim their faults;
for whatever kind of action one performs, one will receive a corresponding fruit.
With a moon-like face brightened by a smile, he should always be the first to speak toward both the elders and the novices; humble in spirit and gentle in nature.
"You should show them favor with robes and alms-food;
thus you should direct your mind: 'All shall become leaders.'"
If they should entreat you for the sake of the gift of Dharma, you should speak these first words: "I am not trained in the Vaipulya."
Thus you should speak these words: "Venerable one, you are wise and learned;
how could I possibly speak in the presence of such great beings?"
One should not speak to them impulsively, but rather after having weighed their capacity as a vessel;
if one recognizes them to be a suitable vessel, one should teach even without being requested.
If you see many who are of immoral conduct present in the assembly, do not speak of ascetic austerity; rather, you should proclaim the praise of giving.
If they should be few in desire, pure, and established in ethical discipline,
you should generate a mind of loving-kindness and deliver a discourse conducive to ascetic refinement.
If those with evil desires are few and those endowed with ethical discipline are many, then,
having gained a following, one should proclaim the praise of ethical discipline.
Having first ascertained the assembly, if it should be pure,
then one should reveal all wholesome dharmas to them.
One should always praise and proclaim generosity, ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, and learning, as well as contentment, fewness of desires, and austerity.
One should speak in praise of dwelling in the forest, the bliss of meditative concentration, and the avoidance of living in a crowd; for by doing so, one will maintain happiness.
One should not abandon dwelling in the forest, nor should one become solely intent on moral discipline; one should cultivate solitary retreat, yet not become solely intent on generosity.
And having established oneself in the aggregate of ethical discipline, one should acquire great learning;
seeking this samādhi, one should honor the relics of the Teacher.
Seeking peaceful samādhi, one should perform worship of the Buddha with parasols, banners, flags, perfumes, garlands, and ointments.
One should employ musical performances with delightful instruments;
one should worship the relic of the Buddha, being neither dejected nor indolent.
With as many perfumes, garlands, incense, powders, and garments as there may be,
one should worship the Lord for the sake of the Buddha-knowledge.
Whatever worship there may be— immeasurable and inconceivable—
one should perform it for all the Buddhas while seeking this peaceful samādhi.
One should impartially give one's own share to all sentient beings, being without dependence,
while seeking unattached knowledge, the unsurpassed knowledge of a Buddha.
I too have performed inconceivable worship to former Buddhas,
having become non-reliant while seeking this peaceful samādhi.
The arising of Buddhas is difficult to encounter; human existence is difficult to obtain;
faith in the teaching, the going forth, and full ordination are difficult to find.
Since you have pleased the Teacher and directed your mind toward awakening,
do not waver from your vow, but remain steadfast in your practices.
Whoever should uphold this sūtra when the time of destruction has arrived will quickly obtain eloquence, provided they maintain it as it has been set forth.
The mass of merit from retaining even a single verse is inconceivable;
how much more so for one who seeks the meaning of what they have heard and retains the entire sūtra?
Whoever, indeed, unweariedly honors all sentient beings who have attained awakening, and whoever always acts with reverence toward them for as many eons as there are sentient beings; SRS_24.65.
Compared to this samādhi, even one who should retain a single verse does not approach even a sixteenth part of all that former merit.
Through the wisdom of a Buddha, I know the inconceivable benefits for one who,
having heard this samādhi here, shall harbor no doubt.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter of the *Śrī-Samādhirāja*, titled "The Entrance into the Analytical Knowledges" (*Pratisaṃvidavatāra*).
(Vaidya 155) Chapter 25: On Rejoicing.
Then the Blessed One addressed the youth Candraprabha once again: "Therefore, young man, a bodhisattva mahāsattva must be skillful in means."
And how, young man, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva become skilled in means?
Here, young man, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should generate the perception of kin toward all sentient beings.
Having established a mind of kinship toward all sentient beings, he should rejoice in every mass of roots of goodness and merit belonging to all sentient beings.

Having rejoiced in the mass of roots of goodness and merit of all sentient beings for three nights and three days, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should dedicate it to those very same sentient beings with the production of a thought directed toward omniscience.
By means of this root of goodness, the bodhisattva mahāsattva quickly attains this samādhi and quickly awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
"All these beings here are my kinsmen; whatever vast mass of merit they possess, I rejoice in it three times by night and three times by day, having generated such a thought."
I rejoice in those whose ethical discipline is perfectly pure, who do not commit evil even for the sake of their lives;
I rejoice in whatever merit belongs to those Bodhisattvas who are endowed with resolute faith.
I rejoice in those who have faith in the Buddha, who have faith in the Dharma, and likewise in the Saṅgha;
I rejoice in those who perform worship to the Sugata while aspiring for awakening.
I rejoice in those who have no view of a self, no view of phenomena, and no view of a living being;
I rejoice in those who have no evil views and who, having seen emptiness, give rise to joy.
I rejoice in those who, within the teaching of the Sugata, obtain the going forth and full ordination;
those who dwell in the forest with few desires and contentment, whose conduct is peaceful, and whose sphere of activity is meditative concentration.
I rejoice in those who dwell alone without a second, always like rhinoceroses in the forest;
pure in livelihood, always with few duties, they do not practice deceit for the sake of gain.
I rejoice in those who have no intimacy with others, nor envy, nor craving for families;
they are constantly terrified of the three realms and wander in the world unstained.
I rejoice in those for whom there is no conceptual proliferation, who are weary of all rebirths in existence,
who are free from conflict and possess peaceful minds— for them, this samādhi is not difficult to attain.

I rejoice in those sons of the Sugata who, seeing the faults of the crowd, have abandoned all disputes; having taken refuge at the roots of trees in the forest, they dwell in the wilderness, making liberation their essence.
I rejoice in those who dwell in the forest, who do not exalt themselves nor disparage others;
I rejoice in those who have no negligence and are heedful in this teaching of the Buddha.
However many extensive factors conducive to awakening there may be, this heedfulness is indeed the root of them all;
for those sons of the Buddha who are always heedful, this samādhi is not difficult to attain.
The teaching of the Sugatas is the attainment of a treasure; the attainment of going forth is the second treasure;
the attainment of faith is the third treasure; and this samādhi is the fourth treasure. (SRS 25.12)
Having heard this emptiness, the domain of the Buddhas, not rejecting it is the attainment of a treasure;
infinite eloquence is the attainment of a treasure, and that which is dhāraṇī is the supreme treasure.

Whatever wholesome qualities have been proclaimed—virtue, learning, generosity, and likewise patience—the root of them all is indeed this heedfulness; it is taught by the Sugata as the attainment of a treasure-store.

For those who are heedful here in the teaching of the Buddha, and whose aspiration is perfectly formed, this samādhi is not difficult to obtain; it has become near for them within this teaching of the Buddha.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter of the *Śrīsamādhirāja*, titled "The Chapter on Rejoicing."
(Vaidya 158) Chapter 26: The Praise of Giving.
Therefore, O youth, you should train yourself in this way: "I shall be heedful."
For, O youth, for a diligent bodhisattva mahāsattva, unsurpassed perfect enlightenment is not difficult to attain; how much less so this samādhi!
And how, O youth, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva become diligent?
In this regard, young man, a bodhisattva mahāsattva possesses completely pure ethical discipline.
In this regard, young man, a bodhisattva who possesses completely pure ethical discipline becomes heedful.
In this regard, young man, a bodhisattva mahāsattva possesses completely pure ethical discipline.

In this regard, young man, a bodhisattva mahāsattva whose ethical discipline is completely pure is never separated from the mind of omniscience regarding the six perfections. He possesses these benefits; listen to them, and attend to them well and thoroughly.
I shall speak to you, O youth. There are these ten benefits for a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is devoted to giving. What are the ten?
Namely, his affliction of stinginess is subdued;
his mind is always fortified by generosity;
and he extracts the essence from enjoyments shared with many people.
He is reborn into families of great wealth;
as soon as he is born, a mind of renunciation manifests before him,
and he becomes beloved by the fourfold assembly.
Confident and unshrinking, he enters the assembly;
and his noble reputation, fame, renown, and verses of praise rise up throughout the world in every direction and intermediate direction.
His hands and feet are soft and tender, and he stands with the soles of his feet level and well-set.
And he remains never separated from spiritual friends until he sits at the seat of enlightenment.
These, young man, are the ten benefits for a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is devoted to giving.
In this regard, it is said:
"Jealousy is subdued by you, and the mind of renunciation is increased;
having grasped the essence, one is born into a prosperous family. (SRS 26.1)
As soon as he is born, his mind is directed toward renunciation;
he becomes beloved by all beings, both those who live at home and those who have gone forth.
Confident in assemblies, he enters among them with a majestic form;
his noble reputation spreads throughout the villages and cities.
Their hands and feet will become soft and not difficult to obtain;
they will find virtuous friends, as well as Buddhas and even Śrāvakas.
A mind of stinginess never arises in him; his mind always delights in acts of generosity.
He becomes beloved by many millions of sentient beings—these are the benefits for one who is free from stinginess.
He is born into a family of great wealth, and once born, his mind delights in renunciation; having extracted the essence, he passes away without envy—these are the benefits. (SRS 26.6)
Confident, he enters the assemblies, and his noble fame spreads throughout the quarters.
His hands and feet are always born soft; these are the benefits for one who is free from envy.
For one who beholds the Buddhas and their disciples, virtuous friends will not be difficult to find;
having seen them, they worship them with serene faith and without stinginess—these are the benefits.
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter of the *Śrīsamādhirāja*, titled "The Chapter on the Benefits of Generosity."
Chapter 27: The Exposition of Ethical Discipline.
Young man, there are these ten benefits for a bodhisattva mahāsattva whose ethical discipline is completely pure.
What are the ten?
Namely: he purifies and fulfills his knowledge;
he trains himself in emulation of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones.
He is not censured by the wise;
he does not waver from his commitment;
he stands firm in practice.
He flees from saṃsāra,
attains nirvāṇa,
and dwells free from the outbursts of the defilements.
He attains meditative concentration and becomes free from poverty;
these, young man, are the ten benefits for a bodhisattva mahāsattva of pure ethical discipline.
In this regard, it is said:
He brings wisdom to full completion and trains in the footsteps of the Buddhas;
he is never censured by the wise and is always confident.
He does not waver from his vow and remains steadfast in practice;
by means of this, he inclines toward nirvāṇa and flees from saṃsāra.
Free from the outbursts of affliction, he dwells and swiftly attains meditative concentration;
established in the aggregate of ethical discipline, he becomes free from poverty.
His knowledge becomes fully perfected, and he trains himself further in the ways of the Tathāgatas; for his morality is utterly pure, the wise do not reproach him. (SRS 27.4)
That wise one does not waver from what has been promised, for he is a hero established in practice;
having seen that saṃsāra possesses many faults, he flees toward that by which he goes to nirvāṇa.
The mind of such a person does not become agitated, for they are thus established in the power of ethical discipline;
they quickly attain a concentration free from afflictions—these are the benefits of pure ethical discipline.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter of the *Śrī-Samādhirāja*, titled "The Exposition of Ethical Conduct."
(Vaidya 161) Chapter 28: The Ten Benefits.
Young man, there are these ten benefits for a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is established in patience and dwells in loving-kindness.
Which ten?
One is not burned by fire;
one is not killed by a weapon.
Poison does not take effect upon him;
he does not die by water;
and deities protect him.
He obtains a body adorned with the primary marks;
the doors to all miserable rebirths are closed for him,
and his rebirth occurs in the Brahma-world.
His days and nights pass in happiness,
and the joy and bliss do not leave his body.
These, young man, are the ten benefits for a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is established in patience and dwells in loving-kindness.
In this regard, it is said: He is not burned by fire, nor is he slain by a weapon;
poison does not affect his body, and he does not die in water.
The deities protect him, and he possesses the thirty-two marks;
for him, the miserable states of existence are closed off—these are the benefits of patience.
Then, the state of Brahmā and the state of Śakra will not be difficult for him to attain;
he dwells in constant happiness, and his joy becomes inconceivable.
He is never slain by fire or weapon, nor does he die from poison while in the water;
likewise, gods, nāgas, and yakṣas protect him—these are the benefits for one who dwells in loving-kindness.
Thirty-two marks appear upon his body, and he shall never again undergo downfall;
having passed away, he is reborn in the city of Brahmā—these are the benefits for one who abides in patience.
His days and nights pass in happiness, and his body becomes suffused with joy;
established in the power of patience and gentleness, that wise one is always possessed of a serene mind.
Young man, there are these ten benefits for a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has initiated vigor.
What are the ten?
Namely, he becomes difficult to overcome.
He obtains the protection of the Buddhas,
he becomes protected by the deities,
and having heard the teachings, they do not decline from him.
One attains dharmas never heard before,
attains the lineage of meditative concentration,
and becomes free from illness.
Furthermore, his food is properly digested,
and he becomes like a lotus, not like a pestle.
Prince, these are the ten benefits for a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who has initiated vigor.
In this regard, it is said:
He is always difficult to assail, and no burning affliction exists for him.
The deities protect him, and he quickly beholds the Buddhas.
What has been heard is not lost for him, and what has not been heard comes before his face;
he fulfills his vow—these are the qualities of the energetic one.
He attains the lineage of meditative concentration, and illness does not arise in him;
his food and drink are digested with ease, and he does not fall into despondency.
Just as a blue lotus grows gradually in the midst of the water,
even so does the bodhisattva increase by means of pure qualities.
His nights and days pass not in vain;
such will be the fruit for him at the time of death.
These benefits have been proclaimed for those bodhisattvas endowed with vigor, by the Tathāgata who, having exerted vigor, attained [enlightenment] over many eons.
One who has initiated vigor becomes difficult to overcome and is embraced by the Victors;
even the gods conceive longing for such a person, and before long they shall attain the awakening of a Buddha.
His learning never diminishes, and he acquires other vast dharmas as well;
his inspired eloquence increases exceedingly—these are the benefits for one who has initiated vigor.
He quickly attains the lineage of meditative concentration, and he never suffers from illness;
just as when he eats food there, it is digested by him with ease.
For one who has initiated vigor and is untiring, there is a bright fortnight day and night;
for such a person, endowed with the powers of vigor, awakening will also be attained before long.
"Furthermore, young man, there are these ten benefits for a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is devoted to meditative concentration. What are the ten?"
That is to say: he abides in proper conduct,
he moves within his proper sphere,
and he dwells free from the fever of affliction.
He has his sense faculties guarded;
he experiences joy;
he is secluded from sensual desires.
Unsatiated by meditations,
liberated from the realm of Māra,
and established in the realm of the Buddhas.
He brings liberation to full maturity.
These, young man, are the ten benefits for a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is devoted to meditative concentration.
In this regard, it is said:
He does not become one of improper conduct, for he is firmly established in proper conduct;
the yogi moves within his proper range and avoids what is not his range.
Dwelling free from burning anguish, with senses guarded and well-restrained,
he experiences the sublime joy that is the domain of one who meditates in dhyāna.
Detached from the thirst for sensual desires, he cultivates the bliss of meditative concentration;
liberated from the realm of Māra, he abides within the sphere of the Buddhas.
For this is the distinction of the yogin: that he alone delights in the forest and brings liberation to full maturity; that is the tenth stage.
That bodhisattva stands in right conduct, having abandoned all improper conduct;
having avoided what is not a proper sphere of activity, he abides in the proper sphere. These are the benefits for one endowed with meditative concentration.
For one who has touched the noble, non-material happiness here, no fever ever arises;
they become cool in body and mind—these are the benefits for one endowed with meditative concentration.
He dwells in forest retreats, guarded, and for him there is never any distraction;
he attains therein a joy free from worldly desire, for he is thus physically secluded.
Unstained by desires and undefiled, for he is thus liberated from the realm of Māra;
established in the domain of the Tathāgatas, his liberation reaches full maturity.
Young man, there are these ten benefits for a bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices wisdom.
What are the ten? Namely: he becomes one who relinquishes all his possessions, yet he does not consider himself purified by that giving.
He possesses unbroken morality and yet does not rely on that morality;
he is well-established in the power of patience and yet does not dwell upon the perception of a "being";
and he is one who has initiated vigor while remaining physically and mentally secluded.
He becomes one who meditates in meditation, yet he is one whose meditation is non-abiding;
he becomes invincible to the Māras and unshakable by all opponents.
He gains insight into the course of all conditioned phenomena,
and his great compassion toward all sentient beings becomes supreme;
furthermore, he no longer aspires to the levels of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.
He enters into the meditations, concentrations, and attainments of a Buddha.
These, young man, are the ten benefits for a bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices wisdom.
In this regard, it is said:
The wise person renounces all possessions, yet does not consider that as purification;
he maintains unbroken ethical discipline, yet has no dependence upon it.
That wise one cultivates patience, having turned away from the perception of a sentient being;
he exerts vigor, being detached in body and mind.
He becomes one who meditates in meditation, unestablished and independent;
he becomes invincible to Māras—these are the qualities of the wise.
He becomes unshakable by all those who propound opposing views;
having attained light within saṃsāra, such are the qualities of wisdom.
He attains great compassion toward all sentient beings;
he never yearns for the knowledge of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
One does not consider purity to come from the renunciation of all possessions, nor is one dependent on moral conduct while possessing unbroken virtue;
one cultivates patience without the perception of a "being"—
these are the benefits for one resolved upon wisdom.
One becomes one who has initiated vigor, liberated, meditating without dependence and without a fixed abode;
that wise one becomes invincible to Māra—these are the benefits for one resolved upon wisdom.
One becomes unshakable by the proponents of other doctrines and attains a firm footing here within the conditioned;
one generates intense compassion for sentient beings—these are the benefits of being resolved upon wisdom.
Neither toward the Pratyekabuddhas nor toward the Śrāvakas does a longing for them ever arise in him;
for he is established in the qualities of a Buddha. These are the advantages of being resolved upon wisdom.
Young man, there are these ten benefits for a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is learned.
What are the ten?
Namely, that he does not produce affliction.
He does not give rise to ill will; he dispels doubt;
and he straightens his view.
He avoids the wrong path,
stands firm upon the path,
and abides at the gateway to the deathless.
One stands close to awakening;
one becomes a source of light for sentient beings;
and one has no fear of the miserable realms.
Young man, these are the ten benefits for a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is learned.
In this regard, it is said:
These ten benefits of great learning have been proclaimed by the Tathāgata, the Buddha, who knows things as they truly are.
He understands both sides: defilement and purification;
having completely abandoned defilement, he stands upon the path of purification.
The wise one dispels doubt and straightens his view;
he abandons the wrong path for the road and stands upon the straight path.
He stands at the gateway to the deathless and draws near to awakening;
becoming a light for sentient beings, he fears no miserable rebirths.
He understands the manifold phenomena that lead to affliction, and likewise he understands the side of purification.
Having completely abandoned affliction, he trains himself in the supreme Dharma of purification.
He dispels the doubt of all living beings, and his vision becomes ever-shining;
having abandoned the wrong path, he always abides on the straight and auspicious way.
He always stands at the gateway to the deathless; he is near to vast awakening.
He becomes a great light for all living beings, and he does not fear the miserable realms.
Young man, there are these ten benefits for a bodhisattva mahāsattva who values the gift of Dharma and bestows the gift of Dharma upon others.
What are the ten?
Namely, that he avoids non-action.
He enters into action;
he establishes himself in the dharma of true persons;
he purifies the buddha-field.
He offers up the seat of enlightenment,
relinquishes material things,
and subdues the afflictions.
He gives a share to all sentient beings,
cultivates loving-kindness directed toward them as its object,
and attains happiness pertaining to the present life.
Young man, these are the ten benefits for a bodhisattva mahāsattva who values the gift of Dharma and bestows the gift of Dharma upon others.
In this regard, it is said:
"For whoever gives the supreme gift of Dharma without stinginess, ten benefits for him have indeed been proclaimed by the Lord of the World."
The wise person avoids all non-action and engages in purposeful action;
the true person, established in the Dharma, cultivates a mind of renunciation.
He purifies a buddha-field and that field becomes unsurpassed;
having ascended to the seat of awakening, this is the fruit of the gift of Dharma.
He renounces all things and trains under the King of Dharma;
his afflictions are subdued, and for him, awakening is not difficult to attain.
With a mind of loving-kindness, he bestows a share upon all sentient beings;
he becomes free from envy and attains superhuman happiness.
The wise one avoids non-action; he is always established in action.
The wise one who always gives the gift of Dharma is forever established in the qualities of the Great-Souled Ones.
His field shall always be pure, and the factors conducive to awakening will increase;
he will always remain near the seat of awakening—these are the benefits of giving the Dharma.
Afflictions do not exist for one who has relinquished all things and thoroughly understood things by their own specific characteristics;
being liberated from all forms of grasping, he never experiences attachment.
When the mind of the wise one is thus established, [he thinks: "May all sentient beings be happy.
With a mind of loving-kindness and free from envy, he experiences no small amount of happiness in this very life.
Young man, there are these ten advantages for a bodhisattva mahāsattva who dwells in emptiness.
What are the ten?
Namely, he dwells by means of the dwelling of a Buddha.
He meditates without dependence;
he does not crave rebirth;
he does not cling to his moral conduct.
He does not disparage the noble ones;
he dwells without conflict;
he does not apprehend any objective entity.
He remains secluded;
he does not slander the Buddhas;
and he upholds the true Dharma.
Young man, these are the ten benefits for a bodhisattva mahāsattva who dwells in emptiness.
In this regard, it is said:
That dwelling which belongs to the lords of men and is the sphere of all Buddhas—
in that the yogi dwells, where no living being is to be found.
Unreliant upon anything in the entire world, he does not abandon noble meditation;
having seen the intrinsic nature of phenomena, he does not pray for rebirth.
For one whose ethical discipline is untainted, there shall be a discipline that is non-reliant;
such a person does not disparage any other noble one who is free from outflows.
He dwells without conflict; no dispute exists for him.
The yogi does not perceive any objective entity; he always dwells in solitude.
Relying on the dharmas of emptiness, a fearless one who has realized the truth with his own body would not slander the Buddha even for the sake of his life.
He reverently upholds the Dharma of all the Protectors of the World— the inconceivable awakening of the Buddhas— and has no doubt regarding the qualities of a Buddha.
Those abodes of the bulls among men, wherein there is no ground for the many heretics—
in those, the bodhisattva dwells here, wherein there is no sentient being, no life-force, and no person.
He never has any dependence; independent, he cultivates the bliss of meditation.
Having realized that phenomena are without self and without sentient beings, the perception of arising never occurs to him.
For one who understands the intrinsic nature of phenomena, there is here no reliance whatsoever even upon ethical discipline;
such a person never considers purification to come through discipline, yet always maintains serene confidence toward the noble ones.
No contradiction ever arises for one who has discerned that all intrinsic natures are empty;
nor does such a person misrepresent the Leaders, having upheld the true Dharma of the Tathāgatas.
Young man, there are these ten advantages for a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is devoted to solitary retreat.
What are the ten?
That is to say: his mind becomes untroubled;
he dwells with vigilance;
and he recollects the Buddha.
He has faith in the practice;
he does not doubt wisdom;
and he is grateful.
He does not reject the Dharma of the Buddhas;
he dwells well-restrained;
and he attains the stage of the tamed.
He realizes the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).
These, young man, are the ten benefits for a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is devoted to solitary retreat (*pratisaṃlayana*).
In this regard, it is said:
The mind becomes untroubled, and all forms of negligence are abandoned; Free from negligence, one dwells within the sphere of solitary retreat.
Having heard the conduct of the Buddhas, the Lords of the World, the yogi places faith in them; he has no doubt regarding the inconceivable wisdom of the Buddha.
He is grateful toward the Buddhas and has no doubt regarding the Buddha-dharmas;
he dwells well-restrained, established on the stage of the tamed.
He who always delights in solitude, having abandoned gain and honor, and whose sphere of activity is secluded meditation, attains the analytical knowledges.
His mind becomes untroubled, and all forms of negligence have been abandoned by him;
this great being is always heedful—these are the benefits for one endowed with concentration.
Remembering the Buddhas, the supreme among bipeds, one has faith in their unsurpassed conduct;
one does not doubt the wisdom of the Tathāgatas—these are the benefits for one endowed with samādhi.
He is always grateful toward the Buddhas; he would never cast away the Dharma for the sake of his life.
He dwells perpetually well-restrained and endowed with meditative concentration—these are the benefits.
Having attained the stage of self-mastery, he quickly realizes the analytical knowledges;
possessing unassailable speech and eloquence, he speaks millions of billions of sūtras.
He quickly grasps the enlightenment of a Buddha and protects the teaching of the Guide;
having defeated all rival disputants, he makes the enlightenment of a Buddha widespread.
Having passed away from here, that bodhisattva goes to the world-realm of Sukhāvatī;
and having heard the supreme and excellent Dharma of Amitāyus, he will attain the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena.
Young man, there are these ten benefits for a bodhisattva mahāsattva who values dwelling in the forest.
What are the ten?
Namely, he dwells with few duties.
He avoids the crowd;
no dispute arises for him;
he becomes free from affliction.
He does not increase the outflows;
he does not engage in legal disputes;
he conducts himself in tranquility.
He dwells well-restrained;
his mental continuum becomes favorable to liberation,
and he quickly realizes deliverance.
Young man, these are the ten advantages for a bodhisattva mahāsattva who values dwelling in the forest.
In this regard, it is said:
One who dwells alone in the forests always has few concerns and avoids the crowd from afar; no dispute arises for him who lives in solitude.
With a mind free from malice, one should not increase the outflows;
for such a forest-dweller, there arises no ground for dispute—these are his virtues.
Tranquil, he conducts himself restrained in mind, speech, and body;
he becomes favorable to liberation and quickly touches liberation.
The yogin always has few tasks, having avoided the faults of large crowds;
the liberated yogin never quarrels—these are the qualities that belong to him who dwells in the forest.
When one becomes disillusioned with the conditioned, no longing for anything in the world arises;
nor do the outflows increase, and while dwelling in the forest, these benefits accrue to him.
He never has any legal disputes; delighting in tranquility, he dwells in seclusion.
For one who is restrained in speech, mind, and body, many virtues arise from living in the forest.

Liberation becomes favorable for him, and he quickly attains peaceful release. For one who dwells in the forest practicing for liberation, all these qualities belong to that forest-dweller. (SRS 28.76)
Young man, there are these ten benefits for a bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices alms-gathering and is established in the ascetic qualities of refinement.
What are the ten?
Namely, he has no desire for fame.
He has no desire for fame; he has no desire for gain and honor;
and he is established in the noble lineages.
He is free from hypocrisy and flattery;
he does not exalt himself,
nor does he disparage others.
Having abandoned both attachment and aversion, he wanders among the houses of others; he bestows the gift of Dharma free from worldly motives,
and for him who is established in the ascetic practices and self-effacement, his teaching of the Dharma becomes worthy of acceptance.
Young man, these are the ten benefits for a bodhisattva mahāsattva who subsists on almsfood and is established in the ascetic practice of purification.
In this regard, it is said:
