One who is established in the dhūta practices does not desire to be known, nor does he delight in fame;
his mind is equanimous toward gain and loss.
He does not abandon the lineage of the noble ones, nor does he engage in hypocrisy or flattery;
he does not exalt himself, nor does he disparage others.
When he teaches the Dharma free from worldly motives, his speech becomes acceptable because of his freedom from aversion and attachment; these are the virtues found in alms-gathering.
He does not seek fame or gain through his knowledge; he is established in the four noble lineages.
The wise one is neither a deceiver nor a chatterer—such are the qualities of one who is devoted to the ascetic practices (dhūta).
He does not exalt himself nor disparage others; even when spoken to by someone, he never becomes angry.
Even upon hearing praise, he does not give rise to joy—he who is content with whatever alms-food he receives.
He gives the gift of Dharma without worldly motive and does not seek gain or honor;
his speech becomes acceptable to others—these are the benefits for one who is devoted to the ascetic virtues (dhūta).
Thus, young man, a bodhisattva mahāsattva established in such ascetic qualities (dhūtaguṇa), dwelling in the forest, attains the treasure of the Buddhas, attains the treasure of the Dharma,
and attains the treasure of gnosis.
He attains the treasury of knowledge regarding the past, the future, and the present.
And how, young man, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva attain the treasury of the Buddhas?
Young man, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in solitude attains these five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñā*).
With the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, he beholds immeasurable and incalculable Buddha Bhagavāns in the eastern direction;
likewise, he beholds immeasurable and incalculable Buddha Bhagavāns in the southern, western, and northern directions.
Thus he becomes never separated from the vision of the Buddhas.
For in this way, young man, a bodhisattva mahāsattva obtains the treasure of the Buddhas.
And how, young man, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva obtain the treasure of the Dharma?
And whatever Dharma those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, teach,
that the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva hears in its entirety with his divine ear-element;
he thus remains never separated from hearing the Dharma.
In this way, young man, a bodhisattva obtains the treasury of Dharma.
And how, young man, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva obtain the treasury of knowledge—
that knowledge by which he masters all dharmas?
Having propitiated [the Buddhas], with unclouded mindfulness, he teaches the Dharma to sentient beings;
and he understands its true meaning.
In this way, O youth, a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains the treasury of knowledge.
And how, young man, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva obtain the treasury of knowledge regarding the past, the future, and the present?
Through supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*), he penetrates the knowledge of the mental conduct of sentient beings in the past, the future, and the present.
In this way, young man, a bodhisattva mahāsattva obtains the treasury of knowledge regarding the past, the future, and the present.
In brief, young man, a bodhisattva mahāsattva established in such qualities and dharmas attains all the buddha-dharmas, wherein there is no ground for any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas,
let alone for any proponents of other doctrines.
In this regard, it is said:

The wise one who always remains in the forest quickly attains the treasure of the Buddhas, the treasure of the Dharma, the treasure of knowledge, the treasure of the past limit, and the five superknowledges.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter of the *Śrī-Samādhirāja*, titled "The Chapter on the Ten Benefits."
(Vaidya 172) Chapter 29: The Chapter on Tejaguṇarāja.
Then the Blessed One addressed the youth Candraprabha once more: "Therefore, O youth..."
"Prince, you should always train yourself thus: 'Having abandoned the divine pleasures of sovereignty as a universal monarch, I shall go forth into homelessness.
Prince, once gone forth, you must abide in the ascetic virtues and self-effacement, dwelling in solitude, and be endowed with patience and gentleness.
And you, Prince, must always exert vigor, like one whose head or clothing is on fire; for this [sūtra] is the manifestation of the equality of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena."
This samādhi should be heard, taken up, mastered, set in motion, maintained, recited, taught, studied, cultivated through the meditation on the absence of conflict (*araṇā*), practiced extensively,
and explained in detail to others.
"O youth, you must always be like the rhinoceros horn—solitary and dwelling in the forest.
O youth, you must always act for the benefit of all sentient beings, even at the cost of sacrificing yourself."
Then, at that time, the Blessed One, elucidating this very matter, revealed in detail through the singing of verses this chapter on the narrative of past lives concerning the youth Candraprabha:
"I remember many hundreds of past eons when there was a Leader of infinite renown."
The Jina named Tejaguṇa, who was honored by hosts of men, gods, and nāgas, was a king.

At that time, his community consisted of ten million monks who had attained the six superknowledges, who had reached mastery in the analytical knowledges, who were purified by the ascetic practices, and whose minds were tranquil.
At that time, in this Jambudvīpa, there were seven hundred and sixty million cities, all equal in size, measuring fifty yojanas each, and distinguished by the excellence of the seven precious gems.
At that time, all those excellent cities were adorned with many hundreds of parks;
every park resembled a dense cloud, filled with trees adorned with fruits and flowers.
Those excellent gardens were filled with various beautiful species of fruit trees, abounding in *lakucas*, mangoes, rose-apples,
and jackfruits; they were further adorned by hundreds of *karṇikāras*, *campakas*, and *punnāgas*.
At that time, O Nyagrodha, there were the cries of all the flocks of birds— the sounds of hundreds of sparrows,
cuckoos, and peacocks, as well as parrots, jīvañjīvakas, and kuṇālas— along with the calls of many other flocks of birds.

Resembling royal swans, king Dhṛtarāṣṭra, they have the hue of bees and kuṇāla birds; they possess excellent voices and calls, with wonderful bodies and the radiance of great red colors, their sounds being most charming, sweet, and joyful.
Thus, at that time when the birds had assembled, there were the cries of sparrows and peacocks,
and various kinds of sounds from many birds— the cuckoos, the mynas, and the diverse species of twice-born winged creatures.
Those hundreds of gardens were frequented by *mucilinda*, *vārṣika*, and hundreds of *aśoka* trees;
they were filled with *atimuktaka* flowers and leaves, as well as *javapuṣpa*, *padma*, *utpala*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka* lotuses.
These lotuses, consisting of hundreds and thousands of petals, beautify the lotus ponds;
adorned with the finest fragrances, these radiant ponds shine forth.
At that time, in this Jambudvīpa, there was a king named Dṛḍhadatta, a lord of men;
he had five hundred sons who were gracious and most beautiful to behold.
At that time, the kingdom was auspicious, secure, free from affliction, and most delightful;
this Jambudvīpa was covered with flowers, being no different from the celestial realms.
At that time, the Jina, the Daśabala, the Inexhaustible One, spoke this supreme samādhi:
"All states of existence are like a dream; nothing at all is born, nor does anything die."
No sentient being is found, nor a life-principle, nor a person; these phenomena are like foam and the trunk of a plantain tree.
They are like an illusion, like lightning in the sky, resembling the moon reflected in water, and like a mirage.
No person whatsoever, having died in this world, transmigrates to or goes to another world;
yet the action performed never perishes, and its fruit—whether dark or bright—follows one as they wander through saṃsāra.
There is neither permanence nor again annihilation; there is no accumulation of karma, nor is there any abiding.
One who has performed [an action] does not fail to experience its result, yet one does not experience what was performed by another.
There is no transition, nor is there returning; nothing exists, yet again, nothing does not exist.
Here there is no station for views, no purification of the path, no conduct of beings, and no state of tranquility.

Unborn, peaceful, and signless is the state of the Sugatas; it is the qualities of the Jinas, the power of the powers, and the strength of those who possess the ten powers. This is the supreme bull-like majesty of the Buddhas.
It is a collection of the qualities of excellent, pure dharmas; it is the supreme power of retaining qualities and knowledge;
it is the method for attaining the supreme way of the five excellent higher knowledges (*pañcābhijñā*) and the performance of miraculous transformations (*ṛddhivikurvaṇā*).
And one who understands here does not perceive any intrinsic nature anywhere, nor any coming or going in the subtle course of phenomena;
the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) does not go anywhere here— such is the course, the non-course, the course of phenomena.
The nature of the range of sounds is not a collection; the movement of intrinsic nature does not abide anywhere.
This non-abiding, non-reliant nature of movement is the domain of the Jinas—the stainless, peaceful state.
Peaceful, profoundly tranquil, and having reached the state of utter stillness, that state does not abide anywhere;
entities and their intrinsic natures are constantly followed [by it], yet this skillful, immovable state is exceedingly difficult to perceive.
For it is not unstable, being established by its very nature; it is unestablished, yet established in the nature of the future.
It is impossible to describe the stability of its intrinsic nature; it is empty, immovable, and the stability of phenomena.
Sound has been described, yet there is no going within sound; the nature of sound is the nature of phenomena (dharmagati).
There is no accumulation of sound, nor does it abide anywhere; such is the nature of things, the nature of phenomena.
The word "going" has been spoken, yet there is no going of a sentient being; it is the nature of phenomena, the path of subtle meaning.
The sound has also been spoken, yet there is no going of a sentient being, nor is the sound found, nor is there any going of a sentient being.
It is neither infinite nor finite, nor does it have a middle course; it neither exists nor does not exist, nor does it go to any place.
Such is the nature of reality as it is known, and this is the equal teaching of the supreme Victors.

Stainless, supreme purity, the state of ultimate reality—tranquil, utterly serene, dustless, and free from passion; the Conqueror, possessed of supreme compassion, teaches this state of peace that is beyond conceptual construction and mental fabrication.
Moreover, there is no movement of syllables here; it is a vast range, a vast progression of meaning.
It is practiced by the Buddhas and praised by the Jinas—a radiance, the subtle progression of the method of Dharma.
In that vast and stainless treasury of Dharma where the peerless Sugatas abide,
they teach the jewel of the Dharma— stainless, ultimate, empty, and leading to the subtle realization of the true meaning.
Then, O King Dṛḍhadatta, you heard that the Lord of Men was teaching this samādhi;
at that time, accompanied by eighty koṭis of nayutas, you approached the Compassionate Victor.
Having generated powerful reverence and having paid homage to the feet of the Jina,
the lord of men then stood before the One of Ten Powers with his ten fingers joined in salutation, filled with joy.
The Jina, having understood his perfectly pure conduct, he who has mastery over the senses and has gone to the further shore,
that supreme man skilled in discerning dispositions, taught him this excellent samādhi.
When that king heard the ultimate truth, a vast and noble joy arose within him;
having abandoned all four continents and renounced sensual pleasures, he went forth into homelessness.
When the king, having abandoned the earth, goes forth as one seeking awakening, he will become a future Victor;
then all humans here in Jambudvīpa, having abandoned the pleasures of desire, will go forth.
At that time, the assembly of the One Possessing the Ten Powers was vast; many monks and nuns were applied in mind.
Then, medicinal herbs that had not been ploughed and not sown appeared, attended by the Maruts.
The three saffron robes appeared, perfectly cut and well-sewn, beyond compare;
stainless, free from dust, with minds like gold, they were worthy of the Buddha’s virtues and possessed the power of merit.
Behold, O Prince, for that excellent king, having abandoned the entire earth, has gone forth into homelessness;
yet in this age of the destruction of beings, many will have meager wealth and will not renounce their homes.
They will endure beatings, imprisonment, unjust punishment, much verbal abuse, threats, and undesirable suffering;
they will suffer many afflictions from royal households, and their enjoyments will be very meager, with no food in their homes.
Their lifespan is short and they possess no wealth; their negligence is great and they lack the power of merit.
These fools are unskilled in the various arts and crafts, and though they are impoverished, there is no property in their homes.
Greedy for the wives of others, with impure minds, envious, and extremely reckless; their conduct defiled and not established in right behavior, they will say, "We shall become Buddhas."
Those who take bribes, those who deceive, the violent, the arrogant, and those wealthy in worldly wealth—who are destroyers, fraudulent, and deceitful—will say, "We shall become Buddhas. (SRS 29.41)
Delighting in the slaughter, binding, and harassment of others, they will be of evil conduct, cruel, and corrupt-minded;
ungrateful, divisive, and established in violence, they will say: "Tell us, speak of the practice of awakening! (SRS 29.42)
Toward the very person from whom they have heard the conduct of awakening, they give rise to resentment;
and having heard even a single word of a lapse by that wise one, they speak hundreds of disparagements. (SRS 29.43)
Therefore, O Prince, having heard these words of mine, do not cultivate intimacy with them;
remain distrustful even in your dreams if you wish to touch the conduct of awakening.
Though they may proclaim for many hundreds of eons the numerous virtues of the austere conduct that is so well-refined,
one who speaks of these virtues yet does not abide within them does not awaken to the words of supreme enlightenment.
Always be entirely sweet and ever pure in conduct with a very serene mind;
remain constantly pure in virtue, and before long you shall attain the supreme samādhi.
Do not harbor pride, do not give rise to stubbornness; always remain with a completely pure mind.
Having abandoned intoxication, pride, and hypocrisy, you shall then attain this supreme samādhi.
One should constantly recollect the Jina according to his qualities: he who possesses hands that radiate the luster of excellent gold;
and just as the sky is filled with stars at night, so too is the body of the Sage adorned with the marks of excellence.
Taking up many excellent banners, parasols, canopies, and flags, as well as powders and ointments, always perform worship of the Sugata; before long, you shall obtain the supreme samādhi.

Always perform worship at the stūpas of the Jinas with excellent perfumes, garlands, and beautiful flowers, and with many musical instruments and cymbals held aloft; before long, you shall attain this supreme samādhi.
With hand-drums, hundreds of sweet-sounding mṛdaṅgas, kettledrums, lutes, and the sounds of excellent flutes—
with various ensembles of musical instruments possessing sweet tones— worship the Leader with a serene mind.
Have a beautiful image of the Buddha made, fashioned from jewels, well-crafted, pleasing, and most excellent to behold; before long, you shall attain the supreme samādhi.
Always frequent secluded forest groves, abandoning delight in villages and cities;
always remain peerless like a rhinoceros, and before long you shall attain the supreme samādhi.
"The Lord of Dharma said to me, 'You are my sons; train yourselves in my practice of samādhi.
I was that one who became renowned throughout the directions, the lord of men named Dṛḍhadatta."
In the city of Ananta, I made offerings to the Buddhas; with a pure mind, I guarded my ethical discipline;
I showed reverence toward those endowed with the ten powers, seeking this peaceful, supreme samādhi.
In former lives, I abandoned my sons, wives, head, hands, feet, and excellent eyes;
yet never once did I allow my mind to become dejected while seeking this peaceful, supreme samādhi.
I have relinquished wealth, grain, many hundreds of male and female slaves, and abundant jewels; I have fully satisfied many supplicants while seeking this peaceful, supreme samādhi. (SRS 29.57)
In former lives, I gave away crystal, gold, much lapis lazuli, conch shells, and stone for the sake of liberation;
I gave mani-jewels, pure silver, coral, and clouds [of wealth], seeking this peaceful, supreme samādhi.
I have cast away various kinds of ornaments, excellent pearl necklaces, and likewise lion-shaped pendants;
I have discarded these vast and distinguished lattices of jewels while seeking this supreme, peaceful samādhi.

I gave away many tens of millions of most exquisite garments, pure and excellent Kāśika and dukūla silks, and various wonderful golden ornaments; all this was sacrificed by me while seeking this supreme, peaceful samādhi.
I abandoned elephants, horses, chariots, and various kinds of women who were dear to me;
yet I never once gave way to dejection while seeking this supreme, peaceful samādhi.
In the past, I saw men who were very poor, distressed by the search for wealth, and fallen into hardship;
I made them free from poverty with my riches, as they sought this peaceful, supreme samādhi.
In the past, seeking this peaceful and supreme samādhi, I gave to supplicants millions of elephants, chariots, and horses, adorned with nets of hidden jewels and gems.
In the past, having adorned many billions of gardens, I gave them away;
gladdening my mind and generating compassion, I sought this supreme, peaceful samādhi.
In the past, having adorned villages, kingdoms, cities, and market towns, I gave them away;
and having given them, I always experienced joy while seeking this supreme, peaceful samādhi.
In the past, seeking this supreme, peaceful samādhi, I gave heaps of jewels equal to Mount Sumeru, as well as many robes and ornaments, to those who begged for them.
I have made the very poor wealthy, and many who had fallen into great distress have been rescued by me;
I have brought happiness to those afflicted by much suffering—seeking this supreme, peaceful samādhi.
When I was the lord of the great earth and saw the many people in such distress, I renounced my kingdom for their sake; having given rise to compassion, I acted so that they might be happy.
O youth, the wonders I have performed and the difficult deeds I have accomplished over many hundreds of eons could not be fully exhausted even if I were to speak for billions of trillions of eons.
Those people went to a state of madness,
having no faith in the conduct of the Sugata;
they performed difficult and wondrous deeds while seeking this peaceful, supreme samādhi.
And I announce this to you, O youth: believe my words, for they are not false.
For the Sugata never speaks a lie; the Jina, the compassionate one, is always a speaker of truth.
These many other modes as well were practiced and purified by me for hundreds of eons;
how may I obtain this supreme samādhi so that I might liberate millions of suffering beings?
At the very moment this samādhi, the path of great primordial wisdom, was attained by me,
having obtained this supreme samādhi, I beheld many millions of Buddhas.
I have attained infinite supernormal powers; manifesting them, I travel to hundreds of buddha-fields.
Having gone there, I ask those compassionate ones many millions of billions of questions.
And whatever questions you, O Sugata, spoke to me then—those millions of billions—I have grasped them all and maintain them; not even a single word has slipped from my memory.
Having heard that true principle regarding many millions of billions of questions,
and having taught that stainless, peaceful state, I establish many beings on the path of wisdom.
Abiding in this samādhi and training in the true method for hundreds of eons,
I have previously established many millions of billions of beings upon the supreme, stainless path.
Those who have not seen the previous Sugatas who taught this stainless method will be unable here to have faith in the supreme samādhi of ultimate emptiness.
Those people who are faithful, wise, and know the ritual procedures, who have attained the method of the profound and true principle,
do not tremble nor will they be terrified; having heard it, they are always joyful at heart.
They all uphold supreme enlightenment; they are my sons, born after me.
They are indeed as rare as the udumbara flower; for their sake, I have practiced for hundreds of eons.
There is no fear of falling into the lower realms for him; the eight inopportune states have forever departed from him.
That person who maintains this samādhi shall behold many billions of Buddhas.
Just as the Victorious One Maitreya of infinite fame will become a benefactor of many beings,
so do I prophesy Anantamati, in whose hand this supreme samādhi rests.
He becomes possessed of mindfulness, possessed of intelligence, and with wisdom arisen, he becomes a bearer of what he has heard; vast eloquence belongs to that person who maintains this samādhi.
He becomes worthy of worship by the gods and always worthy of homage by the Maruts;
he is constantly protected by the hosts of deities, that person who maintains this samādhi.
The person who maintains this samādhi does not die in the midst of fire, nor in water; neither weapon nor poison affects them, and they do not become subject to their enemies. SRS_29.85.
May he always dwell in forest glades, where the winds perform excellent service for him;
and many hundreds of yakṣas shall be his attendants—he who maintains this samādhi.

Through wisdom, he becomes equal to the ocean and does not cling; even if one were to speak of the qualities of the Sage, he who maintains this samādhi proclaims the true qualities of the Buddha. (SRS 29.87)
It has no end and no limit; no measure can be found for it through hearing, just as in the sky.
The person who maintains this samādhi, holding the torch of wisdom, dispels the darkness.
One who maintains this samādhi speaks words that are smooth, well-composed, and always pleasing when addressed in assemblies; like a lion, he roars as he speaks. SRS_29.89.
He becomes a physician, a healer, a refuge, a resort, a protection, and a shelter for many;
he becomes a light in the world—the person who maintains this samādhi.
The mind of such a person does not delight in sexual intercourse; devoted to tranquility, he touches the bliss of meditative concentration.
He who maintains this samādhi speaks with peaceful and perfectly calm speech.
And for him there is no delight in signs within his mind; all extensive signs have been eliminated.
The wise person who maintains this samādhi remains constantly in a state of meditative concentration.
And he obtains a vision that is not ordinary, by which he beholds infinite Jinas;
he becomes one of infinite vision, a bull among men, who maintains this samādhi.

The person who maintains this samādhi possesses a voice like that of a curlew, speech endowed with sweetness, and a tone like that of a kalaviṅka bird or a drum; their voice is harmonious with song and their speech is charming.

The person who maintains this samādhi has a voice like the thundering of clouds; he utters a sweet-toned cry with the voice of a swan, possessing a voice endowed with five hundred musical qualities. (SRS 29.95)
For countless millions of billions of eons, that person who maintains this samādhi emits an inconceivable voice, endowed with various sweet-toned qualities of speech.
The person who maintains this samādhi does not have a greedy mind regarding food, nor does he take delight in bowls or robes; having few desires, being contented, and well-restrained, he remains so.
Such a person does not exalt themselves, nor do they ever speak ill of others;
always delighting in meditation with a subtle mind is the person who maintains this samādhi.
One who maintains this samādhi constantly becomes a contemplator of the self and does not seek out the faults of others; such a person remains unopposed by the entire world.
One who maintains this samādhi becomes a person with an undefiled mind and pure conduct; they are always free from guile and deceit, ever gentle, and always delighting in liberation. SRS_29.100.
One who maintains this samādhi becomes constantly intent on renunciation; a mind of stinginess finds no pleasure in him. He becomes one who is always endowed with ethical discipline. SRS_29.101.
Handsome, beautiful, and lovely to behold, with a complexion like the finest gold that radiates light—
one who maintains this samādhi becomes a possessor of the thirty-two marks. (SRS 29.102)
He is always serene and distinguished, beloved by many people;
men never tire of gazing upon him who maintains this samādhi.
The gods, as well as the hosts of nāgas and yakṣas, are always satisfied, uplifted, and joyful;
they proclaim his praises whenever he enters families while maintaining this samādhi.
Brahmā, Śakra, and the Vaśavartin gods always perform many services for him;
yet, the mind of that person who maintains this samādhi does not become arrogant.

And for that person who maintains this samādhi, there is no fear of an evil rebirth, nor of the inopportune states, nor fear of falling into ruin; they are completely liberated from all fears of falling into ruin and the like.
And having heard the subtle, excellent qualities of the Buddha, no doubt or uncertainty arises in him;
he comes to possess profound wisdom—that person who maintains this samādhi.
Whatever subtle dharma they hear, they become masters and have reached the further shore in all respects;
they become powerful and skilled in causes—he who maintains this samādhi.
When the Jina has spoken such words, I am always one who has attended upon him;
and that person who maintains this samādhi attains the most excellent and sublime dhāraṇī.
And when he meets his death, Amitābha stands before him together with a multitude of monks— the Compassionate One— before the person who maintains this samādhi.

The person who maintains this samādhi becomes an attainer of dhāraṇīs, a master of the treasury of Dharma who has reached the further shore, possessed of inspired eloquence and an uninterrupted voice.
Wheresoever that upholder of the Dharma goes, he becomes a light for the world—
he who, with a mind perfectly purified and conduct thoroughly stilled, maintains this samādhi.
He is a master of the various and subtle treasury of the Dharma, having attained mastery and reached the further shore;
he cuts through the doubts of all the world—the person who maintains this samādhi.
If all sentient beings were compassionate, and the Sugata, the Blessed One, were to act as the ender of existence,
one might honor them for many hundreds of eons, even more than the sands of the Ganges.
And whatever person, in this final age of destruction, having heard this samādhi here,
should utter the single word "I rejoice," the mass of merit of that former [person] would not equal even a fraction of it.

O youth, that wise Dharma-preacher who possesses this supreme samādhi of ultimate emptiness and peaceful course, whether it be in his possession or even written in a book, remains established therein.
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter of the *Śrī-Samādhirāja*, titled "The Chapter on Tejaguṇarāja."
(Vaidya 188) Chapter 30: On the Benefits.
Then the Blessed One addressed the youth Candraprabha once again: "Therefore, then..."

"O Kumāra, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva should desire: 'How may I master the cries of all sentient beings, and having discerned the superior and inferior nature of their faculties, teach the Dharma?'— then, O Kumāra, that bodhisattva mahāsattva [should cultivate] this samādhi called 'The Manifestation of the Equality of the Essential Nature of All Phenomena.'"
It should be heard, taken up, mastered, retained, recited, cultivated through the meditation on non-contention, practiced extensively, and revealed in detail to others.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
"Countless leaders of the past were seen by him; he questioned those Lords of the World regarding how they had applied themselves.
A Bodhisattva who desires liberation, abiding in supreme roots of goodness, maintains this stainless samādhi."
He obtains exquisite happiness, both divine and human,
and he receives supreme worship, both divine and human;
he obtains exquisite happiness, the bliss of meditative concentration and the bliss of the noble ones.
One who desires liberation should maintain this stainless samādhi.
Upon hearing praise, he feels no exultation;
nor, again, upon hearing dispraise, does he fall into dejection.
Like a mountain, he remains unshaken by the eight worldly concerns.
One who desires liberation should maintain this stainless samādhi.
One whose speech is entirely sweet, who speaks with gentle words and is well-reasoned, who is free from frowning and speaks first;
whose face is always smiling and who is trained by the leaders—such a person, desiring liberation, maintains this stainless samādhi.
He dwells in happiness; he is gentle and affectionate in heart, always well-tamed and established on the stage of the tamed.
Possessing very sweet and pleasant speech, he speaks with affectionate truth—such is one who, desiring awakening, maintains this stainless samādhi.
He does not engage in contentious speech nor in disputes; free from all stubborn faults, he has abandoned all remaining defects.
Always joyful, gentle, and mild, he who desires awakening maintains this stainless samādhi.
The wise one is always a renunciant, ever-diligent; seeing people in great suffering, he gives them food.
Desiring awakening, he who maintains this stainless samādhi is a constant and excellent giver, ready to relinquish even that which is most dear.
They arouse the longing of hundreds of thousands of gods; nāgas, asuras, and yakṣas constantly attend upon him.
Whether in the forest or in the wilderness, they provide protection for that person who maintains this stainless samādhi.
He utters speech that is unimpeded, with a voice like the sound of Brahmā, a voice like the cry of a swan, and a voice like the song of the kinnaras;
his voice possesses five hundred musical qualities, it is gladdening, and his resonance is like thunder, a proclaimed sound, a well-sounding voice.
Even if some man were to reduce the vast expanse of the earth into subtle dust particles such that they could be counted,
the sounds that issue forth from one who maintains this stainless samādhi would be even more numerous than those particles.
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter of the *Śrī-Samādhirāja*, titled "The Chapter on Benefits."
Chapter 31: The Exposition on the Essential Nature of All Dharmas.
Thereupon, the Blessed One again addressed the youth Candraprabha: "Therefore, O youth, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva should desire: 'How might I [realize] all dharmas...'"
"How should one know the intrinsic nature?"—

for this reason, O youth, this samādhi called "The Manifestation of the Equality of the Intrinsic Nature of All Phenomena" should be heard, taken up, mastered, retained, recited, taught, and studied by a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
It should be cultivated through the meditation on non-contention, practiced repeatedly, and explained in detail to others.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
"Passion never arises in him, nor does hatred; delusion never arises in that bull among men.
By him all afflictions have been cast away without remainder—he who knows the nature of phenomena to be perfectly tranquil."
Such a person never abandons the training of the Sugatas; such a person is a hero who never falls under the power of women;
such a person finds joy in the teaching of the Sugatas—he who knows the perfectly peaceful intrinsic nature of phenomena.

He is the wise and intelligent one who knows the rules of knowledge; he is the Buddha who perceives the infinite and the boundless. He is the one who understands the limitless knowledge of dhāraṇīs—he who knows the nature of phenomena through the application of method.
Before long, he shall become a lord of bipeds here; he shall be a physician and a healer, a bestower of happiness.
He shall completely extract the thorn from those who suffer—he who knows the perfectly tranquil intrinsic nature of phenomena.
Having recognized those beings as afflicted and suffering, he shall always beat the drum of the Deathless;
he who understands the perfectly peaceful intrinsic nature of phenomena will before long become a Leader, a Victor.
He is the preeminent physician, skilled in the methods of medicine; he knows the origin of all diseases and where liberation from them lies.
Trained in the method of reality, that wise one, having trained himself, liberates many vast numbers of lost beings.

He is skilled in the systems of emptiness, a hero of wisdom; he is unattached to the world and always eats his alms-food. He establishes many beings in supreme enlightenment—he who knows the nature of phenomena to be perfectly tranquil.
That moon among men, exalted by the power of patience, does not become angry even when struck with clods of earth or sticks;
he is not disturbed even if his limbs are severed one by one—he who knows the nature of phenomena to be perfectly tranquil.
Established in the power of patience, he is strong; such is the object of his patience, being perfectly tranquil.
By the power of patience, that hero of intelligence does not conceive pride—he who knows the nature of phenomena to be perfectly tranquil.

Such a person never conceives of a real entity; therefore, all states of existence have been analyzed by him as always empty. All perceptions have been entirely and completely abandoned by him who knows the nature of phenomena to be perfectly tranquil.
They shall teach that most excellent nature of phenomena; they shall before long touch unsurpassed awakening.
To those for whom the nature of phenomena is a well-ascertained domain, an infinite and boundless gift has been bestowed.

He speaks millions of sūtras, as limitless as the sands of the river Ganges, and even more than that; yet his eloquence is never exhausted as he describes it, for he knows the nature of phenomena to be perfectly tranquil.
For thousands of millions of billions of eons, he is ever exalted in wisdom like Mount Meru;
for him who knows the nature of phenomena to be perfectly tranquil, there is no exhaustion of the Dharma as he speaks it.
For one who constantly seeks supreme enlightenment, there arises an extensive, vast, and inconceivable eloquence;
he who knows the perfectly tranquil intrinsic nature of phenomena always speaks millions of boundless sūtras.
Whatever Dharma these Jinas, supreme among bipeds, have spoken—all that she hears and grasps in its entirety;
not even a single word of it remains a subject for doubt, for she knows all these phenomena to be non-existent.
Such a person is always distinguished and possessed of renunciation; he becomes a lord of giving who bestows happiness upon those who suffer.
Having seen suffering beings, he satisfies them with jewels—he who knows that the intrinsic nature of phenomena is eternally empty.
In every Jambudvīpa, he will always be a king who shall bring infinite happiness to sentient beings;
endowed with loving-kindness toward living beings at all times, he knows that the intrinsic nature of phenomena is eternally empty.
Having renounced sons, daughters, male and female slaves, that steadfast one likewise renounces his hands, feet, head, and even his kingdom;
yet his mind does not waver, for he, like a bull, always knows the nature of phenomena to be empty.
Even if each and every limb of his body were to be severed, his mind would not be disturbed even in a dream;
by him the Leaders, the lords of bipeds, are honored—he who always knows the nature of phenomena to be empty.
By this, all the Leaders who have passed away are honored, as well as those Lords of Men yet to come;
by him all the Leaders who stand present are honored, who always knows that the intrinsic nature of phenomena is empty.
That wise one who holds this treasury is established in the supreme *dhāraṇī* of the Sugatas;
having heard this sutra, he who maintains it during the age of destruction will before long become a leader of the world.
Such a wise person shall never be blind, nor shall they ever be deficient in their limbs for many eons;
thus, these eight unfavorable conditions are forever avoided by one who has spoken this sutra without forgetting it.
He shall never again go to the miserable realms; always possessing the marks, he will be handsome.
These five superknowledges will be constantly cultivated by him; that hero will always stand before the Sugatas.
Having emanated many created forms, this wise one sends them to many millions of fields for the sake of disciplining beings;
by those who have seen these many emanated Buddhas, many beings are established in supreme enlightenment.
Possessed of mindfulness, of movement, of wisdom, and of fortitude, he will always be endowed with steadfastness and the power of vigor;
having attained the perfection of Dharma, he will become one of great splendor—he who, hearing this sutra, should uphold it in the age of destruction.
Thousands of millions of rays constantly issue forth from them, making all the skies into circles like those of the suns;
by those through whom these phenomena have been realized as empty, they become heroic leaders before long.
This peaceful sphere of conduct was cultivated by me in the past for many thousands of millions of billions of eons.
My vigor never faltered on this path, so that I was prophesied by Dīpaṃkara for the stage of a Jina.

You too should train yourselves in my conduct according to this sutra; for this guiding principle teaches the profound ultimate truth, wherein many misguided non-Buddhists, having lost their way and rejected awakening, fall into terrifying states of woe.
Having experienced there for many thousands of millions of billions of eons those bitter and intense sensations,
after the passing of many billions of eons, that very cause will once again lead to the attainment of the deathless.

Those who, in the terrible final age, protect such a peaceful sūtra as this of the Sugata—for them, supreme enlightenment is not difficult to attain; they, upholding the teachings, have been prophesied for that highest state in the final age.
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter of the *Śrī-Samādhirāja*, titled "The Exposition of the Essential Nature of All Phenomena."
Chapter 32: The Benefits of Retaining the Sūtra.
Then the Blessed One addressed the youth Candraprabha once again: "Therefore, then..."
O Kumāra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to maintain the purification of the great supernormal knowledges should maintain this samādhi;
it should be taken up, mastered, retained, recited, promulgated, taught, studied, and cultivated.
And it should be proclaimed in detail to others.
And what, O Youth, is that preparation for the higher knowledge of all phenomena?
It is this: the non-appropriation and non-clinging to all phenomena, and the absence of conceit regarding the aggregate of ethical discipline and the aggregate of meditative concentration.
The non-activity of the aggregate of wisdom, the vision of seclusion of the aggregate of liberation, the vision of things as they truly are of the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation,
and the vision of the emptiness of intrinsic nature of all phenomena:
endowed with which superknowledge a bodhisattva mahāsattva performs all the miraculous transformations of meditative concentration and teaches the Dharma to all sentient beings.
This, young man, is called the preparation for the great supernormal knowledges.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
"The preparation for the great superknowledges is taught as being free from dispute.
But he who engages in dispute, even while grasping [the teaching], is not liberated."
That superknowledge is his wisdom, the inconceivable knowledge of a Buddha;
for one who remains fixed in grasping, such knowledge does not exist.
Many inconceivable phenomena have been revealed by means of sound;
whoever becomes attached to that sound does not understand the intentional language of the Saṅgha.
Not understanding the discourse of the Saṅgha, what has been spoken for the sake of the Saṅgha,
one who is untrained in the nature of reality speaks non-dharma as dharma.
The various expressions and the single meaning of the sūtras that have been spoken by me throughout thousands of world-systems cannot be fully recounted.
By contemplating a single entity, all those many dharmas that have been proclaimed by all the Buddhas become cultivated.
For those people who are skilled in the meaning of the selflessness of all phenomena,
having trained in this state, the qualities of a Buddha are not difficult to attain.
All phenomena are Buddha-phenomena for those who have trained in the true nature of phenomena;
those who thoroughly understand the true nature of phenomena do not contradict that true nature.
All speech is indeed the speech of the Buddha, for every sound is devoid of intrinsic reality;
even if one searches throughout the ten directions, the speech of the Buddha cannot be found.
This speech is indeed the speech of the Buddhas; though sought throughout the ten directions, this unsurpassed speech is not found—it has not been found, nor will it ever be found.
The speech of the Buddha is unsurpassed; the speech of the Buddha is beyond compare.
Not even an atom can be found therein; therefore it is called "unsurpassed."
No phenomenon arises as an atom; it is taught by means of the word "atom.
Not even so much as an atom is found in the world, yet it is taught by means of words.
There is no attainment in the attainment of dharmas that have already been attained;
those who understand dharmas in this way awaken to supreme enlightenment.
Those Buddhas attained unsurpassed awakening and turned the wheel of Dharma;
having turned the wheel of Dharma, they revealed the qualities of a Buddha.
And the bodhisattvas awaken to the unsurpassed knowledge of a Buddha;
therefore, they are called "Buddhas" because of their awakening to the knowledge of a Buddha.
Non-existence, the wishless, the signless, and emptiness—
through these doors of liberation, the Buddha has revealed the gateway.
The eye, the ear, the nose, the tongue, the body, and likewise the mind—
these are empty by their own nature, as proclaimed by the perfectly awakened ones.
One who thoroughly understands the intrinsic nature of such phenomena does not engage in dispute, having realized the characteristic of phenomena.
This is the sphere of activity of the heroic Bodhisattvas, the protectors;
they never have any doubt, for they know the emptiness of all phenomena.
Because he knows the intrinsic nature of phenomena, he is indeed called a Buddha;
for he disciplines immeasurable and inconceivable beings for the sake of awakening.
He is honored by the word "Buddha" and he is honored by the word "virtue";
both the word "virtue" and the word "Buddha" have but one single characteristic.
However many words have been proclaimed— whether inferior, superior, or middling—
they are all taught by means of the single word "concentrated," which is the word "Buddha."
The Buddha-dharmas are not proclaimed to be situated in a location nor situated in a specific place;
they have neither arisen nor ceased, neither as one nor as distinct.
They are neither new nor old, nor do they possess any conceit;
they are neither blue, nor yellow, nor white, nor red.
Inexpressible and ungraspable, they are thus taught by means of sound;
yet that is not the domain of sound—this is the miracle of the Sage.
For those dharmas are indeed called "outflow-free" (anāsrava);
they are spread throughout and not confined to the ten directions—this is the teaching of the Buddhas.
The form of the Buddha is seen even when the Buddha has entered final nirvāṇa;
by attending to that place in the mind, he beholds the miracle.
And yet no such being is found who has touched nirvāṇa;
and thus the Dharma has been taught, and many beings have been liberated.
Just as the moon and the sun are seen in a bronze bowl,
yet their own forms do not go there, such is the characteristic of phenomena.
Those who know phenomena by their very nature to be like reflections do not perceive the form of a Buddha through a physical body.
For this Dharma is indeed without form; herein there is no form whatsoever.
That which is the formless Dharma is the very form of the Buddha.
Those who see [the Buddha] by means of the dharma-body, they see the Guide;
for the perfectly awakened ones are indeed the dharma-body—this is the vision of the perfectly awakened one.
They are designated through dependence, yet they are taught as non-dependent;
understand this course for those who truly seek the goal of the ascetic life.
Having understood the inclinations of sentient beings, non-attainment has been taught as attainment; he who transcends through intentional language is not hindered by anything.
He who thinks "I have attained" has not attained;
he by whom the state of a recluse (śrāmaṇya) has not been attained is called a recluse (śramaṇa).
How can these profound dharmas be explained to those who have not trained in them? And it is not possible to fully proclaim them by means of the name "profound" alone.
The five aggregates are without substance; having not previously existed, they have arisen.
For there is no agent here who causes them to arise, nor does there exist one to whom these aggregates belong as they arise.
Whatever are the characteristics of the five aggregates, all phenomena have those same characteristics;
they are taught as having those characteristics, yet no characteristic exists at all.
Just as the atmosphere is the very sky, such is the characteristic of all phenomena;
thus do they perceive the past, the future, and the present.
The sky is said to be ungraspable; herein nothing graspable is found.
This is the intrinsic nature of phenomena: ungraspable and like the sky.
When the teachings have been taught in this way, the disciple does not perceive them;
and for one who does not perceive the Dharma, those dharmas are inconceivable.
These phenomena are without intrinsic nature; their intrinsic nature is not to be found.
For this is the domain of yogins who are disciplined for the enlightenment of a Buddha.
Whoever understands phenomena in this way does not cling to phenomena;
not clinging to phenomena, they awaken to the very notion of phenomena.
All phenomena have been analyzed by the Bodhisattva, the Protector;
having analyzed away the very notion of "phenomena," he does not conceive of the qualities of a Buddha.
For that limit, being non-conceptualizing, is expressed as a limit by means of conceptualization;
one who understands the limit in this way does not conceive of ten million eons.
Having imagined a prior limit, the fool wanders on in saṃsāra;
yet no location for him can be found, even if one searches throughout the ten directions.
Having realized that cyclic existence is empty, the bodhisattva does not cling to it;
yet they practice for the sake of awakening, though no such practice can be apprehended.
Just as the track of birds in the sky cannot be found,
so too is that nature of awakening (bodhi), which is realized by Bodhisattvas.
Just as a well-trained illusionist displays various kinds of forms through an illusion, yet no form is actually perceived; so it is with this.
I do not consider non-attainment to be attainment, nor is attainment found in what has been attained;
that gnosis is like an illusion, yet it does not abide within the illusion.
Thus, regarding phenomena that are empty, the intellect of the foolish discriminates;
for those who course in such discrimination, the six realms of existence are their destination.
Sentient beings are subject to birth and old age; for them, birth does not cease.
For those who possess the aggregates of birth and death, suffering is endless.
The cycle of birth is suffering, imagined by those of childish intellect;
their eons do not diminish, as they wander through ten million eons.
Whether unassociated or associated, they remain fixed in the application of karma; those who delight in the appropriation of karma are not liberated from karma.
For those who are carried away by the flood of karma, their karma is never exhausted;
remaining always on the side of Māra, they die again and again.
Overcome by Māra and possessed of poor wisdom, they indeed experience birth and death through afflicted karma in their various successive rebirths.
Blind, foolish, and ordinary worldlings fall into death;
they are slain and struck down, and their destination is not auspicious.
Those of childish intellect strike one another with weapons;
as they thus engage in such conduct, their suffering increases.
"Mine are sons, mine is wealth"—thus is it imagined by those of childish intellect;
having imagined the actions of the non-existent, cyclic existence increases further.
Increasing cyclic existence, these ordinary persons wander through it;
because they go about individually and separately, they are therefore called "ordinary persons" (*pṛthagjana*).
Abandoning the Buddha’s teaching, those of broad learning will preach [false doctrines];
having fallen under the power of Māra, they shall not attain liberation.
Fools, driven by desire, serve women who are like rotting corpses;
they go to a rotten destination and fall thereby into an evil rebirth.
The Buddhas do not praise sensual desires, nor the cultivation of intimacy with women;
this snare of women is a most dreadful and terrifying serpent-noose.
The wise avoid him as they would a fierce venomous serpent;
they do not place their trust in women, for this is not the path to enlightenment.
They cultivate the path to awakening practiced by all Buddhas;
and having cultivated that path, they become unsurpassed Buddhas.
They become unsurpassed and worthy of being monuments for the world;
through unsurpassed knowledge, they become unsurpassed Buddhas.
They observe the poṣadha and encourage others in the aggregate of ethical discipline;
they inspire inconceivable millions of beings toward awakening.
They accomplish for sentient beings an immeasurable and inconceivable benefit;
those heroes of great wisdom beat the drum of the Deathless.
They cause the abodes of Māra to tremble and shake the hosts of Māra’s followers;
they incite inconceivable millions of Māras toward awakening.
They subdue and utterly defeat the proponents of other doctrines and the heretics;
they cause the entire earth, along with its oceans and mountains, to tremble.
Displaying themselves through their bodies with manifold miraculous transformations,
those of great wisdom manifest inconceivable miracles.
They cause millions of fields to tremble, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
having conquered those Māras, they awaken to unsurpassed enlightenment.
And they create trees beautifully adorned with jewels,
endowed with fruits and flowers, fragrant and delightful.
Those heroes construct palaces, celestial mansions, and joyful gabled houses, as well as delightful lotus ponds.
Those who drink from that water— which is endowed with the eight qualities, clear, cool, and undisturbed— abandon the three types of thirst.
Having drunk this unsurpassed water, they become irreversible;
through unsurpassed wisdom, they become unsurpassed Buddhas.
"Know that they are going to the unsurpassed, peaceful state;
not knowing this state, all the non-Buddhist teachers have gone astray."
And those beings who have gone to that state and rely upon them will fall into the most terrible Avīci hell, having no other refuge.
The terrible sensations that exist there cannot be fully described;
yet I know them, as do the Bodhisattvas who are protectors.
Those who have doubts regarding this Dharma so profound and difficult to see— for them, there is no ground, as they are fools established in the perception of objective existence.
They manifest arrays of emanations displaying many forms,
by which they all go to the unsurpassed Buddha-fields.
Whatever perfections of the manifestation of forms exist throughout all Buddha-fields,
all those the Bodhisattvas of great supernatural power display here.
Armed with the Great Dharma, those great heroes of immense strength deliver blows with the vajra of the meaning of great emptiness.
Thousands of millions of rays, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
issue forth from their bodies, by which the world is illuminated.
They do not take delight in women, nor is there detachment for them;
they have analyzed the perception of "woman" as being by its very nature merely a perception.
Those buddha-fields in which these heroes dwell are not empty;
what obstacle can Māra, the Evil One, create for them?
Those who, remaining fixed in their dogmatic views, have alienated many Buddhas;
who are propped up by malice and established in desire and greed.
Having dissolved all perceptions and remaining in the state of non-retrogression from perception,
whoever understands such knowledge will understand the inconceivable wisdom of a Buddha.
One perceives the past, the future, and the present;
thus have the dharmas been taught, yet herein nothing at all has been taught.
One does not know by means of knowledge, nor does one despair through ignorance;
having transcended the conceptualization of both knowledge and ignorance, it is called "the Buddha-knowledge."
The Bodhisattva understands the conventions of informative speech and signs;
he accomplishes for sentient beings an immeasurable and inconceivable benefit.
Perception is demonstrated by way of grasping for the purpose of perceiving;
yet that perception is taught as being devoid of grasping by way of its meaning of solitude.
That which is secluded is perception; that which is secluded is the teaching.
When the intrinsic nature of perception is known, in this way, perception will no longer arise.
We shall abandon this perception; for one in whom perception arises, that perception moves within conceptual proliferation, and such a person is not liberated from perception.
Whose is this perception that has arisen? By whom was this perception produced? By whom was that perception touched? By whom was the perception ceased?
No phenomenon was attained by the Buddha for which a conceptualization could arise;
reflect upon that meaning here, and then conceptualization will no longer exist.
When does perception not arise? Whose perception is it that is obstructed? How does liberation arise therein for one who courses in the mind?
When one touches liberation, all thoughts become unthinkable;
when thought itself is unthinkable, then one becomes unthinkable.
Having first remained on the stage of thought and having abandoned all thought, one will thereafter become inconceivable.
This is the ripening of pure dharmas; through non-conditioning, one sees and knows in a single moment the thoughts of all sentient beings.
As are sentient beings, so is thought; as is thought, so are the Victors.
This thought has been revealed by the inconceivable Buddha.
Whoever reflects alone in solitude, when will thought cease?
For one who does not think upon thought, all thoughts vanish.
When one has passed away, died, and reached their end, for whomsoever contemplation proceeds, consciousness follows that contemplation; this is called the "end of contemplation."
For those who abide in the perception of "woman," passion arises;
but when that perception has been thoroughly analyzed, one is no longer defiled by passion.
This reflection is a great reflection, an unsurpassed reflection on the Dharma;
through this reflection on the Dharma, the reflection on reality proceeds.
For a long time, many inconceivable thoughts have been contemplated;
yet, by reflecting in an improper manner, no end to such thinking has arisen.
He who contemplates that name [thinks] that knowledge does not exist in cessation;
yet there is no cessation of the knowledge of the stages—this is the true nature (dharmatā) of cessation.
Sound, the path of speech, and communication are taught by the word "cessation";
those phenomena are without distinction, for as is knowledge, so is cessation.
Unarisen and unceasing, signless and characterless;
even if spoken for ten million eons, they are taught by means of the signless.
Having analyzed all phenomena, those who are established in non-existence do not point to existence as one thing,
nor do they indicate non-existence as something other.
The manifestation of non-existence is expressed by the word "existence," yet that non-existence cannot be perceived even by all the Buddhas.
That which is the non-existence of all things is shown to be existence;
having understood existences in this way, non-existence is revealed.
That non-existence can never be touched by anyone;
yet, through the touching of non-existence, this nirvāṇa has been taught.
If one should have such a thought as "May I become a Buddha in the world," that wise person, afflicted by the thirst for existence, will never awaken to enlightenment.
A bodhisattva who is poised in meditative concentration does not long for any phenomenon;
this awakening is said to be without possessions and without effort.
Many will speak thus: "We have set out for enlightenment," yet being ignorant of this path, they remain far from the enlightenment of a Buddha. (SRS 32.116)
All phenomena taught by means of words are empty of conditioned existence;
and the intrinsic nature of sound is profound, subtle, and difficult to perceive.
This sutra is proclaimed as the exposition of the great superknowledges;
it was taught by all the Buddhas for the sake of the bodhisattvas.
All their defiled adversaries have been destroyed;
established in the superknowledges, their miraculous powers are well-cultivated.
They abide in the knowledge of their vows, and that knowledge has been fully cultivated;
there is no satiety in their attainment of knowledge, which is immeasurable and inconceivable.
For them, there is no volitional effort; concentration and the cause of supernatural power are the maturation of these heroes, who are at all times in a state of meditative equipoise.
Traveling by means of supernormal power born of maturation to millions of fields,
they behold the lamps of the world as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Their birth and death proceed according to the movement of their minds;
having attained mastery over the mind, their bodies are luminous.
The disciples of the Buddha who abide in the supernatural power consisting of cultivation do not approach even a sixteenth part of the supernatural power of conditioned formations.
Their intention cannot be known by all the gods,
except for the Lords of the World or those who stand on an equal footing with them.
They have no baldness, nor indeed any graying of the hair;
there is no coarse old age, nor likewise any painful death.
They have no doubt, no perplexity, and no hesitation;
day and night they seek out hundreds of millions of sūtras.
All their defiling latent tendencies have been abandoned;
they always maintain a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings.
They teach millions of billions of samādhis throughout the ten directions,
answering thousands of millions of questions while remaining unattached.
The perception of woman and the perception of man—all perceptions have been dissolved;
established in the perception of non-existence, they teach the certainty of reality.
They teach the Dharma exactly as it is with perfectly pure knowledge;
they are devoted to the communal recitation of the Dharma and have the range of meditative concentration and wisdom.
Even their practice of meditation is not established in any entity;
their speech is never in vain, and their teaching of the Dharma is never fruitless.
Well-gained is the human state by those for whom this sutra is dear; they have abandoned all unfavorable conditions and are grateful to all the Buddhas.
Inconceivable are the eons by which those who have cast off cyclic existence [have been purified],
by whom even a single four-line verse from this supreme sūtra has been upheld.
They have been seen by all the Buddhas, and they have honored those Buddhas;
they will swiftly attain enlightenment, for this sūtra is dear to them.
No doubt or uncertainty regarding any phenomena will arise for those who hold dear this sutra; for them, nirvana is near.
The Great Hero, the Tathāgata, was seen by them on Vulture Peak;
all were prophesied by the Buddha that they shall behold the Jina Maitreya.
Having seen the Perfectly Awakened Maitreya, those who have established themselves here in this sūtra during this age of destruction will attain auspicious patience.
They abide at the limit of reality; the limit of reality is inconceivable.
For those who are at this inconceivable limit, no doubt exists.
Not even the slightest atom of doubt exists in them in any respect;
when this [doubt] has been abandoned down to its subtlest atom, enlightenment is not difficult for them to attain.
Even while practicing what is difficult during this most terrifying age of destruction,
having trained in this jewel of a sutra, one possesses inexhaustible eloquence.
Having made this sutra dear, they are the guardians of the treasury of the Buddhas;
this is an offering to all Buddhas, an inconceivable offering of the Dharma.
For them, the inconceivable wisdom of a Buddha will not be difficult to attain,
as they shall uphold this sūtra during this terrible age of destruction.
And those by whom these sūtras were upheld for previous Buddhas—
in their bodies these shall abide when the time of destruction arrives.
They shall raise their voices throughout millions of Buddha-fields,
in the presence of the Protectors of the World, regarding the conduct of Śākyasiṃha.
Roaring the lion’s roar, they shall proclaim the inconceivable roar of the Buddha;
with infinite eloquence, they will declare supreme enlightenment.
Those born of the Ikṣvāku clan who shall protect this awakening during the time of destruction and great terror have all been prophesied by the Buddha. (SRS 32.147)
Endowed with various forms and adorned with diverse marks,
they will travel, performing miracles, to pay homage to tens of millions of Buddhas.
With flowers like illusions, appearing the color of gold,
with flowers made of silver, and those of beryl and crystal;
All kinds of jewels appear in their hands,
with which those seeking the path to enlightenment scatter [offerings] over the perfectly awakened ones.
Various and manifold offerings, accompanied by the excellence of musical instruments,
issue forth from the pores of the skin like the sands of the Ganges.
And those inconceivable millions of beings who hear that sound become irreversible from the unsurpassed wisdom of a Buddha.
And they proclaim the inconceivable praise of those millions of Buddhas;
their voice is heard throughout inconceivable realms.
And those who hear that sound, their perceptions cease;
when perception has ceased, they behold many Buddhas.
Having practiced the conduct of awakening with such knowledge,
and having accomplished the welfare of all sentient beings, the Victors become those who bring about benefit.
These are the qualities and benefits that the wise indeed obtain;
there are others, immeasurable, by which this awakening has been upheld.
Even a woman, having heard this sutra, should retain even a single verse;
having turned away from the female state, she shall become a preacher of the Dharma.
She shall not assume the female state again hereafter;
she will always be gracious and adorned with the primary marks.
Furthermore, in this supreme sūtra, the most excellent qualities have been revealed;
all of these shall belong to him, and he will swiftly attain awakening.
And having upheld this sūtra, which is the domain of bodhisattvas, he shall always be confident in all births.
The peaceful samādhi of the Bodhisattvas has been proclaimed as "the progenitor. Whoever desires to awaken to enlightenment should set forth this sūtra.
They are close to the lords of sages; they are close to the awakening of a Buddha. Being composed and tranquil, they shall before long attain this peaceful stage.
In this state of awakening, those heroic bodhisattvas always abide,
beholding millions of Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Having become a king, a sovereign lord of the earth and a universal monarch,
he will behold the stainless Buddhas whose minds are perfectly tranquil,
and he will praise those Lords of the World with hundreds of verses.
Having attained this peaceful, stainless samādhi.
Having performed incomparable worship for the Leaders of great renown, the supreme among gods and men,
he abandoned his kingdom as if it were a lump of spittle.
Pure and utterly purified, he will practice the holy life.
Having gone forth into the teaching of the supreme Victor and having attained this stainless, peaceful samādhi,
he became one of virtuous speech and sweet voice.
The wise one will possess the empowerment of ten million sūtras.
Practice the Dharma that is empty, signless, supremely excellent, peaceful, thoroughly calmed, subtle, and unattached;
it is by nature empty, eternally stainless, and serene—reveal this extensively to many beings through the attainment of meditative concentration.
With profound intelligence, with constant and infinite intelligence, with vast intelligence, and with intelligence regarding immeasurable meanings—
one who attains this profound and peaceful samādhi will cause the entire world to reach the light.
He will be eternally pure, a perpetual celibate, free from the odor of raw flesh, and always undefiled;
and there he will establish millions of other beings who have attained this peaceful, stainless samādhi.
He will possess extremely sharp wisdom and supreme intelligence; he will be an ocean of learning, with infinite intellect at all times.
His speech will be auspicious, he will be skilled in thought and knowledgeable in the ritual methods, having maintained this stainless, peaceful samādhi.

Whether it be fields of professional activity, or likewise fields of craftsmanship, fields of medicine, or even medicinal herbs— in all these, the steadfast one will become a master who has reached the further shore, by upholding this stainless samādhi and this sūtra.

Having maintained this peaceful, stainless samādhi, he will at all times become a teacher in the world, highly skilled and having reached the further shore in poetry, treatises, as well as in comedy, dance, and song.

He will always possess a retinue; his faction will be indivisible, ever united and harmonious, as he practices the supreme, excellent, and auspicious conduct of awakening while upholding this stainless sūtra and meditative concentration.
Neither sorrow, nor thorns, nor likewise mental affliction shall ever arise for that wise one;
he will be healthy at all times by upholding this peaceful, stainless samādhi.
Whatever pains of the body, as well as pains of the mind, whatever pains of the teeth, and likewise pains of the head—
none of these diseases shall befall him in the world of the living, having maintained this peaceful, stainless samādhi.
Whatever various diseases there are in the world of mortals— both those diseases of the body as well as those of the mind—
those diseases never at all arise for one who maintains this peaceful, stainless samādhi.
Whatever various afflictions there may be of the mind, or whatever various kinds of diseases there may be in the body—
none of those various defilements exist for one who has maintained this peaceful, stainless samādhi.
Just as the atmosphere and the sky are unstained, naturally pure, stainless, and luminous,
so too does the mind become pure for one who maintains this peaceful, dustless samādhi.
Just as the radiance of the moon and likewise the radiance of the sun are pure, ungraspable, and luminous,
so too does the mind become luminous by maintaining this peaceful, stainless samādhi.
Just as it is not easy to paint the sky with many kinds of various colors once one has taken up the pigments,
even so it is not easy to paint the mind unless one cultivates this peaceful, stainless samādhi.

Just as the wind, blowing in the four directions, moves everywhere through the quarters without attachment, so too does the stream of that person’s mind become like the wind; he moves through the world unattached and unsmeared.
It might be possible to catch the blowing wind with a net, or it might be possible to bind the wind with a rope;
but his mind is not easily understood by anyone who has not cultivated this peaceful, stainless samādhi.
It may be possible to grasp a reflection appearing in water or to obtain water from a vessel of oil;
yet it is not easy to understand the mind of one who has cultivated this peaceful, stainless samādhi.

The clouds thunder and lightning flashes; it might be possible for a human hand to seize them, but it is not easy to know the measure of his mind once he has cultivated this peaceful, stainless samādhi.
It is impossible to grasp the sounds and cries of the beings who exist within the Buddha-fields of the ten directions;
nor is it easy to know the limit of the mind of that bodhisattva when he has attained such a samādhi.
Having attained that stainless stage of concentration, he becomes undefiled and unsullied;
he never again enters into the three realms of existence, for by him this peaceful concentration has been attained.
Neither greedy for sensual pleasures, nor greedy for forms, nor greedy for women, and not having a deluded mind;
when one becomes tranquil, thoroughly pacified, and undefiled, then this stainless samādhi has been attained.
He is not greedy for sons, nor again for daughters, not greedy for a wife, nor greedy for a retinue;
he becomes one whose conduct is perfectly peaceful and remains unsullied when this stainless samādhi has been attained.
Neither greedy for gold nor again greedy for wealth, nor longing for heaven, he is unattached to riches and jewels;
his mind is perfectly pure and free from conceptual construction—this is the attainment of samādhi, and this is its distinction.
The wise one does not practice the holy life for the sake of heaven, nor does he ever give gifts out of a longing for heaven;
desiring perfect awakening, he practices virtuous conduct.
Having attained meditative concentration—this is his distinction.

He does not practice asceticism or vows for the sake of kingship, nor does he seek sovereignty over the three worlds; longing for perfect awakening for the benefit of many beings, he has accomplished this stainless samādhi.
Passion never produces suffering for him who is not lustful for women and whose mind is not deluded;
nevertheless, by means of his natural wisdom, he attains this passionless, peaceful samādhi.
That fault never produces pain for him, nor does he ever harbor ill-will or resentment;
for by means of loving-kindness, that element of hatred is destroyed, as he attains this stainless, peaceful samādhi.
Delusion never produces suffering for him, for that delusion and ignorance have been destroyed by his wisdom.
Having attained that immeasurable knowledge free from darkness, these immeasurable qualities arise upon the attainment of meditative concentration.
Passion is constantly and thoroughly restrained by the meditation on the foul; hatred is always destroyed without remainder by loving-kindness;
delusion is dispelled by wisdom, and having shattered the web of afflictions, one who has attained meditative concentration shines forth throughout the entire world.
Sleep never causes him pain, nor do his various underlying afflictions trouble him when well-cultivated;
he remains unstained and fully liberated—these are the immeasurable qualities attained through meditative concentration.
Delusion never produces suffering for him, for he is always delighted in renunciation;
the bodhisattva who maintains this samādhi becomes a giver of all his possessions and a bestower of happiness.
He becomes endowed with incomparable power and is always possessed of strength;
there is never anyone in the world who is his equal, that bodhisattva who maintains this samādhi.
Even when he becomes a universal monarch (cakravartin) among men, having arrived in Jambudvīpa in this world,
even then he becomes one worthy of worship by many people, having attained excellence, wise, and possessed of distinguished insight.
Those who are leaders, distinguished jewels of noble families, possessing abundant enjoyments and great wealth;
where there are horses, elephants, excellent chariots, and vehicles for transport, as well as copious quantities of silver, gold, and precious gems.
Those who become faithful here in this supreme Buddha-knowledge are endowed with the jewels of noble families in Jambudvīpa.
Reborn there in that distinguished jewel of a family, they bring about vast benefit for the assembly of their kinsmen.
Those in this world, in the family of Jambudvīpa, who lack faith—heedful, he generates faith in them;
by establishing them in the thought of awakening within the assembly of beings, they become Buddhas, the most excellent Jinas, the Self-Arisen Ones.
And having touched that incomparable, supreme enlightenment, they shall turn the peerless wheel in Buddha-fields;
and those who understand this wheel of Dharma at that time will all be firmly established in the dharma of non-arising.
At that time, these bodhisattvas are of great benefit to sentient beings; they are always worthy of worship.
They constantly perform incomparable service for beings and produce for them the eye that is free from the dimness of ignorance.
Many hundreds of thousands, infinite millions of beings, whose roots of merit were established there upon hearing [the teaching],
they too attain the supreme mind of enlightenment when the Jina instructs the great-souled Bodhisattva.
Their fields are never empty and they are always joyful; unstained by defilements, these ones then become Buddhas.
Wherever these Bodhisattvas abide, they bring about immeasurable benefit for sentient beings.
They guard their ethical discipline and practice incomparable celibacy; for vast and infinite eons, they cultivate meditative concentration.
Always firmly established in dhyāna and liberation, those bodhisattvas shall forever be sons of the Buddha.
Constantly cultivating those bases of psychic power, they go to many various and infinite realms;
there they hear the Dharma spoken by the excellent Sugatas and, established in dhāraṇī, they grasp it all.
The Bodhisattvas who are established in the dhāraṇīs proclaim immeasurable and infinite sūtras;
the Bodhisattvas who are established in the dhāraṇīs bring about immeasurable benefit for sentient beings.
He knows the passing away and rebirth of sentient beings, their coming and going;
whatever kind of karma they have performed, such is the ripening of its result.
Not even the slightest transference of karma can be found;
yet those highly renowned Bodhisattvas understand them as well.
Emptiness is the supreme dwelling of the great-souled ones;
they establish inconceivable millions of sentient beings in the Mahāyāna.
As they give these instructions, the notion of a "sentient being" does not arise for them; rather, the bodhisattvas reveal the non-arising of all phenomena.
For those who proclaim the Dharma, the perception of a graspable object does not arise;
they dwell in emptiness, firmly established in steadfast knowledge.
With reference to this samādhi and the dwelling of all Teachers,
the notion of "woman" does not occur to them, for it is their very nature.
Having eliminated the perception of "woman," he sits upon the seat of enlightenment;
having sat upon the seat of enlightenment, the perception of "Māra" ceases.
And there the wise one perceives neither Māra nor Māra’s army;
nor does he even see the three daughters of Māra.
As he sits upon the seat of enlightenment, all conceptual perceptions are abandoned;
when all conceptual perceptions have been abandoned, the entire earth trembles.
The Sumeru mountains and the oceans as far as they exist in the ten directions—
all those beings in all ten directions perceive them.
At that time, as the Bodhisattva was awakening to supreme enlightenment, this earth shook with a sixfold tremor through his miraculous power.
All conditioned phenomena and those phenomena which are unconditioned—
all those phenomena taught by means of the word "dharma," he understands them all.
And herein no one at all is awakened, yet the lion’s roar resounds;
having understood that which is to be practiced, one becomes a Buddha, a maker of light.
Phenomena exist dependently and arise dependently;
those who understand the dependent nature of all phenomena are the wise.
Knowing the rules regarding all phenomena, they have mastered the course of emptiness;
having mastered the course of all phenomena, they thoroughly understand that course.
Having sought this destination, the Bodhisattva is not to be found;
for by him this inconceivable destination of all Buddhas has been known.
He has reached that state who understands all states of existence;
having known the characteristic of the true Dharma, all illusion has been cut off for him.
Having sat upon the seat of awakening and likewise let out a lion’s roar,
he made himself known to immeasurable and inconceivable millions of buddha-fields.
And all those [worlds] the Buddha-heroes of great renown caused to tremble,
as the Charioteer of Beings disciplines those beings who are ready to be trained.
Having touched supreme enlightenment, he rises from the seat of awakening and disciplines immeasurable and inconceivable beings who are to be trained.
Then the Perfectly Awakened One emanated infinite Buddha-emanations,
who went to thousands of millions of fields as teachers of the Dharma.
They establish inconceivable millions of beings in supreme enlightenment,
teaching the sublime Dharma for the benefit of all living creatures.
Such is that great wisdom, the inconceivable wisdom of the Buddhas;
therefore, generate the aspiration, the unsurpassed aspiration for enlightenment.
Generate reverence for the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha of supreme virtue,
and for the heroic Bodhisattvas who cultivate the foremost awakening.
With unshrinking minds, pay honor without weariness;
then you will before long become Buddhas, makers of light.
And those bodhisattvas who have come here from thousands of fields behold the Light of the World teaching the supreme Dharma.
The great heroes scatter great jewels over the Leader;
