they scatter māndārava flowers for the sake of awakening.
They adorn this field, the unsurpassed buddha-field;
they cover it all around with nets of jewels throughout the ten directions.
Banners were hung and millions of flags were raised;
this field was adorned with infinite ornaments.
And they construct gabled halls adorned with every kind of jewel, as well as countless delightful palaces, mansions, and turrets.
Celestial palaces, crescent moons, windows, and likewise lattices;
incense-burners and banners variegated with various jewels.
With the incense being burned, a delightful fragrance, clearly like a mass of clouds,
wafts through thousands of millions of buddha-fields.
Having pervaded all those places, they rained down a shower of fragrance;
and those who smell that fragrance become Buddhas, the Leaders.
The thorn of passion has been abandoned by them, and the thorn of hatred no longer exists;
the web of delusion is shattered, and all darkness vanishes.
There they attain supernatural powers, the strengths, the factors of enlightenment, and the faculties;
they attain the meditative concentrations and liberations, and they become worthy of offerings.
Five koṭis were designated, strewn with millions of garments;
they were covered with nets of jewels and adorned with millions of parasols.
Seated there were those heroic bodhisattvas who had gathered together;
they shone with the primary marks as well as with the secondary characteristics.
The entire buddha-field was adorned with trees made of jewels,
and there were created lotus ponds filled with water possessing the eight qualities.
Having drunk that water and standing on the bank of the lotus pond,
they all dispel their thirst and become shrines for the world.
And bodhisattvas gathered from various fields speak the praises of the Buddha, the Lion of the Śākyas, the Protector.
And those who hear that description shall become leaders of the world;
inconceivable benefits have been revealed by me here in this sutra.
Inconceivable millions of lotuses with petals made of gold were there,
their pericarps fashioned from pure uragasāra sandalwood.
There, beautiful stalks of lapis lazuli and cages of crystal were fashioned,
and the filaments of emerald were beautifully arranged.
And those who smell that delightful fragrance as it issues forth—
their every diseases are pacified, their minds being filled with joy.
Passion, hatred, and delusion—all these are exhausted by them;
having destroyed the three defects, they become Buddhas who bestow happiness.
From that, the inconceivable sound of "Buddha" issues forth;
and the sounds of "Saddharma" and "Saṃgha" likewise issue forth from every direction.
Having heard that sound of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, many millions of beings become irreversible.
And as this sound issues forth, it reaches millions of fields;
it establishes inconceivable millions of beings in the wisdom of a Buddha.
The śakuntas, the kalaviṅkas, and the jīvaṃjīvaka birds—
they too uttered sounds that were the unsurpassed word of the Buddha.
And those trees made of jewels have been fashioned here in this field;
they are exquisite, beautiful to behold, jewel-trees that are delightful to the mind.
Upon those trees hang rows of all kinds of ornaments;
by the majestic power of the Buddha, they have been manifested here in this field.
There is no such array in any of all the fields in every respect that is not seen here in this field, which at that time is even more distinguished than them.
This has been declared in brief by the Protector, the Lion of the Śākyas:
"The Bodhisattvas of great renown have no doubt regarding this knowledge."
Those who awaken to this [teaching] by the millions have inconceivable destinies;
they increase in wisdom like the ocean with its rivers.
Indeed, no end can be found to those who drink from the great ocean;
for this method of the bodhisattvas is said to be inconceivable.
In this pinnacle, the heroic and renowned bodhisattvas emit qualities of voice as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Therefore, even the sound to be contemplated is likewise not conceptualized by the bodhisattva;
when conceptualization has been abandoned, he becomes near to awakening.
He does not violate his ethical discipline even for the sake of his life;
with unimpaired conduct and firm vows, he proceeds as a bodhisattva.
He shall no longer be corrupted by any perception of desire whatsoever;
having abandoned all perceptions, his meditative absorptions are immeasurable.
Concentrated in mind, he moves about and does not cling to meditative absorptions;
unattached and vigilant, he does not cling to the worlds.
Having transcended the world-systems, he goes to Sukhāvatī;
having arrived there, he beholds the Perfectly Awakened One Amitābha.
And those heroic bodhisattvas, adorned with the [major] marks,
having attained the perfection of the five superknowledges, range within the domain of dhāraṇīs.
They go to tens of millions of fields to pay homage at the feet of the Buddhas;
illuminating them as they travel, they go to inconceivable Buddha-fields.
Having abandoned all faults and purified themselves of all afflictions,
the Victors have utterly severed all defilements and abide in their final birth.
And those people do not go to the states of woe from that field;
all states of woe have been utterly eradicated in that field without exception.
You have been awakened by Amitābha, the supreme Buddha and protector;
do not harbor any doubt in that regard—you shall go to Sukhāvatī.
Any woman who, having heard the praise of the Best of Fields, attains clarity of mind,
will quickly become a most wise and excellent man.
And by means of supernormal power, he travels to billions of fields.
Whatever various and immeasurable offerings there may be throughout millions of billions of world-systems,
even if one were to constantly perform those offerings to the Best of Men, they would not equal even a fraction of the merit of one who possesses a mind of loving-kindness.
Constantly practicing ethical discipline and meditative concentration, as well as the dhyānas, the liberations, and the immeasurables;
constantly practicing emptiness and the signless—he indeed becomes a Sugata in the world before long.
For this is the supreme and most distinguished worship for me: the bodhisattva who is established in the aggregate of ethical discipline;
by him all the Buddhas are truly worshipped at the time of the end of the eon, he who remains steadfast in the thought of awakening.

Those bodhisattvas who, in this terrible age of decay, protect the Dharma taught by the excellent Sugatas, have been well entrusted by thousands of millions of Buddhas; they are my sons, the final guardians of the Dharma.
Thus ends the thirty-second chapter of the *Śrī-samādhirāja*, titled "The Chapter on the Benefits of Upholding the Sūtra."
(Vaidya 218) Chapter 33: The Chapter on Kṣemadatta.
Then the Blessed One addressed the youth Candraprabha once again: "In the past, youth, in a time long gone, in an incalculable, even more incalculable, vast eon—"
At that time, in that age, when it was immeasurable, inconceivable, and limitless, there appeared in the world a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Ghoṣadatta—
one perfected in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans.
And for human beings, there was the Buddha, the Blessed One.
Furthermore, young man, that Tathāgata Ghoṣadatta, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened one, having established immeasurable, inconceivable, limitless,
and incalculable beings in arhatship through the destruction of the outflows, and having led immeasurable and incalculable beings to final nirvana in unsurpassed [enlightenment],...
Having established [beings] in the state of non-retrogression toward perfect enlightenment, he passed into parinirvāṇa.
And at that time, young man, during that period, there was a king named Śrīghoṣa.
For the sake of making offerings to that Tathāgata, he had eighty-four thousand million stūpas constructed, containing the relics of the Tathāgata within them.
And at each and every stūpa, he established eighty-four thousand times ten million billion offerings of lamps;

likewise for musical instruments, cymbals, flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, and flags— at each and every stūpa, he established eighty-four thousand times ten million such offerings.

Indeed, young man, after King Śrīghoṣa had performed worship to the relics of the Tathāgata and convened a great assembly of eighty-four hundred thousand *koṭī-niyuta-śata-sahasra* bodhisattvas, he applied himself to honoring those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas with every kind of provision for their comfort.

And all those bodhisattva mahāsattvas were Dharma-preachers with unassailable eloquence, who had attained meditative concentration, who had attained the unimpeded dhāraṇīs, who taught the Dharma with genuine qualities, who taught the Dharma with complete purity, and who had reached the perfection of the bodhisattva-mastery.
And at that time, O youth, on that occasion, in that very assembly, there was a bodhisattva named Kṣemadatta.

The Mahāsattva was a youth, tender, with black hair, abiding in the auspicious prime of his first youth; having not yet sported in sensual pleasures, he was a celibate from childhood, and his full ordination (*upasaṃpadā*) took place at one year [of age].
And at that time, O Prince, on that occasion, King Śrīghoṣa requested that great assembly of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, namely, for the recitation of the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*).

Having exhorted those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas for the sake of accomplishing the Bodhisattvapiṭaka, the great dhāraṇīs, skill in means, mastery, discipline, and non-attachment, he lit many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of lamps before the Tathāgata’s stūpa as the night drew on.
He prepared a circular area that was sprinkled, swept, and purified, strewn with flowers, and furnished with various wonderful couches and seats.
King Śrīghoṣa also went forth, accompanied by his harem, the people of the villages, cities, and provinces, his courtiers, and his citizens.

Having performed worship at the stupa of the Tathāgata with musical instruments, cymbals, drums, flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, and flags— all held aloft— he ascended to the palace terrace together with his harem.
"For the sake of hearing the sublime Dharma,
a great assembly of gods and humans has gathered, desiring to hear the Dharma.
Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Kṣemadatta saw those hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of great lamps burning brightly."
It became clearly illuminated by that very radiance.
And perceiving the multitude of gods and humans assembled to hear the Dharma, this thought occurred to him: "I too have set out upon the Mahāyāna."

"What if, desiring this samādhi, I were to perform an offering to the Tathāgata such that the world with its gods, humans, and asuras would be struck with wonder, become uplifted, joyful, delighted, and filled with gladness and happiness, and attain the light of the Dharma;
and so that I might surpass all these offerings to the Tathāgata which have been made by King Śrīghoṣa?"
And King Śrīghoṣa, together with his harem and retinue, would be filled with wonder, becoming uplifted, delighted, and possessed of joy and gladness.

Then, indeed, the bodhisattva Kṣemadatta, his mind thus disposed and filled with joy and gladness, perceiving that great multitude of people assembled as listeners of the Dharma, stood before the Tathāgata’s shrine at night; having wrapped his right arm in his robe and soaked it in oil, he set it ablaze.

Then, indeed, as the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Kṣemadatta was seeking unexcelled, perfect enlightenment with his resolute intention, even though his right hand was thus set ablaze, there was no change in his mind or in the color of his face. Then, O youth, as soon as the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Kṣemadatta’s hand was set ablaze, fully ignited, turned into a mass of light, and reached a single flame, it happened thus.
Then, at that very moment, a great earthquake occurred;
by the radiance of his blazing hand, those many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of lamps were eclipsed,
and a great light appeared in all directions.
By that radiance, all directions were illuminated and completely pervaded.

Having become filled with joy and gladness, he [the Bodhisattva] addressed the entire assembly at length with a beautiful and delightful voice, with distinguished speech, and with continuous words and syllables, concerning this samādhi called "The Manifestation of the Equality of the Essential Nature of All Phenomena."
He made his request and proclaimed it;
there, twelve thousand gods belonging to the Trāyastriṃśa host assembled to hear the Dharma.
Filled with joy and gladness, they performed various kinds of divine worship.

And divine hosts of apsaras performed celestial songs. King Śrīghoṣa, situated upon the upper terrace of his palace, surrounded by his kinsmen and amidst his harem, having undertaken the eightfold poṣadha vows, beheld the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Kṣemadatta illuminating him with his arm.

Having seen him illuminating [the area] with a divine light that surpassed all other radiance and transcended the human, it occurred to him: "Ah, this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Kṣemadatta must have attained the superknowledges (abhijñā)!
Having established intense love, serene faith, and reverence, he, together with his retinue, was supported by a great mass of merit from roots of virtue.
Then, together with eighty women of the inner apartments, she threw herself down from the palace roof in order to see the Bodhisattva Kṣemadatta and to greet him with joy.
By virtue of that root of merit born of her reverence, in this very life, she and her retinue obtained the protection of the gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas.

Supported by the gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas, King Śrīghoṣa, together with his retinue, descended once more from the palace a full hundred thousand cubits high;
yet there was no injury to his body, no affliction to his mind, nor any despondency.
Then King Śrīghoṣa, raising both his arms together with a great multitude of people,
raised a loud cry and a great clamor of lamentation for the sake of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Kṣemadatta.
Seeing his arm burning and blazing intensely,
the king, together with that great multitude of people, wept aloud, shedding tears.
Then the bodhisattva mahāsattva Kṣemadatta addressed King Śrīghoṣa:
"But why, Great King, together with this great multitude of people, do you weep and shed tears, making such a great outcry and clamor?"
Then King Śrīghoṣa addressed the Bodhisattva Kṣemadatta with these verses:
“Seeing this wise and learned Dharma-preacher, Kṣemadatta, who is great in wisdom,
people weep because they perceive him to be deficient in his limbs.”
Indeed, having recognized that this form, which had arisen like a mass of radiance,
was now deprived of arms, I too became even more sorrowful.
The arm which was ignited by you has released a radiance that pervades the ten directions;
these other lights have been eclipsed by this divine splendor produced from you.
This earth has been shaken, yet your mind does not falter;
therefore, this mind that has arisen is not that of one who is ignorant.
Indeed, I fell from a palace a hundred thousand cubits high here together with the women of the inner court, yet my body was not harmed.
Excellent is your wondrous wisdom; excellent is your unsurpassed mind; excellent is the vigor you have well-initiated; and excellent is your great resolute intention.
He whose hands are burned never experiences agitation here;
filled with joy and gladness, he further proclaims the Dharma.
Like the moon on the full-moon night, or like the sun in the vault of heaven,
or like Sumeru, the king of mountains— thus do you shine, O worthy one!
May I, as a wise one, likewise fulfill this vow;
having abandoned attachment to the body, may I accomplish the welfare of living beings.
I rejoice because of my love for the Dharma, and my affection for this is inconceivable;
yet, that you are deprived of your limbs causes me the greatest sorrow.
For Kṣemadatta, honored by gods and nāgas, spoke these verses with infinite eloquence to the king: SRS_33.11 //
One is not truly deficient in limbs merely because one lacks an arm;
rather, one is deficient in the limbs of a god if one lacks virtuous conduct.
With this putrid body, I have made offerings to the Tathāgatas—
those inconceivable ones who are worthy of gifts and are the shrines for the entire world.
One who seeks the wisdom of a Buddha might give away as many infinite trichiliocosms as there are, offering them to the Lords of the World.
This is a worldly form of worship; there is another, inconceivable worship:
those who know that all phenomena are empty renounce both body and life.
"I shall make a declaration of truth; O Great King, listen to me!
And you, all these people present, understand this verse!"
By that truth that I shall become a Buddha, a shrine for the world,
by that truth may the earth tremble in six ways!
As soon as these words were spoken, the earth trembled;
ten million gods, having attained a state of wonder and amazement, were filled with great joy.
Delighted, gods and humans gave rise to the thought of awakening;
immeasurable and inconceivable numbers set out upon this supreme vehicle.
To as many beings as have had their purpose fulfilled by the monk Kṣemadatta,
there extends the wisdom of the Buddhas, which is inexhaustible and inconceivable.
By that truth that this dharma does not exist as something called "an arm," by that truth may my arm quickly become as it was before.
By that truth, this Dharma called Kṣemadatta does not exist;
even when sought throughout the ten directions, it is not apprehended because of its emptiness.
Whatever sound issues forth, know that to be empty;
sound is like an echo—know all phenomena to be thus.
One who has mastered the course of emptiness is always fearless;
by his word of truth, the entire world is not consumed by fire.
As many beings as there are in the three worlds— whether they be gods or humans—
all become composed through the splendor of omniscience.
Whatever calamities there may be, whether divine or human,
they all become extinguished through the power of irreversibility.
These verses were spoken, and his arm rose up once more;
Kṣemadatta’s body was adorned with the various marks of excellence.
Thousands of millions of deities, stationed in the sky,
at that very moment showered that monk with mandārava flowers.
Indeed, this Jambudvīpa is filled with superhuman flowers,
and millions of billions of apsarases have performed musical concerts.
At that moment, as Kṣemadatta uttered this roar,
thousands of millions of Buddhas beheld this miraculous manifestation.
In their respective fields, the one of great renown shall announce [this] to the monks,
the nuns, the laymen, and the laywomen.
For that monk Kṣemadatta was wise and possessed of great power,
by whom this arm was set ablaze for the sake of the Buddha’s wisdom.
By that lamp, thousands of fields, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, were illuminated as if at the time of the conflagration at the end of an aeon.
All the fields became filled with flowers and sandalwood powder;
from the ground upward, they were covered knee-deep.
The buddha-field became filled with all kinds of jewels and all kinds of flowers;
for the sake of honoring Kṣemadatta, the nāgas rained down pearls.
This field is adorned with arrays consisting of all kinds of jewels;
it is strewn with pearls and gems as an offering to Kṣemadatta.
Gods, nāgas, yakṣas, kinnaras, apsarases,
and mahoragas have set out for supreme enlightenment, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
The Lion of the Śākyas, the perfectly awakened one, the Victor, uttered a lion’s roar before the assembly of monks on Vulture Peak Mountain.
I was Kṣemadatta, and Śrīghoṣa was Ajita;
for thousands of millions of eons, he practiced the conduct leading to perfect enlightenment.
At that moment, upon merely seeing the monk Kṣemadatta,
the female nature of those women was instantly transformed by those inconceivable powers.
They have been prophesied by the Lord of Men; there is no turning back for them.
They shall all become self-arisen ones, the guides of the world.
Having heard this sutra which reveals the virtues of ascetic refinement, the wise one,
well-trained in this Dharma, should not cherish attachment to the body.
Thus ends the thirty-third chapter of the *Śrīsamādhirāja*, titled "The Chapter on Kṣemadatta."
(Vaidya 223) Chapter 34: Jñānāvatī.
Thereupon, the Blessed One again addressed the youth Candraprabha: "Therefore, then, O youth..."

A bodhisattva mahāsattva who desires this samādhi and wishes to quickly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment should apply themselves to the giving of Dharma or the giving of material goods once they are established in roots of virtue. That bodhisattva mahāsattva should dedicate that gift through four types of dedication.

By which four? Namely, for the sake of attaining those skillful means by which the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, have fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, I plant this root of merit consisting of giving.
This is the first transformation:
that from whichever spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) I may hear, grasp, master, and retain those skillful means (upāyakauśalya),
by which one fully awakens to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment (anuttarā samyaksaṃbodhi).
May there be an encounter with those very spiritual friends;
in this way, I plant this root of merit consisting of generosity. This is the second dedication.
May I come to possess those acquisitions of wealth that would serve as the livelihood for all the world;
it is with this intent that I plant this root of merit.
This is the third dedication.

May I obtain such a physical existence that it may benefit sentient beings through two kinds of assistance— both by the assistance of material goods and by the assistance of the Dharma— and with this intention,
I plant this root of merit.
This is the fourth dedication.
O youth, by means of these four dedications, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should dedicate those roots of merit.

Furthermore, young man, a bodhisattva mahāsattva— whether a householder or one who has gone forth— who desires this samādhi and wishes to quickly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, should, with sincerity, serve, associate with, and attend upon bodhisattva mahāsattvas who are virtuous, endowed with good qualities, and possessed of wisdom.
If there should be a monk, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, who is the upholder of this samādhi,
and he should be afflicted and severely ill,
he must resolve to restore that monk from that affliction even by means of his own flesh and blood.

Young man, a bodhisattva mahāsattva endowed with resolute intention, desiring this samādhi and wishing to quickly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, should— remaining unshakable and confident— even give up his own flesh and blood to restore a Dharma-preaching monk from illness.
Therefore, young man, by this method as well, it should be understood in this way.
Long ago, O youth, in the past, in an incalculable, more than incalculable, vast, and immeasurable eon, at that time and in those days,

there appeared in the world a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Acintyapraṇidhānaviśeṣasamudgatarāja— one perfected in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed.
The Teacher of gods and humans,

the Buddha, the Blessed One— indeed, young man, on the very day that the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Acintyapraṇidhānaviśeṣasamudgatarāja fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, on that very same day he passed away.
Having manifested immeasurable and incalculable emanations of Buddhas, having disciplined immeasurable beings,

having established them in arhatship for the exhaustion of the outflows, and having established immeasurable beings in the state of non-retrogression toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, he passed into parinirvāṇa on that very same day.
Furthermore, after that Blessed One had passed into parinirvāṇa, his True Dharma remained for eighty-four hundred thousand nayutas of koṭis of years.

At the time when the teaching of that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Acintyapraṇidhānaviśeṣasamudgatarāja, was disappearing, during the final five-hundred-year period, many monks appeared who held views based on objective apprehension (*upalambhadṛṣṭi*).
Such discourses as these did not please them, nor did they have faith in them; instead, they obstructed and rejected them.
Causing harm to monks who were holders of such discourses, they even deprived them of their lives.
Driven by a craving for honor and gain, they deprived a thousand monks who were holders of such discourses of their lives.
Furthermore, Prince, at that time and on that occasion, there was a king named Jñānabala, the sovereign of Jambudvīpa, who upheld the true Dharma and was endowed with his former vows.

Moreover, Prince, at that time and on that occasion, there was in this Jambudvīpa a certain monk, a preacher of the Dharma named Bhūtamatī, who was a holder of that samādhi and served as a spiritual friend to that king, entering his household.
He was a well-wisher, compassionate, and desirous of their welfare;

and that king was insatiable in his longing to see him, constantly yearning for a vision of him, capable of approaching him, attending upon him, questioning him, receiving, retaining, reciting, and understanding his discourse on the Dharma.
Furthermore, that monk who was a preacher of the Dharma was skilled in the conduct, behavior, inclinations, elements, and latent predispositions of sentient beings.

He was skilled in knowing the variations in the faculties, powers, and vigor of sentient beings, as well as their mental dispositions and latent tendencies; he was skilled in the consistency of truth, skilled in responding to inconsistencies, and skilled in the definitive determination of meaning. He possessed profound eloquence, knew the methods for disciplining sentient beings, was the first to speak, and had a smiling face. With his countenance free from frowns, he dwelt in a state of vast mind and was dedicated to great compassion, remaining unconquered.
By all those who propound other doctrines.

And at that time, O youth, and at that moment, King Jñānabala had a daughter, a girl sixteen years of age, noble by birth, beautiful, pleasing, and lovely to behold, endowed with the highest excellence of a fair complexion; her name was Jñānāvatī.
That monk, Bhūtamati, was her preceptor who instructed, inspired, gladdened, and exhorted her toward wholesome qualities.
And at that time, young man, on that occasion, a severe black erysipelas appeared on the thigh of that Dharma-preaching monk; it was difficult to treat and its remedy was hard to find.
He was rejected by the physicians as being incurable.

Then indeed, the king, together with his harem, his sons, his daughters, and his retinue, having learned that the monk was ill, wept and shed tears along with eighty thousand women, along with the citizens and townspeople, along with the kingdom, the merchants, and the country folk, along with the astrologers and high officials, and along with the ministers, gatekeepers, and members of the assembly.
Having learned that the monk was ill, they all wept and shed tears, saying, "May this monk not pass away!
At that time and on that occasion, O Prince, a certain deity who had been an old kinsman of King Jñānabala remained constantly attached to him.

While the king was in a state of sleep, she appeared to him in a dream and said: "Great King, if this black erysipelas of the monk were smeared with the fresh, untainted human blood of a man, [he would recover]."
"If fresh, undefiled human flesh, prepared with various flavors, were given as food,
this monk would thus recover from his illness.
Then, at the end of that night, King Jñānabala awoke from that dream and, having entered the midst of the inner apartments, related the nature of this dream to the women of the harem.
"Such a dream was seen by me.
For in this way, O Prince, not a single woman from that women's quarters nor from that royal palace ventured to give that medicine to the monk.
The princess Jñānāvatī also saw such a dream as this.
Having seen it and awakened, she reported the nature of this very dream to her mothers and her retinue within the inner apartments;
yet not a single woman dared to give that medicine to the monk.

Then the princess Jñānavatī, satisfied, elated, joyful, delighted, and filled with gladness and cheerfulness, made this resolution: "What if I were to give from my own body this medicine, providing fresh blood and fresh flesh as prescribed?"
"I alone here in this royal household am the youngest of all and the most youthful, and my actions of body, speech, and mind are undefiled.
I seek undefiled knowledge and shall offer my own blood and flesh from my body to this undefiled Dharma-preacher,
so that perhaps this monk may recover from his illness."

Then, indeed, that Princess Jñānavatī, having gone to her own residence, took a sharp blade and, with a mind absorbed in the Dharma, cut the flesh from her own thigh. Having prepared it by mixing it with various flavors into a refined dish, and taking up the blood, she ushered the teacher in, sat before King Jñānabala, and [anointed] him with that blood.
Having applied that ointment to the erysipelas, he satisfied him with food well-prepared from it.
Then, that monk—unknowing, unawakened, and unsuspecting—consumed that meal.
Immediately upon consuming that food, all those pains of that monk were completely stilled.

And every ailment was eliminated. With his fever of passion gone and endowed with all happiness, he taught the Dharma in such a way that from that inner palace and from that gathering of people from the city,
the countryside, and the kingdom, twelve thousand beings conceived the aspiration for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Then King Jñānabala addressed his own daughter with these verses:
"From where, O girl, did you obtain this blood? From where was this human flesh brought?
What food have you prepared today, my daughter, by which the Dharma-preacher has been made well?"

"Is this man killed, or has he died, that you have obtained him? For what purpose have you prepared this dish with various flavors? And from where, girl, did you obtain the blood by which this evil disease is to be cured?"
Having heard her father’s words, the maiden Jñānāvatī spoke this to him; with an undaunted mind, she uttered these words: "Listen, father, to what I say to you."
"O Father, I have seen a dream revealed by a deity;
listen to me, O Lord of the Earth, and understand the truth of what has occurred."
That deity said to me: "If anyone were to give human flesh and blood to this monk, he would be freed from that evil disease. (SRS 34.5)
And having risen from my bed and entered the inner apartments, O King, I then related this dream to my senior mothers.
I said to the maidservants: "Who is capable of preparing such human blood and meat, perfectly seasoned and prepared with a flavorful sauce?"
Food must be provided and an ointment made from blood;
how is this monk to be liberated from black erysipelas?
If this treatment is not performed quickly,
this monk will either die from this illness or [survive] only by means of medicine.
In the three worlds, what being would not give up their own flesh and blood?
Having seen this, what wise person would place reliance upon the body?
"I inform you of the inner apartments: not even a single woman says she will give [herself].
For I hold this monk dear, and I hold my own self dear; yet for the sake of awakening, I have surrendered my flesh and blood."
For them, there is no reliance on devotion toward the body, nor even an atom of affection for a self;
and even having abandoned their own selves, they do not become dejected—those who aspire to the auspicious, sorrowless awakening.
Then, having heard all that, the entire harem was struck with amazement; yet not a single woman there ventured to engage in such an act with her.
Then my mind was turned toward this: "I shall give food to the monk;
having cut off my own flesh, I will provide an ointment with my blood."
Having cut my own thigh with my own hand, I took the flesh and blood;
I cooked a piece of meat, well-prepared with various flavors.
In the presence of my father, I shall give that sick monk human flesh as food and an ointment of blood.
Listen to my words, O lords of men: when human flesh was not to be found,
King Mayūradhvaja cut his own flesh, prepared it, and gave it to this Dharma-preacher.
For the sake of unsurpassed awakening, I have performed this great service by sacrificing my own body;
the monk has been liberated and rendered free from harm, and I have acquired immeasurable merit.
The king also said to his daughter: "How can you cut flesh from your own body for the preparation of medicine, my girl? May there be no suffering or bodily pain for you."
The wise and confident princess addressed him: "O King, Lord of Men, listen!
Having heard this, apply yourself to it thoroughly; such is the inconceivable ripening of karma."
"O dear ones, by performing evil deeds, beings are cooked even in a terrible hell;
having become fleshless, they become possessed of flesh again—behold the inconceivable fruit of karma."
Through evil karma, they become devoid of flesh and blood in an instant, yet in that very moment they possess flesh and blood again;
how much more so, then, does flesh and blood arise through wholesome karma born of resolute conviction?
While my flesh is being cut, I have no sensation; though my blood is being taken away, there is no agitation.
There is neither wound nor breach in the Dharma-body, even if all my own flesh were to be cut away.
O Dharma-practitioner, having generated supreme joy, I cut off and gave my own thigh flesh;
yet, father, I felt no pain from the wound, for my body was just as it had been before.
Just as the udumbara flower, my dear, is seen only once in many millions of eons,
even so is such a Dharma-preacher seen only rarely here in Jambudvīpa. (SRS 34.25)
Just as beings are never satiated when they behold a radiant ornament of Jāmbūnada gold,
even so gods and humans here are never satiated upon seeing such Dharma-preachers.
Just as the thirst of a person overcome by thirst is dispelled when they drink clear water,
even so these wise preachers of the Dharma dispel the thirst of living beings with the nectars of the Dharma.
This flesh and blood of mine was well-sacrificed when it was given to the sick monk;
the erysipelas was pacified for that preacher of the Dharma, and thus I have performed the reverence praised by the Buddha.
For one who possesses virtuous conduct, who is deeply learned, and who maintains this supreme samādhi—
may I become a recipient of these very qualities through the gift of my own flesh that I have offered.
Just as the fragrant, delightful, and auspicious scent of black sandalwood, following the wind,
wafts through the ten directions— even so are the Dharma-preachers like that fragrance.
Just as Mount Meru appears in all directions, beautiful and lovely to behold on every side,
shining and radiant throughout the quarters, even so do the Dharma-preachers resemble Mount Meru.
Just as some wise person might restore and repair a stūpa that was falling down,
whoever should feel faith toward that stūpa— even because it was restored by him— that shall be the cause for them.
In this very way, this Dharma-stūpa, who was ill, has been liberated by the application of blood and by my own flesh; out of reverence for the Dharma, I have lit a lamp in Jambudvīpa. (SRS 34.33)
If this monk had not passed away, even the sound of "samādhi" would have ceased here in Jambudvīpa;
yet, because he has been treated, that samādhi has now been attained by sentient beings.
The monk is the protector of the entire world and the giver of sight to the blind world;
he is the healer of passion, hatred, and delusion—this is my King of Physicians.
Always established in a vast mind, no measure of his conduct can be found;
trained in words whose meanings are well-determined, he is unconquered by the proponents of other doctrines.
I shall have no further fear of falling into the lower realms, nor shall I ever again experience womanhood;
for ten million times a thousand kalpas, I shall instead show supreme reverence toward the Dharma-preacher.
If someone were to give as many Buddha-fields as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, filled with jewels, to the Leaders,
and another were to give even a single toe of their foot, the merit of the latter would be far more distinguished than that.
Having passed away from here, that girl beheld thousands of millions of Buddhas;
having gone forth in the teaching of them all, she taught this supreme, peaceful samādhi.
In the final age after all those supreme among bipeds had passed into parinirvāṇa,
the sons of the Sugatas were always able to attain the going-forth and remained undefiled.
Then, having practiced the holy life under the teaching of the Tathāgata Dīpaprabha,
she turned away from her female state and became a monk, a preacher of the Dharma.
Maitreya, that lord of men was Jñānabala, who always upheld the true Dharma;
he was the Dharma-preacher Dīpaṃkara, and at that time I was the king’s daughter.
At that time, desiring this samādhi and having abandoned all deceit, the Dharma-preacher attended upon me with his own flesh and blood.
Those monks who then wept upon seeing the sick man tormented by pains—
all of them became forever irreversible and never again went to the states of woe.
They never suffered from eye disease, nor head disease, nor ear disease;
they had no nose disease, no tongue disease, and never experienced toothache.

Those by whom a sick monk was then attended became forever pleasing to behold, their bodies blazing with glory and splendor, endowed with the thirty-two marks of excellence born of hundreds of merits.
Having gone forth in my teaching while this awakening of the Buddha is being destroyed,
and having preserved the treasury of the Tathāgatas, they shall behold thousands of millions of Buddhas. (SRS 34.47)
Having well grasped this awakening of the Buddhas and always upheld it with reverence,
they shall accomplish vast benefit for all beings and behold Akṣobhya, the supreme among men.
And having heard this unsurpassed conduct, they will obtain joy and a practice free from worldly taint;
and having heard of their own former conduct, they will perform magnificent worship of the Buddhas.
Having seen monks who are wise and virtuous, one should always attend upon them with sincerity;
having abandoned all harshness and fault-finding, one should then serve those monks who are preachers of the Dharma.
Having abandoned malice and anger, you should honor my sons in the teaching of the Dharma;
lest you become blind for many millions of eons and, having fallen into the lower realms, remain in suffering.
Neither morality nor his learning shall protect him; neither meditation nor dwelling in the forest shall protect him.
Even worship of the Buddha will not protect him at that time when he has committed mutual malice toward one another.
Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "Jñānāvatī," in the *Śrī-Samādhirāja*.
(Vaidya 232) Chapter 35: Supuṣpacandra.
Then, the venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, and placed his right knee on the ground.
Having established himself upon the ground, he bowed with palms joined toward where the Blessed One was and addressed the Blessed One as follows:

"I would like to ask the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened Buddha, about a certain matter, if the Blessed One would grant me the opportunity to have my question answered."

When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Ānanda: "In that case, Ānanda, sit upon your own seat and ask the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One, whatever you desire;
I shall satisfy your mind by answering each and every question.
When this had been said, the venerable Ānanda spoke thus to the Blessed One: "I have been granted leave, Blessed One."
"I have been granted the opportunity, O Sugata, to have my questions answered.
Then, the Venerable Ānanda sat down on a seat before the Blessed One and addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"What, O Blessed One, is the cause and what is the condition that some bodhisattvas here, while practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva..."
Do they undergo the cutting off of hands, the cutting off of feet, the cutting off of ears, the plucking out of eyes, the amputation of limbs and the head, and the severing of various minor members?
Do they experience manifold sufferings?
"And yet they do not diminish, nor do they perish, with respect to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?

When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Ānanda: "If you, Ānanda, were to know the sufferings that I have experienced in order to bring about this unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment..."
This too should occur to you; how much more so that which you consider to be the question to be asked of the Tathāgata?
Ānanda, it is just as if, for example, a man here were to be ablaze, burning, and become a single mass of flame, starting from the sole of his foot up to the top of his head.

Suppose some man were to approach him and say: "Come, my good man! While your body is not yet cooled, being fully endowed and possessed of the five strands of sensual pleasure, play, enjoy yourself, and amuse yourself!
What do you think, Ānanda? Would that man, while his body was not yet cooled and he was fully endowed and possessed of the five strands of sensual pleasure, play, enjoy himself, and amuse himself?
Ānanda said, "Certainly not, Blessed One.

The Blessed One said, "Ānanda, that man might play, delight, and enjoy himself—provided for and endowed with the five strands of sensual pleasure—by means of an unextinguished physical existence based on conceptual construction;

but such was not the happiness experienced by the Tathāgata while formerly practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva, upon seeing beings suffering through the three types of misery and being impoverished."

or joy, or gladness of mind. Ānanda, those bodhisattvas mahāsattvas who, while formerly practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva, were of unbroken morality, flawless morality, unstained morality, unspotted morality, untarnished morality, undisturbed morality, and immovable morality;

They were of a nature not to flee, not of a nature to look toward other doctrines, and not of a nature to be inconsistent; they were upright in character, faithful to their vows, and devoted to the welfare of sentient beings.
Endowed with such morality as this,
Ānanda, those bodhisattva mahāsattvas, while practicing the infinite course of conduct of a bodhisattva, do not suffer the loss of the cutting off of their hands,
nor do they suffer the loss of the cutting off of their feet.
They do not undergo decline through the cutting off of ears or noses;
they do not undergo decline through the plucking out of eyes or the cutting off of heads;
they do not undergo decline through the cutting off of limbs or members.
Nor do they experience various sufferings;
rather, they swiftly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Long ago, Ānanda, in the past, incalculable eons ago— more than incalculable, vast, immeasurable, inconceivable, incomparable, unfathomable, and limitless eons ago—

at that time and in those days, there appeared in the world a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Ratnapadmacandraviśuddhābhyudgatarāja, one perfected in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed.
The Teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.
Furthermore, Ānanda, at that time, the lifespan of that Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Ratnapadmacandraviśuddhābhyudgatarāja, was nine hundred thousand nayutas of koṭis of kalpas;
and every single day, he established nine thousand koṭis of kalpas of sentient beings in the state of non-retrogression regarding the qualities of a Buddha.

Furthermore, Ānanda, at that time, when the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Ratnapadmacandraviśuddhābhyudgatarāja had passed into parinirvāṇa, during the final fifty-year period of the disappearance of the True Dharma while the True Dharma was being corrupted, these very kinds of sūtras were despised by many people and shunned by many people.
They were opposed by the many and abandoned by the great multitude.

This occurred while a time of great fear and terror was present, during a period of great calamity, at a time of excessive rain, at a time of drought, at a time of predatory beasts, at a time like a wilderness of lightning, and at a time of famine.

At a time when false views prevailed, at a time of incorrect views, at a time of seeking the mantras of non-Buddhist sects, and while the era in which the awakening of the Buddhas was being destroyed was unfolding, seven thousand bodhisattvas were banished from villages, towns, market towns, royal capitals, and provinces;
they dwelt together, relying upon a forest grove named Samantabhadra.
The Dharma-preacher Supuṣpacandra taught those monks the method of the dhāraṇī-dharma.
Furthermore, that Dharma-preacher King Supuṣpacandra, having gone alone into seclusion and being in solitary retreat, by means of his divine...
With his superhuman eye, he saw that many millions of bodhisattvas who had planted roots of merit in various other buddha-fields had been reborn here;
and if they were to obtain the opportunity to hear this dharma-discourse on the dhāraṇīs, [they would not be reborn again].
They would not turn back from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment;
however, if they were not to obtain the opportunity to hear this dharma-discourse of the dhāraṇī,
they would turn back from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.

Then the Dharma-preacher Supuṣpacandra, mindful and clearly comprehending, arose from that samādhi and approached where that great assembly of bodhisattvas was; having approached, he said this to that great assembly of bodhisattvas:
"We shall go, sons of good family."
"Having descended into villages, towns, market towns, kingdoms, and royal capitals, we shall teach the Dharma to sentient beings.

Then that great assembly of bodhisattvas said this to the Dharma-preacher Supuṣpacandra: "It is not our wish that the Venerable One should descend from this forest grove to villages, towns, market towns, kingdoms, and royal capitals. Why is that?"
There will be many conceited monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen,
and the time for the rejection of the true Dharma will prevail; they will deprive that venerable one of his life.
The Venerable One was exceedingly gracious, handsome, and beautiful to behold; he was endowed with the prime of youth and was in the flower of his age.

His skin had the luster of polished gold and refined silver, and he was adorned with the *ūrṇā* hair, white as a conch shell, a jasmine flower, or the moon; his forehead was radiant, and his dark, curled hair formed a crown upon his head.
"May no princes or others like them, their minds afflicted by envy and avarice, deprive you of life.

Then the Dharma-preacher Supuṣpacandra said this to that assembly of Bodhisattvas: "If my own self were to be protected, then I would not have performed protection for the teaching of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, of the past, future, and present."
And at that time, he spoke these verses:
"Never dwelling in the notion of a self, it is possible here to provide protection for this teaching;
for the vast canopy of the Sugatas' awakening must be revealed in the dreadful final age."
He who has completely abandoned the notion of a self, and who avoids these beings who rely on the doctrine of a person,
as well as forms, sounds, tastes, smells, and tangibles— he protects the teaching.
One might serve tens of billions of nayutas of Buddhas with food and drink with a devout mind,
and with parasols, banners, and the lighting of lamps, for as many millions of eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges.
And whoever, while the True Dharma is being destroyed and the teaching of the Sugatas is coming to an end,
should attend to disciples for even a single day and night— the merit from this becomes more distinguished than that.
Now, those who, while the True Dharma of those bulls among men is being destroyed, cultivate indifference—
by them no Conquerors whatsoever have been honored, nor has any reverence been shown toward the Leaders.
May you be happy; accomplish your own welfare and protect yourselves. May you be heedful here in this discipline, always dwelling in loving-kindness.
Guard your radiant morality—unblemished, pure, clean, and stainless.
Those who protect this stainless morality praised by the Buddhas.
By those who have honored all the Sugatas, as many as have appeared in the past,
all those people who have set out for enlightenment are thereby protected.
By that very [virtue], many beings who have committed evil deeds are rescued from hell,
provided they protect the stainless morality praised by the Buddhas of old.

"Give gifts of the most excellent jewel of the Dharma; always maintain patience and take refuge in the forest. Skilled in meditative concentration, cultivate gentleness. Do not engage in conflict in any way, but practice the disciplined and auspicious conduct. We are going to the royal capital city for the sake of protecting sentient beings."
While that sage of great intelligence, the essence of the foremost of beings, was descending, these others were weeping most piteously and falling at his feet;
"O wise one of great intelligence, do not descend! Look upon the trees in the forest!"
Possessing a beautiful fragrance, delightful, and most radiant, he is the self that is the nature of protection.
Those former leaders as well— the possessors of the ten powers, with tranquil faculties and gentle natures—
having gone to forests and to the peaks and summits of mountains,
practiced the supreme conduct for the sake of awakening; they were the foremost among those possessing merit and wisdom.
Learn from them as they dwell in the forest; do not go away, O you of noble vows!
Your body is adorned with beautiful marks, and your hair is dark blue;
your complexion, emitting a radiance like gold, illuminates the earth.
Between your eyebrows, your *ūrṇā* is exquisitely beautiful, possessing a luster like that of a conch shell.
May no envy arise in your body, nor may it be scattered among kings and princes.
Then, Ānanda, the Dharma-preacher Supuṣpacandra addressed that assembly of bodhisattvas with a verse:
"As many Sugatas as there were in the past— all those omniscient ones whose outflows were exhausted—
they all, having attained supreme enlightenment, performed [their deeds] in this world within the three realms of existence."
They have practiced the most excellent conduct for the sake of awakening; they are supreme in merit and wisdom.
For the sake of protecting beings, millions of bodhisattvas train in their discipline.
Having all performed circumambulations of the wise seer and having bowed at his feet,
they sighed deeply and uttered piteous cries, wailing with voices of distress;
others, as if their legs were severed, fell to the earth and fainted like sal trees.
And that rishi, who had accumulated merit and desired the welfare of sentient beings, did not turn back.
Taking his bowl and robe, the seer set forth like a maned lion;
established in the intrinsic nature of phenomena, he took neither notice of virtues nor faults therein.
While I was dwelling in this world within dense forests, beings fell into states of misery; desiring to be a protector for sentient beings, I went to that city, the most excellent of towns.
Then, indeed, the Dharma-preacher Supuṣpacandra, having entered villages, towns, market-towns, kingdoms, and royal capitals, taught the Dharma to sentient beings.
Having entered them in the forenoon, he established ninety-nine koṭis of living beings in the state of non-retrogression regarding unexcelled, perfect enlightenment;
yet he had not yet reached that royal capital, Ratnāvatī.
He arrived in due course at that capital city of Ratnāvatī.
Having approached that capital city of Ratnāvatī, he stayed at the foot of a certain *plakṣa*-sāla tree.
At the end of that night, he entered those capital cities of Ratnāvatī.

Having entered, he established thirty-six million living beings in the state of non-retrogression regarding the Buddha-dharmas; yet he had not yet finished his meal. Having been deprived of food, he departed from the royal capital of Ratnāvatī, approached the nail-stūpa of the Blessed One, and spent the night and day standing right there.

When that night had passed, on the second day before the morning meal, he entered the royal capital of Ratnāvatī and established twenty-three koṭis of living beings in the irreversible Buddha-dharmas; yet he did not yet partake of his meal. Having foregone his second meal, he departed from the royal capital of Ratnāvatī, approached the nail-stūpa of the Blessed One, and spent the entire day and night standing upright.

When that night had passed, having been deprived of food for three nights, he entered the royal capital of Ratnāvatī and established nine billion nine hundred million living beings in the irreversible qualities of a Buddha.
He had not yet performed his meal;

having been deprived of food for three nights, he departed from the capital city of Ratnāvatī and approached the nail-stūpa of the Blessed One, where he spent the third night and day standing upright.

At the end of that night, on the fourth morning before his meal, he entered the royal capital of Ratnāvatī and established nine million nine hundred thousand living beings in the irreversible dharmas of a Buddha.
Having fasted for four days, he departed from the royal capital of Ratnāvatī and approached the nail-stūpa of the Blessed One; there, he spent his nights and days standing upright.
At the end of that night, on the fifth day, he entered the royal capital of Ratnāvatī and went into the king’s inner apartments.
Having entered, he established eighty thousand women in the state of non-retrogression toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Furthermore, from that city, he established all sentient beings in the non-retrogressive state regarding the qualities of a Buddha.

At the end of that night, during the sixth meal-period before breakfast, he entered the royal capital of Ratnāvatī and established a thousand princes in the state of non-retrogression regarding unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment;
yet, he had not yet finished his meal.

Having fasted for six meals, he departed from the capital city of Ratnāvatī and went to where the nail-relic stūpa of the Blessed One was located; there he spent his time day and night. At the end of that night, before the seventh meal, Śūradatta entered the capital city of Ratnāvatī and saw King Śūradatta departing for the park in a golden chariot with silver wings and a pole made of uragasāra sandalwood.
It had poles made of lapis lazuli and wheels of beryl; it was adorned with raised parasols and banners, covered with silk cloth and draped with fine cotton fabrics,
wherein eight hundred maidens, holding jeweled cords, [were stationed].

His chariots were drawn by well-proportioned, graceful, and beautiful horses, endowed with the most exquisite and abundant whiteness of color; they were capable of producing joy and exhilaration in the young, yet not in the elderly.
Eighty-four thousand great kṣatriya clans followed closely behind him.
Eighty-four thousand great brāhmaṇa clans and eighty-four thousand great householder clans followed closely behind him as well.
And five hundred daughters, mounted upon palanquins made of jewels, went forth ahead;
at the mere sight of that monk, they became irreversible from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
And eighty-four thousand women of the inner apartments, at the mere sight of that monk, became irreversible from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.

And that great multitude of people, having removed their jeweled earrings and taken off their sandals, dressed themselves in single robes, placed their right knees upon the ground, and bowed with palms joined toward where the monk was, stood there paying homage. Then indeed those maidens also, impelled by their former roots of merit, [descended] from those palanquins.
Having descended, putting on one shoulder his upper robe, and placing his right knee upon the ground,
he bowed with palms joined toward the Blessed One and addressed him in verses:
"Today it has been illuminated all around, just as by the sun."
As the monk was entering, he established his presence before the multitude of people.
Passion and hatred have been utterly severed, and delusions have been dispersed;
anger, malice, and envy—all these have been cut off within that interval.
No one looked at the king, nor did anyone follow him;
such was the retinue of King Śūradatta, including his sons and others.
Just as the moon on the full-moon night is surrounded by the constellations,
so did that monk shine, honored by the prince.
Just as a golden image is wonderfully and beautifully adorned by skilled artisans,
or like a king of *sāla* trees in full bloom— even so does the monk shine.
And Śakra, the lord of the gods, of great majesty, the thousand-eyed sovereign, the destroyer of cities,
the ruler of the thirty-three gods upon the summit of Sumeru— just so does this monk shine as he enters.
I think he is like Brahmā established in the Brahma-world, or like the divine son Sunirmita the lord, or like the god Suyāma in the realm of desire; even so, this monk shines as he enters.

I think it is as if the sun, with its thousand rays, were blazing in the sky, dispelling the darkness and illuminating all the directions on every side; even so does this monk shine as he enters. (SRS 35.22)
Having given vast gifts for infinite eons, having always maintained stainless morality,
and having cultivated incomparable patience throughout the entire world, he is indeed resplendent, adorned with the primary marks.
Having generated the vigor praised by noble beings, having cultivated the four meditative absorptions with an undaunted mind,
and having produced wisdom to destroy the web of afflictions— by this, that monk shines forth in all the world.
Those heroic Buddhas, peerless essences of beings, who have passed away after scattering the most excellent Dharmas—
those in the future time and likewise those in the present— it is for them that this son has come under the power of the King of Dharma.

O monk, may nothing impermanent ever befall you, you who thus radiate such splendor throughout the entire world! Behold your most beautiful brilliance and the sound of your voice; the majesty of kings does not shine forth so intensely.
Since you have realized this Dharma by yourself and, authorized by the Buddhas, wander through the entire world, let us all likewise abandon our female state;
let us all become just like this monk.
Having all joined their ten-fingered palms in reverent salutation and spoken these verses, they cast down their ornaments:
golden garlands, as well as pearl necklaces, ear-ornaments, and earrings.
Just as a powerful universal monarch, while traveling through these four continents, regards all the sons of the earth with the same affection he feels for his own children.
Toward merchants, kṣatriyas, brahmins, householders, and those who are local kings, he does not produce excessive affection for his own people; rather, he maintains equal love for all.
Thus trained and having gained mastery over the dhāraṇīs, this gentle monk discerns the factors of awakening, the powers, the faculties, and the eightfold path;
like the moon shining at night in the midst of the hosts of stars.
Just as the radiant sun, the Vairocana, blazes forth with its orb.

We pay homage to all the Buddhas, who possess the ten powers, whose faculties are tranquil, and who are gentle; no person, even if they were to spend hundreds of eons, would be able to exhaust their praise,
nor could they finish recounting their many virtues even if they spoke for thousands of millions of eons.
One should not disparage even a single hair on the body of one who is the most excellent in the world.
By whom the peerless wheel has been turned, and the basis of wisdom taught; by whom the subtle,
stainless Dharma has been proclaimed, which is nowhere to be seen by any śramaṇas,
brāhmaṇas, gods, nāgas, asuras, māras, or those headed by Brahmā.
The ocean of qualities of the omniscient Buddha cannot be fully described.
"We pay homage to the peerless King of Physicians, the Jina, whose biological sons are such as these.
Having spoken these verses, all the princesses were then filled with joy;
they scattered gold and golden powder and spread out their garments.
And with hundreds of millions of beautiful crest-jewels set in gold,
they joyfully covered that monk, having set out for enlightenment.
Then, this thought occurred to King Śūradatta: "Alas, this inner court has gone astray and the body of people has risen up in revolt!

And those people, having removed their jeweled earrings, draped their robes over one shoulder, placed their right knees upon the ground, and extended their joined palms toward that monk, paid him homage.
King Śūradatta was so pleasing, so handsome, and yet not as beautiful as that bhikṣu;
he became terrified for the sake of his kingdom,
and upon seeing the perfection of that bhikṣu’s physical form, he gave way to extreme rage.
As that monk stood upon the royal highway, he entered the king's sight.
This thought occurred to him: "With a mind full of passion, this monk has gazed upon my harem;
he has even made a signal with his eyes."
The thought occurred to him: "Who now shall deprive this monk of life?
Then, a thousand sons followed behind King Śūradatta;
he addressed them, saying: "O princes, deprive this monk of life!"
Then those princes indeed resisted King Śūradatta on account of that monk.
This thought occurred to him: "Even my sons do not carry out my command."
"I alone have been established as the sole, peerless one.
Who now shall deprive this monk of his life?
Now, King Śūradatta had an executioner named Nandika, who was fierce, violent, and cruel.
Then King Śūradatta, satisfied, elated, and joyful, thought to himself: "This Nandika will deprive this monk of his life. Then the executioner Nandika approached King Śūradatta.
King Śūradatta said to him: "Nandika, will you be able to deprive this monk of his life?"
"I shall give you a magnificent covering.
Nandika said, "Very well, Your Majesty; as you command."
"Today I shall deprive this monk of life!
Therefore, Nandika, do as you deem fit now;
taking a sharp sword, cut off the hands and feet of this monk."
"Cut off his ears and nose!
Since he has gazed upon my inner apartments with a mind full of passion,
therefore pluck out both his eyes with a pair of tongs!"
Then, at that very moment, Nandika the executioner took up a sharp sword and cut off the monk’s hands and feet and gouged out his eyes;
thereafter, that great multitude of people, weeping, wailing, and lamenting, entered the royal capital of Ratnāvatī once again.
Then, after seven days had passed, King Śūradatta went to the pleasure grove, but he did not take delight, nor did he play, nor did he enjoy himself.
Having returned from the grove at the end of those seven days, he entered the royal capital of Ratnāvatī.
There he saw that monk cast away on the royal highway, dead for seven days, yet with a body that was not discolored.
This thought occurred to him: "Since this monk's body is not discolored, there is no doubt that this monk will be irreversible from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Yet, I have committed a sinful deed that leads to rebirth in a great city of hell."
"I shall very soon have to go to the great hell.
As he was thinking thus, eighty-four thousand sons of gods in the sky above raised their voices in a single, harmonious sound, saying: "It is even so, Great King, just as you say;
this monk is irreversible from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment."
At that moment, a great fear, terror, paralysis, and horripilation arose within him, and he was overcome with remorse.
Then King Śūradatta, distressed, dejected, and full of regret, spoke these verses at that time:
"I shall renounce my kingdom as well as the royal capital, my silver, gold, jewels, pearls, and gems."
Taking up a weapon myself, I would slay this self; I am one of base deeds and childish intellect in this world.
This monk Supuṣpacandra was here, armored with the thirty-two marks;
illuminating [the city], he entered the royal capital like the king of stars on the full moon night.
I, being base, was sporting in sensual pleasures and went out joyfully with a host of women;
mounted upon my chariot and surrounded by kṣatriyas, here comes this fragrant, fair-eyed monk.
Seeing that monk, the assembly of women was filled with joy; out of love, they cast down golden garlands.
All of them, joining their ten fingers in reverent salutation, praised the monk with songs of verses.
All those sounds of singing were stilled; the king, mounted upon his chariot and surrounded by kṣatriyas, saw him approaching:
"This is the fragrant, fair-eyed mendicant of great majesty, the son of the most excellent Sugata."
My own mind was exceedingly base; deluded, I gave rise to envy and anger there.
But seeing the vast multitude of women filled with joy upon beholding the monk as he entered the royal capital, [I was overcome].
There he spoke words of most terrible form: "At that very moment, I shall tell my thousand sons:
'Go and cut this monk into pieces! For he is my supreme and most dreadful enemy.'"
O Prince, they were all possessed of supreme virtue, their minds intent on their own welfare, and they took delight in that monk.
O gods, because I did not carry out such an instruction, I was at that time overcome by grief.

Seeing this monk, who was supremely virtuous, endowed with loving-kindness, and acting like a father, my mind became deeply resentful; I set out to kill him, and in the end, I fell into the Avīci hell.
"This Nandika, who stands here on the royal road, is one of extremely fierce deeds who causes suffering to human beings;
he has given me such an order: 'This monk must have his flower garland cut off here. (SRS 35.43)
In that delightful forest of Samantabhadra, filled with birds and sweetly fragrant with blossoming flowers,
that other vast community of monks was like an only son deprived of his mother.
"Arise, O Bhikṣu! Dwell in the forest; you have accomplished a most vast benefit for humanity.
Since you have come here to this royal capital, the Bhikṣus will come seeking you, wailing most piteously."
These flower-banners have been placed to the right, and others, beautiful and lovely to behold, to the left;
the path has been prepared and strewn with robes. Arise, O Bhikṣu, and proclaim the supreme Dharma!
"You have been long established here in this capital; the monks will come, weeping most piteously.
May there be no obstacle to your life at this time when the teaching of the Supreme Victor is being destroyed."
Just as some person of great majesty, whose fame is constantly proclaimed throughout the cardinal and intermediate directions,
falls from a great precipice onto the earth, overwhelming this entire triple world on all sides.

In the very same way, this monk here, fallen upon the earth, possessed of beautiful form and adorned with the excellent marks—though he was free from fault, I, with a sinful mind, have caused him to be cut into pieces; thus Supuṣpacandra now lies in fragments.
"O monks, here everyone is indeed struck by suffering, devoid of joy, and with hearts pierced by thorns;
they will quickly fall into such a state upon seeing this Dharma-preacher Supuṣpacandra struck down and fallen upon the earth."
Supuṣpacandra was like the king of mountains, armored with the thirty-two marks;
yet, seized by a crowd of women as if by a garland of flowers, in an instant he was torn into pieces.
"I have committed an act of supreme and most terrible form; I shall go, helpless, to Avīci, the realm of Yama.
That monk, having been cut here into pieces, will remain at the furthest distance from the Buddhas."
"O son, neither my own sons nor the assembly of my kinsmen, nor those I revere, nor the servants at my feet,
will come to my rescue when I have gone to hell for having myself performed most base deeds."
Those Buddhas of the past, as well as those yet to come, and whoever currently dwells in the ten directions—
those caravan leaders, endowed with the ten powers and free from defilements— I go for refuge to them, whose bodies are as solid as a diamond mass.
Having seen the monk here cut into pieces, a most piteous cry was uttered by the deities;
having gone, they announced it to the community of monks that Supuṣpacandra was here in this royal city.
That wise and learned Dharma-preacher of great majesty, renowned throughout the cardinal and intermediate directions—
that Bodhisattva established in the dhāraṇīs, Supuṣpacandra, has been killed here in this royal capital.
He who for infinite eons gave various gifts, who guarded his morality without blemish or wavering,
and who cultivated a patience unequaled in all the world— that Supuṣpacandra was slain here in the royal capital.
He who was ever-vigorous throughout infinite eons, who meditated upon the four dhyānas with an undaunted mind,
and who cultivated the wisdom that destroys the afflictions— that Supuṣpacandra has been killed here in this royal capital.
Having completely abandoned all attachment to the body and likewise becoming indifferent toward life,
Supuṣpacandra entered the forest of Samantabhadra and was slain here in this royal capital.
Having entered the royal capital, those gentle ones raised a piteous and terrible cry;
seeing the monk here cut into pieces, they all fainted and fell upon the earth.
The community of monks said to that king: "O King, what offense has this monk committed against you—he who is unbroken in virtue, well-restrained, and remembers his inconceivable previous births?"

This self-controlled one has reached the further shore of the knowledge of retention; he understands here that all conditioned things are empty. He demonstrates the signless nature of the world and has abandoned every perception of volitional aspiration.
He has released a charming and beautiful voice; his faculties are tranquil and he is gentle.
He has reached the perfection of dwelling in former lives and stands exalted above the world.
He is the Buddha, the self-arisen one, a bull of wisdom, who is honored by the world.
With pure eyes, he looked upon them free from darkness, possessing exceedingly great loving-kindness and compassion.
Sensual desires are base, lowly, and producers of suffering; they are the destroyers of heaven.
Those men who indulge in sensual desires become deficient in hearing and bereft of wisdom. By indulging in sensual desires, a person becomes blind and may even kill his own mother and father.
One may indulge in sensual pleasures or even kill those who possess virtue; therefore, a person should avoid them.
O King, best of monarchs, if one indulges in sensual pleasures while abandoning this supernatural power,
he goes to terrible, harsh, and painful hells of endless fear.
One who kills such a wise monk always performs an evil deed; therefore, one who desires auspicious awakening should avoid various kinds of evil.
With an undaunted mind, he abandons forms, sounds, tastes, as well as excellent smells, and tangible phenomena;
having understood the body to be as empty as an illusion, he likewise regards the eye, ear, nose, and tongue in the same way.
Trained in generosity, peerless in ethical conduct, he practiced patience and vigor as well as meditation; having reached the perfection of wisdom, he acted for the benefit of sentient beings.
The entire world, including gods and humans, gazed upon the Jina with loving-kindness.
By means of that eye, they awaken to auspicious enlightenment within the dense thicket of great darkness.
With joy, they abandon elephants, horses, and chariots, as well as couches, seats, palanquins, swings, yoked vehicles, oxen, villages, and kingdoms;
having renounced cities, realms, gold, crystal, silver, and coral.
Having renounced their wives, beloved sons, their own steadfast heads, they have set out for enlightenment.
And with joy they perform incomparable worship, taking up flowers and perfumes,
various parasols, banners, and flags, as well as musical instruments;
yet they do not take delight even in the course of existence, having realized that all states of being are empty.
Therefore, those endowed with the ten powers, adorned with the marks, illuminate all directions.
They are not settled in the desire realm, nor in the form realm, nor in the formless realm;
those bodhisattvas who are established in the dhāraṇī do not adhere to any phenomena within the triple world.
They have no perception of a self, nor again a perception of a sentient being, no perception of a life-force, nor even a perception of a person;
those bodhisattvas who are established in the dhāraṇī always practice the stainless holy life.
They have neither the perception of existence nor the perception of non-existence; neither the perception of security nor the perception of insecurity;
neither the perception of happiness nor the perception of unhappiness—those Bodhisattvas who are established in the dhāraṇī.
There is no perception of existence, nor again a perception of non-existence; no perception of woman, nor again a perception of man.
There is no perception of a village, nor a perception regarding cities; no perception of a kingdom, nor even a perception regarding market towns.

For those bodhisattvas who are established in the dhāraṇī, there is no perception of passion, nor again a perception of dispassion; no perception of hatred, nor again a perception of non-hatred; no perception of delusion, nor again a perception of non-delusion.
They are not dependent on the sense-faculties, nor again on the powers; they are not attached to the factors of enlightenment or the meditative absorptions.
Those bodhisattvas who are established in the dhāraṇī have utterly abandoned all faults within the three realms.
They are neither stained by passion nor corrupted by hatred, nor are they deluded by ignorance; they are always free from deceit.
Having seen the Buddhas, the possessors of the ten powers, they pay them honor, and they do not even aspire to heaven, O holder of wisdom.
Having heard the distinguished Dharma from others, they never again have any doubt regarding it;
like a vessel of oil that is clear and pure, they have understood the cutting and the non-cutting according to the views of others.
If one forms attachment, affection arises; that too is indeed a great affliction.
If one commits an offense, resentment toward him arises, along with enmity, fear, and evil.
Those of wise intellect who have set out for enlightenment should abandon both of these.
They become bulls among men here, endowed with the ten powers, arisen preeminent in the world.
Having abandoned both the internal and the external, they abide in the intrinsic nature of phenomena;
their aggregate of ethical discipline is purified— untarnished, unbroken, and flawless.
In them, their conduct is never mottled nor even stained;
having avoided these two, the wise ones awaken to auspicious enlightenment.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
"In the past, while practicing my conduct, I was then a king named Śūradatta.
That royal capital was named Ratnāvatī, the garden-land from which I went forth."
Then, having seen that monk mounted upon the chariot— so serene and beautiful to behold,
armored with the thirty-two marks, illuminating all ten directions on every side— [he was struck with wonder].
Supuṣpacandra, renowned throughout the directions, compassionate for the welfare of others and dwelling in loving-kindness,
entered the city out of compassion for sentient beings, shining with glory and splendor.
And I was so handsome in appearance that a most terrifying envy arose within me;
greedy for sensual pleasures and bound to my kingdom, I thought, "May he not displace me from this sovereignty."
A full thousand sons of mine, mounted upon chariots, follow behind me;
adorned with various crowns and ornaments, they proceed like the sons of the gods following the Lord of the Thirty-three.
In that [chariot], five hundred daughters of mine, beautiful to behold, wearing jeweled sandals,
adorned with bound crowns and ornaments, and decorated with nets of gold, draw the chariot.
Eighty thousand women of mine, all graceful and beautiful to behold,
mounted upon chariots, gazed upon the monk who was pleasing to look at, possessing a splendor as lofty as Mount Meru.
Upon seeing them, they conceived the thought of them as their fathers and generated the mind directed toward supreme, excellent enlightenment;
having then committed themselves to the holy life, they cast away those delightful ornaments.
At that moment, envy arose within me, along with malice, hatred, and cruel stubbornness;
intoxicated by my power, I said to my sons, "Kill the monk who stands before us!"
Then, O youth, having heard my words, they became deeply distressed and dejected:
"O father, do not speak such words; we shall not kill a monk such as this."
Even if one’s body were to be cut limb from limb for as many millions of eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges,
we would never harm a monk, for he has generated the mind set upon awakening.
Then, having heard these words of his son, the king, enraged, spoke to his servant, the executioner:
"Bring this monk quickly; he who stands even before the inner apartments must be executed."
Then that executioner named Sunandin, possessed of a fierce mind, arrived later;
taking up a sword that had been tempered in oil, he cut the monk into eight pieces.
Having committed this most terrible deed, she went out to the park; yet in an instant,
no longer did play or delight arise for her, as she remembered that monk Puṣpacandra.
Hurrying with great speed, he then entered his own capital city;
mounted upon his chariot, he went to that place where the monk had been cut into eight pieces.
Then he heard a voice from the sky, crying out to many tens of thousands of gods:
"O King Kali, you have committed very great evil; having fallen, you will go to the miserable Avīci hell."
Having heard the cry of the Maruts, the king was deeply distressed, dejected, and terrified in heart, thinking:
"I have committed many terrible and evil deeds, by which I have caused Puṣpacandra to be slain."
Even he who was a son of the Buddhas, those bulls among men, the Tathāgatas of infinite wisdom—
