one whose senses were guarded, who was gentle and peaceful in mind— even he was slain by me for the sake of desire.
He who upheld the Dharma of the Tathāgatas, the treasury of the True Dharma while it was still enduring,
and who would have made a lamp of wisdom for the entire world— he has been killed by me through the power of desire.
He who proclaimed for all beings the Dharma that is profound, peaceful, subtle, and very difficult to perceive;
he who is the teacher of the sublime seat of enlightenment—this very person has been slain by me for the sake of my own desires.
He who upholds the treasury of the Dharma of the Leaders, who has become a lamp for the world of the blind—
he who maintains this king of sūtras, how could he have been slain by me for the sake of my desires?
Untainted, possessing perfectly pure knowledge, peaceful, utterly tranquil, and always in meditative equipoise—
he has been slain today by me, who am blinded by desire, because of which I shall go to a most grievous hell.
To all those Buddhas of the past, as well as those of the future, and those Victors, the supreme among men, who dwell in the present—
endowed with infinite renown and like oceans of virtue— I go for refuge with palms joined in reverence.
"Having fallen [from this state], I shall go to terrible hells; there, no protector will be found for me.
For today I have committed an undesirable deed, in that I have killed this preacher of the Dharma."
Fie upon the sinful mind that creates calamity! Fie upon the status of kingship for those intoxicated with pride!
I shall depart alone, leaving everything behind; not even the slightest essence has been taken by me from this world.
One whose nature is pure, who has gone beyond fault and delusion, who speaks kindly, is compassionate, and has conquered himself;
one who does not find fault with others and is the sole kinsman of all people—why was my Varapuṣpacandra killed?

Alas, O you of noble vows, rich in patience and the wealth of austerity! Alas, O you endowed with beauty, courtesy, and virtue! Alas, O you free from guile, O mass of splendor, free from conceptual proliferation! Where have you gone, leaving me behind? SRS_35.106.
Today I understand the words of the Great Seer: desires are indeed impermanent and the slayers of living beings;
they are fevers of the mind and causes of miserable rebirths. Therefore, I shall abandon this pursuit of desire.
"I shall indeed go to the terrible Avīci hell; no protection exists for me,
for I have committed a sinful deed— undesirable and unhappy— that I have killed a monk."
Having renounced the kingdom, I shall be devoted to the supreme life of celibacy; I will offer excellent worship with flowers, perfumes, and beautiful ointments, and I will build a stūpa.
To my sons, daughters, wives, householders, and ministers;
to the guild-leaders, merchants, and various kṣatriyas—to all of them I speak:
of aloeswood, lotus-wood, sandalwood, and whatever fragrances are most beautiful.
"Quickly prepare a beautiful inner chamber for a palanquin, so that the monk may be cremated."
Having heard the king’s words, the entire city brought fragrant substances and constructed an excellent funeral pyre,
beautiful with its exquisite scent; having placed the monk upon it, they prepared aloe-wood,
lotus, sandalwood, *satagara*, *spṛkkā*, and likewise *pāṭalā*.
He lit it with flowers, garlands, ointments, and beautiful oils.
His body was placed in a trough that had been prepared by those monks;
having built a stūpa for them, the king said, "I desire to make offerings to him," and he took flowers, garlands, ointments, parasols, banners, and flags.
The king caused thousands of millions of billions of musical instruments to be played therein.
Then, for three periods of time during the day, the lord of the earth went to the stūpa of that bhikṣu;
throughout the three paths of time, he confessed whatever evil he had committed.
For ninety-five thousand million years, he exhausted that misdeed.
It is better to protect later on a moral discipline that is unbroken, excellent, pure, clean, and stainless.
For ninety-five thousand million years he then observed the *poṣadha* vow;
yet when that [vow] was broken, his physical body fell once more into the terrible Avīci hell.
Having committed merciless deeds, he experienced much suffering on account of sensual desire.
Ninety-five thousand million Buddhas were served by me.
For ninety-five thousand million years I was blind;
furthermore, for sixty-two trillion eons in the past, my eyes were pierced.
For many thousands of millions of billions of eons, my eyes were gouged out and taken away.
For countless millions of eons, his hands, feet, ears, and heads were severed.
Even when born as a human, or throughout millions of billions of other births,
I have long experienced painful sensations, afflicted by the suffering of *saṃsāra*; having committed evil deeds, I have wandered for a long time through *saṃsāra*, experiencing only suffering.
Therefore, one who desires the auspicious awakening should not commit evil throughout the three realms of existence.
Having performed those former deeds, that best of kings was not liberated from his past misdeeds;
and having committed those former actions of terrible form, he passed away and went to the horrific Avīci hell.
My hands were severed, and likewise my feet, ears, and nose were cut off in many various ways throughout endless eons;
and my eyes were forcibly plucked out after being struck with raised staves as I wandered on my journey.
For the sake of awakening, he joyfully gave up his own head, hands, sons, wives, eyes, and even his own flesh; he renounced his hands and feet, yet he did not exhaust the evil karma of his past.
I was King Śūradatta at that time; these sons of mine were my final protectors of the Dharma:
Padmottara was Supuṣpacandra, and Vasunandi was the Ten-Powered Śāntirāja.
If there were a vast multitude of women, as well as kṣatriyas, householders, army commanders, and ministers;
likewise, guild masters, merchants, and kings—all of them became free from defilements under the One Possessing Ten Powers.
O Prince, having seen how you have practiced for infinite eons, and having seen those Buddhas who were free from defilements and possessed of the qualities of asceticism—
those very sufferings which I previously experienced— you now practice this supreme conduct of enlightenment.
The bodhisattva who is established in dhāraṇī, dwelling in loving-kindness, immovable and unshakable—
he never goes to the states of woe after having honored the Buddhas, who possess the qualities of purification and are free from defilements.

Whoever desires to become a Buddha here, the Lord of Dharma, armored with the thirty-two marks— let him guard his morality, stainless and unshakable, and teach the Dharma while established in dhāraṇī.
Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, titled "Supuṣpacandra," in the glorious Samādhirāja [Sūtra]. // 35 //
(Vaidya 254) Chapter 36: The Exposition of the Aggregate of Ethical Discipline.
Therefore, young man, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva should desire: "How may I awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment in happiness? [he should practice this].
Therefore, young man, that bodhisattva mahāsattva should be well-established in the aggregate of ethical discipline,
and he should maintain the perception of teacherly love toward all bodhisattvas.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:

“The bodhisattva who is established in the aggregate of ethical discipline and wanders on his course with a mind intent on the welfare of others, will quickly go to the buddha-field Abhirati; having attained patient endurance, he shall become a King of Dharma.”
Therefore, be complete and free from malice; all enjoyments will constantly bring you delight.
And having seen the immeasurable Buddhas, whose glory is dense, you shall touch enlightenment and become lords of the Dharma.

Therefore, having heard these excellent benefits and having seen monks who possess supreme virtue, the wise should always serve them with sincerity; thus you will attain meditative concentration before long.
If there were storehouses filled with immeasurable and limitless quantities of the seven kinds of precious jewels,
and likewise, if further fields as numerous as the sands of the Ganges were filled with the most excellent gems;
Suppose that Bodhisattva, being devoted to giving, were to bestow gifts here every single night and day;
giving in this manner for many kinds of millions of eons, he would not cease until as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges had passed.
If a bodhisattva here, having heard this samādhi, should retain it— the treasury of the excellent Sugatas—
the mass of merit that would accrue from that does not equal even a fraction of all those various gifts.
This is a supreme, incomparable mass of merit, a treasury of knowledge like an immeasurable mine;
the faithful person who should uphold this conformable, foremost, and stainless samādhi. (SRS 36.7)
One who maintains this stainless, peaceful concentration becomes a Bodhisattva of great wealth;
like the great ocean, a source of many kinds of jewels, there is no measure to his merit.
One who is fully endowed with inconceivable supreme qualities is called a bodhisattva;
for him there is never any doubt regarding awakening if he should teach this samādhi.
Having established as the teacher of the world, the Guide, the Buddha, the Greatly Compassionate One, the Self-Existent;
he who is endowed with a supreme mass of merit, inconceivable, whose measure does not exist.
And there is never any being whatsoever in this great trichiliocosm who could be his equal in terms of the mass of merit, or in his peerless and inconceivable wisdom.
On the other hand, whoever, having heard this samādhi, should uphold it, recite it, and master it—
seeking the incomparable awakening of the Buddhas— there would be no one equal to him in wisdom.

O princes, if this form of the Dharma were to exist as a mass of merit accumulated by one who maintains and recites this samādhi, it would not be exhausted even if searched for throughout these vast world-systems.
Therefore, O youth, whatever bodhisattva here desires to worship all the Buddhas,
being skilled in the meaning of the words of the unattached teaching, should uphold and recite this samādhi for the sake of the Tathāgatas of the past and those yet to arise. (SRS 36.14)
For this indeed is the awakening of the Tathāgatas; have faith in my words, O youths!
The Tathāgata does not speak a false word, for such beings as he do not utter falsehoods.
In this city, throughout hundreds of inconceivable eons in the past, I purified my grasping at a self while practicing the supreme conduct of awakening and seeking this samādhi.
Therefore, having heard this treasury of Dharma, which is the source of tens of millions of billions of sutras,
one gains a vast and inconceivable mass of merit by which one quickly awakens to the wisdom of a Buddha.
Among all sūtras, this is the foremost sūtra, a source of inconceivable merit;
no end to those teachings can be found which the fearless one constantly expounds.
It might be possible to count the collection of atoms in a great trichiliocosm by cutting and breaking it apart;
but it is not possible to measure those hundreds of inconceivable sūtras that he, remaining unshakable, speaks.
It might be possible to count all the inhalations and exhalations of every being here in this buddha-field,
but it is impossible to reach the end of those sūtras which he speaks while established in this samādhi.

The Buddha-fields are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; the beings who have been born within their various realms of existence could perhaps be counted or even conceived of, but not the sūtras that he constantly proclaims.
It might be possible to count, even in tens of millions of eons, the grains of sand that exist here in the great oceans,
in rivers, in pools, and in lakes; yet such is the infinite collection of sūtras that he proclaims.
It might be possible to count the mass of water that always remains there throughout many millions of eons;
but it would not be possible at all to count the tips of a hundredth part of a hair’s end within their individual vocal qualities.

It would be possible, even over many millions of eons, to count those beings who existed there in the past who were attached to the essence of their own bodies; yet they could not know the extraction of this sūtra.
It may be possible to count the cries of all living beings, whatever creatures exist throughout the ten directions;
but it is impossible to count the sūtras that he speaks, constantly and without ceasing.
He understands the instruction of all phenomena, being skilled in etymology, exposition, and the meaning of words;
trained in definitive determination and the principles of reality, he possesses vast intelligence and is always joyful in wisdom.
With undifferentiated intellect, contemplating vast meaning, they always understand that thought is inconceivable;
knowing the extensive nature of all sounds, they do not cling to those words as they are being uttered.
He is called an unattached Dharma-preacher who does not cling while speaking for the sake of the entire world;
he is skilled in explaining questions through words of instruction, for thus has he realized the ultimate truth.
Teaching tens of millions of instructions upon a single sūtra, he is not hindered;
skilled in the meaning of words through unimpeded exposition, he speaks when entered into the assembly and remains unhindered.
The bodhisattva who is well-established in this samādhi becomes unshakable;
having attained the excellence of the empowerment of the Dharma, he brings benefit to many millions of living beings.
Just as Mount Meru is immovable and cannot be shaken by any wind,
even so can a wise monk who is a preacher of the Dharma not be shaken by those who propound other doctrines.

In these great thousands of world-systems, those mountains which are said to be unshakable can indeed be shaken by the wind; but a monk who stands firm in the Dharma, established in emptiness, cannot be moved at all.
One who is constantly engaged in emptiness dwells with certainty in the state of the Buddhas;
knowing for certain that all phenomena are empty, they cannot be shaken by any disputants.
He is unshakable by the proponents of other doctrines and is not overcome by any of their teachings;
being neither overcome nor censured, he has pointed out this peaceful samādhi.
Having attained the state of emptiness, he has no doubt regarding any phenomena;
always firmly established in infinite wisdom, he points toward this peaceful samādhi.

For one who upholds and recites this samādhi, the powers and the factors of enlightenment are not difficult to obtain; the inconceivable modes of supernormal power and the analytical knowledges are likewise not difficult for them to attain. SRS_36.36.
For one who has turned away from existence, it is not difficult to behold the Jinas with infinite wisdom;
he who maintains this samādhi shall see inconceivable billions of perfectly awakened Buddhas.
In the presence of all those Victors, he shall hear this peaceful samādhi;
endowed with supreme knowledge, he will attain mastery and reach the perfection of the analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid).
Suppose this great trichiliocosm were filled with precious jewels—
the most divine, supreme, and excellent gems— starting from the very bottom up to the peak of existence.
As many fields as there are— various and infinite— all filled and strewn with gold from Jambūdvīpa,
one might give all that as a gift to the supreme Victors, reaching from the surface of the earth up to the peak of existence.

Suppose there were as many various and numerous beings as exist, and they were to give diverse gifts for infinite eons; suppose those seeking awakening were to constantly and unceasingly give this mass of gifts to the Buddhas.
And whatever monk, delighting in emptiness, should pay homage to the Buddhas with palms joined in the ten-fingered gesture—
this former mass of giving does not approach even a fraction of the merit of that bodhisattva who delights in emptiness.

Having obtained that, indeed, a meritorious person gives a vast gift, having generated faith while seeking the incomparable enlightenment of a Buddha; this is the analogy made by the Supreme among Men.
And whoever, with a joyful mind, should grasp this excellent and supreme four-line verse of the Samādhi,
the mass of merit accumulated by that person is such that all other giving does not equal even a hundredth part of it.
That bodhisattva who acts for the benefit of others may give gifts, yet he does not attain the wisdom of a Buddha so quickly;
whereas, having heard this stainless, peaceful samādhi, he attains that Buddha-wisdom swiftly. (SRS 36.45)
And whichever bodhisattva, having attained this supreme ground of peace, this stainless samādhi which is the lineage of hearing,
should fill it with joy, will quickly obtain this Buddha-knowledge.
Suppose someone were to obtain such a treasure, as many infinite fields as there are grains of sand in the Ganges,
and suppose those fields were filled with divine and human jewels and gems.
That bodhisattva who attains this samādhi becomes invincible, possessing a vast treasury and great wealth, endowed with riches and jewels; as he masters it, he remains constantly insatiable.
Having obtained a kingdom that is supremely prosperous and flourishing, a wise person is never satisfied by it;
yet, having obtained this stainless samādhi, that bodhisattva becomes satisfied and exultant.
They become constant upholders of the Dharma of all the omniscient Buddhas,
maintaining the vast eye of the sublime Dharma even at the end of the eon;
they are holders of the treasury of Dharma, possessors of great intelligence, and guardians of the storehouse of the Omniscient One.
They satisfy those thousands of millions of billions of beings with the sounds of the Dharma.
Those wise men, endowed with the wealth of ethical discipline and rich in the treasure of training;
those established in and delighting in moral vows, who are the sprouts of the tree of Dharma;
they always wear saffron-colored robes and find satisfaction in renunciation.
For the benefit of those various beings, they have set out for omniscience, being without equal.
They are tamed, well-tamed, tamers of beings, always endowed with self-control; they are peaceful, having attained a state of perfect peace, their faculties calmed and thoroughly stilled.
They constantly awaken with the sounds of the Dharma those beings who are asleep or fast asleep.
Having awakened them with the most excellent and supreme jewels of the Dharma, he established sentient beings [in the truth].
They become those lords of generosity, always and ever free in their renunciation; they are wise, they do not dwell with the stingy, and they always delight in great giving.
Seeing those various sentient beings who are poor and suffering, they satisfy them with enjoyments;
for the welfare and happiness of those various beings, they constantly set out toward omniscience.
They, always trained in wisdom, beat the vast drum of Dharma;
ever set forth in wisdom, they sever the creeping vine of all people's doubts.
They, well-heard keepers of the Dharma, free from dust, [retain] hundreds of millions of sūtras.
Seated upon their thrones in the assembly, those wise ones who possess intelligence spoke forth.

They shall become those of great learning, retainers of what they have heard, and upholders of the Dharma of the Perfectly Awakened One; they hold the treasuries consisting of Dharma, delighting in the treasure-store of the Munis' teachings.
They shall become those of vast wisdom, and they always generate immense joy.
They teach the supreme Dharma, which is peaceful, subtle, leading to liberation, and difficult to perceive.
O wise one, you who know dharma and non-dharma, you who are established in dharma and are gentle;
you rule over the kingdom of dharma, peerless and always practicing the sublime dharma.
You become those who hold the distinguished dharma in high esteem and are established in reverence for the teacher.
Established upon the supreme mountain of the Dharma, these possessors of wisdom raise high the banner of the Dharma.
Having constantly seen those various beings who are intoxicated and heedless, seeing them established in negligence, lost, gone upon wrong paths, and situated on the path of saṃsāra—
having generated toward them sublime loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, he remains established therein.
I shall show them the excellent, auspicious Eightfold Path, which is difficult to perceive.
Having constructed that very firm ship of the Dharma, they carry across many beings who have fallen into the great oceans of existence and are carried away by the current of saṃsāra;
armored with the factors of enlightenment, the powers, and the faculties, they board the ship of the true Dharma.
They always establish sentient beings on the shore of the perfections, which is secure, eternal, and fearless.

Those excellent physicians, who have practiced their vows, who are the best of healers, who possess knowledge and understanding, who have reached the further shore of liberation through wisdom, and who dispense the medicine of the True Dharma—
having seen sentient beings afflicted by many various diseases, they [act].
They give them a purgative of the Dharma and treat them with those very teachings.

Those various speakers, crushers of opponents, lords of speech among the leaders of the world, illuminators of all that is to be known, possessors of intelligence, established on the stage of supreme knowledge;
heroes with the power of wisdom, crushers of [the forces of] strength, they are praised by the wise.
Established in the Dharma, they will satisfy many millions of billions of beings through their wisdom.
Those various lords and caravan leaders, seeking to protect beings from calamities,
see that beings are utterly bewildered regarding the jewel of the path and remain forever ensnared in the noose of Māra.
I shall reveal to them the excellent path— auspicious, secure, and ever-blissful—
that path of knowledge by which they lead hundreds of millions of virtuous beings.
Each of them becomes a refuge, a protection, an eye, and a lamp; they constantly grant fearlessness to those who are afraid and provide consolation to those who are terrified.
Having recognized these most miserable beings as being like those born blind, [they act for their sake].
Having trained in the true method within the jewel of the Dharma, they produce the light of the Dharma.
Whatever supreme crafts exist in the world that are of great utility and bring benefit to sentient beings—
by means of which beings, having been thoroughly trained in those crafts, always become happy—
they have reached the perfection of training, being highly skilled, marvelous, and extraordinary.
Those who have set out for enlightenment, possessors of intelligence, who bestow vision upon the world.
You were never satiated by hearing the supreme Buddha-dharma, which is peerless;
you reached the further shore of ethical discipline, patience, and meditative concentration, and heard the profound Dharma.
And you were never satiated while teaching the jewel of the Dharma, which brings peace, to others.
Raining down the rain of the means to liberation, he satisfies men with the teachings of the Dharma.
As many wise beings as have gathered here seeking the Dharma, we shall hear the most excellent jewel of the sublime Dharma— the straight and direct path.
May he, the bearer of intelligence, cut through their doubts and satisfy them with the Dharma.
Having reached the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, and meditative concentration, they know the inclinations of sentient beings.

The wise ones have reached the supreme pinnacle of knowledge; they are skilled in the dispositions of beings and know the mental conduct of other beings according to whatever discourse is appropriate for them. Through their discourse on wisdom, millions of beings obtain the excellent eye of Dharma.
Each of them has reached the perfection of specific knowledge and provides instruction on the path.
Even ten million billions of Māras could not know the minds of those wise ones;
it is impossible anywhere to know the track or movement of birds in the sky.
They are peaceful, self-controlled, thoroughly calmed, masters of knowledge, and established in noble wisdom.
Having conquered all Māras, the heroic bulls awaken to auspicious enlightenment.
Having attained the perfection of supernatural powers, they constantly travel through hundreds of fields and behold many billions of buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Their vision is not obstructed in the ten directions; they behold many forms, and all those beings who dwell in existence throughout the ten directions—all of them have these leaders as their guides.
Even if they were to speak for hundreds of millions of eons, they could not exhaustively describe all its benefits, nor could they, through their eloquence, finish praising his former conduct;
for it is the inexhaustible and vast wealth of the Buddhas, and an ocean of wisdom.
Whatever person should uphold this stainless, incomparable concentration.
Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter of the *Śrī-Samādhirāja*, titled "The Exposition of the Aggregate of Ethical Discipline."
(Vaidya 264) Chapter 37: Yaśaḥprabha.
Then the Blessed One addressed the youth Candraprabha once again: "Therefore, O youth, listen."
A bodhisattva mahāsattva who desires these immeasurable, marvelous, and wonderful bodhisattva qualities,

and who wishes to quickly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, should hear, take up, master, retain, recite, and propagate this samādhi entitled "The Manifestation of the Equality of the Essential Nature of All Phenomena."
It should be taught, recited, cultivated through the meditation on non-affliction (*araṇā*), practiced extensively, and explained in detail to others;
furthermore, he should cultivate the power of patience (*kṣāntibala*).
Patience should be practiced, cultivated, and frequently developed.
One should be a seeker of the Dharma, a lover of the Dharma, a receiver of the Dharma, and one who has entered upon the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma.
One should be devoted to the worship of the Buddha.
Therefore, one should apply oneself to three points.
Which three?

Namely, by one who desires the wisdom of a Buddha, roots of virtue should be planted for the sake of the exhaustion of afflictions and for the mastery of the power of merit; but certainly not by one who longs for the touch of worldly pleasure.
One should apply effort toward these three points.

Then, at that time, the Blessed One, illuminating that very same meaning for the youth Candraprabha, proclaimed this exposition of the former account of his past lives by means of singing these verses:
"Come now, young man, listen to me as to how I practiced throughout a thousand eons."
Having honored hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, one attains this sublime samādhi.
Inconceivable eons as numerous as the sands in hundreds of fields have thus passed;
this is the illustration proclaimed [of those times] when there was a Jina named Gaṇeśvara.
That supreme assembly of that Jina consisted of no fewer than sixty thousand koṭis;
all were free from outflows, their afflictions exhausted, established in the eight liberations, and meditative.
And during that time, this entire realm was secure, well-supplied with food, and free from turmoil;
all human beings were endowed with happiness and delighted by human pleasures.
And by the power of merit, they were all endowed with beauty, as well as being lovely and pleasing;
they were all wealthy and possessed of great riches, flourishing and their bodies graced with divine happiness.

Gentle, firm in their vows, with few afflictions, they delight in the power of patience; handsome and wise, they are endowed with the qualities of ethical conduct, like the sons of the gods in the celestial cities.
And there, O Kāli, there was a king, a prince named Varapuṣpa;
he had no fewer than five hundred sons, all endowed with mindfulness and intelligence.
And by that prince, six million gardens—
all adorned with flowers and fruits— were offered to that compassionate Victor.
There were hundreds of thousands of diverse gardens, with thousands of walking-paths, couches, and seats;
and those walking-paths and seats were strewn with hundreds of thousands of millions of robes.
In this way, thousands of various kinds of requisites for a recluse were provided by the prince, with a devout mind, to that Sugata.
Thus established by the virtuous people in the ten paths of wholesome action,
the King went forth accompanied by hundreds of thousands of millions of living beings to see the Leader.
Taking flowers, ointments, and incense, as well as parasols, banners, flags, and musical instruments,
he performed worship to that Jina and stood before him with palms joined in reverence.
Then the thousands of monks, as well as gods, humans, yakṣas, and asuras, were filled with joy.
They wondered: "What indeed will the Jina predict regarding this offering? What will the Lord of Men say concerning the Dharma?"
And having personally understood the intention and the unsurpassed mind of that prince, the Self-Existent One,
who had reached the further shore regarding the stages of liberation, taught him this peaceful samādhi.
As soon as the Sugata had uttered his voice, the earth with its groves of trees trembled;
then a rain of flowers fell from the sky, and hundreds of lotuses also rose up from the ground.
Having understood their intentions, the Teacher, the Guide, who is well-trained in the words of meaning, prophesied;
that Lord of Men taught this peaceful samādhi—listen now to these words of meaning.
All states of existence and non-existence are mere conceptual constructions, as empty as a mirage and like illusions;
they are like lightning and clouds, shifting and void—all are without self, without a sentient being, and without a living soul.
From the very beginning, all phenomena are empty and future; they have not yet arrived, they do not abide, and are liberated from any location.
They are eternally without essence, having the nature of an illusion; all are pure, utterly purified, and like the sky.
They are neither blue, nor yellow, nor white; they are nameless, empty, and of the nature of sound.
They are secluded from the mind and have the nature of no-mind, being devoid of all sounds because of their momentariness.
Whether spoken, there is no transition of syllables; nor, when unspoken, does confusion arise. Furthermore, syllables do not go to any location, nor do syllables come from anywhere.
The syllable is imperishable, exhausted, and ceased, whether through speaking or not speaking;
it is eternally called this imperishable syllable, and he who thoroughly understands it becomes imperishable.
Hundreds of thousands of Buddhas who have passed away, having spoken hundreds of thousands of dharmas,
have neither exhausted the Dharma nor the syllables;
because there is no arising, they are therefore inexhaustible.
By which he understands the inexhaustible dharmas, he always understands the inexhaustible dharmas;
having spoken hundreds of thousands of sūtras, he knows all dharmas to be without syllables.
Whatever Dharma the Victor proclaims, he does not conceive of it as having an end, because of its inexhaustibility;
he proclaims these dharmas which are from the very beginning selfless, yet he does not exhaust them.
That wise one speaks all words, yet his mind is not carried away by speech;
all his words resemble the sound of an echo, and for that reason he is never attached to speech.
The very speech by which that Dharma is proclaimed ceases entirely at that very moment;
and whatever the characteristic of that speech may be, all phenomena have attained that same characteristic.
All these phenomena are without marks and devoid of marks; all are markless, yet pure in their very nature.
Always secluded and pure like space, they cannot be reached by any calculation or summary.
All conditioned and unconditioned phenomena are utterly secluded; for those sages, there is no conceptual construction.
Having attained the unconditioned within all realms of existence, they are always secluded from views.
Always free from attachment, aversion, and delusion, their minds are naturally concentrated;
he who understands such phenomena as these is powerful, possessed of the strength of samādhi.
Just as an echo arises in dependence upon mountain caves, rocky crags, or rivers, so should one understand all conditioned things; the entire world is like an illusion or a mirage.
The power of wisdom is the quality of those who have entered the Dharma; by the power of knowledge, the sages possess the superknowledges.
It is through speech and skill in means that this eloquence is expressed, wherein the peaceful samādhi is revealed.
What is conceptualized is said to be mere conceptualization; no end is found while wandering in saṃsāra.
That limit which was previously characterized by the absence of marks, even in the past, is likewise the conditionality of the future.
Karma and action proceed in this way through inferiority and superiority;
always understand that all phenomena are by their very nature secluded, empty, and selfless.
The Victor has taught the Dharma according to conventional truth; thus, behold the unconditioned and the conditioned.
Herein, there is no real self or person; such is the characteristic of the entire world.
Black and unwholesome karma does not perish; having been performed by oneself, it must be experienced.
Yet, there is no transfer of the fruit of karma, nor do beings experience it without a cause.
All states of existence are false and insubstantial; they are empty, hollow, and like foam.
Always void like an illusion or a mirage, they are described as being proclaimed to be utterly secluded.
Knowing thus, there is no conceit; he possesses ethical discipline and a mind that is non-reliant.
By the power of patience, he does not conceptualize anything; practicing in this way, he becomes concentrated.
To whatever extent the Dharma was known, to that same extent it was taught by that Jina;
having heard this Dharma of the Jina, the king, together with his retinue, undertook the training.
Having heard this samādhi, the prince, with a joyful and delighted mind, spoke these words:
"This samādhi is well-spoken; I prostrate at your feet."
And there, eighty thousand living beings, having heard this sublime nature of phenomena,
understood this instruction on the ultimate truth and attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena.
There is neither arising nor cessation for a person; these phenomena are always solitary.
Knowing this, O King, one does not fall away and attains the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena.
Then that king, having relinquished his kingdom, went forth into homelessness under the teaching of that Jina;
all five hundred of the king’s sons, none lacking, likewise followed him into the religious life.
When the king, together with his son, had gone forth, then many thousands of living beings also went forth in the presence of the Sugata, seeking the Dharma of that Jina.
For a full two hundred years that Jina proclaimed the Dharma;
for those two hundred years, the king, along with his sons and those people, practiced the Dharma.
Then, at another time, that Jina also had entered parinirvāṇa;
those disciples of the Jina had also passed away, and that Dharma had become limited.
That king had a son named Puṇyamati, who was always faithful and serene;
and he had a monk as a family friend,
who taught him this peaceful samādhi.
He was entirely gentle and sweet, honored by hundreds of thousands of living beings;
hundreds of millions of deities followed him, and entering the families, they spoke his praises.
He is possessed of mindfulness, intelligence, and wisdom; he is one of excellent vows, gentle disposition, and delight in virtue.
He has a beautiful voice that is neither harsh nor coarse, but sweet; he has attained mastery over the elements and has reached the supreme state.
That monk named Yaśaḥprabha was a recipient of hundreds of millions of robes;
unable to endure his power of merit, a thousand monks then gave rise to envy.
By the power of merit, the power of form, the power of knowledge, and the power of supernormal abilities;
by the power of ethical discipline, the power of meditative concentration, and the power of the Dharma, the monk has arisen.
With a joyful mind, he is dear to the people—monks, laymen, and nuns.
Those beings who have faith in the teaching of the Jina find him desirable and worthy of worship. (SRS 37.51)
And he who was the king’s son, Puṇyamati, always faithful and serene,
having recognized that many monks were of corrupt mind, caused protection to be provided for his teacher.
Surrounded at all times by five hundred thousand beings armed with armor, swords, and clubs, the monk speaks the infinite, true conduct.
He proclaims the Dharma to the assembly: "All phenomena are empty, selfless, and devoid of a living soul.
That which the monk speaks does not please those who grasp at objects and are attached to a self.
O monks, those who do not approve of this peaceful emptiness rose up, taking up weapons, and said:
"This monk speaks what is contrary to the Dharma; let us kill him, and there will be merit [for us]."
And having seen a weapon, the monk is not afraid, recollecting the empty nature of phenomena:
"There is no being here, nor a person, to be slain; these empty phenomena are like a wall."
The bhikṣu placed his palms together at his head and spoke these words: "Homage be to the Victors!
By this truth that these empty phenomena have become so, may these weapons turn into māndārava flowers!"
As soon as the Sage, whose words are never otherwise, had spoken to him who was devoted to vows and observances,
the earth with its forests and groves trembled, and weapons were transformed into māndārava flowers.
At that time, there were monks with bodies bent over, who, having grasped weapons, were seekers of objective perception;
yet when they were able to approach him, they became terrified, struck by a most great wonder.
But those who were faithful and devoted to the Lord of Munis, and to whom this peaceful emptiness was pleasing—
they uttered thousands of "huṃ" sounds and covered the monk with hundreds of fine cloths.
Having generated loving-kindness toward them, that monk speaks before all people:
"I do not practice for the sake of awakening for those beings who harbor malice toward me."
For no less than eighty years, he taught the treasuries of emptiness of the Jinas;
and there were thousands of monks who were adversaries, who were then restrained by the prince.
At that time, he too was treated with contempt, and the monk had only a meager seat;
yet hearing those unpleasant words, he never wavered from the power of his patience.
Then, at another time, the elephant, for the great benefit of hundreds of living beings,
recollecting his entire moral conduct, spoke these words to Puṇyamati:
Having shown great reverence there, Puṇyamatī then said to the monk:
"May nothing whatsoever have been done in my teacher's mind that was disagreeable."
He said: "Listen, O prince! Buddhas have arisen through the power of patience.
Toward those by whom unpleasant words were spoken to me, I maintained noble loving-kindness."
"He who for hundreds of thousands of eons practiced patience in his previous lives—
he was that monk Yaśaḥprabha," said the Blessed One Śākyamuni.
The son of that king, Puṇyamati, who protected the monk Yaśaḥprabhu, has been my companion for thousands of births; he has been prophesied by me as the Buddha Maitreya.
He who worshipped the Teacher, Gaṇeśvara, and who caused the most excellent monasteries to be built—
formerly he was the lord of sages named Padumottara, whose name was Varapuṣpa.
Thus, for many infinite eons, I have upheld this Dharma of the Jinas;
having heard it, O Prince, train yourself according to my example, for the power of patience was fully realized by me in the past.
Furthermore, in the final age when the true Dharma is being destroyed, there will even be those who seek nirvāṇa;
yet monks devoted to the doctrines of non-Buddhists will reject my peaceful Dharma.
Arrogant, haughty, wicked, and impudent; having evil companions, greedy for food, delighting in robes and bowls, and coveting fine cloth—relying on gain, they will reject the Dharma.
Those with malicious and corrupt minds, ungrateful, and born into low and impoverished families—
though they have gone forth in this teaching of mine— they too reject the peaceful Dharma.
Sentient beings are deluded by the mind of Māra; they follow the power of passion and remain attached to it.
Foolish people, deluded by the power of ignorance, do not find pleasure in emptiness, which is peace.
Monks, nuns, and householders, led astray and deluded by those of evil intent,
will always fall under their influence and reject awakening in the final age.
O Prince, having heard these words of mine, let the monk dwell constantly in a forest hermitage; those who delight in emptiness and peace should uphold this Dharma of the Victors.
Having gone forth in my teaching and practiced as monks, performing the rites of full ordination and the poṣadha ceremony,
those who shall uphold this samādhi will eat almsfood without attachment and without fault.
Having abandoned concern for life and body, cultivate emptiness which is perfectly peaceful; being one whose mind is applied with diligence, always dwell in the forest like a deer.
Constantly perform worship of the Jinas with parasols, banners, prosperity, garlands, and monasteries;
worship the shrines and the images, and you shall quickly attain this samādhi.
Have stupas built for the Sugatas, adorned with gold and coated with silver;
have well-finished images variegated with jewels, having generated the mind set on the treasure of awakening.
Whatever offerings there are in the world that are sublime, divine, or human and delightful—
having sought them all, O Buddha, honor them, having made the vow for the treasure of awakening.
Behold the true nature of all the lords of men, as many as exist throughout the worlds of the ten directions;
the parinirvāṇa of all the Victors is seen, for by the nature of phenomena, the Buddhas remain ever present before us.
Furthermore, may you all be intent on renunciation, established in the purity of ethical discipline, and firm of mind;
may you always delight in patience and take joy in loving-kindness, and may you all understand that all phenomena are empty.
Arouse vigor, being neither indolent nor dejected; delight in meditation and take pleasure in solitude.
Understand wisdom and the purification of wisdom; before long, you shall become compassionate ones.
Always subdue passion through the contemplation of the foul; restrain hatred by the power of patience;
subdue delusion by the power of wisdom, and you shall attain the enlightenment praised by the Victors.
Contemplate the body as being like foam—suffering, without essence, putrid, and foul-smelling;
understand all the aggregates to be empty, and you shall swiftly attain unsurpassed wisdom.
Never grasp at evil views, such as "this person is the self" or "this is the soul. Understand that all phenomena are empty, and you will quickly touch supreme enlightenment.
Do not become greedy for gain, nor should you ever feel distressed if you receive no alms-food;
do not waver at blame or praise, but remain unshakable like Mount Meru.
Seeking the Dharma with a sense of reverence, and having heard it, remain intent upon it; abide within the sphere of all the Victors, and you shall swiftly go to the realm of Sukhāvatī.
Having cultivated a mind of equanimity toward all the world, do not harbor thoughts of liking or disliking;
do not seek gain or fame, and you will quickly become Buddhas, the Lords of Munis.
And constantly proclaim the qualities of the Buddha through words of true meaning and etymological analysis, so that beings here,
hearing those qualities, may become serene and conceive a longing for the qualities of a Buddha.

Always maintain reverence toward your teachers, as well as toward your mother and father, and toward all living beings; do not follow the influence of pride, and you shall obtain the thirty-two marks.
Abandoning all social company without exception, always delight in solitude;
being gentle, eternally radiant, and peaceful, be devoted to your own welfare and the welfare of other beings.
Cultivate loving-kindness as well as compassion; always delight in sympathetic joy and equanimity.
Constantly behold the teaching of the Teacher, and you will swiftly become benefactors of the world.
One should never associate with evil friends; rather, one should serve those friends who are noble, who delight in peaceful emptiness, and who have set out for supreme enlightenment.
Never train in the stage of the śrāvakas, nor should you take delight in that conduct;
do not abandon the mind set on the qualities of a Buddha, and you will quickly become Buddhas, the lords of Jinas. (SRS 37.96)
Always speak pure words of truth; do not speak falsely, nor speak harshly.
Always speak what is pleasant and sweet, and you shall obtain the speech of the teachers of the world.
Be indifferent to the body and to life; do not exalt yourselves nor disparage others.
Cultivating your own virtues, remain equanimous toward the conduct of others.
Always delight in the liberation of emptiness; do not form aspirations for the realms of existence. Abandoning all signs without exception, always dwell in the signless.
Always avoid extremes; do not abide in the views of eternalism or nihilism.
Always understand everything through the nature of conditions, and you will become just like the Teacher.
Having abandoned delight in sensual pleasures, having abandoned faults, stubbornness, and impurities,
and having abandoned all the darkness of delusion, O Lion among Men, may you abide in peaceful delight.

Behold both the permanent and the impermanent; having liberated all states of existence from pleasure and pain, and by meditating upon the impure and non-self within what is considered self and pure, one may become a lord of men.
By those Victors who act as lamps for the world, through whom the Dharma has been well-guided here with systematic reasoning—
having struck down the forces of Māra here, they have attained the noble, unsurpassed enlightenment.
"O youth, as many virtues as have been spoken by me here, and whatever hundreds of faults have been revealed by me—
having abandoned those faults and trained in these virtues, you shall become a Buddha right here."
Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, titled "Yaśaḥprabha," in the *Śrī-Samādhirāja*.
Chapter 38: The Chapter on the Restraint of Body, Speech, and Mind.
Therefore, O youth, you should train yourself in this way: "I shall be one who is restrained by the restraint of body."
In this regard, young man, what is bodily restraint?
That bodily restraint endowed with which a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains non-attached knowledge regarding all phenomena—
this, young man, is called bodily restraint.

The restraint of body endowed with which a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains the thirty-two marks of a great person— this is called [the restraint of body]. The restraint of body endowed with which a mahāsattva attains the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha— [this is called the restraint of body].
This is called—
[the means] by which a mahāsattva attains the three gateways to liberation.
What are the three?
Namely, emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
these three are the gates of liberation, and this is called— [the perfection of wisdom].
By which [practice] does the Mahāsattva attain the four Brahma-abodes?
Which four?
Namely, loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity—these are the four Brahma-abodes.
This is called—
[the means] by which a mahāsattva attains the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).
What are the four?

Namely: the analytical knowledge of meaning (arthapratisaṃvid), the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dharmapratisaṃvid), the analytical knowledge of expression (niruktipratisaṃvid), and the analytical knowledge of eloquence (pratibhānapratisaṃvid).
These are the four analytical knowledges;
this is called—[blank].
By means of which the Mahāsattva attains the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment.
What are these thirty-seven?
Namely, the four foundations of mindfulness.
The four right efforts,
the four bases of psychic power,
and the five faculties.
The five powers,
the seven factors of enlightenment,
and the noble eightfold path.
He attains these thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening;
this is called—
[the dwelling of great compassion]— by which the Mahāsattva attains the dwelling of great compassion.
He attains the dwelling of great equanimity,
he attains secure thoughts,
and he attains qualities of seclusion.
This is called restraint of the body.
Furthermore, young man, by means of that restraint of body with which a bodhisattva mahāsattva is endowed, he abstains from taking life;

he abstains from taking what is not given, unchastity, false speech, malicious speech, harsh speech, and idle chatter; he abstains from covetousness, malice, and wrong view. He abstains from cheating with scales, cheating with measures, and cheating with metal weights; he abstains from seizing, binding, confining, beating, cutting, piercing, robbing, and acts of violence.
He is not fidgety with his hands nor fidgety with his feet; his hands and feet are well-restrained.
All the depravity of his body, speech, and mind has been abandoned and cut off at the root, such that it is of a nature never to arise again in the future, like the top of a palmyra tree.
This, young man, is called the restraint of the body.
Therefore, young man, by this method as well, it should be understood in this way.
Long ago, O youth, in the past, in an incalculable, more than incalculable, vast, immeasurable, inconceivable, and infinite eon,

there appeared in the world a Tathāgata named Jñānaprabhāsa— Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, perfect in knowledge and conduct, Sugata, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, Buddha, Blessed One.
Furthermore, O youth, at that time and on that occasion, the lifespan of that Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Perfectly Enlightened Buddha Jñānaprabhāsa, was sixty koṭis of years;
his community of disciples consisted of sixty koṭis of arhats;
and there were immeasurable bodhisattva mahāsattvas who upheld the true Dharma.
And at that time, O Prince, on that occasion, there was a king named Viśeṣacintī.
Then King Viśeṣacintī, together with eighty koṭis of living beings, approached the Tathāgata.
Having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of that Tathāgata, circumambulated the Blessed One three times, and sat down to one side.
Seated in a secluded place, King Viśeṣacintin attended upon that Tathāgata.

Then, O youth, the Tathāgata Jñānaprabhāsa— the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One— perceiving the resolute intention of King Viśeṣacintin and his retinue, [taught] from this Dharma discourse this entrance into the concentration on the restraint of the body.
He teaches by means of chanting verses:
"Just as the intermediate space, the sky, is pure, utterly pure, and luminous by nature;
even so is this pure restraint of the body, which can never be taught by means of sound. (SRS 38.1)
This restraint of the body is secluded and empty; such are these two characteristics of the body.
They are without characteristics, like the atmosphere; such is the restraint of the body taught by you.
For one who knows that the very nature of restraint is such, there is never a lack of restraint;
and for those who have not engaged in [unwholesome] actions, that is their sphere of activity—for the untainted, there is no rebirth.
It is not possible for those who indulge in sensual desires, who have not abandoned craving for forms and enjoyments,
and who do not recognize the faults in states of existence, to know this restraint of the body.
For one who understands the untainted restraint, there is never again rebirth;
such are these qualities of an Arhat, which are not easy for outsiders to understand.

Those whose minds are terrified of the entire triple world and do not give rise to longing for sensual enjoyments, who never seek after kingship or wealth— they shall understand such restraint of the body. (SRS 38.6)
This meaning is called bodily restraint; yet this meaning cannot be taught by means of words.
He who understands such a way of guiding the Dharma is established in this restraint.
I have taught the meaning for those engaged in the meaning who are wise and devoted to the guidance of the meaning;
those who, being intent on the meaning, avoid what is not the meaning, are constantly established in this restraint.
How does that meaning which has been taught in the teaching of the Jinas become understood by one who knows?
He who understands the intrinsic nature of the guide to the meaning is said to be established in the restraint of the body.
By whom the signless has been understood through selflessness, as empty or as void—
for such a person there never arises a lack of restraint, for they have trained in the certainty of reality.
He who understands that things are both existent and non-existent never becomes attached to any phenomena;
he who is never attached to any phenomena touches the signless samādhi.
He by whom the dharmas here have been understood as selfless, empty of intrinsic nature, and luminous by nature—
for him there never arises a lack of restraint, for he has thus trained in the certainty of reality.
He who knows emptiness, having understood that the five aggregates are empty by nature and devoid of self,
will never at any time lack restraint in whatever action he performs with his body.
For one who grasps at signs, who is unrestrained, and who always dwells in the perception of a self—
a person who has become attached to the relish of forms, passion erupts within that unrestrained being.
Those who have trained in the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) and attained mastery in the gentleness of emptiness—
passion never again arises in them, nor does that lack of restraint by which one would go to an evil destiny.
Just as the great Mount Sumeru, being immovable, cannot be shaken by all the ants in the world,
so too the wise one, trained in the principles of reality, is not shaken even by divine forms.
The sky might be painted with colors, and space might be grasped by the hand;
yet he cannot be moved by passion, nor by hatred, nor even by ten million Māras.
An echo might be grasped by someone, or even a stone might float in the midst of water;
yet it is impossible here to perceive the disposition of one who is trained in such restraint of the body.
However many sounds there may be throughout the vast entire world, they could be gathered and placed within a casket;
yet it is impossible to discern the stability or instability of one who is established in the restraint of the body.
It might be possible to grasp the light from the solar disk, or the lightning from a thundering cloud;
but it is not possible to know the intrinsic nature of that body for one who has trained here in the restraint of the body.
A whirlwind blowing from the four directions can be bound with nets and snares;
but it is impossible to comprehend the body of one who is established here in the restraint of the body.
This is not the domain of any living beings here, wherein one who is wise abides in the restraint of the mind;
abiding therein in the sphere of bodily restraint, he is not defiled by worldly conditions, like space.
It might be possible for all living beings wandering separately in the four directions to see his footprints;
yet no one here is able to know the measure of that body or the range of his mind.
For one who thus abides here in this restraint of the body, all various afflictions do not arise;
his secondary afflictions are abandoned here, for he has trained himself in the restraint of the body.
Neither fire nor weapon affects him; nevertheless, his body is ungraspable, for he abides in a peaceful and utterly tranquil samādhi, having thus trained in the restraint of the body.
For one who stands thus, neither fear nor terror arises, nor agitation of mind, nor envy;
he is liberated from all calamities who has trained in such restraint of the body.
He who is trained in such restraint of the body never fears poison or weapons, nor fire, nor the midst of water; he is liberated from all calamities.
One who has entered into the midst of thieves, rogues, evildoers, and venomous serpents does not fear;
for he has abandoned the notion of a self, and for one liberated from such notions, no fear exists.
For one who is liberated from fears, terror does not arise; for one who is not terrified, there is no agitation.
For one who is unagitated, whence can there be fear? He cannot be shaken even by millions of Māras.
This restraint for the benefit of a bodhisattva has been declared, taught, and fully revealed;
one who trains in such restraint of the body shall not be shaken by tens of millions of Māras.
Knowledge that is signless regarding all phenomena, the eighty minor marks,
and the thirty-two major marks— these, arising from the purity of mind, are not difficult to obtain for one who abides in the restraint.
Whoever desires to awaken to the inconceivable Buddha-qualities, for which there is no measure, should train in such restraint of the body; he shall become a shrine for the whole world.

Whoever desires this Dharma of the great seers—the ten inconceivable powers of a Buddha—should train in such restraint of the body; for one who has so trained, those powers are not difficult to attain.
Furthermore, those eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, in which the Victors are established—
these too will not be difficult to attain for one who trains in such restraint of the body.
The seven factors of enlightenment of the great seers, as well as the analytical knowledges and the bases of psychic power—
these too are not difficult to obtain for one who trains in such restraint of the body.
The four divine abodes, the four meditative concentrations, and the three doors to liberation have been fully revealed;
for one established in restraint, secure thoughts and those of seclusion are not difficult to attain.

Dwelling in compassion and likewise attaining equanimity, he practices here the supreme conduct of loving-kindness; he whose mind is intent on the welfare of the entire world is one who stands firm in the restraint of body.
The foundations of mindfulness, the right exertions, the five faculties, and the five powers of the Great Sages;
the wonderful, supreme Eightfold Path is not difficult to master for one who trains in bodily restraint.
Furthermore, whatever other supreme Buddha-qualities there are— those inconceivable ones for which no measure exists—
all of those will not be difficult to obtain for one who trains in such restraint of the body.
Having heard such a teaching on restraint of the body here, the prince attained a state of excellence;
joyful, elated, and with incomparable delight, he went forth into homelessness in the teaching of that Jina.
Having gone forth, he practiced pure and excellent celibacy for ten billion years;
having cultivated the four sublime abodes for the sake of the world including its gods.
Having well-cultivated the divine abodes, he beheld eighty million Buddhas;
thereafter, for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, he practiced this supreme holy life.
Having gone forth into homelessness under the teachings of them all, he practiced the pure and supreme holy life;
he became an excellent monk, a preacher of the Dharma, learned and possessed of eloquence.
Possessing unbroken morality, flawless morality, pure morality, and untarnished morality,
he abides in that noble, untainted morality,
clearly understanding this restraint of the body.
"O Prince, it might be that you think there was someone else at that time who was the elephant among kings, reflecting with such distinction;
but it should not be viewed thus, for he was none other than I, practicing my spiritual career."
Therefore, young man, training yourself, remain established here in this restraint of the body;
teach it to other millions of living beings, and before long you will become just like me.
Therefore, young man, you should train yourself in this way: "I shall be one whose bodily conduct is completely pure.
For what reason? Because, young man, a bodhisattva mahāsattva whose bodily conduct is completely pure does not fear the hells.
He does not fear the animal realm, nor the world of Yama, nor any of the miserable destinies; he does not fear water,
nor weapons, nor lions, nor tigers, nor bears, nor elephants, nor bulls, nor humans.

Young man, a bodhisattva mahāsattva whose physical conduct is completely pure may take even this great trichiliocosm world-system and, holding it in the palm of his hand, toss it up to the height of one palm tree, two palm trees, three palm trees, four palm trees, five palm trees, six palm trees, or seven palm trees.
Or rather, he may toss it up for as long as he desires.
Furthermore, young man, a bodhisattva mahāsattva whose conduct of body is completely pure attains the supreme perfection of the miraculous power of *ṛddhi*.

Purified by the fruition of the bases of miraculous power (*ṛddhipāda*), embraced by merit, secluded in solitude, all-pervading, having attained this samādhi, perfected through untainted merit, and possessing unimpeded vision throughout all world-systems, he manifests such miraculous powers of *ṛddhi*.
He becomes thus endowed.
In this context, what is supernatural power (*ṛddhi*)?
It is that by which supernatural power there is the complete accomplishment of the fulfillment of one's aspirations.
This is called supernormal power (*ṛddhi*).
In that regard, what is the miracle of supernormal power (*ṛddhiprātihārya*)?
It is that by means of which supernormal power, the bodhisattva mahāsattva, endowed with it, experiences various kinds of spheres of supernormal power.
Having been one, he becomes many;
having been many, he becomes one.
He experiences both manifestation and disappearance.
He passes through walls, through enclosures, and even through mountains without obstruction;
he walks upon the sky just as a winged bird does;
and he performs the act of diving and surfacing in the earth just as one does in water.
He walks upon water without breaking through it, just as if on earth;
he even smokes and blazes like a great mass of fire.
He touches and strokes with his hand even these two, the moon and the sun, who possess such great supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), such great majesty (*anubhāva*), and such great splendor (*ojas*).
Desiring it, he exercises mastery with his body over sentient beings even as far as the Brahma-world.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
"He goes rising up and sinking down into the earth; he walks upon water without breaking through it."
Just as a bird travels through the expanse of the sky, he emits smoke and blazes with supernatural power.
Just as the wind is not obstructed in the atmosphere, yet many masses of clouds move within it,
even so the yogin travels through the sky, unattached like the wind and the cloud.
Just as when the wise yogin is seated, he rubs the sun and moon with his hand;
he knows that the world of Brahmā is near, and he teaches the Dharma to millions of Brahmās.
And whenever he desires to speak the Dharma, he makes it known throughout the great trichiliocosm; desiring to do so, he teaches the Dharma to many millions of beings across many millions of fields.
Therefore, young man, you should train yourself in this way: "I shall be one whose physical conduct is completely pure.
For what reason?
Because, young man, a bodhisattva mahāsattva whose physical conduct is completely pure hears sounds with the divine ear-element, which transcends that of humans—both divine and human sounds.
Whether they be among those in the hells, or those born as animals, or those in the world of Yama;
whether they be gods or humans, far away or nearby, dwelling at a distance or dwelling in close proximity.
Therefore, young man, you should train yourself in this way: "I shall be one whose conduct of body is completely pure.
For what reason?

Because, young man, a bodhisattva mahāsattva whose conduct of body is completely pure understands, as they truly are, the mental deliberations and behaviors of other beings and other individuals by means of his own mind.
He understands a mind with lust as "a mind with lust" according to reality;
he understands a mind free from lust as "a mind free from lust" according to reality. ... [and so on] ...
With hatred, free from hatred; with delusion, free from delusion; with grasping, without grasping; contracted, distracted; perverted, non-perverted;
afflicted, unafflicted; exalted, not exalted; luminous, non-luminous; limited, unlimited.
He understands as it really is a mind that is inferior, unsurpassed, concentrated, unconcentrated, liberated, or unliberated;
he understands as it really is a mind with blemish as "a mind with blemish," and a mind without blemish as "a mind without blemish."
Thus, indeed, he understands, as it truly is, the mental deliberations of all beings and other persons with his own mind.
Young man, a bodhisattva mahāsattva whose conduct of body is completely pure recollects his manifold previous existences with their modes and details;
he recollects even a single birth,
two, three, five, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, and even a hundred births.
He recollects even a thousand births;
he recollects even a hundred thousand births, up to many hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kotis of eons;
he recollects even the eon of dissolution and the eon of evolution.
He recollects even many eons of dissolution and evolution;
he recollects one eon, a hundred eons, a thousand eons, a hundred thousand eons, and even up to many hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kotis of eons.
He recollects even as far back as the prior limit:
"In that place I had such a name, such a clan, such a birth, such a complexion, such food, such a livelihood, such a lifespan, such a duration of stay, and such an experience of pleasure and pain;
passing away from there, I was reborn in that other place."
"Having passed away from there, I have been reborn here"—
thus he recollects his manifold previous existences with their modes, their characteristics, and their details.

Young man, a bodhisattva mahāsattva whose conduct of body is completely pure perceives with the divine eye—purified and surpassing that of humans—all beings as they pass away and are reborn; whether beautiful or ugly, fortunate or unfortunate, lowly or exalted;
seeing beings going to happy destinies or going to miserable destinies, exactly as they are, according to their karma.

He understands: "Alas, these beings, being possessed of misconduct of body, possessed of misconduct of speech, and possessed of misconduct of mind; revilers of the noble ones and holders of wrong views—on account of undertaking actions based on wrong view, after the breaking up of the body, after death, have been reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, in the hells."

Moreover, these beings, endowed with good conduct of body, endowed with good conduct of speech, and endowed with good conduct of mind, not reviling the noble ones, through the cause of undertaking right view, after the breaking up of the body, after death, have been reborn in a happy destination, in the heavenly world, among the gods.

Thus, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, he sees beings passing away and being reborn— fair and ugly, inferior and superior; he understands, as it truly is, how beings fare according to their karma, going to happy destinies or going to miserable destinies.

Young man, a bodhisattva mahāsattva whose conduct of body is completely pure, through wisdom associated with a single moment, understands, hears, sees, and realizes according to reality everything that is to be known, resolved upon, or manifested.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
"The stages of the superknowledges have been taught for the protecting Bodhisattvas;
by remaining established in meditative concentration, a Bodhisattva attains them."
They also purify their ears, attaining the inconceivable divine ear,
by which they hear the teachings spoken by all the Buddhas.
They know the minds of living beings— whether with passion or free from passion, with hatred or free from hatred, and with delusion or free from delusion.
They know their former abodes where they dwelt in the past;
for thousands of millions of eons, no attachment exists within them.
They purify your eye and attain the unsurpassed divine eye;
they behold sentient beings passing away and being reborn.
Through wisdom conjoined with a single moment, throughout all births,
whatever is to be known here— the true characteristic of phenomena— [is realized].
Thereupon, the Blessed One addressed the youth Candraprabha once more: "Therefore, O youth, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should train himself thus: 'I shall be restrained by the restraint of speech.
In this regard, O youth, what is the restraint of speech?"

By means of which restraint of speech, the bodhisattva mahāsattva endowed with it attains the inconceivable, unimpeded voice and sound of a Buddha, characterized by sixty aspects— this, O Youth, is called the restraint of speech. By means of which restraint of speech, the bodhisattva mahāsattva endowed with it attains the quality of having speech that is worthy of being heeded.
This, young man, is called the restraint of speech. Endowed with this restraint of speech, a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains the thirty-two marks of a great person and the ten powers of a Tathāgata.
He attains the four fearlessnesses of a Tathāgata and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
this, O youth, is called the restraint of speech.
By means of which restraint of speech, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva is endowed with it, he attains the three gateways to liberation and attains the four divine abodes;
this, O youth, is called the restraint of speech.
By means of which restraint of speech a bodhisattva mahāsattva, being endowed with it, attains the four foundations of mindfulness,
the four right efforts,
and the four bases of psychic power.
the five faculties, the five powers,
and the seven factors of enlightenment;
He attains the noble eightfold path;
this, young man, is called the restraint of speech. Endowed with this restraint of speech, a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains the dwelling of great compassion.
He attains the dwelling of great equanimity,
and he attains thoughts of security and thoughts of seclusion.
This, young man, is called the restraint of speech.
Furthermore, young man, the restraint of speech is described as follows: endowed with this restraint of speech, a bodhisattva mahāsattva abstains from false speech;
he abstains from slander, harsh speech, and frivolous chatter;
and in the presence of his parents and teachers, he does not utter indecent words.
Furthermore, the bodhisattva abstains from those other words associated with faults;
he understands those words to be like an echo,
like a dream, like a magical creation, like a mirage, like an echo, like a reflection, and like an illusion.
He does not perceive such speech as it is,
he does not conceptualize it, and he does not imagine it.
He does not grasp,
nor does he adhere;
this, young man, is called [the perfection of wisdom].
Restraint of speech:
For, O youth, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who possesses completely pure restraint of speech does not fear any of the lower realms and attains all the qualities of a Buddha.
One attains all the miraculous powers of a Buddha and all the superknowledges.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
"By means of this restraint of speech practiced here, that bodhisattva indeed attains mastery;
for he is said to possess the restraint of speech which consists of non-attached knowledge regarding all phenomena."
By means of this restraint of speech, the wise obtain the thirty-two marks, the ten powers, and the unique qualities of a Buddha; for this indeed is called the restraint of speech.
By means of this restraint of speech, the wise one attains all these qualities of a Buddha which were previously proclaimed by me; for this indeed is called the restraint of speech.

By means of this restraint of speech, the wise one shall obtain the meditative abodes and the analytical knowledges, as well as most wonderful and inconceivable qualities; for this indeed is called the restraint of speech.

By means of this restraint of speech, the wise one attains the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, as well as the bases of psychic power, the powers, and the faculties; this is called the restraint of speech.
By means of this restraint of speech, the wise and confident one attains great equanimity, great compassion, and pure dwelling; for this indeed is called the restraint of speech.
By means of this restraint of speech, the wise one attains pure and secure thoughts;
likewise, those thoughts that are tranquil through seclusion— this indeed is called the restraint of speech.
By means of this restraint of speech here, the wise one does not speak falsehoods or malicious words;
nor idle chatter or harsh speech—this indeed is called the restraint of speech.
By means of this restraint of speech, the wise person never casts aspersions on the True Dharma, nor would they slander the Buddha or the Saṅgha; this indeed is called the restraint of speech.
By this restraint of speech, the wise one does not utter untruthful words in the presence of mother, father, or teachers; this indeed is called the restraint of speech.
By this restraint of speech here, the wise one becomes entirely desisted from whatever other words in this world are associated with faults; this indeed is called the restraint of speech.
By means of this restraint of speech, the wise and fearless one crosses over even speech, which is like an echo or a dream; this indeed is called the restraint of speech.
When a bodhisattva transcends speech regarding that which is selfless, soulless, and effortless; which arises dependently, is like a dream, and is false—this indeed is called the restraint of speech.
The truth of cessation is just like a dream, and likewise, the nature of dreams is extinction;
whatever a bodhisattva transcends through speech—this indeed is called the restraint of speech.
He does not acquire any speech whatsoever; he neither conceptualizes nor conceives of it.
He never takes up an object of perception nor becomes attached to it; this indeed is called the restraint of speech.
Then the Blessed One addressed the youth Candraprabha once more: "Therefore, O youth, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should train himself thus: 'I shall be restrained by the restraint of the mind.
In this regard, O youth, what is the restraint of the mind?"

Young man, that restraint of the mind endowed with which a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains the diamond-like samādhi is called the restraint of the mind. That restraint of the mind endowed with which a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains the ray of light named *Jvalanāntarābhā* (Blazing Interior Radiance) is called the restraint of the mind.
This is called the restraint of the mind.
Endowed with this restraint of the mind, a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains the perfection of a voice possessing the eight qualities.
This is called the restraint of the mind.
By means of that restraint of the mind, with which a bodhisattva mahāsattva is endowed, he attains the thirty-two marks of a great man,
the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, and the four analytical knowledges.
He also attains the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
this is called the restraint of the mind.
Endowed with this restraint of the mind, the bodhisattva mahāsattva attains the three gateways to liberation.
One attains the gateways to liberation: emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
This is called the restraint of the mind.
Endowed with this restraint of the mind, the bodhisattva mahāsattva attains the four divine abodes.
He attains great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity;
this is called the restraint of the mind.
Endowed with this restraint of the mind, the bodhisattva mahāsattva attains the four foundations of mindfulness.
the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power,
and the five faculties.
One attains the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path.
This is called the restraint of the mind.
Endowed with this restraint of the mind, a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains the dwelling of great compassion;
he attains the dwelling of great equanimity.
He attains thoughts of security and thoughts of seclusion; he attains a disposition of wishing for the welfare [of others], as well as proper deportment and conduct.
This is called the restraint of the mind.

Furthermore, young man, the restraint of the mind is described as follows: endowed with this restraint of the mind, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, for the sake of abandoning wrong views, does not dwell together with wrong views;
and for the sake of abandoning covetousness, he becomes free from covetousness.
For the sake of abandoning ill-will, he does not dwell together with ill-will;
for the sake of abandoning laziness, he does not dwell together with laziness;
and in the presence of his teachers, his parents, and his preceptors, he does not give rise to a deceitful mind.
He does not give rise to a mind of attachment, aversion, or delusion,
nor does he dwell together with them;
he does not relinquish the mind of awakening.
He does not abandon the mind of resolute intention (*adhyāśaya-citta*),
and he refrains from all other mental volitions associated with faults;
he does not dwell together with them.
This is called the restraint of the mind.
And one enters into the understanding that this mind is like an illusion,
like a dream, and like a mirage.
He enters into it as being like a magical creation, as being like a reflection;
he does not enter into it from the perspective of coming from anywhere.
He enters into pleasure as being like a dream.
One enters [into reality] by way of its being like a dream through impermanence;
one enters it by way of its being like a dream through the absence of a living soul;
one enters it by way of its being like a dream through emptiness.
And that he does not perceive, does not conceptualize, does not conceive, does not grasp, and does not adhere to— this, young man, is called the restraint of the mind.
For, young man, a bodhisattva mahāsattva whose mental conduct is completely pure avoids all unfavorable conditions and attains all the inconceivable qualities of a buddha.
